papers.abstract: Novel view synthesis and 3D reconstruction have advanced rapidly with radiance fields and splatting, yet their memory and computational demands limit their use in resource-constrained settings. We introduce Hexels: novel planar hexagonal surface elements with a first-order spatial color field for efficient 3D scene and 2D image representation. Hexels exploit locally planar regions with smoothly varying appearance using fewer, larger primitives. Their hexagonal support provides an area- and boundary-efficient domain, while the local color field captures appearance variation within each primitive. Across 34 scenes, Hexels improve PSNR over memory-matched 2DGS by 4.53-7.38 dB across datasets while requiring lower training VRAM. We further ablate Hexels by showing that per primitive, Hexels outperform 2DGS by upto 4.74 dB while using lower training VRAM and having 2.31 times faster FPS. Even in unconstrained settings, Hexels offers complementary quality-memory trade-offs. For efficient 3D surface reconstruction, Hexels reduce error by 28.9% compared with memory-matched 2DGS across 15 DTU scans. On 6 Tanks and Temples surface scenes, Hexels achieves the highest mean F1 among compared methods (34.38%, versus 31.72% for 2DGS). We further also show that Hexels, as a general primitive, improves 2D image representation over Image-GS. Hexels push the Pareto frontier on the quality-efficiency trade-off of surface-aligned primitives.
authors: Prakhar Kaushik, Soumava Paul, Alan Yuille
bullets: Addresses the memory and compute costs of radiance-field and splatting methods in resource-constrained settings.
Represents scenes and images with larger, locally planar hexagonal elements and first-order spatial color fields.
Across 34 scenes, improves PSNR over memory-matched 2DGS by 4.53–7.38 dB while using less training VRAM.
Delivers 2.31× faster FPS and up to 4.74 dB higher per-primitive quality than 2DGS in ablations.
Reduces reconstruction error by 28.9% on 15 DTU scans and achieves the highest mean F1 among compared methods on 6 Tanks and Temples scenes.

papers.title: Honeycomb-Surfels: Compact Hexagonal Primitives for Efficient Scene Rendering and Reconstruction
papers.tldr: Hexels use compact hexagonal surface primitives with local color fields to improve rendering and reconstruction quality while reducing memory and computation.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have made substantial progress in robotic manipulation, but their generalization remains constrained by the diversity and coverage of action-labeled robot demonstrations. Human videos provide much broader behavioral and environmental experience, while learning from them faces a fundamental trade-off between scalable data and explicit action grounding. We introduce ThinkWorld, a VLA learning framework that grounds action reasoning in world dynamics and strengthens it through reinforcement learning with world imagination. ThinkWorld represents each action thought as a Chain-of-Dynamics (CoD), a sequence of discrete motion tokens that captures the intermediate dynamics connecting the current world to a future state and serves as a common action representation across embodiments. We first initialize CoD with action-labeled demonstrations, then predict the future induced by each CoD and reinforce those whose predictions better match the observed outcome. This enables videos without action annotations to provide direct supervision from observed state transitions, allowing human and robot experience to refine the same reasoning space. Experiments in simulation and on real robots demonstrate effective human-to-robot transfer and strong generalization to unseen tasks and environments.
authors: Chaehyun Kim, Chi-Pin Huang, Jisoo Kim, Min-Hung Chen, Yu-Chiang Frank Wang, Seungryong Kim, Fu-En Yang
bullets: Addresses limited diversity and coverage of action-labeled robot demonstrations.
Represents each action thought as a Chain-of-Dynamics (CoD) linking the current state to a future state through discrete motion tokens.
Initializes CoD from labeled demonstrations, then reinforces chains whose predicted futures match observed outcomes.
Uses unlabeled human videos as supervision through observed state transitions, aligning human and robot experience in one reasoning space.
Simulation and real-robot experiments show human-to-robot transfer and generalization to unseen tasks and environments.

figures.caption: Figure 2: ThinkWorld architecture and training stages. In stage (b), reinforcement learning (RL) uses the alignment between imagined and observed futures as a scalable reward for CoD reasoning over human and robot videos, strengthening action reasoning without motion annotations and improving guidance for continuous control.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a VLA framework that grounds action reasoning in world dynamics and uses world imagination, strongly fitting 'Vision-Language-Action' and 'Interactive World Models'.
papers.title: ThinkWorld: World Imagination Reinforces Chain-of-Dynamics Reasoning
papers.tldr: ThinkWorld improves VLA robot generalization by representing actions as dynamics-aware motion-token chains and refining them with imagined-world reinforcement from both robot demonstrations and unlabeled human videos.

papers.abstract: Test-time adaptation helps a deployed model respond to changing inputs, but the same intervention can rescue one batch and damage the next. Updating normalization statistics, for example, can improve corrupted images yet fail when a batch contains mostly one class. Average accuracy hides these failures and cannot tell a model when to use an intervention. Target labels can guide this decision, but they are scarce and some choices are already clear. We introduce PORTAL, a controller that chooses when to deploy an intervention, which inputs to label, and when to stop querying. Each available prediction rule is a candidate, and its predictions are fixed before current feedback arrives. Every acquired label therefore evaluates all candidates on the same input. PORTAL combines these shared comparisons and directs queries toward candidates that can still overtake the current leader. It stops when the remaining labels cannot change the choice or when the possible accuracy gain no longer justifies another query. Our analysis links the required feedback to accuracy gaps and shared mistakes, explaining why some choices need much less evidence. Experiments show that this control turns an intervention that loses accuracy overall into a useful choice on selected batches. It prevents severe failures caused by changes in arrival order and preserves gains across complete corruption streams. When a fixed rule already works well, PORTAL uses little feedback to retain its performance. Periodic label checks reveal when past evidence needs refreshing and help the controller recover as conditions change. The acquired labels also train stronger candidates for future batches, and selection brings nearly all of their accuracy gains into deployment. The same feedback therefore improves both the choice made now and the predictions available to later batches.
authors: Jiahao Zhang, Xinling Wen, Liangliang Li, Yu Chen
bullets: Test-time interventions can help some batches but hurt others, and average accuracy does not reveal when they are safe.
PORTAL treats each prediction rule as a candidate, uses shared labeled comparisons, and queries inputs that could change the current choice.
It stops querying when further labels cannot alter the decision or the expected gain no longer justifies the cost.
Experiments show it avoids severe order-dependent failures, retains effective fixed rules with little feedback, and adapts as conditions change.
Collected labels also improve future candidate models, bringing most of their gains into deployment.

papers.abstract: We introduce Heads of Security (HoS), a prompt injection defense that enforces instruction-data separation via a small set of learned per-head attention gates. HoS learns how each head should redistribute attention between trusted and untrusted tokens, enabling models to reason over untrusted content without following injected instructions. We evaluate HoS on Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and GPT-OSS-20B. We compare it against SecAlign++, a state-of-the-art finetuning-based defense, and ASIDE, a defense that, like ours, builds instruction-data separation into the model architecture. We show that HoS offers greater robustness to adaptive attacks, better performance on standard utility benchmarks, and matches top performance on standard agentic prompt injection benchmarks. More specifically, the black-box RL-Hammer attack reaches 97% ASR against GPT-OSS-20B and 85% against SecAlign, but only 10% against HoS. Claudini, a state-of-the-art white-box attack, strengthened against HoS through autoresearch, requires 3 times more FLOPs to reach the same ASR on HoS as it does on GPT-OSS-20B or SecAlign. HoS preserves base-model utility across standard multiple-choice benchmarks and prompting setups, whereas SecAlign and ASIDE degrade in few-shot settings. On agentic benchmarks with static attacks, HoS and SecAlign perform similarly and substantially improve the security-utility trade-off over the base model. ASIDE struggles with tool use, achieving only 10% utility. These results show that prompt injection robustness can be achieved and improved through targeted attention interventions.
authors: Igor Shilov, Xiaoxue Yang, Alexander Panfilov, Evgenii Kortukov, Matthieu Meeus, Peter Romov, Wojciech Samek, Jonas Geiping, Yves-Alexandre de Montjoye
bullets: Targets prompt injection by preventing untrusted content from controlling instruction-following behavior.
Uses lightweight, learned per-head gates to redistribute attention between trusted and untrusted tokens.
Evaluated on Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and GPT-OSS-20B against SecAlign++ and ASIDE.
Reduces RL-Hammer attack success to 10% on GPT-OSS-20B, compared with 97% for the base model and 85% for SecAlign.
Preserves standard benchmark utility and matches top performance on agentic prompt-injection benchmarks; ASIDE struggles with tool use.

Each point is a separately trained model with a different learning rate. The y-axis reports utility under attack (higher is better), and the x-axis reports attack success rate (lower is better). The undefended GPT-OSS-20B is Pareto-dominated by both HoS- and SecAlign-defended models. ASIDE consistently fails to perform tool calls and achieves near-zero utility on all four benchmarks.

Figure 1: (Top) Heads of Security (HoS) learns to redistribute attention between trusted and untrusted tokens. Green, red, and blue denote trusted, untrusted, and chat template tokens. Learned gates preserve trusted and chat template tokens (1× and 0.9×) while suppressing untrusted tokens (0.1×), shifting attention toward the trusted request. Gates are learned independently per head, so other heads may retain or increase attention to untrusted tokens. (Bottom) HoS improves security and utility. Compared to SecAlign and ASIDE, HoS is more robust against adaptive attacks (RL-Hammer and Claudini), better preserves utility across standard capability benchmarks, and achieves strong utility and security on static agentic benchmarks.

papers.selection_reason: Learned per-head attention gates for prompt injection defense are an architectural intervention directly relevant to large language models.
papers.title: Heads of Security: Learned Attention Gates Improve Prompt Injection Robustness
papers.tldr: Heads of Security (HoS) improves prompt-injection robustness by learning per-head attention gates that separate trusted instructions from untrusted content while preserving model utility.

papers.abstract: Relations compose through the entity they share - Alice is Bob's mother and Bob is Carol's father, so Alice is Carol's grandmother - and the order matters, since a father's mother is not a mother's father; verifying a composed relation means closing the loop. We show that if each entity's coordinate frame may be rotated independently (per-entity frame freedom), three things follow. In the pure-gauge sector, relations that share no cycle cannot interact at all. The only gauge-invariant score of a triangle is a class function of its holonomy $H = T_{ij} T_{jk} T_{ki}$ - a Wilson loop. And the only equivariant update of an edge is $U = \Psi(H)\, T_{ij}$ with $\Psi$ conjugation-equivariant. Edge attention by Wilson loops is therefore not one design among many but the unique form the symmetry permits. Three communities hold pieces of this form: the commuting-operator embeddings of knowledge graphs are its abelian (commuting) sector; AlphaFold's triangle update and the Edge Transformer have its shape - an edge updated through the third vertex - without its constraints; and lattice QCD builds it equivariantly on lattices. We instantiate the equivariant sub-family on general relational graphs as holonomy attention. With no training and composition alone, it infers unobserved $S_4$ relations on sparse graphs at 0.88 with a fifth of the edges corrupted, at or slightly below specialist synchronization algorithms, where every commutative architecture is capped at 0.083; its holonomy score flags corrupted triangles at AUC 0.99 where commuting scores are capped at 0.76 by a second selection rule, and it separates clusters without labels.
authors: Aakash Sarkar, Ananya Mukherjee, Motoshige Sato
bullets: In the pure-gauge sector, relations that share no cycle cannot interact.
Triangle scores must depend on the holonomy of the composed edge transformations, while edge updates take a conjugation-equivariant Wilson-loop form.
The framework unifies commuting knowledge-graph embeddings, triangle-based edge updates, and lattice-QCD constructions as special or partial cases.
Holonomy attention infers unobserved S₄ relations on sparse corrupted graphs without training, achieving 0.88 accuracy and detecting corrupted triangles at AUC 0.99.
It also separates graph clusters without labels; the reported results concern composition-based inference on relational graphs.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a theoretical framework connecting attention mechanisms to Lattice Gauge Theory, offering a novel perspective on relational reasoning and attention updates applicable to foundation models.
papers.title: Attention as Lattice Gauge Theory: Relations Interact Only Through Wilson Loops
papers.tldr: The paper argues that per-entity frame symmetry uniquely restricts relational attention to gauge-invariant Wilson-loop interactions over cycles.

papers.abstract: Dexterous manipulation with multi-fingered hands is the next frontier of robotics, yet learned hand skills remain limited to simple grasps or basic repeated motions, such as rotating an object. As robots attempt more demanding in-hand maneuvers, safety, such as not dropping the object, becomes critical, yet it is rarely measured. We study in-hand object pose reaching, a task that demands diverse and difficult grasps: moving an object to almost any position and orientation within reach of the fingers, at any wrist orientation, through long sequences of consecutive goals. We present a recipe for training such policies for a LEAP hand in simulation without human data, built on a range of insights, from diverse resets and goals via generated grasp datasets to an adaptive friction curriculum. With careful system identification, the policies transfer zero-shot to the real hand, using either motion capture or a single wrist-mounted depth camera, and prove remarkably capable and robust. On top of the task policy, we add a learned residual safety filter with adjustable conservativeness, letting us tune the balance between performance and safety and greatly reduce object drops. In 13.3 hours of real-robot evaluation over 4,800 unseen goals across 4 objects and diverse wrist orientations, the state-based policy reaches 95.2% of goals within 2 cm and 0.4 rad, and the filter cuts its drops by 75% while still reaching 91.5% of goals. The policies can also spin a lightbulb held in an arbitrary pose, reach out-of-distribution goals, withstand fast arm motion and perturbations, and, needing only a wrist camera, serve as portable skills such as screwing in a lightbulb. We release the full recipe as a platform for studying performance, reliability, and safety in high-dimensional dexterous systems. Videos and more are available at https://ian-chuang.github.io/dexsafe/.
authors: Ian Chuang, Hiya Shah, Vamsi Chilamkur, Iman Soltani, Claire Tomlin
bullets: Targets diverse, long-horizon object position and orientation goals under arbitrary wrist orientations.
Trains a LEAP-hand policy without human data using generated grasp resets and goals, adaptive friction curricula, and system identification.
Transfers zero-shot to hardware with either motion capture or a single wrist-mounted depth camera.
Across 4,800 unseen goals, the state-based policy reaches 95.2% within 2 cm and 0.4 rad; safety filtering reduces drops by 75% while retaining 91.5% goal success.
Demonstrations include lightbulb spinning, out-of-distribution goals, fast arm motion, perturbation recovery, and portable camera-based screwing skills.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in multi-turn agentic workloads that require sustained interaction with complex environments. Existing reflective prompt optimizers such as GEPA learn from failed rollouts, but agentic failures can also come from prompt weaknesses, harness limitations, stochastic execution, or noisy judges. We argue that such failures may not provide useful learning signal, and may even be harmful; and thus it is essential to curate which tasks are provided to the prompt optimizer for better performance. We introduce GEPA-Curator, a framework that augments the prompt optimizer to select which agent experiences should shape prompt optimization. In particular, GEPA-Curator consists of two components: task curation, which filters out tasks that are likely to provide noisy or unreliable learning signals, and prior success retrieval, which selectively retrieves past successful trajectories for a task and provides them as additional context to the prompt optimizer. We evaluate GEPA-Curator on GoBrowse, ALFWorld, AppWorld, and $\tau$-bench, using both Gemini 3.1 Pro and Claude Opus 5 as optimizer models. GEPA-Curator matches or exceeds the mean performance of both baselines, with gains of up to 20.7% over GEPA and 21.2% over ACE.
authors: Zack Yu, Nicholas Lee, Minjae Lee, Lakshya Agarwal, Luca Manolache, Wonjun Kang, Matei Zaharia, Michael W. Mahoney, Kurt Keutzer, Sehoon Kim, Amir Gholami
bullets: Agent failures may reflect prompt flaws, harness limitations, stochastic execution, or noisy evaluation rather than useful learning signals.
The framework filters unreliable tasks before optimization and retrieves selected successful trajectories as additional context.
It is evaluated on GoBrowse, ALFWorld, AppWorld, and τ-bench with Gemini 3.1 Pro and Claude Opus 5 optimizers.
It matches or exceeds both GEPA and ACE on mean performance, with reported gains up to 20.7% over GEPA and 21.2% over ACE.

Figure 1: GEPA-Curator system diagram. The prompt optimizer takes in a minibatch of tasks at each iteration and invokes the actor agent to execute them and performs reflective prompt optimization based on the resulting trajectories. The Curator augments the prompt optimizer by acting as an outer-loop process which traverses through the training dataset and constructs each minibatch to pass into the prompt optimizer. The Curator reads past execution trajectories for each task sampled from the training dataset and decides to run the task if doing so is likely to provide useful optimization signal (Section 3.1). The Curator can also pass prior successful trajectories for failed tasks as context to the prompt optimizer as a trusted reference example (Section 3.2). Once the curated training batch of selected tasks and successful context is constructed, it is passed to the prompt optimizer for execution and optimization. The resulting trajectories and evaluation outcomes are then written back to the task history for use in subsequent curation rounds.

papers.abstract: Scientific discovery often begins with an unexpected observation that prompts a new research question. In a world with altered physical laws, can large language models (LLMs) notice unexpected behavior, such as heavier objects falling more slowly, and discover the law through experiments without being told what to investigate? To evaluate this ability, we introduce LongChang, an automated framework that creates simulated worlds with altered physics, where one or more laws differ from ordinary physics. The evaluated LLMs act as explorers, manipulating objects and building tools to investigate their own questions without research tasks or hints about these laws. Separate LLM agents generate and review scenes, review tool designs, and evaluate reports for correctness and experimental support using the altered physical laws and exploration records. These records guide scene evolution for further exploration, allowing the full cycle to run without human intervention. Among 12 LLMs, GPT-6-Astra achieves a discovery rate of 16.7%, while the other 11 score 0%. The exploration records reveal uninvestigated anomalies and only partial identification of the altered physical laws.
authors: Zhen Yang, Wen Wang, Xander Xu, Ying-Cong Chen
bullets: Creates simulated worlds where one or more physical laws differ from ordinary physics.
LLM explorers choose what to investigate, manipulate objects, and build tools without task hints.
Separate agents generate and review scenes, tools, and scientific reports, using exploration records to evolve experiments.
GPT-6-Astra discovered altered laws in 16.7% of trials; the other 11 evaluated LLMs had no successful discoveries.
Exploration records showed that agents often noticed anomalies but only partially identified the underlying laws.

papers.abstract: Weight decay and explicit weight-norm constraints improve optimizer performance in language model pretraining, yet a unified understanding of why such control helps and how much is needed remains incomplete. We analyze norm control in Muon over the entire training trajectory using the \emph{accumulated effective learning rate}, $C_T=\sum_{t<T}\eta_t/\|W_t\|_F$, where $\eta_t$ is the nominal learning rate and $\eta_t/\|W_t\|_F$ is the effective learning rate relative to the weight norm. For bounded update directions, accumulation over any training interval bounds relative weight displacement. We show that vanilla Muon can accumulate only logarithmically, potentially limiting exploration and helping explain its slower empirical progress, whereas MuonW and MuonH guarantee at least linear accumulation under the stated conditions. Going beyond bounded-norm control, we show that sufficiently slow norm growth guarantees faster accumulation than the logarithmic worst case, opening up less restrictive optimizer designs. Based on this insight, we propose MuonGS, which uses Gram--Schmidt (GS) projection to remove the radial component of each Muon update without fixing the weight norm. With bounded update directions and a constant nominal learning rate, we prove that the weight norm grows at most proportionally to $\sqrt{t}$ after $t$ steps. Consequently, MuonGS guarantees $C_T=\Omega(\sqrt{T})$, with accumulation sustained even in later training. Further, for smooth scale-invariant objectives we establish its $O(T^{-1/2})$ stationarity guarantee. In pretraining experiments with 160M- and 400M-parameter dense models as well as a 135M active- and 1B total- parameter MoE model, MuonGS achieves lower validation perplexity than MuonH at long training horizons. In particular, for the dense model it achieves an estimated token-equivalent speedup up to about $15\%$ at matched validation loss to MuonH.
authors: Athanasios Glentis, Dawei Li, Mingyi Hong
bullets: Weight-norm control affects Muon’s effective learning rate; vanilla Muon may accumulate it only logarithmically, limiting exploration.
MuonGS applies Gram–Schmidt projection to remove each update’s radial component without fixing the weight norm.
Under bounded updates and constant nominal learning rate, MuonGS grows weight norms at most as √t and guarantees Ω(√T) accumulation.
For smooth scale-invariant objectives, MuonGS has an O(T⁻¹ᐟ²) stationarity guarantee.
In experiments across dense and MoE models, MuonGS achieves lower long-horizon validation perplexity than MuonH, with up to roughly 15% token-equivalent speedup at matched loss.

Each point represents a learning-rate and weight-decay setting; solid curves connect settings with the same weight decay (WD). WD= 0 is vanilla Muon, and positive WD corresponds to MuonW. Numbers beside the points report perplexity. Stars mark the lowest perplexity among the tested learning rates for each WD; the dashed line connects these stars for MuonW.

Figure 1: One step of vanilla Muon, MuonW, MuonH and MuonGS from the same Wt and the same direction Ot, for a small (left) and a large (right) weight norm. Vanilla Muon’s radial part (dashed) grows the norm at first order; MuonH retracts to ∥W∥F = R (dotted); MuonGS keeps the tangential part only, so the norm changes at second order. MuonW’s decay −ηλWt scales with ∥Wt∥F but the actual step depends on the size of Wt; the decay therefore hardly slows down the norm growth for a small norm but can shrink the norm for a large one.

papers.selection_reason: Presents an optimizer for LLM pretraining with norm-control analysis and token-equivalent speedups, directly relevant to large language model training.
papers.title: MuonGS: Pretraining LLMs with Relaxed Weight-Norm Control
papers.tldr: MuonGS relaxes strict weight-norm control in Muon by removing radial update components, preserving effective learning-rate accumulation and improving long-horizon LLM pretraining.

papers.abstract: Self-attention plays a key role in long-sequence modeling, but its quadratic time complexity fundamentally limits the scaling of Large Language Models. Recently, Multi-State Linear Attention (MSLA) mechanisms have been proposed to make sequence modeling more efficient by splitting the context into segments and compressing each in its own memory state. MSLA aggregates the information extracted from each memory state using only the mean alignment between a query and each segment's keys, ignoring how the alignment is distributed within the segment. In order to model the relevance of a segment to a query more comprehensively and incorporate the variance of the alignment in the aggregation, we propose MERLIN (MomEnt Routing for multi-state LINear attention), a method that tracks the first and second moments of each segment's keys. Using the moments of keys, a query can recover both the mean and the variance of its alignment with each segment to perform a more content-aware aggregation of per-state readouts. Experiments on multi-state variants of Gated DeltaNet-1.3B and Mamba-2-780M show that MERLIN consistently outperforms existing aggregation methods on various long-context tasks. In particular, MERLIN outperforms baselines on RULER needle-in-a-haystack and long-context QA (+8.3% for Gated DeltaNet-1.3B and +7.0% for Mamba-2-780M) and diverse subtasks in LongBench (+13.5% and +12.0%). It even outperforms baselines that consume 4x more memory. MERLIN provides a simple and general routing mechanism for improving long-context capabilities of MSLA models.
authors: Hee Seung Hwang, Sanghyuk Chun, Xindi Wu, Olga Russakovsky, Zhiwei Deng
bullets: MSLA reduces the cost of long-sequence modeling by compressing context segments into separate memory states, but standard routing uses only mean query–key alignment.
MERLIN tracks each segment’s first and second key moments to estimate both mean and variance of query alignment.
This enables more comprehensive, content-aware aggregation of per-state readouts.
On RULER, long-context QA, and LongBench, MERLIN consistently outperforms existing routing methods, including baselines using 4× more memory.
Reported gains include up to 8.3% on RULER/QA and 13.5% on LongBench for the evaluated models.

figures.caption: Figure 1: (a) A multi-state linear attention (MSLA) model aggregates segment-level outputs via a weighted sum. Prior methods compute the weights λt,i from position or from the mean of each segment’s keys. MERLIN instead reads both the first and second moments of the keys. (b) On retrieval-augmented generation samples in HELMET (Yen et al., 2025), we measure the aggregation weight each method places on the ground truth (GT) segment at the query token. Position-based aggregation largely misses the GT and mean-based aggregation recovers more, while MERLIN places the most weight on it.

Figure 2: MERLIN Overview. The context is split into segments Ci (middle row). Each segment stores a memory state (top row) and the first and second moments of its keys (bottom row). At position t, the query qt reads segment-level outputs from memory states (step 1). The query computes the mean and variance of the key-query alignment from the moments (step 2). The final output is a weighted sum of segment-level outputs, where the weights are derived from a gated mix of the alignment mean and variance (step 3).

Figure 4: MERLIN Outperforms Baselines Across Segment Length. Average score as the segment size that defines each state varies over {64, 128, 256, 512}. MERLIN leads at every segment length, and its margin over mean-based aggregation persists as segments grow. Vanilla (dashed) is segment-independent.

Figure 3: Position-Controlled Retrieval. Retrieval accuracy as the gold passage sweeps from the start (1/6) to the end (6/6) of the context. Vanilla is recency-biased: it recovers the gold only when placed near the end and is otherwise flat, while Position and mean-based aggregation are flatter but weaker. MERLIN stays high and roughly uniform across positions.
Figure 5: Dimension of Moments. Average LongBench scores as dr varies over {16, 32, 64, 128} (log axis). Performance saturates around dr =32 for GDN and dr =64 for Mamba-2.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes moment-based routing for multi-state linear attention, improving efficient attention and long-context modeling.
papers.title: Multi-State Linear Attention with Generalized Second-Order Routing
papers.tldr: MERLIN improves long-context multi-state linear attention by using first- and second-order key statistics for more content-aware routing across memory states.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models offer a promising path to efficient agents through parallel token generation. However, efficient interaction requires adapting both where computation is spent and how much text is generated. We introduce a metacognitive controller that guides diffusion generation according to the needs of the current response and the agent's interaction with the environment. It learns when to finalize tokens and how far generation should extend, reducing overall computation within responses. Our controller, a lightweight plug-in for the diffusion backbone, is trained on agent trajectories to balance correctness and generation cost. This approach connects the agent's generation process to the interaction the agent serves. Experiments across five benchmarks demonstrate that our approach reduces inference FLOPs by 20.6% on average compared with the most efficient baseline, while maintaining competitive task accuracy. Ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of our approach.
authors: Mingyu Zhao, Shuhang Lin, Ligong Han, Xiaojing Yu, Zhenting Wang, Yifei Pang, Yang Zhou, Dimitris N. Metaxas
bullets: Targets the challenge of reducing computation while preserving agent response quality.
Learns when to finalize tokens and how far generation should continue.
Trained on agent trajectories to balance correctness with generation cost.
Reduces inference FLOPs by 20.6% on average across five benchmarks versus the most efficient baseline, while maintaining competitive task accuracy.
Ablation studies support the controller’s effectiveness.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of our approach. The metacognitive controller monitors the generation state and interaction progress, then guides backbone predictions through the confidence alignment policy and flux policy. Tool calls provide environmental feedback for subsequent generation.

Figure 1: Metacognitive control of environment-aware diffusion decoding. Left: fixed-range decoding computes positions beyond the response consumed by the environment. Right: our controller guides content commitment and adjusts the active computation range during interaction. Orange denotes controller-guided revelation, gray denotes computed tail positions, and dashed cells lie outside the active range.

Figure 4: An interaction comparison using the same backbone and search queries. Green highlights the tokens in three structural segments; Red marks post-call generation; gray denotes padding. Blank blue cells have no saved token text. Flux decoding reduces the active range (gray). With the metacognitive controller, the agent uses 24.3% fewer FLOPs over the complete interaction and answers correctly in this example.

Figure 3: Accuracy versus FLOPs reduction on BFCL and multi-hop tasks. Gray points denote evaluated checkpoints; blue points and lines highlight their empirical Pareto frontier. The upper-right direction is better.

papers.selection_reason: Adaptive token finalization and generation-length control reduce inference FLOPs for diffusion language agents, fitting efficient token-level computation.
papers.title: Metacognitive Decoding: Efficient Inference for Diffusion Language Agents
papers.tldr: A lightweight metacognitive controller makes diffusion language agents more efficient by adapting token finalization and response length to interaction needs.

papers.abstract: Language models pretrained on web corpora collected over multiple years learn both general and domain-specific knowledge. How these different kinds of knowledge are learned as pretraining progresses remains unclear. Recent point-in-time models trained on web snapshots from different years provide a way to probe how knowledge prevalence varies over time. Using these models, we propose a temporal variability score (TVS), defined as the coefficient of variation of an item's negative log-likelihood across models. A higher score suggests that the knowledge may be less consistently represented across years of web text. We evaluate six benchmarks covering diverse topics using six models from multiple open-source model families. We find that low- and high-TVS items are learned similarly early in training, but high-TVS items improve faster later on. At the end of the pretraining run, high-TVS items outperform low-TVS items in 34 of 36 model-benchmark settings, with an average advantage of 7.3 points of chance-normalized accuracy. This pattern is most robust on knowledge-intensive tasks, even when comparing items of similar difficulty. Our findings reveal differences in how knowledge is learned over the course of pretraining, with temporal variability providing a diagnostic of these learning dynamics beyond aggregate benchmark scores.
authors: Chang Su, Bin Wu, Emine Yilmaz, Yao Lu
bullets: Introduces temporal variability score (TVS), measuring variation in an item's negative log-likelihood across models trained on web snapshots from different years.
Across six benchmarks and six models, low- and high-TVS items improve similarly early in training, while high-TVS items improve faster later.
High-TVS items outperform low-TVS items in 34 of 36 model–benchmark settings, with a 7.3-point average advantage in chance-normalized accuracy.
The effect is most robust on knowledge-intensive tasks, including comparisons between items of similar difficulty.
TVS offers a diagnostic for knowledge-acquisition dynamics beyond aggregate benchmark scores.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Chance-normalized accuracy over pretraining for temporally variable (high TVS, red) and temporally stable (low TVS, green) items, by model (columns) and benchmark (rows). Groups are length-matched; training tokens are on a log scale. Pythia and OLMo show little early separation; high-TVS items generally pull ahead later.
Figure 2: Main result with five TVS quantiles. The most variable quintile ends ahead of the least variable one in 32 of 36 settings; all four exceptions are on WinoGrande.

papers.abstract: When an LLM group's discussion is compressed into a short memory for a final decision maker, what should the memory keep? Two natural heuristics keep the rarest claims or the claims relevant to the decision criteria. On hidden-profile tasks both look attractive, because how widely a fact is held is confounded with whether it helps. We introduce CrossProfile, a diagnostic benchmark of 60 templates with automatically verified answer keys, in which the ownership of supporting, decoy, and irrelevant facts is crossed while their text is held fixed (480 tasks). Across Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, and two DeepSeek models, both heuristics fail in predictable places. Selecting by relevance readmits decoys, because decoys are on topic: even a perfect relevance filter loses 23 to 31 points to rarest-first selection in the classic hidden-profile configuration. Rarest-first selection is no better than random selection on average and wins only where the rare facts happen to be the useful ones. In both cases accuracy follows the balance of evidence the memory keeps, not the policy that kept it. The decision model adds a third failure, a form of social proof: it gives extra weight to facts attributed to many agents. Removing the attribution tags, or reassigning them at random with line order fixed, raises accuracy in the classic configuration by 13 to 24 points. In natural discussions the evidence is lost before any memory acts: the complete transcript yields lower accuracy than no notes at all.
authors: Anouar Imel, Imad Charradi, Abderrahman Sghir, Khalil El Khammar
bullets: CrossProfile tests 480 hidden-profile tasks across 60 templates by independently varying who holds supporting, decoy, and irrelevant facts.
Relevance-based memory can retain on-topic decoys; in classic hidden profiles, it trails rarest-first by 23–31 points.
Rarest-first is no better than random on average, succeeding only when rare facts are actually useful.
Decision models overweight facts attributed to more agents; removing or randomizing attribution improves classic-task accuracy by 13–24 points.
Natural discussions can degrade evidence before memory compression: full transcripts perform worse than providing no notes.

papers.selection_reason: Directly investigates memory mechanisms in LLM group decisions, analyzing heuristics for memory compression and retrieval, which fits the LLM Memory subtopic.
papers.title: Rare, Relevant, and Still Wrong: How Memory Fails LLM Group Decisions
papers.tldr: LLM group memories fail because rare or relevant facts can be misleading, while attribution creates social-proof bias and evidence is often lost during discussion.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought reasoning has substantially advanced video understanding in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, language-based reasoning traces do not provide a reliable mechanism for models to revisit relevant visual evidence, leading to visual forgetting and impairing their ability to reason over video content. Existing approaches maintain visual grounding during reasoning in two main ways: they either refer to evidence using textual coordinates, which specify symbolic locations rather than the visual content itself, or reinsert cropped regions or frames into the multimodal context, preserving visual details at the cost of substantial context expansion. To address these limitations, we introduce VideoLVR, which constructs latent visual evidence from local regions at relevant video moments, thereby providing visual support for intermediate reasoning steps. To supervise latent visual evidence generation, we introduce a visual token prediction objective that formulates visual token reconstruction as prediction over a vocabulary derived from the input video, thereby unifying visual evidence reconstruction and text generation within the same token prediction framework. This shared prediction framework enables MLLMs to reason over interleaved text tokens and latent visual states while integrating evidence from different moments. We further extend VideoLVR to reinforcement learning by treating sampled visual tokens as actions alongside text tokens and jointly optimizing the policy using final-answer rewards. By efficiently revisiting task-relevant visual information during reasoning, VideoLVR improves video understanding without substantially expanding the multimodal context. Experiments on multiple video benchmarks demonstrate its effectiveness, especially on tasks requiring fine-grained visual evidence.
authors: Shilong Li, Xingyuan Bu, Hao Shi, Yun Xing, Weixin Feng, Qiangpeng Yang, Shilei Wen
bullets: Addresses the weakness of language-only reasoning traces, which can lose access to relevant video evidence.
Constructs latent visual evidence from local regions at relevant video moments instead of relying only on coordinates or pasted crops and frames.
Uses visual token prediction over an input-video-derived vocabulary to unify visual reconstruction and text generation.
Supports interleaved text and visual latent states, with a reinforcement-learning extension that jointly optimizes visual and text token actions.
Improves performance across multiple video benchmarks, particularly on tasks requiring fine-grained visual evidence.

(c) At inference with the supervised model, each decoder hidden state is projected into a latent visual state and fed back as the input for the next decoding step, enabling autoregressive reasoning over latent visual evidence without additional visual observations.

papers.selection_reason: Improves video reasoning in multimodal LLMs via latent visual evidence generation, directly relevant to video understanding and multimodal large language models.
papers.title: VideoLVR: Latent Visual Reasoning over Grounded Video Evidence
papers.tldr: VideoLVR lets multimodal models revisit compact latent visual evidence during video reasoning, reducing visual forgetting without greatly expanding context.

papers.abstract: As executable environments for language agents scale, generating and verifying their rollouts becomes increasingly expensive. Under finite rollout budgets, this raises an important question: can data management at the environment level make agentic reinforcement learning (RL) more efficient by organizing, evaluating, and scheduling task instances together with the environments that determine their tools, states, transitions, and verification? To address this question, we introduce EnvSched (Environment-aware Scheduling), an online scheduler that learns from rollout history. EnvSched assigns scheduling value through two complementary modeling choices: exploitation prioritizes tasks likely to provide informative reward differences, while coverage spreads each batch across underobserved environments and interaction patterns. EnvSched organizes environment--task pairs as nodes in a dual-relation graph, with within-environment edges capturing task semantics and shared tool, state, and verifier structure, and cross-environment edges capturing abstract execution and reward topology. By propagating historical rollout statistics along both edge types, it predicts within-task reward variance. These predictions guide a scheduler that allocates each batch to tasks with high predicted reward variance and underobserved environments and tasks. Environment quotas and a similarity penalty further limit concentration and redundancy, yielding informative and diverse batches without additional pilot rollouts. In RL on Qwen3-8B, EnvSched achieves an average score of 48.81 across BFCL-v3, tau-Bench, and ACEBench-Agent after 40 training steps, exceeding the highest score attained by random task selection after 120 steps. It also improves downstream performance across model sizes at the same training budget.
authors: Sihan Yang, Weichen Bai, Ruichuan An, Yiming Cheng, Zhiyuan Feng, Tianyi Jiang, Renye Yan, Ning Ding, Yifan Zhang, Renrui Zhang, Yehui Tang, Wentao Zhang
bullets: Addresses the high cost of generating and verifying agent rollouts under finite budgets.
Uses exploitation of tasks with predicted high reward variance and coverage of underobserved environments and interaction patterns.
Models environment–task pairs as a dual-relation graph linking semantic, tool/state/verifier, execution, and reward structure.
Applies environment quotas and similarity penalties to reduce concentration and redundant batches without pilot rollouts.

On Qwen3-8B, reaches an average score of 48.81 across BFCL-v3, tau-Bench, and ACEBench-Agent after 40 steps, outperforming random selection’s best score after 120 steps; gains extend across model sizes.

papers.selection_reason: Environment-level scheduling to reduce rollout costs in agentic RL directly targets computation/data efficiency and is transferable to broader efficient-training pipelines.

papers.abstract: Developing on-device image models requires considering practical user needs, task types and device resource constraints. However, existing benchmarks provide limited guidance on identifying capability gaps between on-device models and server-side models. We introduce MoI-Bench, a benchmark grounded in mobile user needs, comprising 64 subtasks and 1150 samples. It defines 16 operations, such as removal and replacement, and eight visual target categories covering content such as portraits and text. These form two orthogonal axes whose applicable combinations define specific tasks, such as removing facial makeup. To better guide model improvement, we further propose MoI-Eval, which introduces task-specific criteria covering instruction following, visual quality and detail preservation. We further construct sample-level evaluation questions and aggregate their scores into overall quality and capability profiles along the operation, target and criteria axes. We evaluate representative on-device and server-side models and measure mobile deployment costs. Results show that this decoupled Operation x Target design provides finer-grained guidance for improving compact models. For example, it highlights the need to prioritize specific capability gaps (e.g., text-replacement) over broad application-level goals (e.g., improving text editing). Unlike conventional benchmarks that rank models using a single score, we introduce a two-dimensional Quality-Deployability capability map to assess models for practical mobile use. The map shows that current on-device models can achieve efficient generation or editing but expanding their task coverage deserves greater attention than further improving deployment efficiency. Further progress requires improving editing quality, particularly identity preservation and text rendering, while broadening task coverage.
authors: Kailai Feng, Haoxiang Rao, Yuxiang Wei, Bo Chen, Junsong Li, Yang Pan, Chengkun Cai, Jagmohan Chauhan
bullets: Covers 64 subtasks and 1,150 samples across 16 operations and eight visual target categories.
MoI-Eval assesses instruction following, visual quality, and detail preservation using task-specific criteria.
Its Operation × Target design exposes specific capability gaps, such as text replacement, rather than broad application-level weaknesses.
A Quality–Deployability map evaluates practical mobile suitability beyond single-score model rankings.
Findings emphasize expanding task coverage and improving editing quality, especially identity preservation and text rendering.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmark and evaluation protocol for on-device image generation and editing that explicitly measures deployment efficiency, relevant to efficient AI.
papers.title: MoI-Bench: A Benchmark for Image Generation and Editing on Mobile Devices
papers.tldr: MoI-Bench evaluates mobile image generation and editing models with fine-grained task and deployability analysis grounded in practical user needs.

papers.abstract: World models are widely proposed as core components for enabling agents to reason over long temporal and spatial horizons. Yet current evaluations often emphasize task performance while providing limited insight into whether learned world models acquire predictive latent dynamics that reflect the underlying structure of the environment. Here we introduce the concept of faithful latent world models as an equivariance condition between the environment's transition map and the learned latent dynamics. We propose latent rollout consistency (LRC) as a metric to evaluate action-conditioned latent prediction. Strikingly, we find that across the studied state of the art latent world models, none solves the task by actually faithfully modeling the dynamics of the environment.
bullets: Motivates evaluating latent dynamics beyond task performance, especially for long-horizon reasoning.
Defines faithful latent world models through an equivariance condition linking environmental transitions to learned latent dynamics.
Introduces latent rollout consistency (LRC) to measure action-conditioned latent prediction.
Finds that none of the studied state-of-the-art latent world models faithfully models the environment’s dynamics.

figures.caption: Figure 7: World modeling under nonlinear observation mixing on CartPole. (a–b) Pixel rendering is contrasted with approximately invertible mixing of the underlying state. papers.abstract: Automatic soccer event spotting supports highlight generation, video indexing, and sports analytics, but existing methods depend on large annotated datasets and soccer-specific training. We present a zero-shot framework that detects, classifies, and temporally localizes events in full-length soccer broadcasts without task-specific parameter training. Each match is segmented into overlapping clips represented by a compact visual storyboard and the aligned commentary transcript, which a general-purpose multimodal model processes jointly. On three manually annotated matches containing 130 events, the best configuration achieves 72.0% F1@5s and outperforms SoccerNet-trained CALF and NetVLAD++ in a cross-dataset setting, while the storyboard representation reduces inference cost by 72% compared with individual frames. We further analyze the effects of model family, input representation, and prompt optimization, and introduce an evidence-grounded excitement-scoring stage that ranks detected events with natural-language explanations for highlight selection.
authors: Sadia Kamal, Mahmudul Hasan, Tony Braskich
bullets: Addresses the need for soccer event detection without large annotated, soccer-specific training datasets.
Processes overlapping clips using compact visual storyboards aligned with commentary transcripts.
Achieves 72.0% F1@5s on 130 events across three manually annotated matches and compares favorably in a cross-dataset evaluation.
Storyboards reduce inference cost by 72% versus using individual frames.
Adds evidence-grounded excitement scoring with natural-language explanations for highlight selection.

papers.abstract: Supernumerary robotic fingers augment human dexterity by enabling a single hand to perform complex "hold-and-manipulate" tasks that typically require bimanual coordination. However, existing devices are often hindered by bulky hardware that limits interaction to large objects and rely on explicit hand motion triggers that lack environmental context. To address these challenges, we present EgoThumb, a fully open-source, vision-driven supernumerary robotic thumb. EgoThumb features a compact, dual tendon-driven finger whose actuation is relocated to the forearm, reducing distal weight while enabling precise active joint control. The system utilizes a visual imitation learning policy that maps egocentric images from a palm-facing camera directly to continuous joint positions. By implicitly decoding human intent from visual cues capturing both the hand and the object of interest, EgoThumb achieves robust autonomous manipulation and strong generalization across diverse users and environments. All hardware designs and software implementations are fully open-sourced at https://ego-thumb.github.io.
authors: Jianyu Hou, Jiawei Fu, Weikang Wan, Minghui Jiang, Jiajun Li, Hao Su
bullets: Addresses bulky supernumerary fingers and hand-motion triggers that limit object interaction and environmental awareness.
Uses a compact dual tendon-driven finger with forearm-mounted actuation for lower distal weight and precise joint control.
Maps palm-facing camera images directly to continuous joint positions through visual imitation learning.
Infers user intent from the hand–object scene to support autonomous manipulation across users and environments.
Hardware designs and software are fully open-sourced.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of the EgoThumb System Design. 1) On-body View: The system comprises a wearable thumb and a forearm-mounted actuation module. 2) Wearable Thumb: The thumb features dual tendon-driven joints for precise control and PLA phalanges with a silicone-gel coating for stable grasping. A palm-facing fisheye camera provides egocentric visual feedback. 3) Actuation Module: The actuation module houses three Dynamixel XL430-driven ratchet spools. This forearm-mounted configuration significantly reduces distal weight. 4) Control System: Our EgoThumb interfaces with teleoperation and deployment systems via custom communication middleware.

papers.abstract: Films introduce characters incrementally as they progress. We study the problem of identifying principal characters and assigning their names directly from the movie itself, without using external cast lists, actor photographs, or pre-built character banks. We introduce the character naming task: given a name mentioned in dialogue and the associated video context, the model must determine which visible character bears that name. This task is challenging because name resolution often depends on cinematic cues such as shot-reverse-shot structure, self-introduction, direct address, third-party reference, gaze, and temporal continuity. We provide a dataset and annotations for evaluating character naming and first character appearances, develop a video-and-dialogue model for the task, and compare it with proprietary multimodal large language models. We further introduce a progressive framework for building a character bank as the film unfolds. Together, these contributions support online, human-like movie understanding in which character identities are inferred from the film itself.
authors: Zhongrui Gui, Junyu Xie, Tengda Han, Weidi Xie, Andrew Zisserman
bullets: Studies identifying principal characters without cast lists, actor photos, or pre-built character banks.
Defines character naming: linking a dialogue-mentioned name to the corresponding visible character.
Uses cinematic cues including shot structure, self-introduction, direct address, references, gaze, and temporal continuity.
Provides a dataset and annotations for character naming and first appearances, plus a video-and-dialogue model.
Introduces progressive character-bank construction and compares the model with proprietary multimodal language models.

figures.caption: Figure 11: Example of the constructed character bank for Meet the Parents. We show another example of a character bank constructed by our streaming pipeline. Our method correctly identifies the most prominent characters, but errors remain for the bottom three entries. These characters often appear in complex multi-person scenes, making reliable name binding more difficult. In addition, transcription errors can introduce noisy name variants; for example, Fonker and Falker should both be resolved to Focker for Greg Focker.

Figure 2: Example annotations from the MCN dataset. The MCN dataset provides manually annotated timestamps for each character’s first visual occurrence and first naming, along with ground-truth name-to-face correspondences for the Character Naming task.

Figure 10: Example of the constructed character bank for Juno. We show the character bank constructed by our streaming pipeline. Each row (apart from the last two) corresponds to one character entry and includes representative face tracks, the predicted canonical name with confidence, and discovered aliases. The example illustrates that the bank captures major characters with clean visual clusters and resolves name variations, such as mapping Mama Bear to Juno, Bren to Brenda, and McGovern to Mac. Some naming errors remain, typically due to noisy or ambiguous character-name associations.

Figure 4: Qualitative results for Character Naming. Examples are from Four Weddings and a Funeral and Jerry Maguire. In each case, our default “Qwen3VL-4B-Thinking (SFT + RL)” model reasons jointly over subtitles and video frames to link a queried name to the correct face — in the first, by following a verbal introduction to a later podium shot; in the second, by resolving direct address across a shot–reverse-shot exchange.

Figure 6: Qualitative results for character naming. We associate character names with their facial appearances in movies, mirroring how audiences infer who is who while watching. Characters may be introduced through diverse cues, including direct address by other characters (top), visual reasoning with common knowledge (middle), and third-party reference (bottom). In each case, the model grounds the name to the correct colored box by combining the spoken cue with visual evidence such as gaze, gesture, and scene role. Correctly linking character identities is central to movie understanding, enabling coherent character tracking across scenes. The examples are taken from Sleepless in Seattle, Four Weddings and a Funeral and Meet the Parents.

Figure 7: Comparison of reasoning efficiency on character naming. We compare our model against Qwen3.5-9B on the same scene. Our model produces a concise, well-grounded answer that directly links the spoken cue (“Congratulations, Walter”) to visual evidence (gaze and handshake direction), correctly identifying the orange box as Walter. In contrast, the baseline generates a lengthy chain of thought with repeated re-examinations and self-verifications, yet arrives at an incorrect mapping (green). This illustrates that longer reasoning does not guarantee better grounding: our model achieves more accurate character naming with substantially fewer tokens.

Figure 8: Examples of failure cases for both our model and Gemini-3.1-Pro-Preview. We show three examples in which Gemini-3.1-Pro-Preview, the strongest proprietary baseline, fails. These cases suggest that it struggles to capture subtle actions that are important for character naming. In the last example, Gemini is given the original audio rather than the erroneous subtitles for inference. The examples are taken from Four Weddings and a Funeral and Jerry Maguire.

Figure 5: Examples from the MCN dataset. Six character-naming annotations illustrating the range of problem types covered: direct address with shot–reverse-shot structure, direct address with eyeline match, direct address over the telephone, on-screen text, and OCR-based reasoning. Clips are drawn from Moneyball, Gangs of New York, Sleepless in Seattle, The Help, Four Weddings and a Funeral, and The Ides of March.

Our fine-tuned Qwen3VL-4B-Thinking closes most of the gap to proprietary frontier models despite being substantially smaller in terms of model size.

papers.abstract: AI agents have made substantial progress in domains where they have a non-trivial amount of time to deliberate between actions, such as mathematics, software engineering, and performing tasks on desktop applications. It is less clear how such models fare in settings that demand real-time interaction, such as playing a video game or operating a physical device. In these settings, the environment state may evolve as the agent is reasoning, or even as the underlying model is performing a forward pass. To gain insight into the real-time interaction capabilities of vision-language agents, we introduce Gym-Anything-RT. Our key idea is to construct visual minigames that demand a portfolio of capabilities required for interactive real-time settings. Gym-Anything-RT uses an agentic pipeline to automatically generate such environments based on a taxonomy of six capabilities required for real-time interaction, including the ability to perceive the environment and act under an evolving environment state. A key feature of Gym-Anything-RT is that it allows for controlled comparison of real-time interaction capabilities: we can run the same minigame in real time, or pause or slow down the environment to relax the requirement for real-time actions. We use Gym-Anything-RT to construct 100 real-time minigames and evaluate AI agents on them. We find large capability gaps in real-time interaction. For example, GPT-6 Astra (xHigh) achieves a pass rate of only 9.0% on the real-time minigames, which rises to 75.0% when the environment is paused. We also identify intriguing behaviors by the most powerful frontier agents: for instance, when given the ability to write code, these agents write code that bypasses the need to perceive and act in real time. We publicly release Gym-Anything-RT and the generated minigames to spur further research on AI agents in real-time interactive settings.
bullets: Targets real-time settings where the environment may change during reasoning or model inference.
Generates visual minigames from a taxonomy of six real-time interaction capabilities.
Supports controlled comparisons by running environments in real time, paused, or slowed down.
Agents show substantial real-time capability gaps: GPT-6 Astra (xHigh) scores 9.0% in real time versus 75.0% with the environment paused.
Some frontier agents exploit code-writing access to bypass real-time perception and action.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of our construction method. An independent auditor checks the implementation and evidence, returning issues for revision until the minigame passes the audit. Review agents calibrate difficulty and annotate capability requirements for controlled model evaluation.

papers.abstract: Injecting new subjects naturally during streaming video generation requires integrating newly supplied visual references into the existing video while preserving established subjects and the scene. Encoding references independently of the current scene provides little guidance for this integration, while keeping their features in persistent memory can interfere with established context. We propose ReferStream, a framework that requires no additional training and combines reference construction using the current scene with transient cache injection. Joint Latent places reference latents in target regions of the latest scene latent, allowing reference features to be extracted in context. Cache Restoration uses these features to condition the injection chunk, then restores the overwritten global cache entries while retaining the newly generated history. This procedure incorporates new visual conditions without retraining the generator or revising emitted frames. We further introduce ReferStream Bench, a new benchmark with scheduled reference arrivals, evolving instructions, and explicit annotations of subject presence for InShot and MultiShot generation. Evaluation follows the event schedule and measures both the fidelity of new subjects and the preservation of established subjects, alongside video quality, text adherence, and count accuracy. Experiments on ReferStream Bench show higher scores for text adherence, subject similarity, and count accuracy than the compared baselines, including offline methods given all references in advance. Project page: https://xushuolin.github.io/ReferStream/.
authors: Shuolin Xu, Guanyuan Li, Boyu Li, Kelu Yao, Xiaogang Xu, Hongchuan Yu, Shuicheng Yan, Xiaobin Hu
bullets: Addresses reference integration during ongoing video generation without revising already emitted frames.
Uses Joint Latent to construct references in the current scene context and Cache Restoration for temporary feature injection.
Introduces ReferStream Bench with scheduled reference arrivals, evolving instructions, and subject-presence annotations.
Reports improved text adherence, subject similarity, and count accuracy over compared baselines, including offline methods.
Evaluates both new-subject fidelity and preservation of established subjects, alongside video quality and text adherence.

papers.abstract: Threading a quadrotor through a moving narrow gap is a demanding test of agile flight, requiring centimeter-level spatial alignment and precise temporal execution. We address this challenge using a control policy that operates directly on onboard visual and inertial measurements to output collective thrust and body-rate commands. The task is difficult because success lies on a thin feasible manifold: small errors in timing, position, attitude, or visual observability cause collision. Prior planning and learning methods rely on privileged state, teachers, planners, or distillation; learning dynamic narrow-gap traversal directly, from scratch, remains open. We introduce a differentiable moving-gap formulation that gates centering, alignment, and smooth collision terms by signed distance to a time-varying gap plane, turning a sparse traversal event into a dense pathwise objective. We integrate this formulation into a visual-feature-to-command policy trained in one stage from random initialization, without a teacher, planner, or distillation. We validate our approach in both synthetic and real-world experiments. In controlled benchmarks, we demonstrate that pathwise gradients significantly outperform score-function gradients for precision-critical tasks, yielding a 99.3% success rate in simulation after only a few minutes of training on a single GPU. Furthermore, the policy transfers directly to a real quadrotor, successfully crossing a dynamic narrow gap from varied initial conditions using onboard sensing and inertial measurements, achieving an 80% success rate over 10 physical trials.

papers.abstract: Label-free reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) rewards a language model for agreeing with its own majority vote. It improves reasoning at first but eventually collapses: the self-assessed reward goes to one while accuracy falls, often until the model gives the same answer to every problem. The collapse appears only when training uses many problems. We explain this dataset-size dependence as a collective instability. In a solvable many-problem model in which problems share parameters, a population whose problems prefer different answers amplifies any shared perturbation for as long as the population-averaged slope $\langle F'\rangle$ of the single-problem self-reinforcement drift $F$ is positive. This holds while problems are still uncertain about their answers. Per-problem sharpening, slowed by $1/N$ for $N$ training problems, races against the shared mode, which grows at a rate $\propto\lambda^2$ independent of $N$, where $\lambda$ is the strength of the shared coupling. This yields a critical number of problems $N_c\simeq\ln(1/\delta)/(\lambda^2G)$, where $\delta$ seeds the shared mode and $G$ decreases with the initial confidence. Simulations of the model confirm the predictions: a sharp transition, $N_c\propto\lambda^{-2}$ up to a logarithmic correction, a single critical amplification $\lambda^2NG$ across couplings, confidence profiles and training variants, a logarithmic dependence on batch size, and no collapse for confident initial models. A kernel version of the theory identifies a protective coupling (generalization of sharpening) and a marginal-entropy bonus that stabilizes the uniform collective mode. In label-free RL of a small Transformer, removing the shared direction prevents collapse entirely, restoring it causes collapse, and collapse grows with training-set size and base-model entropy.
bullets: Collapse occurs when shared parameter perturbations are amplified while individual problems remain uncertain.
Per-problem sharpening slows as the number of training problems grows, while the shared mode grows at a rate set by coupling strength.
The theory predicts a critical problem count scaling roughly as $N_c\propto\lambda^{-2}$, with logarithmic dependence on perturbation size and batch size.
Simulations support the predicted transition and a shared critical amplification across couplings and training variants; confident initial models avoid collapse.
In a small-Transformer experiment, removing the shared direction prevents collapse, while restoring it makes collapse worsen with dataset size and model entropy.

papers.abstract: Manipulation policies are evaluated predominantly by binary task success, which cannot tell whether the commanded gesture is the one the object's kinematics admit. We introduce Constraint-Referenced Strategy (CRS), which projects the commanded end-effector twist onto the object's joint axis, separating progress along the joint from off-constraint waste. CRS requires a joint model and a joint-following scripted controller derived from it, but no recorded demonstration or learned judge. On 74 simulated articulated objects, success registers three transfer failures as lower rates but attributes none, while the two CRS channels give each a distinct signature. A door-trained behavior-cloning policy opens drawers in 59 of 110 episodes, and in these passes it commands about $40\times$ the off-axis rotation of a drawer-trained policy's passes ($1.27$ vs.\ $0.032$~rad/s). Relative to a scripted controller scored with the same axis, CRS verdicts are unchanged under joint-axis errors up to $30^\circ$; absolute thresholds tolerate about $8^\circ$.
authors: Baptiste Bonin, Caro Strickland, Audrey Durand
bullets: Binary task success cannot distinguish kinematically valid gestures from inefficient or invalid commands.
CRS projects the commanded end-effector twist onto the object’s joint axis, producing progress and off-constraint motion signals.
It uses a joint model and a model-derived scripted controller, without demonstrations or a learned evaluator.
Across simulated articulated objects, CRS differentiates transfer failures that success rates only aggregate.
Its verdicts remain stable with joint-axis errors up to 30°, while absolute thresholds tolerate about 8°.

papers.abstract: Event cameras offer low latency, high dynamic range, and milliwatt-level power consumption, making them ideal for agile robots such as tiny drones navigating through cluttered environments. However, existing simulators generally render photorealistic images before converting them into events, making large-scale reinforcement learning prohibitively slow. We propose an analytic event simulator that exploits what event cameras fundamentally measure - moving contrast edges - to synthesize event streams directly from scene geometry and ego-motion without visual rendering. Our simulator generates a 64x64 event observation in 17 microseconds on a single GPU - over 400x faster than a state-of-the-art rendering pipeline - enabling end-to-end reinforcement learning for goal-directed obstacle avoidance to converge in under 30 minutes - three orders of magnitude faster than training on rendered events. Policies transfer zero-shot to physically based event simulations (ray-traced Isaac Sim). Our policy reaches 83% success in cluttered courses unseen during training (mid-difficulty, traversability probability approx. 0.57), at 2.4 m/s average goal velocity, and retains 70% in a simulated texture-dense indoor hall. Furthermore, we quantized the policy to a 1.2 MB int8 network running fully onboard a 56-gram Crazyflie equipped with a Prophesee GenX320 event camera and an OpenMV N6 microcontroller board. Without any fine-tuning, external processing, or positioning, the policy achieves an average success rate of 82% (5/5, 5/6, 4/6 flights) across three real-world obstacle courses of increasing difficulty. Code: https://github.com/tudelft/rendering-free-event-nav
authors: Dequan Ou, Austin Lopez, Quentin Missinne, Christophe De Wagter, Guido C. H. E. de Croon
bullets: Generates event streams directly from scene geometry and ego-motion, avoiding photorealistic image rendering.
Produces 64×64 event observations in 17 μs on a single GPU, over 400× faster than a rendering-based pipeline.
Enables obstacle-avoidance policies to converge in under 30 minutes and transfer zero-shot to ray-traced simulation.
Achieves 83% success in unseen cluttered simulated courses and 70% in a texture-dense indoor hall.
A quantized 1.2 MB policy runs onboard a 56 g Crazyflie, reaching an average 82% success rate across three real-world courses.

papers.abstract: A joint of pipe run into the hole swings from the elevator over the well and strikes a fixed stabbing guide at whatever speed the swing has. StabBot, a robotic stabbing system, predicts the swing and meets the pipe at its own speed. A pendulum Kalman filter tuned from the pipe tally tracks the joint in stereo images. A six-axis arm with an open V-shaped roller head closes in at matched velocity, confirms the last millimetres by touch, aims the pin over the box when the elevator hangs off centre, and follows the block down with lateral compliance. A ResNet-18 keypoint network locates the pipe, pin nose and box mouth in 3-D, and a residual reinforcement-learning policy refines the capture. On 200 paired random jobs with nine sizes from 2-3/8-in. tubing to 20-in. casing, StabBot seated every joint with the pipe touching only rollers, against 74% for a conventional fixed guide. Median contact speed fell from 18.4 to 2.3 cm/s and median peak head-pipe force from 11.3 to 1.4 kN, and the force was lower in all 200 jobs (Wilcoxon $p < 10^{-30}$). The network locates the pipe with 0.4-mm median error in 2.3 ms per stereo pair. With the network in the loop, success stayed at 100% under 20 mm of added noise, 300-ms delay, 85% frame loss, 20-mm calibration offset, 20-cm elevator offset and 40-cm swings. All results come from a 1:4 Froude-scaled MuJoCo model and are reported at full scale.

papers.abstract: Self-attention mechanisms have established the Transformer as the dominant backbone across natural language processing, source code intelligence, and automated theorem proving. However, all-to-all pairwise token comparison enforces a quadratic $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ compute and memory barrier alongside severe softmax attention dilution as sequence length $N$ scales beyond the training horizon. Inspired by recent advances in algebraic graph learning (\textbf{WPNet}), this work introduces \textbf{GTFormer}, a syntax-free hierarchical Graph Neural Network (GNN) that replaces flat self-attention for general long-context sequence modeling. GTFormer organizes raw token streams into a bounded-degree hierarchy combining a balanced binary reduction tree ($\lceil \log_2 N \rceil$ depth), horizontal boundary-bridging shift edges, random expander shortcuts, multi-channel convex highway gating, and a top-down broadcast pass. Across eight long-context code, log, and multi-hop retrieval benchmarks trained exclusively on sequences of length $N \le 512$, GTFormer extrapolates zero-shot to $N = 4{,}194{,}304$ ($8192\times$) on a single commodity GPU in linear $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, maintaining near-perfect accuracy where standard and RoPE Transformers suffer from out-of-distribution attention collapse and out-of-memory exhaustion.
bullets: Targets quadratic compute and memory costs, plus attention dilution, in very long sequences.
Uses a bounded-degree hierarchy with binary reduction, boundary-bridging edges, expander shortcuts, convex highway gates, and top-down broadcasting.
Trained only on sequences of length ≤512 and evaluated zero-shot at lengths up to 4,194,304 tokens.
Across eight code, log, and multi-hop retrieval benchmarks, it reportedly maintains near-perfect accuracy on a commodity GPU.
The abstract reports scope limited to the benchmarked long-context tasks and extrapolation setting.

papers.abstract: In smart factory environments, passive entities such as humans and movable obstacles may interfere with autonomous robot operations, posing significant safety risks. Detecting potential conflicts between robots and entities outside their field-of-view (FoV) is therefore of paramount importance. However, conventional passive object detection systems rely on sensors such as LiDAR, radar, or cameras, which operate under direct line-of-sight (LoS) and are limited by obstacles and occlusions. To overcome these limitations, integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) enables environmental perception via the communication infrastructure thanks to cooperation among distributed wireless devices. In this paper, we propose a framework for passive entity sensing beyond the robot's FoV that relies solely on distributed channel measurements from the communication infrastructure to perform risk-aware classification. These measurements are embedded into high-dimensional representations using hyperdimensional computing (HDC), enabling robust and scalable learning without explicit channel reconstruction. Numerical simulations based on a commercial ray tracer and ROS-based validation in realistic smart factory scenarios demonstrate improved safety and enhanced path planning with up to 89% accuracy under severe occlusions, while maintaining low computational complexity.
authors: Placido Mursia, Marco Rossanese, Francesco Devoti, Adrian Lendinez Ibanez, Lanfranco Zanzi, Xi Li, Xavier Costa-Perez
bullets: Addresses robot safety risks from humans and obstacles hidden by occlusions in smart factories.
Uses distributed communication-channel measurements rather than direct line-of-sight LiDAR, radar, or camera sensing.
Maps measurements to high-dimensional representations with hyperdimensional computing for risk-aware classification without reconstructing channels.
Validated through ray-tracing simulations and ROS-based smart-factory scenarios.
Supports safer path planning under severe occlusions, with scope demonstrated in simulated and realistic validation environments.
