papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has emerged as an effective post-training paradigm for enhancing the video reasoning capability of Large Multimodal Models (LMMs). Despite its empirical effectiveness, we show that outcome-level optimization can introduce an undesirable shortcut amplification effect, whereby models increasingly favor text-prior answers even when they are not supported by the visual evidence. To characterize this behavior, we investigate the training dynamics of video RLVR through the lens of perceptual uncertainty, analyzing how predictive uncertainty evolves under video-conditioned and text-only contexts. Our analysis identifies a perceptual uncertainty collapse phenomenon, in which RL training continuously sharpens the model's answer distribution while the uncertainty reduction attributable to visual evidence progressively diminishes. A further gradient-direction analysis reveals that such confidence enhancement becomes increasingly less aligned with visually grounded uncertainty reduction and is instead dominated by text-prior compression. Motivated by these findings, we propose Bifocal Self-distillation Policy Optimization (BSPO), a self-distillation framework that regulates policy updates with two complementary distributional signals. Specifically, BSPO derives empirical reasoning principles from intra-group correct and incorrect rollouts to identify reasoning-sensitive tokens, and introduces shortcut-aware visual perturbation to penalize predictions that remain invariant when task-relevant visual evidence is weakened. By adaptively reweighting the original RL advantage, BSPO preserves the task-solving benefits of RLVR while promoting updates that are both reasoning-sensitive and visually grounded. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of BSPO in improving video reasoning performance and strengthening visual faithfulness.
authors: Jiafeng Liang, Xianhao Ou, Tao Ren, Rongchuan Mu, Runxuan Liu, Dandan Tu, Ming Liu, See-Kiong Ng, Bing Qin
bullets: RLVR may make models increasingly confident in text-prior answers unsupported by video evidence.
Perceptual uncertainty collapse occurs as visual evidence contributes less to uncertainty reduction during training.
Gradient analysis links this confidence growth more to text-prior compression than to visual grounding.
BSPO combines self-distillation from correct/incorrect rollouts with shortcut-aware visual perturbations to guide policy updates.
Experiments show improved video reasoning performance and stronger visual faithfulness.

papers.abstract: The success of large language models in real-world applications relies on parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods such as Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), which inserts compact, trainable adapters into selected layers. In this paper, we propose SimplexLoRA, a LoRA variant that adaptively adjusts adapter ranks during fine-tuning based on their learned importance. Unlike standard LoRA, which employs a fixed rank across all layers, SimplexLoRA optimizes per-adapter importance weights on the $n$-scaled simplex during a short warm-up and then freezes them, dynamically allocating capacity where it is most beneficial without increasing the overall parameter budget or inference cost. We evaluate SimplexLoRA across 12 language understanding, summarization, and reasoning tasks using DeBERTaV3, BART-large, Llama 3.1 8B, and Qwen3-8B. Our results show that SimplexLoRA consistently matches or outperforms standard LoRA and recent adaptive baselines, with the largest gains at low ranks. Our code is available at https://github.com/brain-lab-research/SimplexLoRA.
authors: Igor Shalygin, Grigorii Davydenko, Andrey Veprikov, Aleksey Antonov, Nikolay Bushkov, Stanislav Moiseev, Aleksandr Beznosikov

papers.abstract: Humanoids and other legged robots operating in complex environments must remember information that leaves their field of view and only becomes relevant much later. Reinforcement learning policies address this using memory networks such as LSTMs that are trained end-to-end with the policy to memorize such task-relevant aspects. Yet, such architectures often fail to preserve sufficient information over long horizons. In this work, we propose a network architecture based on Hadamard memory that specifically targets robot navigation. Our Local Spatial Matrix Memory (LSMM) enables RL agents to store generic task-relevant information at specific, position-based memory cells, enabling flexible and spatially grounded memorization. We evaluate LSMM on the task of autonomous maze exploration, where it matches the maze coverage of strong recurrent and finite-history baselines while being the only architecture that remembers the maze layout, reducing the reconstruction error threefold.
authors: Leon Magnus, Nico Bohlinger, Jan Peters, Oleg Arenz
bullets: Long-horizon navigation requires remembering information beyond the robot’s current field of view.
The proposed Local Spatial Matrix Memory (LSMM) stores task-relevant information in position-based memory cells.
LSMM is evaluated for autonomous maze exploration against recurrent and finite-history baselines.
It matches baseline maze coverage and is the only evaluated architecture to remember maze layout, reducing reconstruction error threefold.

papers.abstract: Current 3D scene understanding pipelines typically concatenate vast numbers of 3D object tokens with text tokens and feed the resulting sequence to a Large Language Model (LLM). However, existing 3D-LLMs for scene understanding encounter two major limitations: (i) excessive inclusion of task-irrelevant object data, introducing noise that reduces reasoning accuracy and increases hallucinations; and (ii) reliance solely on point cloud data, which inherently lacks the rich semantic information available in complementary 2D modalities, such as color, material properties, texture, and high-level contextual relationships. To address these challenges, we introduce 3D-SceneQ, a 3D LLM that unifies adaptive token pruning with multimodal semantic enrichment, markedly advancing scene understanding, reasoning, and grounding. Specifically, we propose a Query-Guided Adaptive Pruning (QGAP) module that adaptively selects task-relevant objects based on the intended meaning of user instructions, leveraging a learnable latent query to retain critical information while effectively suppressing irrelevant noise. In addition, we introduce a Multi-modal Object-level Feature Enhancement (MOFE) module, which integrates 2D feature embeddings from pre-trained models into 3D representation to enrich object-level semantic information. Evaluations show that 3D-SceneQ outperforms current state-of-the-art methods across multiple benchmarks (e.g., +5.7 CIDEr on Scan2Cap and +17.0 EM@1 on SQA3D), demonstrating its remarkable capabilities in various 3D language reasoning tasks.

Outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods on multiple benchmarks, including +5.7 CIDEr on Scan2Cap and +17.0 EM@1 on SQA3D.
Targets 3D scene understanding, reasoning, and grounding tasks.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) predict the visual consequences of the actions they generate, which makes test-time selection a natural way to improve a fixed policy: imagine the futures of candidate actions and execute the best one. The benefit of selection is bounded by the selectable headroom, how much better the best candidate truly is, but the standard estimate, which executes each candidate once and keeps the best outcome, conflates candidate quality with the randomness of everything that follows. We introduce a denoised counterfactual protocol, based on bitwise-reproducible branching, repeated continuations, held-out oracles, and common random numbers, that measures the headroom a selector can realize, and use its measurements to build a fail-gated selector. Across four WAMs, two benchmarks, over 100,000 branched rollouts, and pre-registered tests, we find that (i) the standard estimate overstates the selectable headroom of native samples: bounds from 17 continuations per candidate place its selectable share between 24% and 66% for three WAMs; (ii) structured action perturbations create up to 16 points of selectable headroom; and (iii) in both WAMs with action-conditioned imagination, imagined futures carry candidate-outcome information with no detectable loss relative to real futures, information that the value head of Cosmos Policy leaves unused. Deviating from the policy chunk only when a readout of the WAM predicts failure, the selector raises closed-loop task success from 76.9% to 81.6% on held-out episodes of training tasks, with the largest gain where the policy fails most often, and from 62.6% to 69.8% on unseen tasks.
authors: Haojia Gao, Yue Cao, Yumin Liu, Haohua Que, Mingkai Liu, Guanqiu Guo, Zhuo Zou, Bokui Chen, Xueqian Wang
bullets: Standard one-shot estimates overstate selectable headroom because they mix candidate quality with downstream randomness.
A counterfactual protocol uses reproducible branching, repeated continuations, held-out oracles, and common random numbers to measure realizable headroom.
Structured action perturbations add up to 16 points of selectable headroom; native-sample selectable share is estimated at 24–66% for three WAMs.
Action-conditioned imagined futures retain candidate-outcome information comparable to real futures, but Cosmos Policy’s value head does not exploit it.
A fail-gated selector improves success from 76.9% to 81.6% on held-out training tasks and from 62.6% to 69.8% on unseen tasks.

papers.selection_reason: Measures and exploits selectable headroom in world action models through closed-loop test-time selection, core interactive world-model research.
papers.title: How Much Can Best-of-N Help a World Action Model? Measuring Selectable Headroom and Realizing It in Closed Loop
papers.tldr: A denoised evaluation protocol shows that best-of-N selection can provide meaningful but limited gains for world action models, enabling a fail-gated selector that improves closed-loop success.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning for long-horizon agents relies on feedback from sequences of interactions, making credit assignment to individual actions difficult. Existing methods such as GiGPO compare actions at shared states to compute relative advantages, but estimate each action's value from a single sampled continuation. The resulting local credit remains sensitive to decisions made later in the trajectory. To address this problem, we propose ConCal (Continuation Calibration), a recursive continuation-value estimator that incorporates continuation evidence already present in a rollout batch. ConCal matches visits from the same task by their incoming state-action-state transitions, combines shared continuation evidence with each visit's own transition estimate, and propagates calibrated values backward to refine earlier action-value estimates. This reduces dependence on individual sampled continuations and mitigates local credit distortions without additional rollouts. Held-out return diagnostics show lower error in within-group value differences and higher agreement with reference action orderings than estimates based on individual continuations. With Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, ConCal improves success rates over GiGPO by 3.39 and 5.86 percentage points on ALFWorld and WebShop, respectively. Our code is available at https://github.com/Yingjian-Chen/ConCal.
authors: Yingjian Chen, Lang Zhou, Zixin Zhao, Pingfan Li, Weishi Zheng, Zhilin Zhao
bullets: Targets local credit distortion caused by estimating each action from only one sampled continuation.
Matches same-task visits through shared incoming state-action-state transitions to reuse continuation evidence.
Recursively propagates calibrated values backward to refine earlier action-value estimates.
Held-out diagnostics show lower within-group value-difference error and better agreement with reference action orderings.
Improves success rates over GiGPO by 3.39 percentage points on ALFWorld and 5.86 points on WebShop with Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of ConCal. (1) ConCal matches visits across same-task rollouts by their preceding state, executed action, and current state to identify shared continuation evidence (Left). (2) It recursively combines continuation evidence from matched visits while retaining each visit’s own transition contribution, producing calibrated continuation values for action evaluation. At each recursion depth, all visits are updated using successor estimates from the previous depth (Right). (3) Each action is evaluated using its immediate reward and its actual successor’s calibrated continuation value. The resulting action values are compared within state groups to obtain local advantages, which are combined with episode-level advantages for PPO updates (Bottom).

papers.selection_reason: Action-value calibration for long-horizon RL is a general credit-assignment technique transferable to embodied robot policy learning.
papers.title: Action-Value Calibration via Continuation Sharing for Long-Horizon Agentic Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: ConCal improves long-horizon reinforcement-learning credit assignment by sharing and recursively calibrating continuation values across matching transitions, yielding better value estimates and higher task success without extra rollouts.

papers.abstract: Image quality assessment (IQA) aims to evaluate the perceptual visual quality of images. Recently, the rapid development of Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) has significantly advanced the IQA field. By integrating chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning and reinforcement learning (RL), these models can generate more accurate and interpretable results while relying on less training data. However, existing MLLM-based methods are predominantly constrained to holistic, image-level evaluations and lack the capability to produce fine-grained, localized assessments, which substantially limits their practical applicability. To address this limitation, we propose VGIQA, a novel IQA model endowed with both local and global quality assessment capabilities. VGIQA is trained via a two-stage paradigm comprising a cold-start phase followed by reinforcement learning. Driven by carefully designed local quality assessment reward functions, our model exhibits exceptional image quality understanding on VGSR-2K, a new dataset we propose specifically for local quality evaluation, significantly outperforming existing open-source MLLMs such as Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct and Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct. Furthermore, the local quality evaluation task can effectively enhance the model's performance on the degradation perception task.
authors: Weichang Wang, Liyu Chen, Shuyue Guan, Jie Hu, Fei Gao, Wei Li, Nannan Wang
bullets: Addresses the limitation of existing MLLM-based IQA methods that mainly provide holistic, image-level evaluations.
Uses a two-stage training strategy: cold-start training followed by reinforcement learning with local quality assessment rewards.
Introduces VGSR-2K, a dataset designed for local image-quality evaluation.
Reports strong local quality understanding and outperformance of the compared open-source MLLMs on VGSR-2K.
Finds that local quality assessment also improves degradation perception.

figures.caption: Fig. 3: Overview of the proposed VGIQA framework. The framework follows a two-stage training paradigm. Stage 1 (Cold Start): The Qwen-based foundation model is initialized via SFT using CoT reasoning data distilled from Qwen3-VL-Plus [2] to establish structural formatting and inject IQA priors. Stage 2 (Multi-Task GRPO): Reinforcement learning jointly optimizes Local Quality Assessment, Degradation Perception, and Score Regression. Alongside a shared format reward, task-specific rewards are dynamically routed: a dedicated local reward exclusively supervises the local task (computing zero for non-local tasks), evaluating spatial bounding boxes via Hungarian Matching, negative DIoU, and F1 Score. Meanwhile, global tasks are optimized via verifiable score and classification/intensity rewards, unifying local-and-global quality evaluation.

Fig. 4: Overview of the VGSR-2K dataset construction pipeline. The dataset is curated via a rigorous human-in-the-loop pipeline. (1) Candidate Generation: Qwen3-VL-Plus [2] and Seed1.6-VL independently process LR-SR image pairs, yielding six candidate spatial bounding boxes. (2) Double-Blind Selection: Two annotator groups select the most consistent candidate; consensus establishes the baseline, while divergence prompts expert resolution. (3) Double-Blind Correction & Merging: Annotators refine baselines by adding or removing boxes. Corrections are merged via the Hungarian algorithm with a negative DIoU cost metric, extracting the MBR for matched pairs. (4) Final Review & Balancing: After expert review, pristine LR-HR image pairs are introduced as negative samples (with empty annotations) to calibrate spatial predictions and prevent trivial over-generation.

Fig. 2: Example applications of the proposed VGIQA framework. Built upon a Qwen-based foundation model, VGIQA achieves comprehensive quality understanding via multi-task reinforcement learning. While existing models (e.g., Q-Insight) are limited to holistic Score Regression and Degradation Perception, VGIQA explicitly bridges the gap in fine-grained Local Quality Assessment. Driven by novel visual grounding rewards, it adopts a rigorous "look and then judge" paradigm—precisely localizing spatial artifacts before formulating final judgments.

Fig. 1: Qualitative visualization of the local quality assessment results. Given a reference image, a distorted image to be evaluated, and a user query, VGIQA produces more reliable and accurate responses compared with the state-of-the-art RL-based IQA method Q-insight and the general large vision-language model Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct [1].

All methods except handcrafted ones are trained on the KonIQ dataset. The best and second-best results are highlighted in bold and underlined, respectively.

Table 1: Quantitative comparison of the local quality assessment task on the VGSR2K dataset. Qwen2.5-VL-72B and Qwen3VL-32B denote Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct and Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct, respectively. VGIQA significantly outperforms both large-scale general MLLMs and the IQA-specific baseline. The best and second-best results are highlighted in bold and underlined, respectively.

Table 3: Quantitative comparison of the Degradation Perception task. VGIQA significantly improves the perception accuracy of global physical degradations, especially in Noise and Null(no degradation). The best and second-best results are highlighted in bold and underlined, respectively.

papers.title: VGIQA: Fine-Grained Image Quality Assessment with Visual Grounding Rewards
papers.tldr: VGIQA enables MLLMs to assess image quality both globally and at localized regions by using visual-grounding rewards and reinforcement learning.

papers.abstract: We trained four widely used imitation-learning policies, ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA and $\pi_{0.5}$, on nested subsets of 12, 25, 50, 100 and 200 teleoperated demonstrations of one pick-and-place task with distractor objects, using one fixed training recipe per policy. Every trained model was then run on a physical SO-101 arm on a fixed set of object placements: 1,340 scored episodes in 126 blocks. ACT, trained from scratch, rose from 1 success in 40 episodes at 12 demonstrations to 37 in 40 at 100. $\pi_{0.5}$ with its action expert fine-tuned was the best policy when data was scarce (16 of 40 at 12 demonstrations, 28 of 40 at 25) and then stayed near 70%; from 100 demonstrations ACT was ahead, by a margin this study does not fully resolve. SmolVLA and Diffusion Policy peaked near 50%, and both were affected by a failure to start: SmolVLA's arm never started moving in 47% of episodes, and Diffusion Policy hardly ever started until an idle lead-in was trimmed from the demonstrations. For $\pi_{0.5}$ the fine-tuning recipe mattered more than the amount of data: low-rank adaptation succeeded in 4 of 110 episodes, against 130 of 200 for action-expert fine-tuning. From the joint and camera recordings we place every episode on a four-stage ladder (started, reached the ball, carried it, delivered it) and show that for ACT more data moves failures from reaching, to grasping, to none, while the failures $\pi_{0.5}$ retains are in grasping. We also measure how weak a ten-episode block is as a measurement (the same checkpoint tested twice differs by 2 successes in 10 on average), separate seed-to-seed variation from that noise, and audit the human scoring against the recordings. Training length was fixed within each recipe, so the amount of data and the number of times it was seen change together; we state which conclusions survive that confound and which do not.
bullets: The study compares ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA, and π₀.₅ using 12–200 demonstrations for one distractor-heavy pick-and-place task.
π₀.₅ performs best with 12–25 demonstrations, whereas ACT improves sharply with more data and reaches 37/40 successes at 100 demonstrations.
SmolVLA and Diffusion Policy peak near 50%; startup failures substantially limit both, especially SmolVLA.
For π₀.₅, action-expert fine-tuning is far more effective than low-rank adaptation under the tested recipes.
A four-stage failure analysis shows ACT’s errors shift from reaching toward grasping as data increases, while π₀.₅ mainly retains grasping failures.

papers.title: From 12 to 200 Demonstrations: How ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA and $\pi_{0.5}$ Scale on a Low-Cost Arm
papers.tldr: On a low-cost arm, imitation policies scale very differently with demonstrations: π₀.₅ leads with scarce data, while ACT becomes strongest from 100 demonstrations onward, with evaluation noise and training confounds limiting some conclusions.

papers.abstract: Accurate forecasting of global total electron content (TEC) is important for space weather monitoring and the reliable operation of satellite communication and navigation systems. We propose a physics-guided generative artificial intelligence (AI) framework for day-ahead global TEC forecasting. The framework builds on flow matching, which learns to gradually transform samples from an initial distribution into new samples that share the statistical characteristics of the target data. The proposed model incorporates ionospheric dynamics described by a partial differential equation (PDE) into this transformation process, guiding the changes between initial and target samples using physical knowledge. The model further combines the physical dynamics with statistical patterns captured from data to learn this transformation, adaptively adjusting their relative contributions at each location. The model is trained and evaluated using one year of global TEC data generated by the Thermosphere Ionosphere Electrodynamics General Circulation Model (TIEGCM). The results demonstrate that our model improves both spatial and temporal forecasting accuracy over representative benchmarks, including statistical, deep learning, and generative AI methods at all lead times and across latitudes. The average root mean square error (RMSE) is 39.2% lower than that of ConvLSTM and 23.8% lower than that of the same framework without physical guidance. The learned contribution weights vary systematically with latitude and across geographic locations, showing how the physical contribution changes across the forecast domain. These findings demonstrate that explicit physical guidance improves generative forecasts of global TEC and highlight the value of incorporating physical dynamics into generative AI modeling.
authors: Si-Tong Yang, Feng Ye, Xian Lu, Dong Lin, Benjamin C. Martinez

papers.abstract: Reliable real-time 3D object detection based on LiDAR and camera data is critical for safety in autonomous driving, where systems must accurately perceive their surroundings with minimal latency. Many state-of-the-art systems achieve high-quality detection results but fail to meet real-time constraints, limiting their practical use. To address this challenge, we propose FastBEVFusion, a simple, fast, and robust fusion system for 3D object detection. Based on modality-specific features, FastBEVFusion projects these features into semi-aligned modality-specific BEV spaces, without relying on a computationally intensive and potentially error-prone depth estimation. Given these BEV spaces, we propose a light-weight, soft, and dynamic fusion module based on cross-attention, which adapts dynamically to the scene context and enables feature fusion across the entire BEV spaces. Experiments on the complex nuScenes dataset show that FastBEVFusion outperforms state-of-the-art real-time systems, and achieves over 50 FPS without deployment libraries. Additionally, our system shows strong robustness to calibration errors, making FastBEVFusion a powerful 3D object detection system for real-world applications.
authors: Tom Sanitz, Emre G\"ulsoylu, Simone Frintrop, Christian Wilms
bullets: Targets the latency and reliability challenges of real-time multimodal 3D detection for autonomous driving.
Projects modality-specific features into semi-aligned BEV spaces without computationally expensive depth estimation.
Uses lightweight cross-attention for scene-adaptive fusion across the full BEV representation.
Evaluated on nuScenes, it outperforms state-of-the-art real-time systems and exceeds 50 FPS without deployment libraries.
Shows strong robustness to calibration errors, supporting practical real-world use.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of our FastBEVFusion. Multi-view image data is encoded and projected into an image BEV space using a uniform depth distribution to ensure low latency (color-coded in shades of green for different views). During training, an additional 2D object detection head is added. In parallel, the LiDAR point cloud is encoded into a LiDAR BEV space. The semi-aligned BEV spaces are then fused in our light-weight fusion module using on a single attention block exploiting the semi-aligned nature of the BEV spaces (see Fig. 3 for details). Based on the resulting fused BEV space, a detection head generates multi-modal 3D object detections.

Fig. 1. Results of real-time capable 3D object detection methods on the nuScenes dataset. Here, the two versions of our proposed FastBEVFusion based on different backbones offer the best detection quality and latency. Table I presents detailed results. Some latencies are estimated (see Sec. IV).

Fig. 4. Qualitative results of TransFusion-L [1] and our FastBEVFusion in three scenes of the nuScenes dataset. Only one of six views per scene is presented for brevity. Detected objects are color-coded by predicted classes: blue (pedestrians), orange (cars), and red (trucks).

Fig. 3. Detailed view of our light-weight fusion module based on a single multi-head attention block. The modality-specific BEV spaces are encoded and downsampled, before being tokenized and enriched with positional encodings. Subsequently, one multi-head attention layer is applied with tokens from image features as keys/values and tokens from LiDAR features as queries to efficiently learning a soft and dynamic fusion exploiting the semi-aligned nature of the features. Finally, an MLP is applied and a skip connection from the original LiDAR BEV space is added, before upsampling the features, yielding the fused BEV space. Note that we omit typical normalization steps in Transformers for brevity.

Fig. 5. Visualization of the attention scores in image BEV space (heat-map in right parts) given a feature from the LiDAR BEV space (position marked in left parts) as a query in our cross-attention fusion module. All figures show BEVs with the vehicle in the center.

papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary 3D occupancy prediction represents scene geometry and semantics in a unified voxel grid, enabling recognition beyond predefined categories. One approach reconstructs scenes with 3D Gaussians and converts them into voxel occupancy. However, Gaussian scale inflation and excessive overlap can distort voxel occupancy predictions, while semantic mixing can arise within Gaussians spanning multiple categories and during 3D--2D semantic feature alignment. We propose GCSR-OCC, which combines geometry calibration and multi-mode query-conditioned semantic routing for indoor occupancy prediction from a single RGB image. The Evidence-Conserving Gaussian-to-Occupancy operator (EC-G2O) uses kernel mass normalization, $p$-norm aggregation, and a learnable gain to suppress scale inflation and excessive local evidence accumulation while calibrating occupancy responses. Multi-mode Query-First Gaussian Semantic Routing (MM-QGSR) matches multiple semantic modes per Gaussian to text queries and aggregates query-specific evidence into voxels through a learnable text-conditioned router. Fine-grained subclass queries and smoothed semantic aggregation further refine voxel-level predictions. Without 3D semantic annotations, GCSR-OCC achieves state-of-the-art performance in open-vocabulary occupancy prediction on Occ-ScanNet, with 63.31% geometric IoU and 27.44% semantic mIoU. It also reduces geometric aggregation latency from 19.76 ms to 12.88 ms. Our code will be made publicly available.
authors: Bohua Wang, Congyang Zhao, Tianxiong Lv, Chenxu Zhao, He Zheng, Hangqi Fan, Leigang Luo, Zhihao Liao, Yihong Guo, Yang Cai
bullets: Addresses occupancy distortions from inflated, overlapping 3D Gaussians and semantic mixing across categories.
Uses EC-G2O to normalize Gaussian evidence, aggregate it with a p-norm, and calibrate occupancy responses with a learnable gain.
Uses MM-QGSR to match multiple semantic modes per Gaussian to text queries and route query-specific evidence into voxels.
Adds fine-grained subclass queries and smoothed semantic aggregation for more precise voxel semantics.
Achieves 63.31% geometric IoU and 27.44% semantic mIoU on Occ-ScanNet, while reducing geometric aggregation latency from 19.76 ms to 12.88 ms without 3D semantic annotations.

papers.abstract: We present a variational control framework that connects sampling-time guidance and reward-based model adaptation through a shared Jacobian pullback. Starting from terminal reward maximization with a path-space KL penalty, the Gibbs variational principle and Doob transform yield a correction to the generative dynamics. A local denoising approximation exposes the pullback that transports output preferences to the controlled variable. This construction gives Variational Optimal Guidance (VOG) in state space and extends to Distilled Variational Optimal Control (DVOC) by amortizing locally improved endpoints into model parameters. The resulting controls share a local variational rule: VOG acts through the denoising Jacobian, while DVOC realizes the parameter pullback by endpoint distillation. Under a linear MMSE model, VOG's exact correction lies in the data subspace. On ImageNet, VOG reduces DiT-XL/2 FID from 2.27 to 2.04 at 250 sampling steps and from 7.58 to 4.44 at 25 steps. After 20 updates on Z-Image-Turbo, DVOC improves HPSv3++ and four held-out evaluator scores over the untrained model, with the highest corresponding means among the trained methods compared. These results connect inference-time control and reward adaptation through a common geometric principle.
authors: Ruoyu Wang, Xinyi Ye, Yunshuo Shi, Liangyu Yuan, Beier Zhu, Chi Zhang
bullets: Formulates guidance from terminal reward maximization with a path-space KL penalty using the Gibbs variational principle and Doob transform.
Introduces Variational Optimal Guidance (VOG), which transports output preferences to diffusion states through the denoising Jacobian.
Introduces Distilled Variational Optimal Control (DVOC), which amortizes locally improved endpoints into model parameters.
VOG reduces DiT-XL/2 FID from 2.27 to 2.04 at 250 steps and from 7.58 to 4.44 at 25 steps on ImageNet.
DVOC improves HPSv3++ and four held-out evaluator scores on Z-Image-Turbo after 20 updates; the abstract does not specify limitations.

papers.abstract: In replay-free continual learning, Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) uses Fisher information matrix (FIM) to protect acquired knowledge by penalizing changes to historically important parameters. However, a local importance estimate at the retained solution does not in general characterize sensitivity after finite parameter displacement. This motivates controlling Fisher sensitivity over a neighborhood of potential future updates. We propose Fisher-Shaped EWC (FS-EWC), which extends the role of FIM from parameter protection to solution formation for future retention. During task learning, FS-EWC minimizes the worst-case empirical FIM trace within a prescribed neighborhood, explicitly favoring solutions that are less sensitive to bounded future displacement. At task completion, trajectory-based model merging constructs the retained solution from multiple optimization states rather than a single terminal iterate, after which FIM is estimated for subsequent consolidation. Experiments across multiple benchmarks show that FS-EWC improves performance over EWC, while controlled studies indicate a more favorable stability--plasticity balance and greater tolerance to parameter drift. These results suggest that effective knowledge retention requires both forming solutions with future retention in mind and protecting acquired knowledge.
authors: Liying Wang, Simone Magistri, Joost van de Weijer
bullets: EWC’s local Fisher estimate may not reflect sensitivity after finite parameter changes.
FS-EWC minimizes worst-case empirical Fisher trace within a prescribed update neighborhood during task learning.
Trajectory-based model merging forms the retained solution from multiple optimization states before later consolidation.
Experiments report improved performance over EWC, with better stability–plasticity balance and tolerance to parameter drift.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Beyond protection: shaping solutions for future retention. Complemented by model merging over task trajectory, our approach incorporates future retention into how solutions are learned and retained for subsequent protection.

papers.abstract: Equilibrium Propagation (EqProp) offers a biologically grounded and hardware-aligned alternative to backpropagation for training Hopfield Networks. However, its behavior in continual learning settings remains largely unexplored. This work confronts catastrophic forgetting in EqProp-trained Hopfield Networks from the inside out, eliminating the need for external data buffers or architectural overhead that standard Experience Replay \textbf{(ER)} and Generative Replay \textbf{(Gen-Replay)} inevitably require. We introduce an Energy-Based Generative Replay strategy \textbf{(EB-Gen)} which exploits the intrinsic generative dynamics of Hopfield Networks, allowing a single model to act as both classifier and replay samples generator. Samples capturing past task knowledge are generated by relaxing a frozen copy of the network, enabling rehearsal solely through internally generated pseudo-data. We evaluate the proposed method in the Class-Incremental setting, using the split versions of the MNIST and CIFAR10 benchmarks and compare it with FineTune, Experience Replay, Generative Replay, Sleep-Like Replay Consolidation (SRC) and Joint training. Our results show that EB-Gen significantly improves stability while preserving plasticity, achieving a 75\% and 64\% average accuracy on Split MNIST and Split CIFAR10 respectively. These findings show that Equilibrium Propagation can be adapted to alleviate catastrophic forgetting without forgoing the traits which made it compelling in the first place.
authors: Victor Cook (LIRMM | ADAC), Gilles Sassatelli (LIRMM | ADAC), Thierry Gil (LIRMM), Mohamed Watfa (LIRMM | ADAC), Marina Reyboz (CEA-LETI)

Evaluated on Split MNIST and Split CIFAR10 against FineTune, Experience Replay, Generative Replay, SRC, and Joint training.
Reports average accuracies of 75% on Split MNIST and 64% on Split CIFAR10, with improved stability while retaining plasticity.

papers.abstract: Coronary guidewire navigation during percutaneous coronary intervention requires continuous interpretation of vessel anatomy, guidewire position, and target stenosis under two-dimensional X-ray fluoroscopy. While existing approaches commonly address vessel segmentation or device localization as separate tasks, a robotic system requires a more structured perception of the coronary scene to support downstream navigation. In this work, we present a simulation-driven framework centered on a Multi-Task Coronary Perception Network (MCP-Net) for robotic guidewire navigation, integrating coronary vessel segmentation, vascular topology extraction, and roadmap generation. Starting from three-dimensional coronary CT angiography, we generate simulated fluoroscopy images containing vascular structures, simulated guidewires, stenotic lesions with varying severity, and diverse vascular geometries, together with simulation-derived ground truth. MCP-Net jointly performs coronary vessel segmentation, guidewire-tip localization, and stenosis localization from a single fluoroscopic frame. These predictions are subsequently converted into a structured vascular graph containing centerlines, bifurcations, endpoints, branch directions, and branch angles. By associating the predicted stenosis with this graph, the framework generates a roadmap from the automatically selected graph root toward the target lesion. The results demonstrate that the proposed framework can jointly recover coronary perception targets and transform them into an interpretable vascular representation suitable for downstream robotic navigation.
authors: Sahar Nasirihaghighi, Tianyuan Wang, Kenan Niu, Stefano Stramigioli
bullets: Addresses the need for structured, continuous coronary-scene understanding beyond separate vessel segmentation or device localization.

Transforms predictions into a vascular graph with centerlines, bifurcations, endpoints, branch directions, and angles.
Generates an interpretable roadmap from a selected graph root to the target lesion; evaluation is demonstrated in simulation.

papers.abstract: Pruned language models are judged almost entirely by accuracy and perplexity, which assumes that preserved output behaviour implies preserved internal computation. We test this assumption with a factorial pruning study on GPT-2, crossing two importance criteria (magnitude, random), two component types (attention heads, MLP neurons) and three sparsity levels (3%, 50%, 70%). Using the fully characterised indirect object identification (IOI) circuit as ground truth, we measure circuit integrity with activation patching, path patching and direct logit attribution. We find two qualitatively distinct failure modes. Magnitude head pruning >= zeroes the circuit: output-facing heads are removed, and the model falls to near-chance. Magnitude neuron pruning at 30% inverts it: all 26 circuit heads remain intact, but Name Mover contributions flip sign, and the model systematically prefers the wrong name (17.7% accuracy). Perplexity ranks it as less damaged than random head pruning (74.6 vs 140.1). A replication of the Greater-Than circuit shows that the critical component type depends on the circuit's architecture. These results show that output metrics and structural checks can both miss mechanistic damage, motivating circuit-level causal analysis as a complementary evaluation of compressed language models.
bullets: The study tests magnitude and random pruning of GPT-2 attention heads and MLP neurons across multiple sparsity levels.
Circuit integrity is evaluated using activation patching, path patching, and direct logit attribution, with IOI as the primary ground truth.
Magnitude head pruning can remove output-facing circuit heads and reduce performance to near chance.
Magnitude neuron pruning can leave all circuit heads intact while reversing Name Mover contributions, yielding systematically wrong predictions.
A Greater-Than circuit replication shows that pruning sensitivity depends on circuit architecture; circuit-level causal analysis is therefore needed alongside perplexity and structural checks.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates mechanistic failure modes of weight pruning in Transformers using mechanistic interpretability. This provides a deeper understanding of how pruning affects internal computation, relevant to LLMs and model efficiency.
papers.title: Mechanistic Failure Modes of Weight Pruning in Transformer Language Models
papers.tldr: Weight pruning can preserve or obscure output-level performance while severely damaging the internal circuits that produce model behavior.

papers.abstract: We introduce SERF (Self-Regularized Flow Language Models), a simple self-supervised framework for improving continuous diffusion language models by exploiting the denoising trajectory itself. While continuous flow-based language models offer a promising alternative to autoregressive generation, their training objectives typically rely on supervision from clean target tokens, leaving the denoising trajectory underexploited as a learning signal. SERF addresses this limitation through noisy-to-clean self-distillation: an exponential moving average (EMA) teacher receives a cleaner version of the student's noisy input along the same interpolation path and provides additional supervision. We investigate two variants: SERF-L, which aligns the student's intermediate representations with deeper teacher representations, and SERF-P, which aligns their output token distributions, either at the student's output or at an early student layer. All variants augment the standard training objective without requiring external pretrained models or modifying the inference procedure. Experiments across three continuous language-model paradigms (one-hot FLM, latent ELF, and hyper-spherical S-FLM) demonstrate substantial improvements in training efficiency, generation quality, and few-step generation. In particular, SERF achieves up to 7.7x wall-clock training acceleration on OpenWebText, improves MAUVE by 24.3% and GSM8K accuracy by up to 28.8%, and matches baseline performance with up to 64x fewer sampling steps. These results establish noisy-to-clean self-distillation as an effective approach to improving continuous diffusion language models.
authors: Theodoros Kouzelis, Spyros Gidaris, Nikos Komodakis
bullets: Addresses the underused denoising trajectory in standard continuous flow-language-model training.
Uses an EMA teacher that receives a cleaner input on the same interpolation path to supervise the noisy student.
Introduces representation-level SERF-L and distribution-level SERF-P variants without external pretrained models or inference changes.
Improves training efficiency, generation quality, and few-step generation across one-hot FLM, latent ELF, and hyper-spherical S-FLM.
Reports up to 7.7× faster wall-clock training, 24.3% higher MAUVE, 28.8% higher GSM8K accuracy, and comparable performance with 64× fewer sampling steps.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of SERF. In flow language models, the clean data lies at x1 (one-hot token embeddings) and pure noise at x0. SERF corrupts x1 at two noise levels along the same interpolation path using shared noise: the noisier input xs is fed to the student fθ, while the cleaner input xt (t > s) is fed to the EMA teacher fθ̄, whose outputs are detached via stop-gradient. The student is supervised by the standard cross-entropy loss against the ground-truth one-hot target xl 1, plus a distillation loss weighted by λ, which takes one of two forms. Left: In Latent Distillation, (SERF-L) the hidden states of an early student block ks are mapped through a lightweight projection head gθ and aligned with those of a deeper teacher block kt > ks using a per-token cosine distance. papers.selection_reason: Introduces SERF, a self-supervised framework for continuous diffusion language models using noisy-to-clean self-distillation. This improves training efficiency and generation quality for a specific class of generative LLMs.
papers.title: Self-Regularized Flow Language Models
papers.tldr: SERF improves continuous diffusion language models by self-distilling from cleaner points along their own denoising trajectories, enabling faster training and high-quality generation with fewer sampling steps.

papers.abstract: Distribution-matching distillation enables high-quality image generation in only a few denoising steps. However, distilled student models often map different initial noise samples to similar outputs under the same prompt. To locate where diversity is lost, we compare the teacher and student along the sampling trajectory. The largest measured reduction in the response to different initial noises occurs during the first, high-noise step. When we replace the first step with the teacher's corresponding trajectory and leave the final three student steps unchanged, most of the output diversity returns. This suggests that the first step is a key point for restoring diversity. Motivated by this finding, we introduce \emph{ReSeed}, a post-distillation method that adds a seed-response bias adapter only to the first student step and aligns its velocity with the teacher's first-interval secant velocity. All student weights and later denoising steps remain unchanged. We evaluate ReSeed on three text-to-image models (SD3-Medium, SD3.5-Medium, and FLUX.1-dev) and one text-to-video model (Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B). For a distilled 4-step FLUX.1-dev model, \emph{ReSeed} requires only $0.00196\%$ additional trainable parameters relative to the base model and is trained on 8,000 prompt--noise pairs, while keeping the distilled student fully frozen and requiring no target images, perceptual losses, or adversarial losses. It improves DINO diversity by $48.3\%$ while maintaining competitive visual quality. These results show that substantial diversity can be recovered through a lightweight, data-efficient tuning of only the first denoising step, without finetuning the full student model.
authors: Wenwu Tang, Dong Wang, Yun Cheng, Olga Saukh
bullets: Diversity is lost primarily during the first, high-noise denoising step.
Replacing that step with the teacher’s trajectory recovers most output diversity while leaving later student steps unchanged.
ReSeed adds a first-step seed-response bias adapter aligned with the teacher’s first-interval velocity; the student remains otherwise frozen.
Evaluated across three text-to-image and one text-to-video model, it improves DINO diversity by 48.3% for a distilled 4-step FLUX.1-dev model while preserving competitive visual quality.
The method uses 0.00196% additional trainable parameters and 8,000 prompt–noise pairs, without target images, perceptual losses, or adversarial losses.

papers.title: A First-Step Bias Restores Lost Diversity in Diffusion Model Distillation

papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) incorporate the prediction of future observations into robot policy learning. However, most WAMs build on billion-parameter vision-language or video-generation backbones, which incur high training cost and inference latency. In this letter, we present GAWM (Geometry-Aware World Model), a compact multi-task WAM that predicts future observations in the latent space of a frozen DINOv3 encoder. GAWM compresses the features of each camera view into a small set of tokens. A lightweight predictor, conditioned on the task rather than on actions, forecasts these tokens at two future horizons. The forecast is supervised with the dense patch features of future frames, which requires it to encode the spatial layout of the future scene. An action decoder directly regresses a chunk of future actions from the current and predicted tokens. With fewer than 100M parameters and no robot or video pretraining, GAWM outperforms billion-parameter WAMs on RoboTwin 2.0 and performs comparably to billion-parameter VLAs on LIBERO. On a dual-arm robot, it achieves lower action-prediction error on held-out demonstrations than a fine-tuned billion-parameter VLA, with substantially lower inference latency. Ablation studies show that the latent world model substantially improves performance when training data or training time is limited. Code is available at https://github.com/gaoxiang12/ga-wm.
authors: Yang Liu, Xiaoli Liu, Liuzhao Li, Yuduo Song, Muyuan Liu, Xiang Gao
bullets: Addresses the high training cost and inference latency of large world-action and vision-language models.
Predicts future multi-view observations in the latent space of a frozen DINOv3 encoder using compact tokens.
Forecasts task-conditioned future tokens at two horizons and uses dense future-frame patch features to preserve scene geometry.
Directly predicts chunks of future robot actions from current and predicted latent tokens.

Uses fewer than 100M parameters, requires no robot or video pretraining, and performs strongly across RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO, and a dual-arm robot; benefits are especially pronounced with limited data or training time.

papers.selection_reason: Compact latent world-action model for multi-task manipulation; directly combines robot action learning with future visual prediction.
papers.title: GAWM: A Compact Latent World-Action Model for Multi-Task Robot Manipulation
papers.tldr: GAWM is a compact, geometry-aware latent world-action model that enables effective multi-task robot manipulation with lower computational cost and latency than billion-parameter alternatives.

papers.abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) has been widely adopted for aligning language models with human preferences. Recent empirical work has revealed that DPO induces remarkably sparse parameter updates, yet no theoretical explanation for this phenomenon has been offered. We analyze DPO's optimization dynamics under a neural tangent kernel linearization and show that the logistic structure of the DPO loss gives rise to an implicit maximum-margin bias. Building on this observation, we introduce the concept of dual sparsity: the DPO update direction is a sparse linear combination (data-level sparsity, driven by support vectors) of sparse gradient feature vectors (parameter-level sparsity, arising from gradient cancellation between preferred and dispreferred responses). We formalize this structure in our main theorem, bound the number of support pairs by a margin-dependent spectral quantity, and present a framework relating dual sparsity to weight disentanglement---a condition favorable for model merging. Experiments on GPT-2 Small and Medium and on 7--9B instruction-tuned models (Llama-3-8B, Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-9B) with the Anthropic HH-RLHF and UltraFeedback datasets confirm both sources of sparsity, and experiments on GPT-2 show that DPO reduces cross-task interference by up to $35{\times}$ compared to supervised fine-tuning.
bullets: DPO’s logistic loss creates an implicit maximum-margin optimization bias.
Its update is sparse at two levels: support-vector-like data sparsity and gradient-cancellation-driven parameter sparsity.
A theorem bounds the number of support pairs using a margin-dependent spectral quantity.
The framework connects dual sparsity with weight disentanglement, a property useful for model merging.
Experiments across GPT-2 and several 7–9B instruction-tuned models confirm both sparsity mechanisms; on GPT-2, DPO reduces cross-task interference by up to 35× versus supervised fine-tuning.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes the sparsity of Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) updates, providing a theoretical explanation for weight disentanglement. This connects alignment (LLMs) with efficiency (sparsity) and model merging.
papers.title: On the Sparsity of Direct Preference Optimization: Weight Disentanglement in the NTK Regime
papers.tldr: DPO’s sparse parameter updates are theoretically explained by dual sparsity in the NTK regime, which also promotes weight disentanglement and reduces cross-task interference.

papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods adapt large models by introducing a small number of trainable parameters. However, we find that these parameters still contain redundancy and can be further compressed while maintaining strong task performance. To this end, we propose a novel hierarchical low-rank reparameterization method. Its core idea is to reorganize the trainable parameters of PEFT methods into an approximately square matrix and then express it via a low-rank decomposition, which can be applied recursively. This forms a multi-level structure with factors compressed level by level, drastically reducing the number of trainable parameters. In our experiments, we combine this reparameterization with LoRA, DoRA, MoSA, and RaSA. We evaluate commonsense reasoning on LLaMA-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B, with additional GSM8K math reasoning experiments on LLaMA-3.1-8B. Under comparable trainable-parameter budgets, our method combined with LoRA or DoRA achieves better performance. Furthermore,when the parameter count of the original methods is compressed by approximately an order of magnitude, our method can still maintain competitive task performance and even surpass the corresponding baselines in average accuracy across the eight commonsense reasoning benchmarks.
authors: Rong Huang, Yi Xiong, Yuan-Yuan Cheng, Xiao-Ming Fu
bullets: Targets redundancy in the trainable parameters of existing PEFT methods.
Reorganizes parameters into an approximately square matrix and applies recursive low-rank decomposition to create a multi-level compressed structure.
Combines with LoRA, DoRA, MoSA, and RaSA, evaluated on commonsense and GSM8K reasoning tasks.

With comparable parameter budgets, LoRA- and DoRA-based variants perform better; roughly tenfold compression can retain competitive performance and sometimes exceed baselines on average commonsense accuracy.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of HiLoRA (our method HiLoRR applied to LoRA). (a) Standard LoRA adds a rank-r update ∆W = αr BA to the frozen weight W0. (b) HiLoRA reshapes each LoRA factor into a Near-Square matrix (Breshape/Areshape) and represents it by a second low-rank product UBVB (resp. UAVA). The factor is then reshaped back into the reconstructed B/A (blue boxes), so the maximum rank of the matrix product BA remains bounded by r. HiLoRA directly parameterizes and trains only UB,VB,UA,VA, from which the factors (B/A (blue boxes)) are reconstructed on the fly.

papers.abstract: Self-supervised vision transformers are increasingly used as reusable encoders for Earth observation, but their inference cost on the hardware available in the field is rarely characterized. We deploy a pretrained SAR-optical masked-autoencoder encoder on three commodity x86 nodes, from a low-power CPU without AVX2 to an AVX2+VNNI reference, at FP32, FP16 and INT8 on the CPU and, where present, the integrated GPU, and report latency, energy (RAPL and wall plug) and linear-probe accuracy. Quantization is accuracy-neutral: INT8 changes micro-mAP by only +0.0006, within the seed spread, so precision becomes a pure cost decision. INT8 lowers CPU latency on every node, by 1.45x even on the CPU without AVX2, and CPU energy wherever it is measured, and the VNNI reference (1.53x) suggests a further gain beyond AVX2. The Pareto-optimal device shifts from the integrated GPU, which is 4.38x faster than the CPU on the weakest node, to the CPU as the CPU class improves.
bullets: Evaluates a pretrained self-supervised SAR-optical masked-autoencoder encoder across three commodity x86 nodes.
Compares FP32, FP16, and INT8 inference on CPUs and, where available, integrated GPUs using latency, energy, and linear-probe accuracy.
INT8 is accuracy-neutral, changing micro-mAP by only +0.0006 within seed variation.
INT8 reduces CPU latency on every node, including 1.45× on a CPU without AVX2; VNNI hardware suggests further gains.
The Pareto-optimal device shifts from the integrated GPU on weaker hardware to the CPU on more capable systems.

papers.abstract: Multimodal perception forms the foundation of multimodal intelligence. In particular, spatial perception and multimodal long-context understanding are two pivotal tasks that underpin embodied AI and multimodal agents. However, synthesizing targeted, high-quality training data for these tasks remains difficult and costly. Our key insight is that these tasks share an underlying capability, which we call connecting evidence: identifying relevant visual facts, binding them to the correct entities, recovering their relations, and composing them into an answer. Crucially, targeted training data are far easier to synthesize for this capability than for these tasks themselves. To strengthen this capability, we propose EvidenceConnect, an easy-to-implement data synthesis framework that uses zoomed views of related regions within a single image to generate questions requiring comparison, aggregation, or chaining of visual evidence. To ensure quality, a reference answer is retained only when independent VLMs agree on it, and region-ablation tests discard questions whose answer survives the removal of selected regions. We then train base VLMs on the resulting data with RLVR, obtaining Zooming without Zooming v2 (ZwZ2). Although the synthesized data are not tailored to any downstream benchmark, ZwZ2 improves fine-grained and spatial perception, with further gains on embodied spatial reasoning, multimodal long-context understanding, multimodal agent tasks, and general visual reasoning. These results establish EvidenceConnect as an effective framework for supervising evidence connection and suggest that strengthening this shared capability leads to more generalizable multimodal perception.
authors: Lai Wei, Yatai Li, Liangbo He, Jun Lan, Renjie Gu, Linhan Cao, Junkai Lin, Huijia Zhu, Weiqiang Wang, Linghe Kong, Yue Wang, Zhuosheng Zhang, Weiran Huang
bullets: Targets the shared capability of connecting evidence: finding relevant visual facts, linking them to entities, recovering relations, and composing answers.
Generates comparison, aggregation, and multi-step visual questions from zoomed views of related regions within one image.
Filters data using agreement among independent VLMs and region-ablation tests to verify answer quality and evidence dependence.
Trains base VLMs with reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) to obtain ZwZ2.
Although not tailored to downstream benchmarks, ZwZ2 improves fine-grained and spatial perception, with broader gains across several multimodal reasoning settings.

papers.abstract: Embedding-level scaling expands the capacity of language models through lookup-based memory rather than by increasing model depth, width, or dense computation. Extending this idea to vision-language models (VLMs) is challenging because visual features are continuous, spatially structured, and query-dependent, unlike discrete text tokens that naturally support n-gram lookup. We introduce V-LUMEN, a visual lookup memory for VLMs. V-LUMEN discretizes visual features with a frozen codebook, builds spatially aware memory keys through spatial aggregation-based hashing, and modulates them with text-conditioned relevance signals; all addressing is non-parametric, and the retrieved embeddings are fused into the backbone through a gated residual pathway. On five reasoning-intensive benchmarks, V-LUMEN substantially improves a frozen Qwen3-VL-2B backbone and transfers zero-shot to three benchmarks whose images are disjoint from the training data. At a matched parameter budget, moving part of a LoRA or MoE adapter's capacity into V-LUMEN preserves accuracy on two backbones, indicating that external visual memory is an independent capacity axis rather than a stronger adaptation method. Because lookup cost is constant in table size and incurred only once at prefill, this capacity grows in storage rather than in per-token compute. Code is available at https://github.com/miso-choi/V-Lumen.
authors: Miso Choi, Daekeun Kim, Eunji Kim, Jungbeom Lee
bullets: Visual features are continuous, spatially structured, and query-dependent, making text-style lookup memory difficult to apply directly.

Retrieved embeddings are integrated into the VLM through a gated residual pathway.
It improves a frozen Qwen3-VL-2B on five reasoning benchmarks and transfers zero-shot to three disjoint-image benchmarks.
At matched parameter budgets, V-LUMEN can replace part of LoRA or MoE capacity while preserving accuracy on two backbones.

papers.abstract: Every neural-network training run produces not only a model, but also evidence about how models learn. Can these accumulated experiments enable us to predict and compare new training runs before executing them? We study meta-models: models that predict the learning behavior of other models. From this perspective, final-performance prediction, learning-curve prediction, and hyperparameter selection are different queries to the same training response function. We take a first, humble empirical step toward this goal: treating real language-model training records as native numeric data, we find that an off-the-shelf tabular in-context learner, TabPFN, can match or outperform a fine-tuned LLM meta-model in multiple evaluated settings. Whereas recent work fine-tunes LLMs on tokenized configurations at a cost of tens to hundreds of GPU-hours, TabPFN requires seconds of fit-and-predict time without task-specific weight updates. We argue that meta-modeling is better treated as its own numeric modality rather than as a text task for LLMs. Going one step further, augmenting TabPFN with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) further improves accuracy on selected prediction tasks. Finally, we pre-registered a forecast of the Marin Hero Run, a 535B-parameter public training run, whose ground truth is revealed point by point as training progresses, putting meta-model predictions to the test against training outcomes not yet observed at the time of forecasting.
bullets: Unifies final-performance prediction, learning-curve prediction, and hyperparameter selection as queries to one training-response function.
Treats language-model training records as native numeric data rather than text.
TabPFN matched or outperformed a fine-tuned LLM meta-model across multiple evaluated settings without task-specific weight updates.
TabPFN required seconds for fitting and prediction, compared with tens to hundreds of GPU-hours for fine-tuning LLM meta-models.
Adding Kolmogorov–Arnold Networks improved accuracy on selected prediction tasks; a preregistered forecast tests predictions against an ongoing 535B-parameter training run.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces 'Meta Models' to predict learning behavior of other models, comparing TabPFN against LLM meta-models. This advances the field of meta-learning and model selection, relevant to Adaptation and Memory and LLMs.
papers.title: Meta Models: Models that Model Learning
papers.tldr: Meta-models use past training records to predict future model-learning behavior, with tabular learners offering an efficient alternative to LLM-based approaches.

papers.abstract: Field applications in chemical sensing, from portable safety monitors to mobile robots, require models that are lightweight, fast to respond, and can be recalibrated from limited labelled data. Current gas classification pipelines assume controlled sampling cycles and offline feature extraction, and rely on computationally expensive models. With a few thousand neurons and sub-milliwatt power consumption, insects reliably classify odours in open environments. Inspired by the insect olfactory system, we present a neural network architecture that classifies raw sensor array readings using a sparse, high-dimensional binary representation. We evaluate it on random sequences of single gases and binary mixtures, introducing new samples dynamically and classifying gas identity from the transient sensor response. In this setting, the architecture out-performs a linear \gls{svm} on gas mixtures and matches an optimised non-linear \gls{svm}, while maintaining online class-level frequency estimates that distinguish familiar from novel stimuli. It relies exclusively on binary weights and Hebbian-based local learning, remaining computationally lightweight and well suited to ultra-low-power neuromorphic processors. We demonstrated the network on-chip with a hazardous gas detection experiment running on the mixed-signal neuromorphic chip TEXEL. The on-chip classifier yielded an accuracy of 74.6\% while running at 482 $\unit{\nano\joule}$ per inference and 27 \unit{\micro\watt} of static-power.
authors: Ton Juny Pina, Hugh Greatorex, Elisabetta Chicca
bullets: Targets fast, recalibratable gas classification for portable and robotic edge applications using limited labelled data.
Processes raw sensor-array transients with a sparse, high-dimensional binary representation and supports dynamically introduced samples.
Uses binary weights and local Hebbian learning, avoiding offline feature extraction and computationally expensive models.
Outperforms a linear SVM on gas mixtures and matches an optimized nonlinear SVM, while estimating familiar versus novel stimuli.
Demonstrated on the TEXEL neuromorphic chip for hazardous-gas detection at 74.6% accuracy, 482 nJ per inference, and 27 µW static power.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: The expand-and-sparsify architecture. As the sensor array responds to a randomized sequence of gas mixtures, the first and second order derivatives of each sensor signal are approximated using backward differences, and the 56 pairwise channel ratios and differences are appended to form a 136-dimensional feature vector. This signal is then projected onto a higher-dimensional space via multiplication with a random sparse binary matrix, and subsequently sparsified through a k-WTA mechanism. A linear read-out layer produces online class-identity estimates.

Fig. 3: Class identity estimates from the read-out neurons activity. The activity of the read-out layer neurons as the sensor array signals are processed through the expand-and-sparsify architecture. The sensor array is exposed to a random sequence of odours (CO, ethylene, methane). During the training phase, learning signals trigger the potentiation of the output synapses, enforcing the output neurons to learn the sparse representations of its assigned category. The weights are then frozen during the testing phase.

Fig. 7: On-chip hazardous emission detection a) The custom mixed-signal neuromorphic processor TEXEL. It hosts 180 neurons distributed across two cores, with each neuron equipped with analogue synaptic circuits that emulate local plasticity mechanisms. b) The network architecture mapped onto the chip. HD input vectors are distributed across neurons and their synaptic inputs, then converted into single spikes at nonzero vector entries with random delays relative to a teacher spike during training. c) Raster plot of the input spike pattern for an inference sample, and the spiking responses of the read-out neurons. d) The ROC curve and the confusion matrix for the operating point with the highest Youden index (0: hazardous, 1: non-hazardous). e) Histogram of the dynamic power consumption per inference across the test sequence. papers.abstract: Continual adaptation of large language models (LLMs) to evolving task distributions while mitigating catastrophic forgetting remains an open problem. Existing strategies often struggle to scale or lack a robust mechanism for zero-shot task-to-expert assignment. We introduce CaLLM, a framework that resolves these tensions by combining metric-based meta-learning with modular parameter isolation via lightweight adapters. First, CaLLM projects each input batch into a task-agnostic embedding space to find its nearest prototype. It then routes the batch to the specific adapter specialized for that data distribution. This formulation provides (i)~controllable cross-task interference by design, (ii)~constant computational complexity regardless of task count, (iii)~seamless integration of novel distributions through prototype expansion, and (iv)~regime agnosticism as the local routing decision enables a unified approach to both online and offline settings. Our experiments demonstrate that this routing mechanism discovers semantically coherent task groupings while facilitating constructive interference between similar tasks, and keeping overhead at a minimum. Across diverse and fine-grained continual learning benchmarks, CaLLM consistently outperforms traditional isolation and replay methods, establishing prototype-based modular routing as a principled and scalable approach to lifelong adaptation of LLMs.
authors: Bilge Celik, Anna Vettoruzzo, Joaquin Vanschoren
bullets: Addresses continual adaptation under evolving task distributions and catastrophic forgetting.
Embeds each input batch, matches it to the nearest prototype, and selects the corresponding adapter.
Uses modular parameter isolation to control cross-task interference while supporting constructive transfer between similar tasks.
Maintains constant routing complexity as tasks grow and incorporates new distributions by expanding prototypes.
Outperforms traditional isolation and replay methods across diverse continual-learning benchmarks with low overhead.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems ground large language models (LLMs) by retrieving external evidence and conditioning generation on the retrieved context. Although dense retrieval is effective for local semantic matching, independently ranked retrieval can return redundant passages, miss cross-chunk dependencies, and provide incomplete evidence for multi-hop reasoning. We propose SpectRAG, a spectral graph-augmented retrieval framework that combines hybrid candidate seeding, weighted chunk graph construction, graph-based expansion, spectral relevance propagation, and token-budgeted context selection. Document chunks are represented by dense semantic embeddings and graph-spectral coordinates derived from a weighted chunk graph whose edges encode semantic similarity, document adjacency, section hierarchy, shared entities, citation links, and similarity between LLM-generated utility questions. At query time, SpectRAG builds a high-recall seed set using exact inner-product search and hybrid relevance signals, expands it over the chunk graph, re-scores candidates using graph proximity and spectral information, and assembles the final context under a fixed token budget. The goal is not merely to retrieve individually similar chunks, but to construct a context that is relevant, diverse, structurally connected, and sufficient for grounded reasoning. Experiments on MultiHopRAG, UltraDomain, and long-document question-answering settings show that SpectRAG improves broad evidence recovery and achieves competitive generation quality against dense, hybrid, HyDE, LightRAG, and NaiveRAG baselines. The results further indicate that graph-spectral structure is particularly useful for inference-oriented and cross-document retrieval, while highlighting trade-offs in early precision, computational cost, and domain-dependent performance.
authors: Zafer Sahinoglu, Abdulazeez Mohammed, Buse Yaren Kazangirler, Cahit Berkay Kazangirler
bullets: Addresses redundant retrieval, missed cross-chunk dependencies, and incomplete evidence from independently ranked dense retrieval.
Combines hybrid seed retrieval, graph expansion, spectral re-scoring, and token-budgeted context assembly.
Constructs chunk graphs using semantic similarity, document structure, shared entities, citations, and utility-question similarity.
Improves broad evidence recovery and delivers competitive generation quality across multi-hop and long-document settings.
Graph structure is especially useful for inference-oriented and cross-document retrieval, but involves precision, compute, and domain-dependent trade-offs.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated remarkable multimodal capabilities but suffer from prohibitive computational overhead due to the massive number of visual tokens. While token pruning is a promising solution, existing methods still suffer from two major drawbacks: 1) unreliable pruning criteria that fail to accurately localize task-specific regions due to inherent attention biases or query-agnostic designs, and 2) suboptimal pruning strategies that employ rigid, non-adaptive schedules, overlooking the dynamic evolution of token redundancy across different model depths. To address these challenges, we propose LearnPrunerV2, which extends the previous two-stage heuristic framework (LearnPruner) into a fully learnable architecture. Specifically, we integrate lightweight learnable modules into every layer of the VLM backbone, which estimate token importance by fusing intrinsic visual saliency with extrinsic query relevance captured via a shadow token. By uncovering a consistent staircase redundancy pattern across VLM layers, we further introduce Budget-Deterministic Pruning (BDP) to establish a hardware-friendly schedule with fixed per-layer budgets. Extensive experimental results across various benchmarks and VLMs demonstrate that LearnPrunerV2 consistently outperform previous state-of-the-art methods. Notably, LearnPrunerV2 preserves 99.8% of the original performance when pruning 77.8% of visual tokens on LLaVA-v1.5, achieving a superior accuracy-efficiency trade-off.
authors: Rinyoichi Takezoe, Yaqian Li, Weiren Wang, Zihao Bo, Huihong Shi, Anzhou Hou, Mo Guang, Jiale Yan, Kaiwen Long

Across benchmarks and VLMs, it reportedly outperforms prior state-of-the-art pruning methods.
On LLaVA-v1.5, it retains 99.8% of original performance while pruning 77.8% of visual tokens.

papers.abstract: Linear threshold functions (LTFs) are a canonical class of Boolean predictors. In the autoregressive setting, the same LTF reads the most recent $d$ bits, generates the next bit, and returns the bit produced after $T$ steps. While the one-step class has VC dimension $d$, for general $T$ the counting upper bound is $O(d^2)$. We prove that the VC dimension is $\Theta(d^2)$ for every $T\ge d^2$, resolving the quadratic gap for deterministic autoregressive LTFs. We then adapt the same technique to show an exponential separation between deterministic and stochastic autoregressive models: replacing the sign of LTFs by logistic sampling can increase the VC dimension of the final majority prediction class from quadratic to exponential in $d$.
authors: Ilan Doron-Arad, Idan Mehalel, Elchanan Mossel
bullets: Studies autoregressive LTFs that repeatedly use the latest d generated bits to produce future bits.
Shows the VC dimension is Θ(d²) for every sequence length T ≥ d², closing the previous quadratic-gap question.
Extends the approach to stochastic logistic models with final majority prediction.
Establishes an exponential VC-dimension separation between deterministic and stochastic autoregressive models.

papers.abstract: Image-goal navigation (ImageNav) requires an agent to reach a location specified by a goal image in an unknown environment. For drones, this task demands exploration, goal- directed navigation, and collision avoidance under limited onboard computing resources. Existing aerial ImageNav methods are built on single-view observations, requiring additional rotation and exploration to search for goal-relevant cues outside the field of view. In this paper, we present Omni-IGN, a fully onboard ImageNav system that integrates quad-fisheye perception, an attention-based reinforcement learning (RL) policy, and a collision-aware safety layer. The policy adaptively fuses goal-relevant features across multiple views to provide directional guidance for continuous navigation. The quad-fisheye RGB images support both ImageNav and obstacle avoidance without a dedicated depth sensor. On Habitat benchmarks, Omni-IGN achieves the best performance among continuous-action baselines. Moreover, flight tests in IsaacSim validate the effectiveness of integrating learning-based depth estimation with the action safety layer for collision avoidance. Finally, real-world experiments demonstrate zero-shot sim-to-real transfer without any fine-tuning or external localization. The code and model checkpoints will be released upon acceptance.

papers.abstract: Proactive LLM agents anticipate service opportunities from ongoing observations and accumulated history. Existing approaches emphasize recent context or retrieval of related memories, providing limited support for validating recurring behavioral regularities and assessing their applicability to the current event. We propose Proactive Memory (ProactMem), which organizes history into recent events, temporal trajectories, and behavioral regularities. Trajectory facts are checked against source events, and regularities are assessed through historical replay before being matched to current conditions. We also construct ProactiveStream, a longitudinal benchmark covering three application scopes, where agents process isolated event streams chronologically under episode-aware opportunity labels. On ProactiveStream, ProactMem achieves an overall effectiveness (F1) of 52.6%, a 21.4% relative improvement over the strongest of five external baselines. Code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ProactMem-5351/.

Organizes history into recent events, temporal trajectories, and behavioral regularities.
Verifies trajectory facts against source events and uses historical replay to assess regularities before matching them to current conditions.
Introduces ProactiveStream, a longitudinal benchmark spanning three application scopes with episode-aware opportunity labels.
