papers.abstract: Maintaining contact in non-prehensile manipulation requires more than nominal friction cone feasibility: a force barely inside the cone and one well inside it are both feasible, but they provide different margins against slip and contact loss. This paper uses signed friction distance to measure friction margin in force space and derives a task-adaptive margin from the force correction needed to balance pivot moment deviations in bimanual tilting. The resulting contact margins are embedded in a sequence of second-order cone programs (SOCPs), each giving a globally optimal contact force solution at a tilt angle. The optimizer balances the object about an environmental pivot while keeping robot and pivot contact forces away from the nominal friction boundary. Optimizer-level results show interpretable force redistribution and adaptation to object property changes. Real-world experiments demonstrate successful execution under object property variations and model mismatch, while fixed margin and no-margin comparisons illustrate the importance of adapting the margin to task demand. These results support signed friction distance margins as a force planning mechanism for maintaining contact in bimanual non-prehensile manipulation. Project page: https://keeping-contact.github.io/
authors: Qian Ying Lee, Lin Yang, Domenico Campolo
bullets: Signed friction distance distinguishes barely feasible contact forces from forces with greater slip and contact-loss margin.
The margin is adapted to the force correction required to balance pivot-moment deviations during tilting.
A sequence of SOCPs computes globally optimal contact forces while balancing the object about an environmental pivot.
Results show interpretable force redistribution and adaptation to object-property changes.
Real-world experiments succeed under property variation and model mismatch; fixed- and no-margin comparisons highlight the value of adaptation.

papers.selection_reason: Contact-aware force planning for bimanual non-prehensile manipulation; directly relevant to robotic manipulation and physical interaction.
papers.title: Keeping Contact: Task-Adaptive Friction Margins for Bimanual Non-Prehensile Manipulation
papers.tldr: A task-adaptive friction-margin planner uses SOCPs to maintain robust contact during bimanual non-prehensile tilting despite changing object properties and model mismatch.

papers.abstract: Streaming multimodal assistants must make response decisions while events are still unfolding. They need to recognize when the available evidence warrants a response, produce an appropriate continuation, and remain silent otherwise. Supervised fine-tuning learns from recorded assistant turns, but does not directly train on the response prefixes produced by the evolving policy itself. We introduce Live-OPSD, an on-policy self-distillation method that uses privileged hints available only during training to supervise the policy on its own outputs. The policy first generates a continuation from the streaming context alone. The same model then re-evaluates that continuation with a hint describing the relevant evidence, and the resulting distributions guide the unhinted policy. On Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B, Live-OPSD attains an average score of 59.64 on LiveProBench, 5.26 points above the strongest continued-SFT baseline, and stays competitive on OVO-Bench (65.84). These results indicate that guiding the policy on its own outputs with privileged hints improves both when and how a streaming assistant responds.
authors: Kaixuan Du, Xin Wan, Dai Guan, Ming Chen, Xiaoxi Jiang, Guanjun Jiang
bullets: Streaming assistants must decide whether to respond, what to say, or remain silent as events unfold.
The method addresses a gap in supervised fine-tuning, which does not train on prefixes generated by the evolving policy.
It generates a continuation from streaming context, then re-evaluates it with training-only privileged evidence hints.
On Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B, it scores 59.64 on LiveProBench—5.26 points above the strongest continued-SFT baseline—and remains competitive on OVO-Bench at 65.84.
The approach improves both response timing and content, within the evaluated streaming-assistant benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Hybrid language models keep a key-value (KV) cache only in their few full-attention layers, but this cache is still the part of a prompt's state that grows with the prompt and that must be stored or moved to reuse it. We present DCKV, a differentiable codec for the KV cache and the first KV-cache codec that is trained end to end. Its transform, its quantizer and its entropy models, which are conditioned on the prompt tokens and on already decoded neighbouring positions, are optimized together against the frozen language model, both for the code length that the entropy models assign and for the change of the model's output. On Qwen3.5-2B, DCKV stores a compressed token in more than 55 times fewer bytes than bf16 at a loss of at most 1.8 points on three long-context benchmarks, and in more than 100 times fewer bytes at a loss of at most 3.6 points.
authors: Egor Maximov, Aleksei Merkelov, Vasiliy Alekseev, Ivan Krivorotov, Valentin Beliaev, Nikita Arsenin, Dmitry Bocharov, Aleksei Goncharov
bullets: Targets the growing, transferable KV cache used by full-attention layers in hybrid language models.
Jointly learns a transform, quantizer, and token-conditioned entropy models.
Optimizes both estimated code length and the frozen model’s output preservation.
On Qwen3.5-2B, achieves over 55× compression with at most a 1.8-point loss on three long-context benchmarks.
Exceeds 100× compression with at most a 3.6-point loss.

papers.selection_reason: Learned KV cache compression for efficient inference in hybrid LLMs.
papers.title: DCKV: Learned Transform Coding of the Prompt KV Cache in Hybrid Language Models

papers.abstract: A large language model maintains conversational content in an external storage that is outside the model and grows as the dialogue continues. This work assumes an environment where a language model has no external memory and no prior knowledge of the future question or its answer. The motivation is to research whether a dialogue can be stored in the model parameters and later answer a question about it. This work proposes self-keyed in-parameter memorization (SKIM), a closed-form method in which the model generates its own questions about each dialogue turn and writes those questions into its parameters as the keys that later retrieve the turn's content. Generating many varied questions for each turn allows a later user question to match one even when phrased differently, and its answer is recalled from the parameters alone. Evaluated on five language models, SKIM recalls most stored dialogue turns from later user questions, and it answers from the model parameters without any external storage.
authors: XinYu Piao, Myunghoon Ryu, Joongheon Kim, Jong-Kook Kim
bullets: Addresses dialogue recall when no external storage or future question knowledge is available.
Generates varied questions for each dialogue turn and writes them with the turn content into model parameters.
Uses matching later user questions to retrieve and answer from parameter-stored content.
Evaluated on five language models, recalling most stored dialogue turns.
Scope: focused on parameter-only recall rather than external-memory systems.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of Skim. From an earlier turn the model extracts candidate spans as values and self-generates questions as keys. Both steps are answer-free, and a closed-form edit installs these pairs into one frozen feed-forward layer. A later question phrased differently forms a key that retrieves the value, and the model answers from its parameters.

Figure 2: Recall (%) for five language models. Panel (a) reports recall at N=32 in five conditions from ceiling to floor, the KV cache upper bound, the answer-given references true-Q and self-Q, the answer-free SKIM, and a no-cache floor that removes all memory. Panels (b) and (c) trace recall and the count of unrecalled facts as N grows from 4 to 32.

Figure 5: A comparison of streaming recall and batch recall for five models, ranging from N=4 to N=32. Every point lies on the identity line because a streamed write reproduces the batch solve without forgetting.

Figure 3: Per-fact outcome at N=32 for five language models. Each model’s 32 stored facts split into correct and four failure classes, the store-time pair missing and selection and the recall-time pair routing and decoding.

Figure 4: Panel (a) reports recall by write position, each model’s facts split into early, middle, and recent groups. Panel (b) reports recall by answer type, proper-noun versus descriptive multi-word, pooled and within each group.

papers.selection_reason: Closed-form in-parameter memorization for dialogue recall, combining test-time parameter updates with LLM memory.
papers.title: Self-Keyed In-Parameter Memorization for External Memory-Free Dialogue Recall in Frozen Language Models
papers.tldr: SKIM stores dialogue turns directly in frozen model parameters using self-generated question keys, enabling later recall without external memory.

papers.abstract: Multimodal transformer models have driven unprecedented performance breakthroughs in modern document understanding. However, the inherent black-box nature of these models remains a major obstacle to their safe deployment in high-stakes sectors. Despite significant progress in explainability for vision and language tasks, explainable AI (XAI) research tailored to multimodal document understanding has received little attention. To address this gap, we present \ourframework{}, the first comprehensive explainability framework that adapts existing XAI methods and evaluation metrics to the multimodal (text, layout, and image) document understanding context, while introducing efficient multi-target adaptations of both methods and metrics for domain-specific tasks such as semantic entity recognition. Using \ourframework{}, we systematically evaluate 13 XAI methods across 3 document understanding tasks, 8 datasets, 4 models, and 17 evaluation metrics, and find that only a few methods perform consistently across all evaluation criteria, with Occlusion emerging as the most faithful and interpretable method overall. Through a dedicated meta-evaluation, we observe moderate to strong agreement among several faithfulness and complexity metrics while identifying certain ones that produce unreliable results. Finally, through multiple dataset-wide diagnostic analyses, we uncover key insights into model behavior, including the contribution of individual modalities across tasks and labels, spatial attribution patterns around target entities, and potential dataset biases. Overall, this work serves as both a benchmark and a practical guide for future XAI research in multimodal document understanding. To support reproducibility, we publicly release our code at https://github.com/saifullah3396/docxeval/.
authors: Saifullah Saifullah, David Dembinsky, Stefan Agne, Andreas Dengel, Sheraz Ahmed
bullets: Addresses the limited XAI research for models combining document text, layout, and images, especially in high-stakes applications.
Adapts existing XAI methods and metrics to multimodal documents and develops efficient multi-target variants for tasks such as semantic entity recognition.
Systematically evaluates 13 XAI methods across 3 tasks, 8 datasets, 4 models, and 17 metrics.
Finds that only a few methods perform consistently across evaluation criteria; Occlusion performs best overall.
Diagnostic analyses reveal modality contributions, spatial attribution patterns, and potential dataset biases; code is publicly released.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of the DocXEval framework. Given a dataset and a trained model, the framework (1) extracts modality-specific inputs from each document, (2) defines feature segmentation masks, reference baselines per modality, and targets, (3) computes modality-wise attribution scores via XAI methods, (4) evaluates explanation quality across four XAI evaluation criteria, and (5) conducts a systematic qualitative and quantitative analysis of results across datasets, models, and tasks.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates explainability of multimodal document-understanding transformers, relevant to interpretation and reliability of multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: DocXEval: A Systematic Evaluation of Explainability in Multimodal Document Understanding
papers.tldr: DocXEval introduces a comprehensive framework and benchmark for evaluating explainability in multimodal document understanding, finding that Occlusion is the most consistently faithful and interpretable method overall.

papers.abstract: Learning from experience is essential for building the next generation of agents that continually expand their capabilities. Pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) already internalize rich world knowledge, yet this knowledge is rarely leveraged to drive policy improvement through online interaction. Realizing this potential efficiently remains challenging, as policy updates shift the agent's interaction distribution, requiring the world model to adapt accordingly, while continually updating large pretrained models is computationally expensive. To address this challenge, we introduce Dwell, a model-based reinforcement learning (RL) framework that reframes a VLM as a recurrent latent transition operator, endowing it with the ability to predict, adjust, and act in latent space. Leveraging the VLM's own representations and its dual role as both world model and policy, the agent continually learns from real interactions to anticipate and evaluate action outcomes, and from latent imagination to improve its behavior. Across five interactive visual environments, Dwell achieves the strongest overall performance among trainable methods while substantially reducing the compute required for imagination, showing that effective world models for VLM agents need not reconstruct the future; they need to predict futures that are useful for action. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Tom111-lhx/Dwell
authors: Haoxi Li, Sikai Bai, Jianfei Ma, Qinglin Hou, Xiaocheng Lu, Tao Han, Jie Zhang, Song Guo
bullets: Addresses the challenge of efficiently adapting pretrained VLM agents through online experience without continually updating large models.
Recasts a VLM as a recurrent latent transition operator serving as both world model and policy.
Combines real-interaction learning with latent imagination to anticipate action outcomes and improve behavior.
Achieves the strongest overall performance among trainable methods across five interactive visual environments.
Substantially reduces imagination compute and suggests useful world models need not reconstruct full futures.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Computational Efficiency. End-to-end GPU-hours required to reach the reported training step on FROZENLAKE, SOKOBAN, NAVIGATION, and EB-ALFRED. GPU-hours include all computation incurred during online training, including world-model updates, imagined rollouts, and policy/value optimization. All methods are evaluated under the same environment-specific training schedule and hardware configuration.

Figure 1: Overview of DWELL. Left: The VLM learns a recurrent latent world by matching action-conditioned priors to observation-conditioned posteriors, while grounding the latent states with a frozen V-JEPA2 encoder. Right: The same VLM backbone serves as both world model and policy, alternating online interaction with latent planning for policy improvement.
Figure 2: Learning Efficiency. Success rate throughout training on SOKOBAN and FROZENLAKE. Left: comparison with model-based approaches. Right: comparison with model-free approaches.

Figure 4: Ablation Studies. Left: effect of removing the representation-grounding objective Lrep or the predictive dynamics objective Ldyn. Right: effect of freezing the world model after initialization instead of continually updating it with newly collected experience. Predictive dynamics provide the primary supervision for useful latent imagination, while representation grounding and continual world-model adaptation further improve policy learning.

All trainable methods use Qwen2.5-VL-3B as the VLM backbone and are trained under the same environmental feedback and interaction budget. Off-the-shelf VLMs are evaluated without online adaptation. papers.selection_reason: Introduces a VLM-based recurrent latent world-model/policy for online interactive learning, directly fitting latent-action and interactive world-model research.
papers.title: Vision-Language Agents Can Learn in Their Own Latent Worlds
papers.tldr: Dwell enables vision-language agents to learn from interaction by predicting and improving actions entirely in their own latent space.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents rely on memory systems to leverage long-term interactions, yet existing systems typically retrieve memories based on their relevance to the current query and use them as contextual evidence. However, relevance alone does not characterize how a memory contributes to task solving: the same memory may serve different roles across tasks, such as directly supporting the answer or linking to complementary memories with weaker semantic relevance but necessary information. We therefore reframe agent memory systems as Task-Oriented Role-Adaptive Workspaces, where memories are selected and organized by their task-oriented roles and relations. Based on this view, we propose TrawMem, which organizes interaction histories into local threads and constructs task-oriented workspaces by assigning roles and jointly selecting complementary memories. Experiments on LoCoMo and MemGallery with four open- and closed-source backbones show consistent improvements over representative memory systems, with macro-F1 gains of 2.23-3.14 points. On LoCoMo, TrawMem improves the LLM-Judge score over SimpleMem by 4.07 and 4.31 percentage points on Qwen3.5-9B and DeepSeek-V4-Flash, respectively, while requiring approximately 12.8% and 5.1% fewer context tokens, respectively.

bullets: Existing memory systems may miss complementary memories whose roles are important but whose semantic relevance is weak.
TrawMem groups interaction histories into local threads and assigns task-oriented roles to memories.
It jointly selects complementary memories to construct workspaces tailored to the task.
Across LoCoMo and MemGallery with four backbones, TrawMem gains 2.23–3.14 macro-F1 points over representative systems.
On LoCoMo, it improves LLM-Judge scores over SimpleMem while using fewer context tokens on the reported backbones.

papers.abstract: Although the recent development of LLMs has paved the way for multi-modal interaction, minority languages face difficulties keeping pace. This work presents the first open Speech Language Model for Basque, designed for low-latency, end-to-end spoken interaction. Based on the LLaMA-Omni architecture, the system integrates a Latxa model as its backbone, transferring its Basque capabilities to the spoken modality by fine-tuning several modules. To address data scarcity, the English VoiceAssistant-400K corpus was translated into Basque, and the audio was synthesized using a Basque TTS. Evaluation results confirm the system's viability, achieving 3.86/5 in content quality, a 9.94% WER for spoken intelligibility, and a 3.07 UTMOS for audio quality. This work demonstrates that advanced spoken interaction systems can be developed using modular architectures and synthetic data even in low-resource languages.
authors: Andoni Sudupe, Inma Hernaez, Ander Arriandiaga, Christoforos Souganidis, Ibon Saratxaga, Eva Navas
bullets: Addresses the limited availability of advanced spoken-interaction systems for minority and low-resource languages.
Builds on LLaMA-Omni with Latxa as the Basque backbone, fine-tuning modules to transfer language capabilities to speech.
Expands scarce training data by translating VoiceAssistant-400K into Basque and synthesizing corresponding audio with Basque TTS.
Evaluation reports 3.86/5 content quality, 9.94% word error rate, and 3.07 UTMOS audio quality.
Demonstrates the viability of modular architectures and synthetic data for Basque speech interaction.

papers.abstract: Long-sequence panoramic reconstruction requires detailed scene geometry and globally consistent camera poses across distant revisits. Panoramic SLAM and incremental SfM rely on feature correspondences, but repeated, similar structures and small partial overlap make reliable long-range connections difficult to establish, leaving accumulated drift unresolved. Feed-forward models offer detailed local geometry, but their high computational costs limit inference window size, necessitating additional constraints for global consistency. This motivates combining continuous feature-based tracking and sparse mapping with rapid, high-quality local reconstruction from feed-forward models to achieve accurate localization and globally consistent dense mapping over long sequences. We therefore propose a panoramic reconstruction framework that couples an ORB-based sparse panoramic mapping frontend with a fine-tuned feed-forward model. Our key insight is that predicted local geometry enables 3D verification of feature matches across distant revisits, yielding long-range camera constraints even between regions. We calibrate predicted depths with sparse landmarks and use verified connections to optimize the global pose graph, updating dense geometry with the corrected camera poses. We also introduce PanoRecon, a seven-scene benchmark with repetitive architecture, large and small loops, and reference camera poses and LiDAR geometry for evaluating global consistency. Our method achieves the lowest mean absolute trajectory error and high F-1 Score among the evaluated methods. Project Page:https://zhuoxiaoli.github.io/HoloRecon_page/
authors: Zhuoxiao Li, Xinyi Liu, Hongye Hou, Jing OU, Kang Du, Shuai Zhang, Dongli Wu, Taoyu Wu, Siyuan Feng, Xiaohui Zhu, Wufan Zhao
bullets: Addresses drift and unreliable long-range feature matching caused by repetitive structures and limited overlap.
Uses an ORB-based panoramic mapping frontend coupled with a fine-tuned feed-forward reconstruction model.
Calibrates predicted depths with sparse landmarks and performs 3D verification of feature matches across distant revisits.
Optimizes a global pose graph using verified long-range connections, then updates dense geometry with corrected poses.
Introduces the seven-scene PanoRecon benchmark and reports the lowest mean absolute trajectory error plus a high F-1 Score among evaluated methods.

papers.abstract: GUI grounding on high-resolution screens fails mostly on small targets, and zooming in is a common training-free remedy. However, most existing zooming pipelines do not match the zoom to the target's size, accept the zoomed answer unconditionally and never revisit a wrong answer. To address these issues, we propose AdaGround, a training-free framework with three components: (1) Token-Normalized Adaptive Zooming, which sets the magnification, field of view and zoom depth of each sample from the model's own estimate of the target size; (2) Verifier-in-the-Loop Refinement, which uses one marked-click Yes/No verifier to keep or reject each zoom, choose between zoom chains, trigger re-grounding and, with an existence query, decide when to abstain; and (3) Compositional Structure Grounding, which composes spreadsheet cells from their headers. On Qwen3-VL models, AdaGround surpasses state-of-the-art training-free zooming methods and many trained GUI models, improving accuracy over the backbone by 7.4 to 20.6 points on OSWorld-G and ScreenSpot-Pro, and its gains carry over to held-out UI-Vision. Code is available at https://github.com/bcwang-sjtu/AdaGround
authors: Bingchao Wang, Yongcheng Jing, Chengyu Wang, Jun Huang, Jie Yang, Wei Liu, Dacheng Tao

Uses a marked-click Yes/No verifier to accept or reject zooms, select zoom chains, trigger re-grounding, and abstain when targets may not exist.
Composes spreadsheet-cell targets from their row and column headers.
On Qwen3-VL, improves over the backbone by 7.4–20.6 points on OSWorld-G and ScreenSpot-Pro, with gains transferring to held-out UI-Vision.
The framework is training-free and evaluated on high-resolution GUI grounding.

papers.abstract: Open-Set Test-Time Adaptation (OSTTA) operates on non-stationary target streams where covariate and semantic shifts coexist. Existing TTA methods often obtain adaptation signals by updating model parameters or maintaining mutable memories, which can be costly and vulnerable to unknown samples. We present TALOR, a lightweight, backward-free rectification module that uses the source linear head as a geometric anchor. The head-induced basis decomposes each normalized feature into high-gain principal coordinates and low-gain tail coordinates. TALOR estimates a soft-routed affine correction in the principal subspace, combining a regime-level principal bias with a tail-conditioned slope that captures sample-level tail-to-principal coupling. Using weighted ridge regression, it subtracts this drift estimate from the principal coordinates, reconstructs the feature and feeds it into the source head. On the ImageNet-C benchmark with six csOOD datasets, TALOR outperforms the next-best UniEnt by 2.2% H-score while running 2.5x faster and using only 12% of its GPU memory; as a post-correction plug-in, it further boosts COME to 68.4% H-score with only 2% additional memory overhead.
authors: Yingkai Yang, Chaoqi Chen, Hui Huang
bullets: Targets open-set test-time adaptation under simultaneous covariate and semantic shifts.
Decomposes normalized features into principal and tail coordinates using the source linear head as an anchor.
Uses soft-routed weighted ridge regression to estimate and subtract principal-space drift conditioned on tail features.
On ImageNet-C with six csOOD datasets, it achieves 2.2% higher H-score than UniEnt and runs 2.5× faster with 12% of its GPU memory.
As a post-correction plug-in, it raises COME to 68.4% H-score with 2% additional memory overhead.

papers.abstract: Real-to-Sim-to-Real (Real2Sim2Real) enables structured world representations for planning, interpretability, and safe execution. Most existing approaches rely on passive perception, which creates real2sim gaps due to imperfect observation. Inspired by how humans perceive actively through actions, we propose ActiveAlign, a framework that leverages active perception to align the Real2Sim2Real gap from interactions. ActiveAlign introduces two complementary modules: (i) ActiveAlign-Waving, which performs hand-eye calibration by exploiting active hand motions and differentiable rendering, and (ii) ActiveAlign-Touching, which refines object alignment through tactile feedback to achieve millimeter-level precision. Together, these capabilities enable strong real2sim alignment. We demonstrate that ActiveAlign-Waving can be used to curate simulation environments for open-sourced uncalibrated robot manipulation datasets, and demonstrate on a real Unitree G1 robot that ActiveAlign enables fine manipulation of millimeter-scale objects such as pressing buttons and moving sliders.
authors: Ri-Zhao Qiu, Bowen Wen, Yifeng Jiang, Chen Tessler, Eric Heiden, Xue Bin Peng, Xiaolong Wang, Stan Birchfield, Erwin Coumans
bullets: Addresses misalignment caused by passive perception in Real2Sim2Real systems.

papers.title: ActiveAlign: Aligning Egocentric Manipulation via Active Perception

papers.abstract: Achieving high-quality reconstruction and responsive camera tracking remains challenging for monocular RGB Gaussian splatting SLAM under a limited optimization budget. We present an online system that addresses this challenge by combining learned geometric priors with explicit geometric camera tracking, which can substantially outperform learned camera prediction in terms of tracking accuracy. A frozen streaming 3D foundation model serves as a virtual RGB-D sensor, providing depth estimation from monocular video. An explicit geometric solver then estimates camera motion through feature reprojection, and a streaming Gaussian mapper integrates the resulting observations into a dense scene representation. We further show that geometric tracking improves camera pose accuracy across representative streaming geometry backbones, demonstrating the broader applicability of our approach. Extensive experiments on indoor and outdoor datasets show that our method significantly improves reconstruction quality over existing approaches, achieving about 7 FPS on a single RTX 4090 and delivering 2-3 times the throughput of the evaluated prior SLAM systems.
authors: Da Li, Yihan Zang, Ivan Viola, Zeyu Wang, Dominik Engel
bullets: Targets the joint challenge of accurate camera tracking and quality reconstruction under limited optimization budgets.
Uses a frozen streaming 3D foundation model as a virtual RGB-D sensor for monocular depth estimation.
Estimates camera motion with feature reprojection and integrates observations using a streaming Gaussian mapper.
Improves reconstruction quality and camera pose accuracy across indoor/outdoor settings and multiple geometry backbones.
Runs at about 7 FPS on one RTX 4090, with 2–3× the throughput of evaluated prior SLAM systems.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of our online Gaussian splatting SLAM system. (a) A frozen streaming foundation model estimates camera intrinsics from the initial RGB frames. (b) Predicted depth and image features support geometric camera tracking through correspondence matching and reprojection error minimization. (c) The Gaussian mapper integrates RGB frames, predicted depth, and estimated poses through keyframe selection, Laplacian-guided Gaussian insertion, and 30-step refinement using RGB and depth losses with keyframe replay.

Figure 3. Qualitative rendering and depth comparison. One representative sequence is selected from each dataset. For 7-Scenes, TUM-D and Oxford Spires, we show both novel-view RGB rendering and rendered depth; RE10K is shown only in RGB because reference depth is unavailable. The 7-Scenes and TUM-D datasets provide dense reference depth, whereas the Oxford Spires reference depth is sparsely projected from the scanned point cloud. All methods are compared using the same valid-depth mask.

Figure 2. Ablation on refinement steps per keyframe. Means over the six Oxford Spires sequences. Rendering quality saturates at 𝑛≈75–100 (dashed line). The filled marker is the default 𝑛=30 used in all main tables.

Figure 4. Qualitative trajectory comparison. We visualize one representative sequence from three datasets after trajectory alignment. Our estimated trajectories closely follow the ground truth. Because OTF is designed primarily for novel-view synthesis and estimates poses only for keyframes and held-out views, its trajectory error is computed only over this available pose subset rather than over all input frames.

papers.selection_reason: Gaussian SLAM combining learned geometric priors with explicit camera tracking; directly relevant to dense 3D reconstruction and 3D perception.
papers.title: LingGS: Decoupling Feed-Forward Geometry Prediction from Camera Tracking for High-Fidelity Gaussian SLAM
papers.tldr: LingGS combines learned depth with explicit geometric tracking to enable fast, high-fidelity monocular Gaussian SLAM.

papers.abstract: Robot foundation models may generalize across tasks and embodiments, but their actions still depend on sensors that can fail. When the policy is frozen or inaccessible, can an external monitor diagnose and repair corrupted inputs without access to its internals? We test a structured surrogate that separates periodic gait from sensor-dependent corrections to guide input repair around a frozen locomotion policy. On simulated Go2, offline diagnosis raises walking success from 259/640 to 429/640 episodes; online repair reaches 382/640, with no triggers in 64 held-out fault-free episodes. A matched boosted-tree surrogate predicts clean actions similarly well but yields no detected repair improvement over no repair. Separate fits improve walking on Go1 and ANYmal C, although phase-aware gradients perform better. Evidence remains limited to one policy and a partly screened simulated fault suite; robot foundation model and hardware validation remain open.
authors: Marc Ziegler, Batu \"Ozen, Sami Mentes, Thomas Waschulzik, Alois Knoll
bullets: Addresses sensor corruption when the robot policy is frozen or inaccessible.
Separates periodic gait dynamics from sensor-dependent corrections to guide input repair.
On simulated Go2, offline diagnosis improved success from 259/640 to 429/640 episodes; online repair reached 382/640.
Produced no false triggers across 64 held-out fault-free episodes; a matched boosted-tree surrogate showed no repair benefit.
Separate surrogate fits helped Go1 and ANYmal C, while phase-aware gradients performed better.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Method overview: Diagnosis and input repair. MBD identifies the faulty sensor from the structured surrogate’s per-sensor contributions, and PRR repairs its input before the frozen policy acts. For a +0.3 rear-left thigh-encoder offset: (a) the sensor explains 49% of the abnormal correction across 16 diagnosis logs; (b) PRR supplies its phase-matched healthy value; and (c) repair removes the sideways drift and raises walking success from 3/16 to 16/16 fresh episodes.

Table 1: Results across three embodiments. For Go2, R2 measures action prediction on 16 clean trajectories, and Diagnosed reports top-1 sensor identification across 37 faults. Go2 Walk and Survive are counts over 640 episodes. Online MBD detects, diagnoses, and repairs faults within each episode. Go1 and ANYmal C report walking over 352 episodes per method. On these two robots, the GBM predicts actions directly and shares neither MBD’s gait model nor its input representation.

papers.selection_reason: The paper addresses sensor failure in robot foundation models by proposing a transparent surrogate for online diagnosis and repair of inputs to a frozen locomotion policy. This falls under robot learning (surrogate modeling) and test-time learning (online adaptation).
papers.title: When Black-Box Robot Policies Fail: Online Sensor Diagnosis and Repair with a Transparent Surrogate
papers.tldr: A transparent, phase-aware surrogate can diagnose and repair sensor faults around a frozen robot policy, improving simulated locomotion but with limited validation.

papers.abstract: Camouflaged object detection (COD) depends on weak texture and boundary cues that can be destroyed by aggressive post-training quantization (PTQ). Existing PTQ methods mainly optimize quantizers or reconstruct network blocks, while using a single precision-allocation domain throughout hierarchical backbones. Instead, we introduce AxisQ, a depth-adaptive bit-allocation framework motivated by the observation that the useful allocation axis changes with feature depth. Under a fixed per-layer average activation-bit budget, AxisQ allocates precision in the channel domain for shallow features and in the local-frequency domain for deep features, using COD-aware sensitivity to better preserve subtle foreground regions and ambiguous boundaries. We also formulate a boundary-aware Hessian approximation for reconstruction by incorporating boundary-weighted gradient and error statistics. Experiments across multiple COD models and diverse benchmarks demonstrate improved accuracy over the strongest baselines at low bit widths, with relative weighted F-measure gains of 12.7% for CFRN and 33.3% for CamoFormer-P on CAMO under W2A2 quantization. These results support adapting the allocation domain to feature depth as a transferable quantization strategy for hierarchical COD models.
authors: Chi Ruan, Tianqi Li, Xin He, Xue Geng, Ming-Ming Cheng, Yun Liu
bullets: Addresses the risk that aggressive PTQ destroys weak texture and boundary cues in COD.
Allocates activation bits in the channel domain for shallow features and local-frequency domain for deep features under a fixed average bit budget.
Uses COD-aware sensitivity to preserve subtle foreground regions and ambiguous boundaries.
Introduces boundary-aware Hessian-based reconstruction using boundary-weighted gradient and error statistics.
Reports relative weighted F-measure gains of 12.7% for CFRN and 33.3% for CamoFormer-P on CAMO with W2A2 quantization.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Qualitative comparison of quantization methods on two COD models at W2A2. Model A is CFRN, and Model B is CamoFormer-P. Each pair of rows corresponds to one model, with IoU reported for each prediction against the ground-truth mask. The compared methods show incomplete foreground regions and false detections in the background. In these examples, AxisQ recovers more complete object shapes and clearer boundaries while reducing background false positives.

Figure 3: Overview of AxisQ for a four-stage hierarchical encoder. Channel-domain allocation is used in shallow and eligible non-frequency paths, while deep encoder features use local-frequency allocation. The strip and grid visualize channel-wise and frequency-wise activation-bit assignments at W2A2; darker orange indicates higher precision, and gray denotes zero-bit bands. (d) sketches the auxiliary boundary-aware Hessian approximation using teacher-derived boundary weights and weighted gradient statistics.

Figure 2: Depth-dependent sensitivity on a selected COD image. (a) shows the input and groundtruth mask, and (b) shows independently normalized S2 and S4 feature responses. In (c), 17 bands in S2 and two in S4 account for 80% of DCT sensitivity. (d) plots cumulative sensitivity above uniform versus the percentage of top-ranked channels or frequency bands, with separate vertical scales. Sensitivity is more concentrated across channels in S2 and across frequency bands in S4, supporting channel-wise allocation in shallow stages and local-frequency allocation in deep stages.

Figure 4: Actual CFRN W2A2 bit assignments in the first attention-output projection of each encoder stage. Channels retain their original order; frequency maps use DCT coordinates. Every shown layer averages two bits. Gray indicates suppressed, zero-bit bands.

papers.selection_reason: Post-training quantization approach for efficient deployment; depth-adaptive bit allocation is a transferable efficiency strategy for vision models.
papers.title: AxisQ: Depth-Adaptive Channel--Frequency Quantization for Camouflaged Object Detection
papers.tldr: AxisQ improves low-bit post-training quantization for camouflaged object detection by adapting precision allocation from channels to local frequencies as feature depth increases.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) learn representations for robot control by coupling future visual prediction with action generation. Successful manipulation depends primarily on how the robot and task-relevant objects evolve, whereas future-video prediction must also reconstruct the appearance and background of the entire scene. We therefore propose Trace-WAM, which augments video-action learning with future 3D motion prediction as an auxiliary objective. This objective supervises temporal point correspondence together with image-plane displacement and depth change, directly describing the interaction dynamics and spatial changes involved in manipulation. To this end, we adopt a three-branch Mixture-of-Transformer (Tri-MoT) architecture to jointly learn video prediction, motion prediction, and action generation. The motion expert predicts future trajectories from current visual features, allowing motion supervision to shape the representations used for action generation. Because the action expert does not consume predicted trajectories, inference retains the current-observation policy path: a single visual forward pass followed by action denoising. Experiments on RoboCasa-GR1, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus demonstrate strong in-distribution performance and out-of-distribution generalization, with particularly clear gains over Fast-WAM under limited demonstrations and distribution shifts.
authors: Xu Hu, Changjie Wu, Linzhe Shi, Hang Zhang, Chen Yang, Lingjun Zhang, Guowen Zhang, Mu Xu, Junran Peng, Qing Li, Zhaoxiang Zhang
bullets: Targets a key mismatch in WAMs: whole-scene video prediction may underemphasize robot-object interaction dynamics.
Adds auxiliary supervision for temporal point correspondence, image-plane displacement, and depth change.
Uses a three-branch Mixture-of-Transformer architecture for video prediction, motion prediction, and action generation.
Keeps the action policy conditioned only on current visual observations, requiring one visual pass followed by action denoising.
Experiments on RoboCasa-GR1, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus show strong in-distribution performance and improved generalization, especially with limited demonstrations and distribution shifts.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of Trace-WAM. Left: three Transformer experts jointly learn future video prediction, 3D motion prediction, and action generation. Right: colored cells allow attention among the illustrated video, motion, and action streams. At inference, future-video and motion prediction are removed, and action denoising uses cached visual keys and values.

papers.selection_reason: Robot manipulation policy learning augmented with future 3D motion prediction; directly fits embodied robot learning and world-action models.
papers.title: Trace-WAM: Learning to Act via 3D Motion Prediction for World Action Models
papers.tldr: Trace-WAM improves robot manipulation policies by adding future 3D motion prediction to video-action learning while preserving efficient action inference.

papers.abstract: Despite significant progress, current models struggle to generate comprehensive video captions, constrained primarily by coarse-grained supervision, which often fails to capture spatial-temporal dynamics and the underlying logical intent. To address this issue, we introduce MVRCap, a novel framework that reformulates video captioning as a reinforcement learning task steered by structured verification. Central to our approach is a Fine-Grained Verifiable Reward mechanism, serving as dense supervision to enforce rigorous visual-semantic alignment. Specifically, we construct this reward system anchored by three complementary pillars: a Hierarchical Concept Coverage Reward utilizing our newly constructed MVRCap-QA dataset to ensure multi-dimensional completeness and semantic depth, a Factuality Verification Reward to enhance factual consistency, and a Conciseness Constraint to maximize semantic density. Furthermore, we curate the high-quality MVRCap-SFT dataset, providing structured annotations across six key dimensions, to serve as a robust foundational initialization for the RL policy in this training pipeline. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MVRCap achieves state-of-the-art performance on authoritative benchmarks including VDC, CAPability, and VC4VG.
authors: Weihuang Lin, Xianing Chen, Zhibin Wang, Congzhi Zhang, Yiwei Ma, Jiayi Ji, Miao Chen, Jun Song, YuCheng, Bo Zheng, Xiaoshuai Sun, Rongrong Ji
bullets: Addresses coarse-grained supervision that misses videos’ spatial-temporal dynamics and logical intent.
Recasts video captioning as reinforcement learning guided by fine-grained visual-semantic verification.
Combines hierarchical concept coverage, factuality verification, and conciseness rewards.
Uses the MVRCap-QA dataset for coverage evaluation and MVRCap-SFT for structured policy initialization.
Reports state-of-the-art performance on the VDC, CAPability, and VC4VG benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The Data Construction Pipeline for MVRCap. The left panel details the construction of the MVRCap-QA dataset. For brevity, only three dimensions are visualized. The right panel illustrates the workflow for generating the MVRCap-SFT dataset. The human icons denote steps involving manual validation.
Figure 3: The Overall Framework of MVRCap.

Figure 1: (a) Coarse Matching RL treats captions as unordered sets of atomic facts, failing to capture dynamic logic. (b) In contrast, our approach leverages Structured Visual Probing. We employ a Fine-Grained Verifiable Reward that integrates hierarchical QA probing and factuality verification to enforce supervision across six key dimensions.
Table 1: Quantitative captioning evaluation results on VC4VG-Bench.
Table 3: Quantitative comparison on the VDC benchmark.
Table 4: Ablation study on the effectiveness of different reward components. Rcov, Rfact, and Rlen denote Coverage, Factuality, and Conciseness respectively.
Table 5: Ablation study on different training stages. We compare the Base Qwen2.5VL-7B with combinations of Supervised FineTuning and Reinforcement Learning.

papers.selection_reason: Video captioning reformulated with RL and fine-grained verifiable rewards; directly fits video understanding and video-language understanding.
papers.title: MVRCap: Towards Comprehensive Video Captioning via Hierarchical Multi-Dimensional Verifiable Rewards
papers.tldr: MVRCap improves comprehensive video captioning by training with hierarchical, verifiable rewards that promote coverage, factuality, and conciseness.

papers.abstract: Generative planners are often evaluated by the trajectories they can generate, although closed-loop driving ultimately depends on the single candidate committed to control. We identify this mismatch as the sample-to-execution gap and show that improving proposal quality alone can worsen the executed decision. Here, we introduce ExecDiffuser, a recurrent proposal-to-execution framework that couples candidate generation, trajectory selection, and subsequent replanning through shared execution semantics. Intent-Guided Diffusion Proposal (IGD) assigns hypothesis responsibility and shapes trajectories with execution-conditioned supervision. Execution-Grounded Selection (EGS) learns a candidate-conditioned publication utility, commits one trajectory to control, and returns it as context for the next planning cycle. Across nuPlan, InterPlan, and NAVSIM, ExecDiffuser achieves leading closed-loop performance against strong state-of-the-art baselines. Under a unified five-seed protocol, it obtains an average score of 85.62, improving over Diffusion Planner and FlowDrive by 4.02 and 1.31 points, respectively. On NAVSIM, it achieves 92.6 PDMS under the official evaluation pipeline. Matched counterfactual analysis further shows that ExecDiffuser more reliably converts strong candidates into committed decisions, while prefix interventions confirm that this advantage persists after physical execution and subsequent replanning.
authors: Shuo Pei, Bosun Liang, Saihui Zha, Chen Sun, Huachun Tan, Yong Wang
bullets: Identifies a sample-to-execution gap: better generated proposals can still lead to worse committed actions.
Combines intent-guided diffusion proposals with execution-grounded candidate selection.
Feeds the committed trajectory back into subsequent replanning through shared execution semantics.
Reports leading closed-loop performance across nuPlan, InterPlan, and NAVSIM, including an average score of 85.62 and 92.6 PDMS on NAVSIM.
Counterfactual and prefix analyses indicate more reliable conversion of strong candidates into executed decisions.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. ExecDiffuser couples proposal learning and publication through a shared online execution interface. IGD assigns and shapes latent hypotheses; EGS filters invalid candidates, ranks the remaining candidates, publishes one trajectory, and returns it as recurrent context.

Fig. 1. A strong candidate can already be available yet remain uncommitted to control. Strengthening proposals alone may raise the available-candidate ceiling while widening candidate-publication regret. ExecDiffuser connects proposal learning and trajectory publication through shared execution semantics: IGD improves candidate availability, while recurrent EGS commits one trajectory to control and returns it to the next planning cycle.

papers.selection_reason: Diffusion-based closed-loop planning with execution-grounded selection for autonomous driving, fitting learned navigation.
papers.title: ExecDiffuser: Closing the Sample-to-Execution Gap in Diffusion Planning
papers.tldr: ExecDiffuser narrows the gap between high-quality diffusion proposals and the single trajectory actually executed in closed-loop driving.

papers.abstract: Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs), which route predictions through a layer of human-interpretable concepts, have substantially improved the interpretability of visual classification by exposing an explicit, language-based rationale for each prediction. Most existing work focuses on static images, and temporal dynamics in videos have been underexplored in conceptual representation. We propose a framework that extends concept-based image recognition to procedural video understanding. It represents a multi-step video as a temporal sequence of segment-level concept score vectors and feeds this sequence into a Transformer encoder to predict the class label. We also explore a way to estimate the contribution of each concept for further interpretability. We evaluated three concept sets of different granularities on cooking and household-activity videos and found that coarser-grained concepts are sufficient for classifying these videos, which implies that fine-grained textual descriptions may be unnecessary.
authors: Ryoya Yoshiyama, Bowen Wang, Yuta Nakashima
bullets: Extends Concept Bottleneck Models from static images to multi-step video understanding.
Represents videos as temporal sequences of segment-level concept score vectors.
Uses a Transformer encoder to predict video classes.
Estimates each concept’s contribution to improve interpretability.
Evaluation on cooking and household-activity videos suggests coarse-grained concepts are sufficient.

Fig. 5: Visualization of the important concepts for an incorrectly classified test video. Concepts are ranked by |qi| with respect to the ground-truth class.

papers.title: Drop the Details, Get the Gist: Dynamic Conceptual Representation for Video Recognition
papers.tldr: A concept-based Transformer recognizes procedural videos from temporal sequences of segment-level concepts, showing that coarse concepts can suffice without fine-grained descriptions.

papers.abstract: Leading GUI grounders score 93 to 96% on ScreenSpot-v2, and reported gaps between new and prior models are about a point. At this level the useful question is what the remaining errors are. Benchmarks count a click as correct only inside one annotated box, but interfaces often expose one action through several elements: a duplicated link, the label of a checkbox, the title next to a logo. The box is not wrong. The rule is incomplete. We call a click correct when executing it produces the same outcome as clicking the annotated target. A probe that executes and fingerprints about a thousand clicks per page turns this definition into outcome maps and an execution judge for live web applications, with no new annotation. We execute the predictions of three strong 7--8B grounders on a code forge and an online shop. About one in five and one in three of the clicks that box scoring rejects reach the intended outcome, and the shares remain one in seven and one in three when the instructions are rewritten as natural tasks. A blind audit of 11 models on ScreenSpot-v2 (three 7--8B grounders and eight 3B variants) finds the same effect on web screenshots, with two independent reviewers on a 60-unit subset. The share is highest for the strongest grounders. Training seeds and test-set sampling add noise that more runs and paired intervals control. Box scoring instead under-counts correct clicks, which repetition does not remove, and the audit-based correction of 0.2 to 1.8 points on ScreenSpot-v2 is as large as the gaps the field reports. The correction is needed in evaluation. In our 3B GRPO study, crediting equivalent clicks in the reward gives no stable gain over box rewards across three seeds and four test sets. We release the probe, the outcome maps, the audit and every prediction.
authors: Xiaokang Yuan, Binhui Yao, Luwei Yang, Ruimin Chen, Zeng Wang
bullets: A click can be functionally correct even when it falls outside the single annotated target box, such as on duplicated links or labels.
The authors execute clicks and fingerprint page outcomes to build outcome maps and an execution-based judge without new annotations.
Across a code forge, online shop, and ScreenSpot-v2 audit, roughly one-fifth to one-third of box-rejected clicks achieve the intended outcome.
Correcting ScreenSpot-v2 scores changes results by 0.2–1.8 points, comparable to reported model gaps.
Rewarding equivalent clicks in a 3B GRPO study produced no stable improvement over box-based rewards.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Outcome-correct clicks that ScreenSpot-v2 rejects. Zoomed audit panels: red box is the annotation, blue circle the model click, instruction in quotes. E-same clicks hit the target control outside its box, E-dup clicks hit another control with the same function. In the last panel the click follows the instruction and the box marks a different control. We release such cases as likely annotation errors and count them as N.

Blue marks intervals that exclude zero (Gitea resamples pages, ScreenSpot-v2 resamples screenshots, Mind2Web resamples tasks). papers.abstract: Humanoid parkour requires robots to reason about future footholds and whole-body motions over highly discontinuous terrain. We revisit the information asymmetry in asymmetric actor-critic learning for perceptive humanoid locomotion: the critic exploits privileged simulator signals during training, whereas the deployable actor operates solely from onboard perception. We argue that the key is not exposing privileged information to the actor, but learning a deployable approximation of it to narrow the information gap between training and deployment. We present HC2Robot, a deployable perceptive humanoid parkour framework consisting of a Predicted Foresight Module (PFM) and a Hyper-Connection (HC) Transformer. PFM predicts from deployable observations the policy-conditioned timing, location, and support quality of each foot's next touchdown event, converting privileged supervision into a deployable latent representation that provides the actor with predicted touchdown information without privileged runtime sensing. The HC Transformer further enhances temporal reasoning through learnable multi-stream routing, while a future motion prediction head provides short-horizon motion priors for regularization. Across stairs, gaps, high platforms, and slopes, HC2Robot achieves a mean simulated traversal success rate of 97.60% and consistently higher safe foothold rates than strong perceptive locomotion baselines, supporting improved traversal performance and geometric foothold support under deployable sensing.

bullets: Addresses the training–deployment information gap in asymmetric actor–critic learning without giving privileged runtime signals to the actor.

Across stairs, gaps, high platforms, and slopes, reports a 97.60% mean simulated traversal success rate and higher safe foothold rates than perceptive locomotion baselines.

papers.abstract: Pretrained video generation models encode rich priors about physical interactions, but leveraging them for robot control typically requires either resource-intensive video generation at test time or action heads trained from scratch that do not fully utilize the pretrained backbone. We introduce Tokenizing Actions as Video Patches in a Shared Transformer Policy (TAPESTRY), a world action model that repurposes a pretrained video diffusion transformer into a robotic policy without requiring video generation at inference. Our key idea is to treat robot actions as single-patch tokens in the video model's latent space. A lightweight linear projection maps each action timestep to the patch dimensions of the pretrained VAE, and the resulting tokens are processed by the same patchifying layers and transformer backbone used for video. The shared backbone is optimized through three diffusion objectives sampled per minibatch element: Video diffusion uses VAE latents from robot and human videos to establish dynamics priors. Joint video+action diffusion trains on robot demonstrations using a coupled diffusion timestep and an asymmetric attention mask. Action-only diffusion denoises actions conditioned on clean image latents. At test time, the model generates a compact action token sequence in a single DDIM step from pure noise, producing smooth action chunks at 84 ms per action chunk on consumer hardware and avoiding the cost of full video generation. Across simulation benchmarks and real-robot experiments, TAPESTRY achieves strong performance with substantially lower inference cost than comparable joint video--action policies. More information can be found at https://tapestry-wam.github.io.
authors: Jeremy A. Collins, Seungjae Lee, Rachanon Wachakorn, Krishnan Srinivasan, Animesh Garg, Vitor Campagnolo Guizilini, Paarth Shah
bullets: Avoids costly video generation at test time and avoids training a separate action head from scratch.
Maps each action timestep into the pretrained VAE’s patch space, then processes actions with the shared video patchifier and transformer backbone.
Jointly trains video diffusion, video–action diffusion, and action-only diffusion objectives to combine visual dynamics priors with robot demonstrations.
Generates smooth action chunks in one DDIM step, achieving 84 ms per chunk on consumer hardware.
Shows strong results in simulation and real-robot experiments with substantially lower inference cost than comparable joint video–action policies.

papers.abstract: Knowledge improvement in large language models is shifting from predefined knowledge incorporation pipelines toward evaluation-guided updating. Existing methods use evaluation to localize model-specific knowledge weaknesses and guide targeted post-training. However, identifying what to improve does not necessarily provide sufficient information for deciding how to improve it. The same localized weakness can be compatible with distinct operational knowledge states: the relevant knowledge may be unavailable, available but difficult to access reliably, or accessible but ineffective for downstream use. We call this ambiguity knowledge-state aliasing. When compatible states favor different interventions, greater diagnostic resolution alone is insufficient for intervention selection. Moreover, model updates can change the underlying knowledge state before the observed weakness disappears, such that an intervention appropriate in one round may no longer address the bottleneck in the next. To address these challenges, we propose Recursive Knowledge Improvement (RKI), which formulates knowledge improvement as a sequential, state-aware intervention process. RKI organizes knowledge into graph-structured units that provide a shared basis for diagnostic evaluation and targeted intervention across rounds. At each round, RKI localizes knowledge weaknesses, estimates the model's operational knowledge state from diagnostic evidence and intervention history, selects a corresponding intervention, and re-evaluates the updated model before determining the next intervention. On HotpotEval and SafeInternalEval, RKI outperforms existing knowledge incorporation methods by 18.41 points on average. Further analyses show that knowledge states provide additional guidance for intervention selection beyond weakness localization and can change across model updates even when the observed weakness persists.
authors: Runze Jiang, Yan Wang, Boran Jin, Bingyu Zhu, Longtao Huang

On HotpotEval and SafeInternalEval, RKI outperforms existing knowledge incorporation methods by 18.41 points on average; knowledge states may change even when weaknesses persist.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models have made substantial progress in visual question answering, but complex visual reasoning often requires locating and comparing multiple pieces of question-relevant visual evidence. Existing methods that move intermediate reasoning into the visual latent space usually follow a single linear reasoning trajectory, which can be limiting when multiple visual hypotheses or competing evidence regions are relevant. We propose Latent Visual Contrastive Reasoning, a branch-aware latent reasoning framework that generates multiple question-conditioned latent visual branches as soft hypotheses over image tokens. To train these branches, our method uses bounding-box evidence annotations to build target evidence representations and introduces a soft contrastive branch-evidence alignment objective. This objective encourages evidence-relevant branches to align with annotated visual regions while contrasting them against negative evidence. We instantiate our method on Qwen2.5-VL backbones and train it with standard supervised fine-tuning. Experiments on perception-intensive visual reasoning benchmarks show that the proposed method achieves overall improvements over the corresponding backbone and single-path latent reasoning baselines at both 3B and 7B scales.
authors: Kegeng Tang, Jingbo Wang, Yangming Zhang, Huanshu Zhang, Shaogang Ren, Zihao Wang
bullets: Targets the limitation of single-path latent reasoning when questions require comparing multiple visual regions or competing evidence.
Generates multiple question-conditioned latent visual branches as soft hypotheses over image tokens.
Uses bounding-box annotations and a soft contrastive branch–evidence alignment objective to associate branches with relevant regions and reject negative evidence.
Implemented with Qwen2.5-VL backbones and standard supervised fine-tuning.
Reports overall gains over the backbone and single-path latent reasoning baselines on perception-intensive benchmarks at 3B and 7B scales.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overall framework of LVCR. Given an image-question pair, LVCR encodes the image and question into visual and textual tokens, and proposes multiple question-conditioned latent branches as candidate visual hypotheses over the image. These branches are contrastively aligned with answer-relevant visual evidence and separated from irrelevant regions. LVCR then ranks the branches using relevance scores computed by cosine similarity with the question representation, and injects the selected branch tokens into the MLLM decoder, which combines them with the original multimodal context to generate the final answer.

Fig. 3. Accuracy (%) of three branch injection strategies on V ∗, MMVP, and BLINK (aggregated). Ranked denotes our default LVCR strategy; Top-1 injects only the highest-ranked branch; Unranked injects all branches without ordering. Results are reported using LVCR-3B with K=4.

Fig. 2. Ablation study on the NCE loss coefficient using LVCR-3B with K=4. We compare the default setting with λNCE = 0.1 against a variant trained without the NCE loss, i.e., λNCE = 0. Removing the NCE loss leads to consistent performance drops on V ∗, MMVP, and BLINK, indicating that contrastive branch-evidence alignment helps latent branches capture questionrelevant visual cues.

papers.abstract: Controlling the personality of a language model usually relies on written profiles or named trait categories, so it can only express what an author writes down or what a taxonomy names. We instead propose Personality Latents (PL), which learn a latent for each person from their own writing, with no personality labels and no authored profile, and inject it into a frozen language model as a soft prefix. Following generative latent optimization, each training person receives a free latent that is optimized through the frozen model itself, while an encoder learns to predict these latents so that a new person needs only one forward pass, with optional refinement at test time. We evaluate on held-out people by having the conditioned model answer neutral and interview questions and reading personality from its answers with scorers trained on real human writing. On the MBTI axes PL reaches an AUC of , ahead of persona embedding and prompt-based baselines under identical settings, and the ranking holds when the answers are scored in three different embedding spaces. A latent learned with Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct also transfers personality to Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct through a new adapter alone.

papers.abstract: Test-time training (TTT) enables a deployed language model to internalize incoming context on-the-fly into a small set of fast-weight parameters, rather than merely treating it as transient context for attention. In-Place TTT recently made this idea practical for large language models by repurposing the down-projection of standard MLP blocks as fast weights. However, we find that its benefit largely disappears on realistic web long-context question answering. We attribute this to In-Place TTT's uniform write schedule: every chunk is written with equal strength, so irrelevant content dilutes query-relevant information in fast-weight memory. Building on this insight, we propose Select-TTT, a model-agnostic, query-conditioned rule for In-Place TTT that scales each chunk's write strength by its relevance to the user query. This relevance signal requires no supervision and no new parameters: it is read directly from the model's frozen output head, as the probability mass that a chunk's hidden states assign to the query tokens. A temperature-scaled softmax turns these scores into learning-rate multipliers, leaving the chunk-wise, context-parallel computation of In-Place TTT intact. Select-TTT consistently improves long-context question answering on two benchmarks and two backbones. These findings highlight the value of query-conditioned fast weight writes for practical test-time training on long-context question answering, which is also potentially promising for long-horizon agent tasks involving multiple user queries over evolving contexts.
authors: Yue Wu, Yang Zhang, Weinan Gan, Chongming Gao, Xinsen Guo, Xiaoyuan Li, Fuli Feng
bullets: In-Place TTT can lose its benefit on realistic web long-context QA because uniform writes let irrelevant content dilute useful information.
Select-TTT conditions each chunk’s write strength on its relevance to the user query.

A temperature-scaled softmax converts relevance scores into learning-rate multipliers while preserving context-parallel computation.
The method consistently improves long-context QA across two benchmarks and two model backbones.

papers.abstract: Learning controllable world dynamics from heterogeneous interaction videos is challenging because robot embodiments use incompatible action spaces, while human videos lack native control labels. We present RynnWorld-Latent, a cross-embodiment video world model that uses the 3D-grounded latent actions introduced by RynnLAM as a shared conditioning interface. This representation enables joint pretraining on human interaction videos, robot demonstrations, and simulation rollouts without requiring a common native action space. Built on a pretrained video transformer, RynnWorld-Latent combines global action tokens with an identity-initialized local pathway that aligns actions with future video latents. We pretrain on 23 datasets comprising approximately 553.5M frames and adapt the model to target robots through post-training. The framework supports two data-generation routes: digital teleoperation uses target robot commands to generate action-video demonstrations, while latent-action synthesis transfers source motion to an edited initial frame and pairs the resulting rollout with retargeted pseudo robot actions. Experiments show improved video prediction metrics on public benchmarks and two real-robot platforms, alongside qualitative action following when different action sequences share the same initial observation. Synthetic mid-training improves policy success rates on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, and both generation routes improve real-world policy success rates over real-demonstration-only training in the evaluated settings. These results support universal latent actions as a scalable interface for learning controllable visual dynamics across heterogeneous embodiments.

papers.abstract: Multi-view tracking extends visual coverage beyond a single camera, providing complementary observations when targets are occluded or leave the view. This raises a question: how can observations from different views be matched to the correct identities without offline scene-specific training or camera calibration? Progress toward this goal remains limited because many offline formulations assume such deployment-specific knowledge, while online adaptation can amplify association errors. We study this problem as online multi-view identity maintenance (OMIM): targets are initialized once per view, with no further identity labels provided after each initialization. To this end, we introduce OmniGlimpse, an asymmetric propose-verify framework that separates adaptive association from stable identity consolidation. At the representation level, short-term local and cross-view evidence is mapped into target-specific adaptive spaces to propose associations, whereas long-term identity distributions are maintained for verification in a canonical space defined by a frozen encoder. At the update level, short-term evidence may guide current associations, whereas, after bootstrapping, only verified observations may update persistent memory or drive adaptation. Under a unified target-specified evaluation protocol, OmniGlimpse improves over the best evaluated online baseline for each metric by 9.1 IDF1 and 22.1 CVIDF1 points on M3Track. The corresponding gains on MvMHAT are 20.3 and 26.2 points. Despite using no offline scene-specific training, it outperforms offline-trained references in IDF1 and remains competitive in cross-view association. These results support an approach to online identity maintenance that adapts to changing appearances while consolidating reliable evidence into stable identity anchors.
authors: Rangya Zhang, Jiaping Xiao, Yujing Shang, Yuhang Zhang, Mingsheng Li, Mir Feroskhan

Improves substantially over evaluated online baselines on M3Track and MvMHAT, while remaining competitive with offline-trained references for cross-view association.
Scope: relies on a target-specified evaluation protocol and does not provide post-initialization identity labels.

papers.abstract: We fine-tuned a separate $\pi_{0.5}$ policy for each of the five tasks in the MetaFine Open Competition, with a task-specific training mixture and number of actions executed per prediction. Training started from the official demonstrations and expert procedures. Local evaluation exposed recurring grasping, pushing, and insertion failures. We addressed them by revising the demonstrated motions and by adding expert continuations from states the policy reached, while keeping nominal demonstrations in training. Checkpoints were compared on every instruction, so that a gain on one instruction could not hide a loss on another. Our submission, MAI, ranked first overall with a score of 96.66.

papers.abstract: Generative recommendation (GR) predicts the next item through its semantic ID (SID). Existing methods commonly fit SID vocabularies to pretrained language model (PLM) representations of item descriptions, incurring additional training costs and making vocabulary coverage dependent on the fitting domains. We observe that pretrained sparse autoencoders expose PLM features with human-interpretable semantic annotations, allowing feature indices to serve as a reusable SID vocabulary. However, reusing this vocabulary requires preserving item distinctions under compact token budgets and learning to favor target items over candidates with shared dominant features. It also requires extending feature interpretability from item content to retrieval decisions. To address these challenges, we propose API, a framework that Adapts the Pretrained Interpretable vocabulary for effective and explainable GR without additional vocabulary learning. Within API, Pretrained Interpretable IDs (PIDs) retain selected feature indices and relative activation strengths for item discrimination. With PIDs as supervision, the Semantic Prediction Adapter (SPA) learns user preferences from interaction histories through joint feature-index and strength prediction. SPA combines both predictions to score candidate items, with item-level supervision encouraging the observed next item to outrank its alternatives. API further explains candidate score differences through feature contributions paired with their pretrained semantic annotations. Extensive experiments show that API achieves competitive performance across backbones and decoding schemes, while preserving item distinctions under compact token budgets and enabling explainable retrieval.

papers.abstract: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) are laboratory systems that couple experimental planning, automated execution, and measurement feedback in a closed loop. Integrating flexible robot control with the typed application programming interfaces (APIs) and continuous measurements exposed by laboratory instruments remains an execution-interface challenge. To address this challenge, we propose a traceable framework comprising four components: LAM (Lab Action Model), OpenSDL, Safe-SDL, and L3-Bench. LAM is a proposed measurement-conditioned policy architecture that extends vision-language-action paradigms to generate both continuous robot trajectories and typed instrument API calls. OpenSDL is an execution substrate with an initial control implementation, designed to map role-level operations to heterogeneous devices, coordinate execution, and record timestamped causal events. The proposed Safe-SDL runtime gate combines pre-dispatch schema and resource checks with signal temporal logic monitoring during execution, including extended waiting periods. L3-Bench (Level-3 Laboratory Benchmark) specifies an episode-level evaluation protocol covering physical outcomes, timing, reproducibility, safety violations, and fault recovery. Together, these components provide an end-to-end design for linking hybrid action generation, monitored device execution, measurement feedback, and experimental evaluation, addressing coordination and traceability challenges in SDL workflows.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the L3-Bench evaluation protocol. Left: adaptive dilution, measurement-conditioned titration, and fault injection with recovery define three scenario families. Two baselines—a vision-only single-arm policy and LAM without measurement tokens—are compared with the full LAM × OpenSDL framework under nominal, measurement-shift, device-transfer, and fault-injection conditions. Center: initialization comprises profiling, matching, activation, and configuration, followed by on-the-fly schema, safety, and replay-readiness checks of manifest and ledger completeness. The safety-gate ablation is restricted to simulation or risk-assessed hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) evaluation. Right: liquid separation/heating and delay/high pressure illustrate task and condition metadata; the evaluated scenario families are defined on the left. Complete episodes are scored, with batch-level clustering for bootstrap confidence intervals. Primary endpoints are normalized physical yield Y , temporal safety violation rate SVR, and operational time cost C; diagnostic measures include mass-transfer error ∆m, temperature-control error ITAE, makespan, and recovery. Photographs illustrate the laboratory scenarios; check marks and miniature plots indicate protocol requirements and metric types.

Figure 1: LAM architecture for measurement-conditioned hybrid laboratory control. Task language, RGB/RGB-D observations, robot proprioception qt, and time-stamped instrument telemetry Mt enter a multimodal context builder comprising a visionlanguage-model (VLM) backbone and a telemetry encoder. Typed measurement tokens retain device roles, units, sampling times, and data-quality information within the shared context. A continuous action head generates robot-trajectory chunks, a discrete function-calling head generates typed instrument application programming interface (API) calls, and an optional dynamics head predicts the next measurement state Mt+1. The execution layer connects the arm controller and the signal temporal logic (STL) safety monitor with event logging to the OpenSDL bus. Parallel dispatch coordinates compatible actions, while updated observations and confirmed execution events supply feedback for subsequent decisions.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward Gaussian Splatting enables efficient novel view synthesis, but pixel-aligned prediction makes the primitive count grow with image resolution and view count, leading to substantial redundancy and increased computational cost. Non-pixel-aligned methods address this limitation by predicting a fixed number of Gaussians. Without explicit ray and depth constraints, these methods yield misplaced Gaussian centers, causing rendering artifacts under large viewpoint changes. To address this issue, we introduce GeoGSplat, a geometry-grounded feed-forward model that explicitly incorporates geometric priors into the non-pixel-aligned framework. A dual-branch encoder constructs Anchors and Triplane to capture coarse 3D structure and fine-grained scene features, respectively. Subsequently, a hierarchical decoder progressively decodes dense 3D points and Gaussian primitives, enabling 3D reconstruction and novel view synthesis. GeoGSplat surpasses both state-of-the-art pixel-aligned and non-pixel-aligned Gaussian Splatting methods on DTU and NRGBD in terms of novel view synthesis and reconstruction. The advantage of our geometry-grounded paradigm further increases as target viewpoints move farther from the input cameras, demonstrating stronger generalization to large viewpoint changes. authors: Jiale Wang, Chen Zhao, Haoyang Zhang, Yanhao Wu, Fei He, Yanhu Shan, Rui Wu, Wei Ke, Tong Zhang
bullets: Non-pixel-aligned methods reduce redundancy but can misplace Gaussian centers without ray and depth constraints.

A hierarchical decoder progressively reconstructs dense 3D points and Gaussian primitives.
The method outperforms pixel-aligned and non-pixel-aligned baselines on DTU and NRGBD for reconstruction and novel view synthesis.
Its advantage grows as target viewpoints move farther from input cameras, indicating stronger large-viewpoint generalization.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Pipeline of GeoGSplat. Image features are encoded in parallel into Anchors and Triplane. Anchors comprise sparse 3D spheres with learnable centers and adaptive radii, accounting for the coarse scene structure; Triplane consists of three orthogonal 2D feature maps that encode finegrained high-dimensional scene features. Anchor-to-Point Decoding (blue) gathers Triplane features within each Anchor region to predict offsets and recover dense 3D points; Point-to-Gaussian Decoding (orange) re-queries the Triplane at these points to predict the corresponding Gaussian primitives.
