papers.abstract: Multilingual multi-hop document question answering (MMHop-DocQA) requires locating and integrating evidence across complex layouts, document pages, and diverse languages. Existing approaches include single-pass processing and adaptive tool use, but learning to coordinate evidence acquisition, cross-page integration, and answer verification remains challenging. To address this challenge, we present DocSkill, an agentic framework with a learned skill-orchestration policy for adaptive evidence acquisition and reasoning. The policy selects, revisits, or skips skills according to the evolving evidence state. To construct supervision for skill orchestration, bounded Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) explores alternative skill trajectories offline. These trajectories provide demonstrations for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and preference pairs for Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). We further introduce MMHop-DocBench, a multilingual multi-hop document QA dataset with training and test splits, containing 60K QA pairs across 10 languages and eight document domains. Its HopGen pipeline builds hierarchical page-element graphs to derive traceable cross-page evidence paths and generate grounded QA pairs with page- and element-level evidence annotations. Experiments show that DocSkill with Qwen3-VL-8B achieves 41.0 accuracy and 49.2 F1 on MMHop-DocBench, exceeding the strongest evaluated baseline by 5.5 and 6.3 points, respectively, and achieving competitive performance on MMLongBench-Doc and DocBench.

papers.abstract: Remote sensing (RS) image-text retrieval plays a critical role in understanding massive RS imagery. However, the dense multi-object distribution and complex backgrounds in RS imagery make it difficult to simultaneously achieve fine-grained cross-modal alignment and efficient retrieval. Existing methods either rely on complex cross-modal interactions that lead to low retrieval efficiency, or depend on large-scale vision-language adaptation, which requires massive data and computational resources. To address these issues, we develop a fast-then-fine (FTF) retrieval framework centered on interaction-free multi-granular recall and parameter-free text-guided cross-modal reranking with the Balanced Text-guided Interaction Block (BTIB). Specifically, interaction-free multi-granular recall pre-computes gallery embeddings and matches them with the corresponding query embedding without full-gallery token-level text-image interaction, while text-guided cross-modal reranking with BTIB refines local semantic correspondence within the top-K candidate set. Furthermore, an inter- and intra-modal loss is designed to jointly optimize cross-modal alignment across multi-granular representations. Extensive experiments on public benchmarks demonstrate that the FTF achieves competitive retrieval accuracy while significantly improving retrieval efficiency compared with existing methods.
authors: Xi Chen, Xu Chen, Xiamgyang Jia, Wei Wang, Xu Zhang, Zhenyuan Shun
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between fine-grained cross-modal alignment and efficient retrieval in complex remote-sensing imagery.
Uses precomputed gallery embeddings for fast, interaction-free multi-granular candidate recall.
Applies the parameter-free BTIB module to refine local image–text correspondence within the top-K candidates.
Jointly optimizes alignment across multi-granular representations with an inter- and intra-modal loss.
Experiments on public benchmarks show competitive accuracy with significantly improved retrieval efficiency.

Fig. 1. Comparison of three paradigms for RS image–text retrieval. (b) VLM-based methods achieve strong generalization, but often require massive data and computational resources. papers.abstract: Gradient-based data attribution has become an important tool for high-quality data selection in the instruction fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs), as it estimates the contribution of training examples through their influence on model optimization. However, we find that existing global gradient attribution methods suffer from surface-form bias: minor changes to semantically irrelevant details, such as wording or formatting, can produce highly inconsistent attribution scores even when the underlying content remains unchanged. To address this issue, we propose Content-Invariant Gradient Attribution (CIGA), a robust framework for instruction data selection. CIGA first identifies layers whose gradients are both influential for attribution and stable under semantics-preserving surface-form perturbations, thereby reducing formatting noise in gradient features. It then dynamically fuses these attribution signals with semantic representations of the input, combining optimization-level influence with content-level information. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks show that CIGA produces more stable rankings under surface-form perturbations while preserving downstream capabilities and improving average performance. CIGA also reduces attribution cost, offering a robust and efficient approach to data selection for LLM instruction tuning.
authors: Jia Gu, Liang Pang, Huawei Shen
bullets: Existing global gradient attribution can assign inconsistent importance scores to semantically equivalent examples because of surface-form bias.
CIGA selects gradient layers that are both attribution-relevant and stable under semantics-preserving perturbations.
It dynamically combines robust gradient signals with semantic input representations.
Experiments across multiple benchmarks show more stable data rankings, preserved capabilities, and improved average performance.
The framework also reduces attribution cost, though its scope is focused on instruction-tuning data selection.

papers.title: Robust LLM Data Selection via Content-Invariant Gradient Attribution
papers.tldr: CIGA makes gradient-based instruction-data selection more robust to irrelevant wording and formatting changes while improving efficiency and downstream performance.

papers.abstract: Computationally expensive simulations and real-world observations often provide data at a lower temporal resolution than downstream tasks require. Averaging observations at fixed grid points can introduce errors, and motion estimates alone do not determine how the physical field values change. In this work, we study whether learning to correct a simple numerical interpolation improves the reconstruction of intermediate scientific fields. Our model, interpolative FLow EXpert (iFLEX), first estimates the missing field by taking a weighted average of the two observations at each grid point, giving more weight to the observation closer to the requested time. During training, subtracting this estimate from an observed intermediate field gives the residual that a conditional diffusion model learns to generate. Both observations condition the model, together with the target time, the interval between observations, and available physical parameters. To reconstruct an unobserved intermediate field, the generated residual is added to the weighted average. We evaluate iFLEX on Navier-Stokes Kraichnan turbulence, Shanghai radar precipitation, and sea surface temperature. Across these datasets, iFLEX achieves lower reconstruction error than the evaluated baselines, including optical-flow and diffusion models developed for video frame interpolation in computer vision. In a controlled turbulence comparison at a Reynolds number of 36,000, learning the residual reduces relative Frobenius norm error from about 13.7 for direct field generation to 10.5, with the diffusion backbone and training setup held fixed. Code is available at https://github.com/paulpuren/iflex.
authors: Pu Ren, Michael W. Mahoney, N. Benjamin Erichson
bullets: Targets missing temporal resolution in simulations and observations, where averaging and motion estimates alone may poorly capture field evolution.
Builds a time-weighted average of two observed fields, then generates a correction residual conditioned on both observations, target time, interval length, and physical parameters.
Evaluated on turbulence, radar precipitation, and sea-surface temperature data.
Achieves lower reconstruction error than evaluated optical-flow and video-interpolation diffusion baselines.
In controlled turbulence experiments, residual learning reduced relative Frobenius error from about 13.7 to 10.5 versus direct field generation.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of iFLEX for temporal interpolation between two observed physical fields. Linear interpolation provides an initial estimate of the intermediate state, while a conditional diffusion model generates the correction needed to reconstruct the missing field. The two endpoint observations are processed by a shared spatial encoder, and their features are combined and supplied to the denoising network through learned gates. The requested interpolation time, observation interval, available physical parameters, and diffusion noise level are incorporated through feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM). After the final denoising step, the generated residual is added to the linear estimate to obtain the reconstructed intermediate field.

Figure 5: Reconstruction accuracy depends on both spatial structure and computational cost. (a) Comparison of the ground-truth and reconstructed spatial spectra for NSKT at Re = 12000. The intended diagnostic is the windowed vorticity power spectrum; the underlying figure export requires the verification noted in the text. (b) RFNE versus inference time for the evaluated methods at the same Reynolds number. iFLEX achieves 4.11% RFNE but requires 35.39ms per generated field, compared with 13.20% and 3.54ms for Super SloMo. Bubble size represents model parameter count.

Figure 1: Interpolation using two observed states achieves lower reconstruction error than the tested one-endpoint predictor on NSKT. (a) Observations are separated by a time interval ∆t, and intermediate fields are reconstructed at a finer temporal spacing δt. Unlike prediction from an initial state, interpolation uses observations from both ends of the interval. (b) At Re = 36000, iFLEX achieves lower relative Frobenius norm error (RFNE) than the one-endpoint predictor (Model A) across the tested intermediate times. Over the full evaluation set, the RFNE is 10.5% for iFLEX and 20.4% for Model A. Reconstruction errors are generally larger near the midpoint, where the requested state is farthest in time from both observations.

Figure 7: Learning the interpolation residual gives the lowest reconstruction error in the NSKT ablation study at Re = 36000. (a) The full model achieves 10.48% RFNE, compared with 20.44% for the one-endpoint predictor (Model A), 12.71% without interval duration conditioning (Model B), 10.75% with fixed-gap training (Model C), and 13.73% for direct generation of the full intermediate field (Model D). (b) Model A uses only the first observation and has larger errors toward the end of the interval, whereas iFLEX uses both endpoints. (c) The full model is compared with Model C, which is trained at a fixed gap of T = 20. The curves show the error at each intermediate time.

Figure 4: iFLEX achieves lower reconstruction error across the observation interval on NSKT, Shanghai radar, and SST. The panels report RFNE at each requested intermediate step, using 20 intermediate states for NSKT at Re = 12000, eight for radar, and ten for SST. Errors are generally largest near the middle of the interval, where the requested field is farthest in time from both observations. The curves display RFNE as a fraction rather than a percentage.

Figure 10: The SST example shows similar broad temperature patterns across the methods, with differences in local gradients and finer spatial variations. The rows compare the ground truth with U-Net, EDEN, Super SloMo, and iFLEX at intermediate indices k = 2, 4, 6, 10. The panel labels t denote target indices. On the held-out South Pacific test set, iFLEX achieves 1.81% RFNE and 0.87 SSIM (Table 2). These scores summarize the full evaluation set rather than the displayed examples.

Figure 6: iFLEX achieves lower reconstruction error than Super SloMo and EDEN across three temporal gaps on NSKT at Re = 36000. The panels show RFNE at each intermediate step for T = 12, 16, and 24. During training, iFLEX samples T ∈ {5, . . . , 20}; therefore, the first two gaps lie within its training range, while T = 24 exceeds it. Errors generally increase toward the midpoint of the observation interval, particularly for the longer gap. RFNE is plotted as a fraction.

Figure 2: In these examples, iFLEX more closely reproduces the vortex structures in the ground-truth NSKT fields than Super SloMo. The panels compare the ground truth with reconstructions from Super SloMo and iFLEX at t = 0.005 s and t = 0.02 s, using the same two endpoint observations. Red boxes highlight differences in vortex shape and fine-scale structures. Each intermediate field is reconstructed independently.

The rows compare ground-truth fields with reconstructions from U-Net, EDEN, Super SloMo, and iFLEX at intermediate indices k = 2, 4, 6, 8. The panel labels t denote these indices. In this example, iFLEX more closely retains localized precipitation structures at the middle target times than EDEN or Super SloMo. Aggregate RFNE is 32.69% for iFLEX, 56.54% for EDEN, and 36.77% for Super SloMo (Table 2).

Figure 8: iFLEX more closely reproduces the vortex structures in the illustrated NSKT fields at Re = 36000. The rows show the ground truth and reconstructions from U-Net, EDEN, Super SloMo, and iFLEX, evaluated at intermediate indices k = 5, 10, 15, 20. The panel labels t indicate target indices, rather than physical time in seconds. Differences are visible in the location and shape of vortices and in smaller vorticity structures. Over the corresponding test set, iFLEX achieves 10.48% RFNE compared with 22.87% for Super SloMo (Table 1); these aggregate values are not errors for the individual displayed fields.

The larger error in the upper-range case reflects the greater reconstruction difficulty of the tested flow, rather than parameter extrapolation distance alone. All methods use 256 × 256 crops and T = 20.

At Re = 12000 and 24000, its RFNE is 4.11% and 7.10%, compared with 7.81% and 12.23% for PIT-UNet. All methods use 256× 256 crops and T = 20. Bold denotes the best value at the reported precision.

Bold indicates the best value at the reported precision.

All methods are trained using Re ∈ {2000, 4000, 8000, 16000, 32000} and evaluated with 20 intermediate states between the endpoint observations. The values Re = 12000 and 24000 are unseen but lie within the training range, while Re = 36000 tests extrapolation beyond that range. At Re = 36000, iFLEX achieves 10.48% RFNE, compared with 22.87% for Super SloMo and 25.52% for EDEN. RFNE denotes relative Frobenius norm error, PC denotes Pearson correlation, and SSIM denotes structural similarity. Inference time (IT) is reported in milliseconds per generated intermediate field. Bold values indicate the best reconstruction scores.

The evaluations use eight intermediate states for radar and ten for sea surface temperature. On SST, iFLEX reduces RFNE from 1.94% for linear interpolation to 1.81%. Inference time (IT) is reported in milliseconds per generated intermediate field. papers.selection_reason: Develops iFLEX, a generative refinement learning method for temporal interpolation in scientific machine learning (e.g., Navier-Stokes). This fits the 'Video World Models' subtopic as it learns to predict and reconstruct intermediate physical field states over time.
papers.title: Generative Refinement Learning for Temporal Interpolation in Scientific Machine Learning
papers.tldr: iFLEX improves intermediate scientific-field reconstruction by learning a conditional diffusion residual on top of time-weighted linear interpolation.

papers.abstract: Continual learning requires large language models to acquire new knowledge and capabilities while retaining what they have learned. Fine-tuning and replay support acquisition and retention, but deciding whether incoming examples need supervision and which historical examples to revisit remains a challenge. We propose Compatibility-Aware Memory Replay (CAMR), an adaptive framework that jointly controls current-example supervision and historical replay. CAMR combines compatibility checks with a learned memory gate to guide an online policy over three actions: learning incoming examples with general replay, jointly reinforcing compatible related examples, and skipping direct supervision of verified mastered duplicates. The policy learns from acquisition, retention, and training-cost feedback under a bounded per-arrival replay budget. We evaluate CAMR with Qwen3-8B-Base on continual factual updating and cross-task and cross-domain learning. On WikiBigEdit, CAMR consistently leads evaluated methods in Original Match from 3K to 100K facts, reaching 93.66% after just 3K facts and surpassing Full-history Replay (LoRA) after 100K facts. It also achieves the highest final scores on all four selected TRACE tasks and maintains or improves earlier-task performance relative to post-acquisition levels in a sequence spanning financial question answering, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and summarization.
authors: Jingpu Yang, Tianhao Li, Fengxian Ji, Yufeng Wang, Shuxin Zheng, Xiaoqing Zhang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of selecting incoming examples for supervision and historical examples for replay in continual learning.
Uses compatibility checks and a learned memory gate to choose among general replay, reinforcing compatible examples, or skipping mastered duplicates.
Optimizes an online policy using acquisition, retention, and training-cost feedback with bounded replay per arrival.
On WikiBigEdit, reaches 93.66% Original Match after 3K facts and surpasses Full-history Replay (LoRA) after 100K facts.
Achieves the highest final scores on four TRACE tasks while maintaining or improving earlier-task performance across diverse domains.

papers.title: CAMR: Compatibility-Aware Memory Replay for Continual Learning in Large Language Models

papers.abstract: Interactive world generation requires models to follow successive commands while preserving relevant history and action consequences. We present Hy-Nomas, a video world model with an 8B diffusion backbone that supports free-form text instructions and continuous camera control across multiple interaction turns. It generates variable-length segments conditioned on current inputs and cached history. Our central design aligns structured video captions with action-aware causal attention: descriptive context remains accessible across segments, while action instructions are restricted to their intended temporal windows. A vision-language Prompt Enhancer (PE) translates user requests and multimodal interaction histories into structured conditions for the next segment. A multi-stage curriculum progressively introduces causal generation, text interaction, camera control, and training on model-generated histories, followed by diffusion distillation. In human evaluation, Hy-Nomas shows superior performance over existing world models. We release model weights, code and benchmarks, together with a lightweight adaptation workflow, to support reproducible research on interactive world generation.
authors: Qiaoling Chen, Jiaxiang Cheng, Xueqing Deng, Tiankai Hang, Ji Hou, Jiaqi Li, Yifan Liu, Tao Lu, Junshu Tang, Yu Tang, Yao Teng, Yu Tian, Heng Wang, Weizhi Wang, Xiyao Wang, Xilun Wu, Mingyu Yang, Yangbin Yu, Rui Zhao, Longjun Cao, Linghao Chen, Haoyi Duan, Jiaming Han, Mingji Han, Enhua Jiang, Shunkai Li, Yanzhe Liang, Qinwei Ma, Cong Wang, Lei Wang, Bing Wu, Ke Xing, Ray Ying, Zhentao Yu, Key Zhang, Yuan Zhou, Zhengguang Zhou, Kai Zou
bullets: Supports successive text instructions and continuous camera control across multiple interaction turns.
Generates variable-length video segments conditioned on current inputs and cached interaction history.
Uses action-aware causal attention to preserve descriptive context while limiting actions to their intended time windows.
A vision-language Prompt Enhancer converts user requests and multimodal histories into structured next-segment conditions.
Human evaluations report better performance than existing world models; weights, code, benchmarks, and an adaptation workflow are released.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Overview of the model architecture. A structured multi-segment prompt, a video clip, and a camera trajectory are encoded into text, video, and camera tokens, respectively. Text and video tokens are processed by N = 54 dual-stream MMDiT blocks. Within each block, segmentwise causal attention with 3D RoPE allows tokens to attend to the current and preceding segments, while diffusion timestep embeddings modulate both streams. The two streams pass through separate MLPs, and camera cross-attention further conditions the video stream on camera tokens. During autoregressive generation, keys and values associated with both text and video tokens are stored in the KV cache as context for subsequent segments. The 3D VAE decoder maps denoised video latents to RGB frames. Purple, blue, and green denote the text, video, and camera streams, respectively.

Figure 10: Overview of Hy-Nomas-Bench. Top: Model outputs for an example case from Bench-3 (interleaved text–camera control). Bottom: (a) World settings span diverse scenes, visual styles, subjects, and viewpoints. (b) 280 cases cover multi-turn text interaction, camera navigation, interleaved control, and spatial memory. (c) Unified control maps instructions to text, binary key states [T, 8] (W/A/S/D and four arrow keys), or per-frame 4 × 4 camera-to-world matrices [T, 4, 4], where T is the frame count. Generation continues across turns without world resets. (d) Three annotators evaluate prompt following, physical plausibility, camera control, and memory consistency through pairwise comparisons. Results are summarized by win/tie/loss rates and net win rate (win minus loss, in percentage points).

Figure 2: Data pipeline. Raw videos are split, transcoded, and filtered by basic video properties and visual quality. Hierarchical clustering supports within-cluster deduplication, and a VLM assigns labels to each video from a predefined taxonomy. Video tagging adds captions and, for selected clips, camera-trajectory annotations. Across each training stage, adaptive sampling adjusts the training distribution in response to weaknesses identified from evaluations of earlier stages.

Figure 1: Interactive world generation with Hy-Nomas. Free-form text instructions and continuous camera control can be interleaved across successive interaction turns. At each turn, a vision-language Prompt Enhancer converts the user request and observed world history into a structured text prompt and a duration for the next video segment. Conditioned on these inputs and cached context, Hy-Nomas autoregressively generates the next segment, allowing the world to unfold through continued interaction.

Figure 6: Comparison of segment-wise and action-aware causal attention. (a) Tokens attend to all video and text tokens in the current and preceding segments. (b) Action-aware masking further restricts access to action-specific text tokens. Colors indicate query-to-key modality pairs; gray cells are masked. head denotes the environment description for the current segment, and a0, . . . , an denote actions within that segment.

Figure 3: Structured video captioning. The VLM annotates segments sequentially, maintains subject identities, interleaves scene and camera descriptions chronologically, and records subject actions separately with timestamps. A final text-only turn reviews, translates, and validates the annotations to produce aligned English and Chinese captions. During training, camera-motion sentences and their tags are removed when camera trajectories are available and retained otherwise.

Figure 4: Structured caption format. Video-level fields define perspective, style, and shared subject profiles. Segment descriptions interleave scene information and camera-tagged motion chronologically, excluding main-subject references. The first segment provides a full description; later segments describe changes. Subject actions and their visible outcomes are recorded separately in action-tagged entries using subject tokens. papers.abstract: This paper presents an approach to achieve side-by-side autonomous motion with a pair of personal mobility vehicles (PMVs). Given a global path, two PMVs plan cooperatively so as to hold a social formation that lets the passengers hold a conversation, while keeping the ride safe and smooth. Each vehicle runs its own sampling-based model-predictive planner; the planners exchange nothing but the odometry each vehicle could observe of the other, and the joint decision is expressed as a pair of utility matrices over pairs of candidate trajectories, resolved by a common rule. The behavioural parameters are fitted by inverse reinforcement learning from 409 minutes of driving by ten pairs of people in human-driven PMVs in an indoor environment, and the lanes the pair can use are derived offline from the corridor itself rather than fixed by hand. A safety layer the cost cannot override executes a move only if the vehicle can still brake clear, measured from its whole body, and a vehicle that is stuck reverses along its own path and continues. In closed-loop simulation over 24 runs in the conditions the drivers were recorded in and 24 in four generated obstacle layouts, no vehicle entered a wall or a cone. The pair holds conversational formation for 60.5 and 68.9 percent of the time among obstacles (anticlockwise and clockwise) and 81.2 and 91.5 percent in a clear aisle, against the drivers' 34.0 and 36.0 percent, and 52.9 and 56.0 percent, and it matches their speed. It keeps one lateral formation where the drivers alternated between a close diagonal and a wide abreast one, and it varies far less. Experimental results are based on a differential drive kinematic simulator running on ROS 2.
bullets: Uses inverse reinforcement learning from 409 minutes of driving by 10 human pairs to fit cooperative behavioral parameters.
Each vehicle runs a sampling-based model-predictive planner and exchanges only observable odometry with its partner.
A common utility-matrix rule coordinates trajectory choices, while corridor-derived lanes and a non-overridable braking-based safety layer support navigation.
In simulation, no vehicle collided with walls or cones across 48 closed-loop runs, and conversational formation was maintained more often than by human drivers.
The system matched driver speed but used a more consistent lateral formation; evaluation was limited to a differential-drive kinematic simulator in ROS 2.

papers.abstract: Personalized spoken agents must identify speakers before accessing user-specific memory, yet memory benchmarks typically assume correctly attributed histories. We argue that voiceprints are observations of identity, not identities themselves, and formulate online speaker-memory construction to maintain persistent user entities as acoustic evidence evolves. We introduce EvoSpeakerMem, a training-free layer for causal speaker routing, selective acoustic-state updates, and identity-partitioned memory writes and retrieval through a replaceable text-memory backend. We also construct LoCoMo-ID, a spoken-memory benchmark with hidden speaker identities, speaker-sensitive queries, simulated recording-condition shifts, and four-speaker identity-confusion tests. On longitudinal SMIIP-TV, genuine-probe rejection under a frozen near-enrollment threshold rises from 29.8% to 55.6% over approximately one year. On LoCoMo-ID speaker-sensitive queries, gated updating improves identity-gated QA over fixed representations by 3.86 and 11.62 percentage points under clean and shifted conditions, respectively, with no wrong-user authorizations. The advantage persists in the four-speaker test. Yet reducing fragmentation and improving QA can coexist with incorrect cross-user links, revealing a fragmentation--contamination trade-off that QA alone cannot capture.
authors: Yucong Zhang, Cancan Li, Bo Xiao, Ke Zeng, Ming Li
bullets: Addresses the gap between voiceprint observations and persistent user identities in personalized spoken agents.
Introduces a training-free system combining causal speaker routing, selective acoustic-state updates, and identity-partitioned memory operations.
Provides LoCoMo-ID, a benchmark with hidden identities, speaker-sensitive queries, recording shifts, and multi-speaker confusion tests.
Improves identity-gated QA over fixed representations by 3.86 and 11.62 percentage points in clean and shifted conditions, with no wrong-user authorizations.
Finds a fragmentation–contamination trade-off: better QA and less fragmentation may still permit incorrect cross-user links.

papers.abstract: Reasoning language models answer math problems by writing long chains of thought, and sampling many chains per problem and taking a majority vote raises accuracy at a large cost in generated text. A popular way to cut that cost scores each chain by the model's confidence in each token it writes, where a token is a word or part of a word. The method averages this confidence over a sliding window of 2048 tokens and keeps or stops chains based on the lowest average. We treat the confidence, recorded token by token, as a signal in the sense of audio or radio, and examine the method with standard signal-processing tools such as spectral analysis and statistical tests for detecting a sudden change. We sampled 16 chains for each of 500 problems from two math benchmarks with a small open reasoning model. The windowed-minimum score turns out to measure mostly how long a chain is. Ranking chains by length alone does as well as or better than the confidence score, and once length is accounted for the score carries no information about correctness. Signal processing explains why: the minimum of a longer stretch of a slowly drifting signal is lower by chance alone, and the confidence signal drifts slowly enough that this effect dominates. The spectrum does hold a small signal that length does not explain, since incorrect chains carry more rapid token-to-token fluctuation, but it is too weak to improve the vote. For stopping chains early, neither the sliding average nor a classical change detector beats the simpler choice of sampling fewer chains.
bullets: The study audits token confidence as a signal using spectral analysis and change-point tests.
Across 16 chains for each of 500 problems from two math benchmarks, chain length matched or outperformed the windowed-minimum confidence score.
After accounting for length, the confidence score contained no useful correctness information.
Incorrect chains showed more rapid token-level fluctuations, but this weak signal did not improve majority voting.
Neither confidence-based stopping method outperformed simply sampling fewer chains.

papers.abstract: Flow-based policies for language-conditioned multi-task manipulation commonly share a single $\textit{Gaussian}$ source prior and a common linear transport path across tasks. However, reliably executing multiple tasks with distinct motion requirements remains challenging for a shared policy. We introduce $\textbf{TOPS}$ ($\textbf{T}$ask-$\textbf{O}$riented $\textbf{P}$riors and $\textbf{S}$chedules), which adapts the flow source prior and interpolation schedule to each task without modifying the network architecture. TOPS first constructs multimodal task sources from reverse-mapped expert action sequences, allowing language instructions to select where generation begins. Guided by source-target covariance mismatch, it then slows the transition toward expert actions early in denoising and accelerates it later along directions requiring expansion. Under a $\textit{Gaussian}$ endpoint model, our analysis shows that this schedule adjustment can lower an upper bound on velocity-prediction risk. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and CALVIN demonstrate improved performance across in-distribution, perturbation and cross-environment settings, alongside better data efficiency. Using one integration step, TOPS raises LIBERO-10 success from $53.44\%$ to $69.67\%$ compared with ten-step Standard Flow Matching (FM), while reducing inference time to approximately one-sixth of the baseline. TOPS also yields consistent gains when transferred to the large-scale flow-based $\pi_{0.5}$ policy across all four evaluated settings. Real-world experiments further demonstrate improved task success, including an increase from $20\%$ with standard FM to $80\%$ with TOPS on the upper-drawer opening task.
authors: Tuo An, Chuhao Zhou, Jiahua Dong, Jingliang Li, Jiaqi Bai, Jindou Jia, Jianfei Yang
bullets: Shared Gaussian priors and transport paths struggle with tasks requiring distinct motion patterns.
TOPS builds multimodal, task-specific source priors from reverse-mapped expert actions, selected through language instructions.
It adapts denoising schedules using source–target covariance mismatch, slowing early transitions and accelerating later expansion directions.
The method improves performance across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, CALVIN, transfer to π0.5, and real-world manipulation settings.
On LIBERO-10, one-step TOPS reaches 69.67% success versus 53.44% for ten-step Standard Flow Matching, with roughly one-sixth the inference time.

papers.abstract: Bimanual robot manipulation plays an important role in real-world robotic applications, but the high cost of collecting bimanual demonstrations limits the scalable development of bimanual policy learning. Meanwhile, existing single-arm manipulation data are difficult to directly transfer to bimanual systems due to the Single-to-Dual gap in action spaces, coordination requirements, and arm-side spatial preference. To address this issue, we propose RoboSTD, a zero-shot Single-to-Dual data construction method for bimanual robot learning. RoboSTD first applies sagittal-plane mirroring to observations, proprioception, and actions to construct executable contralateral pseudo-demonstrations. It then uses an LLM to generate structured spatio-temporal coordination constraints that guide the reconstruction of pseudo-bimanual supervision across workspace regions and task stages. We evaluate RoboSTD on the AgileX ALOHA platform in both RoboTwin simulation and real-world settings. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of RoboSTD for bimanual policy learning. Without requiring additional bimanual demonstrations, RoboSTD increases the average number of collected cups to 2.11x that of the single-arm baseline in the cup collection task. Project page: https://huahungy.github.io/RoboSTD/
authors: Hongyu Wu, Chong Liu, Shaoxuan Xie, Shaqi Luo, Hanyu Feng, Shihan Wu, Guocai Yao
bullets: Addresses the high cost of collecting bimanual demonstrations and the Single-to-Dual gap in action spaces, coordination, and arm-side preferences.

In cup collection, it collects 2.11× as many cups as the single-arm baseline without additional bimanual demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Modern language models are trained on far more language than children experience, but we know much less about learning from small, naturalistic datasets. We train small GPT-2 models on transcripts of speech with children from dense home recordings (BabyView) and on synthetic child-directed dialogue (TinyDialogues), varying the amount, source, and diversity of training data. Models trained on one child's language environment predict that environment substantially better than other children's environments. Much of this specialization is lexical and distributional: a simple 5-gram model reproduces the cross-child pattern (r=.91). Training on data from multiple children clearly improves prediction of pooled held-out language relative to training on a single child's input without a similarly clear improvement on grammatical benchmarks. Across data sizes, naturalistic and synthetic training inputs also produce different grammatical and lexical-semantic patterns, with important differences between grammatical phenomena. Together, these results show that small-data language learning depends not only on how much language a model sees, but on which environments it comes from and how well that input matches what the model is asked to predict.

papers.abstract: Deformable image registration relies on accurate anatomical correspondences. However, explicitly coupling local matching reliability with spatial context selection and deformation update strength remains insufficiently explored in learning-based registration. This challenge is particularly pronounced in homogeneous, weakly textured, and severely deformed regions, where ambiguous matches may induce erroneous deformation updates. We propose ReliMorph, a reliability-routed symmetric framework for 3D deformable registration that couples correspondence assessment with spatial context selection and update strength.Local correlation distributions characterize correspondence ambiguity using shared anatomical features with modality-specific adaptation. These reliability cues guide spatial expert fusion and gate residual velocities during coarse-to-fine refinement. Updated inverse-inconsistency feedback guides routing and gating at finer pyramid levels. To our knowledge, ReliMorph is the first 3D deformable registration framework to jointly condition spatial expert routing and residual velocity gating on correspondence reliability. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ReliMorph consistently outperforms competing methods in anatomical overlap, highlighting its effectiveness across unimodal and multimodal registration tasks.
authors: Chenyu Guo, Wenjie Dai, Yiqian Chang, Zhiyuan Zhang, Yunfan Wei, Shuhan Qi
bullets: Targets ambiguous matches in homogeneous, weakly textured, and severely deformed regions.

Experiments report consistently better anatomical overlap across unimodal and multimodal registration tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of ReliMorph. Stage I (shared encoding) extracts multiscale anatomical features using a shared encoder with modality-specific adaptation. Stage III (symmetric refinement) integrates gated velocities via scaling and squaring, then composes the resulting residual transformations with the accumulated transformations in both directions. Updated inverseinconsistency maps feed back to Stage II at the next finer level.

papers.abstract: Diffusion vision-language models (DVLMs) process their entire input at every denoising step. Since visual tokens make up 89-97% of this input on the benchmarks we study, most of the decoding computation is spent repeatedly processing the same image. Visual token pruning methods partially relieve this burden by removing part of the visual tokens, but they lose the removed information and still process the remaining image at every step. To measure how often the image is actually needed, we compare LLaDA-V's predictions with and without the image at every decoding step and find that removing the image changes a token being unmasked at only 22.8% of steps on average and at as few as 7.9%. We therefore propose LOWN, a decoding method that decides at every step whether to process the image and how many tokens to unmask. LOWN predicts the masked tokens without the image and processes the image only when this prediction disagrees with the last image-conditioned prediction. Agreement certifies the earlier prediction for reuse, and the number of certified tokens sets how many are unmasked in that step. We further observe that the need for the image differs across benchmarks, so LOWN's adaptive decision is needed rather than a fixed schedule. Without training or a tuned threshold, LOWN retains 99.6% of LLaDA-V's score on ten benchmarks at 35.3% of the decoding FLOPs on average. LOWN also generalizes across LLaDA-based DVLMs, composes orthogonally with visual token pruning, and runs under key-value caching for further efficiency gains. Code and project page are available at https://hyeon9698.github.io/LOWN/
authors: Donghyeon Cho, Joowon Kim, Seungho Shin, Eunho Yang

Across ten benchmarks, LOWN retains 99.6% of LLaDA-V’s score while using 35.3% of the decoding FLOPs on average.
It generalizes across LLaDA-based DVLMs, combines with visual token pruning, and supports key-value caching.

papers.abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) enable world models to plan from images by predicting future embeddings. However, their visual prediction objectives do not explicitly incorporate task-relevant state information, so the physical state that determines task progress may not be reliably captured in the latent space. Supervising world models with simulator state can make planning more informative, but it requires deciding which state features matter. Features are typically selected by hand or weighted uniformly, and a uniform weighting gives every standardized state feature equal influence, so redundant coordinates can overcount the same variation, while irrelevant ones can obscure task-relevant differences. To address this limitation, we propose SWIM (State Weighting with Inverse-Dynamics Model), which learns state weights from offline trajectories by predicting recorded actions from current states and observed future displacements. The learned weights quantify each feature's contribution to action prediction and define a weighted state metric for state-supervised training, which we demonstrate by aligning latent and state distances. The inverse-dynamics model is used only during training, so the resulting world model plans from images with no additional planning-time computation. Across five simulated robotic manipulation tasks, SWIM consistently improves planning success over uniform state weighting.
authors: Jiaming Hu, Shi Bo, Yan Zheng, Tian Wang, Florian Dubost, Alejandro Mottini, Junze Liu, Arvind Srinivasan, Kai Zhong, Kun Qian, Sharon Gao, Vianne Gao, Houyu Zhang, Qingjun Cui
bullets: Addresses the problem that visual JEPA objectives may miss physical state information important for task progress.

papers.abstract: Point cloud registration is an essential task for scene reconstruction, requiring the alignment of partially overlapping point clouds. Under low-overlap conditions, this task remains challenging because existing geometry-only methods cannot distinguish geometrically similar but semantically distinct structures (e.g., TV corners vs. desk corners and chair legs vs. table legs), resulting in incorrect correspondences. To address this geometric ambiguity, we present Semantic-Augmented Geometric Experts (SAGE), which integrates frozen pre-trained point cloud semantic representations into the registration pipeline without requiring additional sensors or fine-tuning the semantic encoder. To effectively leverage these semantic distinctions, SAGE employs a Semantic-Guided Mixture of Experts (SG-MoE) architecture. Through semantic-aware routing, SG-MoE enables each expert to specialize in distinct semantic-geometric patterns, reducing mismatches that confound geometry-only methods. With a structure-aware estimator, SAGE achieves the highest registration recall on 3DLoMatch while remaining competitive on 3DMatch. When evaluated with the same number of refinement iterations, SAGE further achieves the highest inlier ratio and registration recall on both benchmarks. These results indicate that frozen semantic representations provide effective cues for resolving geometric ambiguity in low-overlap registration.
authors: Tomoyasu Shimada, Kazuhiko Murasaki, Shoichiro Takeda, Shogo Sato, Riku Inoue, Toshihiko Nishimura, Ryuichi Tanida
bullets: Addresses geometric ambiguity between visually similar but semantically different structures.
Uses frozen pre-trained point cloud semantic features without additional sensors or semantic-encoder fine-tuning.
Introduces a Semantic-Guided Mixture of Experts to specialize in semantic-geometric patterns.
Combines SG-MoE with a structure-aware estimator for registration.
Reports highest recall on 3DLoMatch and strong inlier ratio and recall on both 3DLoMatch and 3DMatch under equal refinement iterations.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overall pipeline of SAGE. Given two input point clouds, the Two-Stage Feature Extraction (Sec. 3.2) first applies a frozen Sonata encoder to extract point-level semantic features from each point cloud, and then feeds these semantic features together with the raw point coordinates into the KPConv encoder to produce semantic-geometric features. The Spatial Feature Aggregation (Sec. 3.3) then maps both the semantic and semantic-geometric features to the superpoint level via nearest-neighbor search and average pooling. The aggregated features are refined through N alternating iterations of Geometric Transformer layers (red box, self-attention) and Semantic-Guided Mixture of Experts (Sec. 3.4) layers (blue box, cross-attention), where semantic features guide expert routing to enable semantic-aware specialization. Finally, the framework adopts GeoTransformer’s coarse-to-fine matching for correspondence estimation and registration.

papers.abstract: Memory helps LLM-based multi-agent systems reuse experience, but stored advice can be flawed or applied in the wrong situation. Team-level success or failure alone cannot reliably show whether a memory needs correction or should not have been used. We propose DiscernMem, a training-free framework that improves both memory quality and memory use. To improve quality, Defect-Aware Memory Refinement (DMR) compares team executions with a single memory and with no memory, diagnoses rule defects, and tests repairs on current and earlier tasks to guard against losing previously useful behavior. To guide appropriate use, Boundary-Learning Meta-Memory (BLM) records each memory's past uses and effects, learning when its owner role should apply or avoid it based on task context and incoming messages. Together, these components help teams correct flawed experience while retaining useful rules that were applied incorrectly. Experiments with Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 on four benchmarks show that DiscernMem achieves the highest average score on AutoGen, CAMEL, and MacNet, exceeding the strongest reported baselines by 0.51-4.32 points. It leads on code generation and symbolic planning across all three systems, including a PDDL score of 37.71 versus 28.48 on CAMEL.
authors: Yipeng Hao, Yuxuan Cai, Wenkai Ji, Jie Zhou, Liyang Yu, Qin Chen, Zhiguo Yan, Shulei Zheng, Liang He
bullets: Multi-agent memories may contain defective advice or be applied in unsuitable contexts, while team-level outcomes alone cannot diagnose either issue.
Defect-Aware Memory Refinement compares executions with one memory versus no memory, diagnoses and tests repairs, and preserves previously useful behavior.

On four benchmarks with Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, DiscernMem achieved the highest average scores on AutoGen, CAMEL, and MacNet, with gains of 0.51–4.32 points over reported baselines.
It led on code generation and symbolic planning across the evaluated systems, including a CAMEL PDDL score of 37.71 versus 28.48.

papers.abstract: System identification, namely the inference of mathematical representations of dynamical systems from measured data, is fundamental to engineering diagnostics, prognostics, and decision-making. Bayesian filtering offers a principled framework for probabilistic state estimation but traditionally relies on prescribed transition and observation models. Recent advances in deep Bayesian filtering address this limitation by embedding learnable representations within probabilistic state-space formulations, enabling data-driven identification of unknown dynamics while retaining physical structure and uncertainty-aware inference. This tutorial provides a systematic introduction to deep Bayesian filtering for nonlinear structural system identification, focusing on the interplay between learned dynamics, physical inductive biases, and posterior inference. The Deep Markov Model serves as a data-driven reference, while the Physics-guided Deep Markov Model (PgDMM) and Neural Extended Kalman Filter (Neural EKF) illustrate complementary approaches based on amortized variational inference and differentiable Kalman filtering, respectively. Their capabilities are examined through dynamic state estimation and joint dynamic state and parameter estimation on a three-dimensional shear-frame benchmark with hysteretic Bouc-Wen connections and sparse acceleration measurements. The results highlight important distinctions between measurement-conditioned reconstruction and open-loop forecasting, demonstrate how physical structure can improve latent-state interpretability without necessarily ensuring predictive fidelity, and reveal differences in the robustness of response and parameter estimation. Practical guidelines for model construction, training, evaluation, and deployment are provided, together with an outlook on remaining challenges in uncertainty calibration, identifiability, and real-world validation.
authors: Wei Liu, Konstantinos Vlachas, Eleni Chatzi
bullets: Addresses data-driven identification of unknown nonlinear structural dynamics from measured data while retaining probabilistic state estimation.
Introduces Deep Markov Models, Physics-guided Deep Markov Models, and Neural Extended Kalman Filters as complementary approaches.
Evaluates dynamic state estimation and joint state–parameter estimation on a three-dimensional shear-frame system with hysteretic connections and sparse acceleration data.
Distinguishes measurement-conditioned reconstruction from open-loop forecasting and compares robustness of response and parameter estimation.
Highlights unresolved challenges in uncertainty calibration, identifiability, and validation on real-world systems.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Common probabilistic state-space skeleton and method-specific realizations of the three deep Bayesian filtering frameworks considered in this work. The top panel shows the latent state zk evolving under the transition model fν and generating observations xk through the emission model hϕ, with the dynamics driven by inputs uk. Inference recovers the latent state from the observation sequence through an approximate posterior q. The bottom panels arrange the three frameworks according to increasing physics-based inductive bias. The DMM constitutes the fully data-driven baseline, with learned transition, emission, and amortized inference models and no prescribed physical organization of the latent state. The Neural EKF introduces an intermediate level of structure by replacing the amortized encoder with the EKF predict-update recursion and, in its structural specialization, by organizing the latent state into displacement- and velocity-like coordinates, while retaining learnable transition and emission models. The PgDMM introduces stronger physics-based bias by embedding a parameter-dependent ROM within the transition and emission models, while retaining the amortized inference architecture of the DMM.

papers.abstract: Test-time adaptation updates a deployed model on an unlabeled test stream. In practice this stream often arrives one sample at a time, with the classes in no particular order. A single sample then provides limited information for estimating distribution-level statistics, and selecting samples by confidence can admit predictions that are wrong yet confident. A corruption, however, shifts the features while leaving the decision regions of the frozen classifier unchanged. We therefore propose Origin-recentered Test-Time Adaptation (OriTTA), which constructs fixed geometric targets from the source model and adapts selected features toward them. Seen from the origin of the feature space, the classes lean toward a common direction. We choose a new origin to bring class scores closer together while keeping it near the mean feature of one synthetic prototype per class. From this origin, prototype directions spread more evenly, and each class obtains an axis and an ideal point before any test data arrives. During adaptation, OriTTA aligns selected features with their predicted class axis and penalizes excessive radius, keeps one input per predicted class in memory to limit feature changes for classes absent from the stream, and resets the model when re-classifying this memory reveals collapse. Without tuning for each setting, OriTTA achieves the highest mean accuracy at batch size 1 on CIFAR-10-C, CIFAR-100-C and ImageNet-C in all sixteen combinations of four backbones, two protocols and two stream orders. On ImageNet-C fog, recent methods collapse in up to two thirds of one hundred runs, while OriTTA never does.
authors: Jaeho Hwang, Yujin Oh, Juhyeon Shin, Juhye Lee, Sungroh Yoon, Uiwon Hwang

Adapts selected features toward predicted class axes, penalizes excessive feature radius, and stores one sample per class to preserve absent-class behavior.
Detects adaptation collapse by reclassifying the stored memory and resets the model when necessary.
Achieves the highest mean accuracy at batch size 1 across the reported CIFAR-10-C, CIFAR-100-C, and ImageNet-C settings; it avoids collapses observed by recent methods on ImageNet-C fog.

papers.abstract: Sparse event responses produce uneven keypoint errors whose effects on spacecraft pose depend on correspondence geometry and the reliability of successive observations. We present a reliability-aware framework connecting polarity--time localization, geometric recovery, event--CAD refinement, and trajectory optimization. A three-branch representation combines positive events, negative events, and recent-event timing through cross-branch attention and gating, followed by spatiotemporal aggregation. An ordered semantic-point head estimates relative correspondence precision for geometrically constrained pose recovery. Event-edge and CAD-projection agreement then guide local pose refinement under keypoint-geometry safeguards. At the sequence level, a ten-dimensional descriptor combines heatmap shape, reprojection consistency, and geometric conditioning to set time-aligned observation scales. On the official SPADES challenge test set, the complete system achieves a combined pose score of 0.0474, approximately 5.4\% below PASAN+IRIS. Validation ablations reduce the score from 0.0772 for base localization with uniform PnP to 0.0514 for the complete cascade; on identical single-frame observations, quality weighting reduces the score from 0.0549 with constant-weight optimization to 0.0514.
authors: Yonglong Zhang, Zongwu Xie, Yang Liu
bullets: Addresses uneven keypoint errors in sparse event data and their impact on pose recovery.
Uses separate positive, negative, and recent-event timing branches with cross-branch attention and spatiotemporal aggregation.
Predicts semantic-point reliability for geometry-constrained pose estimation, then refines poses using event-edge/CAD agreement.
Optimizes time-aligned observation scales from heatmap, reprojection, and geometric-conditioning descriptors.
Scores 0.0474 on the official SPADES test set; ablations show progressive improvement from 0.0772 to 0.0514, with quality weighting improving 0.0549 to 0.0514.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) leverage pretrained video generative models for robotic control by jointly predicting future visual observations and actions. The visual prediction objective plays a key role in adapting pretrained video representations to the target robot domain. Yet standard visual prediction inherited from video pretraining treats all visual regions uniformly, despite their differing relevance to robotic control. We therefore investigate the spatial allocation of visual supervision in WAMs and show that focusing supervision on dynamic regions can substantially improve policy performance. Building on this finding, we introduce Motion-Guided Asymmetric Prediction (MoGAP), which augments WAM training with motion-focused visual prediction. MoGAP allocates noise asymmetrically across regions, training the model to reconstruct more heavily corrupted dynamic regions using less corrupted static regions as context. MoGAP is trained alongside standard video-action prediction through a training-only auxiliary prediction path within the shared video diffusion backbone. It uses motion cues derived directly from training videos, requiring neither an external teacher nor additional modalities. Across robot manipulation benchmarks and WAM architectures, MoGAP consistently improves policy performance, increasing success rates on the GR-1 tabletop benchmark from 38.8% to 47.5% for Fast-WAM (Wan2.2-5B) and from 52.3% to 62.3% for Cosmos3-Nano.
authors: Taeyoung Kim, Junyoung Sung, Heeseung Kwon, Minseop Kim, Jinwoo Shin
bullets: WAMs benefit from allocating more visual supervision to regions that move and matter for control.
MoGAP applies asymmetric noise: dynamic regions are more corrupted, while static regions provide context for reconstruction.
It adds a training-only auxiliary prediction path alongside standard video-action prediction, using motion cues from training videos without extra modalities or teachers.
Across manipulation benchmarks and WAM architectures, MoGAP improves success rates, including GR-1 gains from 38.8% to 47.5% and 52.3% to 62.3%.

papers.abstract: Mamba-2 compresses all context into a fixed-size recurrent state that dominates decoding memory and bandwidth. Existing compressors quantize state values or prune state coordinates, scoring each channel independently in the native basis. We examine trained Mamba-2 states and find that energy is almost rank-one, but the output does not read the energetic directions: energy concentrates in a bias-like direction accumulated by the recurrence, while the content the output reads lives in a low-dimensional subspace that is not aligned with the state's coordinates. Even output-aware scores are computed coordinate by coordinate, so they miss the directions that determine the input--output map. Compression should therefore target the write--read subspace rather than individual coordinates. We propose \method{}, a post-training transform that instantiates balanced truncation with full controllability and observability Gramians and applies the rotation exactly via Mamba-2's scalar-identity transition. Because the useful rank varies widely across layers, we further introduce HARP, which allocates ranks per layer from the Hankel spectrum and protects retrieval-sensitive layers, improving both perplexity and retrieval over uniform budgets. Calibration takes a single forward pass, an order of magnitude faster than GHOST's released protocol, with lower peak memory. With HARP, \method{} halves the state dimension at an average WikiText-2 perplexity increase of $0.3$ points ($1.8\%$) across 130M--2.7B, versus $1.6$ ($9.3\%$) for GHOST, and the gap widens at 25\% retention.
bullets: Mamba-2 state energy is nearly rank-one, but the useful output-read content lies in a different low-dimensional, non-coordinate-aligned subspace.
The proposed post-training method applies balanced truncation using full controllability and observability Gramians, with an exact rotation enabled by Mamba-2’s scalar-identity transition.
HARP allocates layer-specific ranks from the Hankel spectrum and protects retrieval-sensitive layers instead of using uniform budgets.
Using one-pass calibration, the method halves state dimension with a 0.3-point average WikiText-2 perplexity increase across 130M–2.7B models, compared with 1.6 points for GHOST.
The approach is evaluated for perplexity and retrieval; performance degradation increases at 25% retention.

papers.abstract: Enabling a humanoid to interact naturally with human partners requires preserving not only individual motions but also the spatial, semantic, and contact relationships underlying the interaction (i.e., hugging, dancing, hand-shaking, etc.). Furthermore, a practical solution should generalize across various humanoid embodiments with distinct morphologies and kinematic constraints. To tackle this challenge, we propose HumiTransfer, a mimetic embodiment transfer framework that converts in-the-wild human-human interaction videos into physically plausible human-humanoid interactions. HumiTransfer first reconstructs 3D human motion with consistent foot-ground contact, then transfers one participant to a target humanoid embodiment via interaction modeling, using weighted joint-relative directions and anatomical offsets to prioritize interaction-critical inter-body relationships, while post-retargeting optimization enforces balance, contact, and collision avoidance. Subsequently, we apply HumiTransfer to 1,200 in-the-wild videos, producing approximately 500,000 frames of diverse interactions for the 26-DoF Unitree R1 Edu and the 23-DoF HighTorque Mini-hi humanoid robot, resulting in our HumiMimic dataset. Across both robots, HumiTransfer achieves superior motion fidelity, preserves inter-body relationships, and maintains contact accuracy compared with existing baselines. Moreover, we demonstrate that HumiMimic supports motion generation methods for synthesizing interactive humanoid motions following a human partner. Finally, our real robot deployments confirm the physical executability of the transferred motions in real-world settings.
authors: Nghia Le (Hann), Khang Nguyen (Hann), Ba Long Tran (Hann), Thi Quynh Nhu Pham (Hann), Binh Nguyen (Hann), Tuong Do (Hann), Erman Tjiputra (Hann), Hoan Nguyen (Hann), Tung D. Ta (Hann), Baoru Huang (Hann), Hai-Nguyen (Hann), Nguyen (Hann), Anh Nguyen

papers.abstract: Reconstructing dynamic 3D scenes over time (4D reconstruction) from a single moving camera is central to robotics and AR/VR applications, yet state-of the-art feed-forward methods rely solely on RGB frames and therefore inherit the failure modes of conventional cameras, including motion blur and temporal aliasing under fast or non-uniform camera and object motion. Event cameras report per-pixel brightness changes asynchronously at microsecond resolution, offering a complementary signal that is largely immune to these artifacts, but whether this modality can be incorporated into existing RGB based 4D reconstruction pipelines without a full architectural redesign remains an open question. In this preliminary study, we investigate a minimal extension: we augment Monst3R, an existing RGB-only 4D reconstruction model, with an additional event-camera input branch, leaving the rest of the architecture unchanged. Across 3 benchmark datasets, this simple RGB-event fusion reduces Abs Rel by 3.4% on average relative to the RGB-only Monst3R baseline, and a sensitivity analysis shows that the improvement grows with the magnitude of camera and object motion, with the largest gains observed under high object motion conditions where RGB-only reconstruction degrades most. These early results suggest that even a lightweight, non-invasive fusion of event data can meaningfully improve 4D reconstruction robustness, motivating a more thorough architectural investigation in future work.

papers.abstract: Handheld data-collection interfaces such as the Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) allow manipulation demonstrations to be gathered in the wild without a robot in the loop, but the quality of the resulting action labels is bounded by the accuracy of vision-based localization. Existing systems recover end-effector pose from monocular visual-inertial odometry, which is subject to scale ambiguity and drift, or delegate tracking to closed-source modules and external infrastructure that reintroduce cost and setup burden. We present OpenJaws, a fully open hardware and software framework for sensorized UMI that improves localization and simplifies deployment across robot platforms. OpenJaws pairs a modular, 3D-printed gripper exposing a standardized ISO adapter with a low-cost stereo camera to recover metric camera trajectories. We further introduce UMI-Loc-Bench-v1, a benchmark quantifying real-world localization accuracy for handheld data-collection devices, and show that stereo localization substantially outperforms monocular alternatives. Finally, we demonstrate that policies trained on data collected with OpenJaws can be deployed on a real robot across multiple tasks. Hardware, software, and data are released under a commercially permissive license. Code, data, and videos are available at https://open-jaws.github.io/

papers.abstract: Decision models offer fast choices over sup- plied alternatives, while general-purpose large language models interpret open-ended tasks through flexible generation and reasoning at the cost of sequential decoding. Many work- loads expect a generative backend to determine what can be done and therefore provide no well-defined candidate list. We bridge this in- terface gap with a small candidate formalizer trained on offline teacher-generated lists. The formalizer constructs explicit, validated alter- natives from task context, and a frozen deci- sion model selects an entry. A motivating com- parison with official TypeSafe Jev-1.13.0 on 200 CALVIN-D test episodes reports 11% suc- cess with generic motions versus 46.5% with DeepSeek V4 Flash pose candidates. Sepa- rately, a six-arm privileged-state evaluation on 1,011 CALVIN-D validation annotations finds that a locally deployed decision model can achieve at most 52.6% task success rate with the fine-tuned formalizer, compared with 11.8% without it, and the end-to-end latency is kept to 2.09 s, whereas Qwen3.5-27B is 3.67 s with the exact experiment setting.
authors: Chengxuan Pei, Ziyao Wang, Teng Mei, Zhe Li
bullets: Addresses the interface gap between generative language models and decision models that require explicit candidate lists.

In CALVIN-D evaluations, formalization improved reported task success from 11.8% to 52.6% in a privileged-state setting.
A motivating comparison reported 46.5% success with pose candidates versus 11% with generic motions.
End-to-end latency was 2.09 s, compared with 3.67 s for Qwen3.5-27B under the stated experimental setting.

papers.abstract: Autonomous scientific agents must not only reason about experiments but also interact with the physical environments in which they are executed. Existing laboratory simulators typically rely on manually constructed assets and predefined procedures, while laboratory videos capture real equipment, layouts, and interactions but leave this information implicit in pixels. We introduce LabWorld, an agent-driven Real2Sim framework for reconstructing interactive 4D laboratory worlds from monocular RGB video. LabWorld recovers reusable 3D assets, a metric scene, time-varying object states, and procedure events. Multi-frame observations provide complementary evidence for asset and scene reconstruction, while motion reconstruction combines visual and geometric observations with event constraints encoding the spatial and temporal requirements of laboratory interactions. We evaluate LabWorld on real pipetting and vortexing videos collected in our laboratory against general-purpose agentic and dedicated reconstruction baselines. For pipetting, LabWorld achieves a mean Mask IoU of 0.501, exceeding the strongest baseline by 0.033. For vortexing, it achieves a mean Tube-Length-Normalized PCK-AUC of 0.638, exceeding the strongest baseline by 0.035. On five pipetting videos, event-conditioned reconstruction increases the fraction of modeled physical constraints satisfied from 14.3% (5/35) to 100% (35/35). The resulting worlds expose geometry, motion, articulation, and events as explicit, editable state for replay, inspection, and future embodied scientific systems.

bullets: Addresses the gap between pixel-based laboratory videos and simulators with explicit, reusable equipment, scenes, object states, and procedure events.
Uses a Real2Sim pipeline that combines multi-frame visual evidence, geometric observations, and spatial-temporal event constraints.
Evaluated on real pipetting and vortexing videos, achieving Mask IoU of 0.501 and Tube-Length-Normalized PCK-AUC of 0.638.
Event-conditioned reconstruction increased satisfied modeled physical constraints from 14.3% to 100% across five pipetting videos.
Produces editable world states for replay, inspection, and future scientific agents; evaluation is scoped to pipetting and vortexing activities.

papers.abstract: Low-precision training often relies on stochastic rounding (SR) to keep quantized gradients unbiased and prevent small updates from rounding to zero. Standard SR draws an independent random threshold for every gradient element. However, accelerators generate random numbers on vector units whose throughput lags far behind their matrix units. Drawing one threshold per element saturates the vector unit and can make INT8 training with SR slower than BF16 training. Sharing random thresholds across tensor elements removes this cost but forces those elements to round in the same direction and shifts their rounding errors by a common offset. We find that this offset degrades training primarily through the activation gradient, which propagates the error backward into earlier layers. Because earlier layers cannot cancel an incoming offset using their own local rounding errors, the offset must be removed at the layer where it originates. We propose Structured Subspace Stochastic Rounding (S3R), which quantizes each upstream gradient once for both the activation and weight gradient matrix multiplications and shares a single threshold per token across the hidden dimension. Its error correction, S3R-EC, subtracts the structured mean rounding error from the activation and weight gradients while leaving the optimizer unchanged. In LLM pre-training experiments, uncorrected threshold sharing degrades convergence, whereas S3R-EC eliminates this degradation and matches the validation loss of independent SR. Furthermore, S3R-EC accelerates full INT8 training steps of dense LLMs on TPU v5p by 1.24x to 1.32x over BF16 and by 1.11x over independent SR.
authors: Zeyu Wang, Yiheng Duan, Tao Chen, Donghyun Koo, Sihan Liu, Wenbo Zhang, Chuan He, Liang Liu
bullets: Independent stochastic rounding is costly because generating one random threshold per gradient element bottlenecks accelerator vector units.
Naively sharing thresholds reduces randomness overhead but introduces a common rounding offset that harms convergence through activation gradients.
S3R quantizes each upstream gradient once for both activation and weight computations, sharing one threshold per token across hidden dimensions.
S3R-EC removes the resulting structured mean rounding error without changing the optimizer.
In LLM pre-training on TPU v5p, S3R-EC matches independent-SR validation loss and achieves 1.24–1.32× speedup over BF16 and 1.11× over independent SR.

In the backward pass, the upstream gradient Gt is quantized once, and the int8 result is written to HBM once and read by both the activation-gradient product G̃tW⊤ t and the weight-gradient product X̂⊤ t G̃t. papers.abstract: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) are being applied to Web data streams such as network intrusion detection, where they adapt by updating the labelled rows of their context without retraining. When a past concept returns after leaving the context, a TFM faces a recall-or-relearn decision between restoring stored rows of the concept and relearning it from new labels. We propose MICE (Mixture of In-Context Experts), a training-free learner that cuts the stream into segments at detected changes. It merges a closed segment into a stored context when the TFM's estimated additional error on the segment is within a tolerance, under a capacity limit on stored contexts. A fast level weights the stored contexts and first-in-first-out (FIFO) windows by the log-loss of their predictions on the last labelled batch. We show that, with pure stored contexts and a margin condition, this fast level gains over relearning, in expected accuracy, the normalised positive area between the stored context's accuracy and the TFM's learning curve, up to a first-batch term. A slow level mixes the fast level's prediction with that of the FIFO window of the last labelled rows and bounds the discounted half-Brier regret of MICE against this window at every time. Learning curves measured beforehand predict the ordering of the observed recall gains. MICE outperforms reset, which empties the context at detected drifts, on grid streams with random boundary phases. Merging keeps fewer experts than pools that store every segment, and with fixed segmentation a time-matched snapshot pool matches MICE on the shifted grid. On real streams, MICE has the highest mean accuracy of all policies we compare.
authors: Zhangkai Wu, Xu Zhang, Zhihong Cui, Yiqi Wang, Yi Zhang
bullets: Addresses TFMs’ recall-versus-relearning decision when previously seen concepts return after leaving context.
Segments streams at detected changes and selectively merges segments into a capacity-limited pool of stored contexts.
Uses a fast log-loss weighting level over stored contexts and FIFO windows, plus a slower mixture with the latest labelled rows.
Theory links recall gains to stored-context accuracy and learning curves, and bounds discounted half-Brier regret against a recent-data baseline.
Outperforms context-reset policies on grid streams and achieves the highest mean accuracy among compared policies on real streams; fixed-segmentation snapshots can match it on shifted grids.

papers.abstract: To generate landmark-based route instructions, models must understand both map geometry and human landmark preferences. Although large language models (LLMs) show great abilities in language tasks, the best way to structure map data for these models is not yet established. This paper proposes a structured text representation for landmark selection tasks in route navigation, utilizing SVG format to encode spatial features. The structured text maintains a geometric connection with rendered map images, allowing language models to directly access spatial and semantic data. Using a new dataset created from human-written route descriptions and OpenStreetMap data, we evaluate models on two tasks: landmark selection at turns and around destinations. Experiments with five LLMs show that the proposed structured text input performs as well as or better than image-based PNG inputs. In addition, task-specific fine-tuning enables smaller local LLMs to effectively leverage map layouts to achieve high selection accuracy. These results demonstrate that structured text is an efficient and lightweight interface for spatial reasoning in human-oriented navigation.
authors: Mifu Matsumoto, Yuki Nakanishi, Tomoya Hashiguchi, Hiroaki Ohshima
bullets: Addresses the challenge of representing map geometry and semantic information for landmark-based route instruction generation.
Encodes spatial features in structured SVG text while preserving alignment with rendered map images.
Evaluates landmark selection at turns and near destinations using a dataset combining human-written routes with OpenStreetMap data.

Task-specific fine-tuning allows smaller local LLMs to use map layouts effectively.
