papers.abstract: Final-answer accuracy reports whether a vision-language model was right, but not whether its answer was grounded in the image, whether its stated reasoning reflects that evidence, or what the answer cost to produce. Those are the properties that decide whether a system can be deployed. We present PRISM-BENCH, a benchmark of 1,000 expert-curated questions spanning five under-represented reasoning categories, in which every item carries an idealized reasoning trace written by one human annotator and validated by another. The traces support two diagnostics that accuracy cannot provide. A perception probe, in which the model answers from a description it wrote itself, attributes roughly 85% of frontier-model failures to misperception and places the bottleneck at grounding. Trace alignment predicts answer correctness for all 25 systems tested (macro AUROC 0.66) and survives length control, so it measures reasoning content and not verbosity. We further introduce CORE, an efficiency-aware metric that reorders 24.2% of model pairs relative to accuracy while remaining uncorrelated with response length. Across 25 open and closed systems, including GPT-5 and Claude Opus 4.6, the best accuracy is 66.0%. On the four categories with a human baseline the best system trails humans by 18.4 points, and recent frontier gains fall on recognition and not on spatial grounding.
authors: Vansh Bhatia, Mehdi Rezagholizadeh, Parsa Ashrafi Fashi, Igor Gilitschenski, Vikram Appia, Emad Barsoum
bullets: Introduces 1,000 expert-curated questions across five under-represented reasoning categories, each with a validated ideal reasoning trace.
A self-description perception probe attributes roughly 85% of frontier-model failures to misperception, identifying grounding as the main bottleneck.
Trace alignment predicts correctness across all 25 evaluated systems, beyond effects of response length.
CORE, an efficiency-aware metric, reorders 24.2% of model pairs relative to accuracy while remaining uncorrelated with response length.
The best system reaches 66.0% accuracy, trails humans by 18.4 points where comparable, and recent gains emphasize recognition over spatial grounding.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Three deployment-relevant diagnostics that final-answer accuracy cannot provide. (a) Accuracy falls when a model must answer from its own image description instead of the image (drop annotated in red); the white figure inside each bar is the share of that model’s baseline failures that the model itself, judging in a fresh context, attributes to perception instead of inference. (b) For all 25 evaluated systems, responses that are correct align more closely with the human reasoning trace than responses that are incorrect (macro AUROC 0.66, and 0.665 after regressing out response length). (c) CORE reorders models relative to accuracy; dashed arrows connect matched thinking/instruct pairs, which spend more tokens for less accuracy.

Figure 3: (a) Overall accuracy for all 25 evaluated systems, shaded by family, against the 83.9% human baseline (red). Restricted to the four categories where both are measured, the best system trails humans by 18.4 points, and the open/closed gap is larger than any difference within the open families. (b) Best system of any kind versus the human baseline (red tick) per category. The deficit is concentrated in the two spatially grounded categories and nearly vanishes on multi-hop, where the reasoning is largely textual once the scene is read.

Figure 6: Navigation / map reading. Gemma-3-12B-It reads the label adjacent to the church and answers correctly in 74 tokens. Kimi-VL (140 tokens), Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct (172) and Qwen3-VL-30B-Instruct (316) all produce longer, more structured deliberations and all answer “Henry Street”. This item is a compact illustration of why we score cost alongside correctness: the cheapest response here is the only correct one, and a leaderboard ordered by accuracy alone would still rank three of these systems above Gemma overall.

Figure 9: Navigation / spatial orientation. The question asks which street is the odd one out and states explicitly that the criterion is not the name. The answer is Wilfred Ave, the only street running north–south while the others run east–west. Only OpenAI o3 checks orientation on the map. Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct (1,861 tokens), Ovis2.5-9B and Gemma-3-12B all reason from the linguistic distinction between “Court” and “Avenue” despite the hint ruling it out, and Ovis2.5-9B visibly loops before committing. This is the linguistic shortcutting failure, and it is the pattern behind the ∼47% navigation scores in Table 2: the models read the map as text rather than as space.

Figure 2: The five reasoning categories, balanced at 200 items each. The categories mix functional reasoning patterns, such as multi-hop composition, with domain-specific grounding requirements, such as medical interpretation, because deployment demands both.

Figure 4: Visual coreference under occlusion. The question asks for the registration of the aircraft partially occluded behind the silver plane in the foreground. Gemini 2.5 Pro resolves it by enumerating the three visible aircraft, reading each registration, and matching against the referring expression. Kimi-VL, Qwen3-VL-30B-Thinking and Ovis2.5-9B all answer N177XV, the registration of the foreground plane. This is the saliency bias described in Section E: the referring expression is never applied, and the most prominent entity is returned instead. Token budgets of 614, 296 and 753 show this is not a matter of insufficient reasoning length.

Figure 5: Handwriting / OCR reasoning. All five candidate words appear correctly in the handwritten passage, so the answer is “none of the above”, which requires transcribing every option correctly before concluding that nothing is missing. Qwen3-VL-8BInstruct does so. Gemini 2.5 Pro misreads one word and then constructs an elaborate, internally consistent argument for “based”; Gemma-3-12B and VL-Rethinker each settle on “favour”. This is the cascade pattern: the reasoning is valid given the misperception, so the trace looks sound and the error is invisible without the ground truth.

Figure 7: Multi-hop reasoning. Answering requires chaining what the scene shows (people playing a Wii boxing game) to a fact about the game (each player needs a remote and a nunchuck) to a count. Ovis2.5-9B, Gemma-3-12B and Skywork-R1V3-38B chain correctly. OpenAI o3 counts three players from the image and propagates that into three controllers, an error at the first hop that the subsequent reasoning faithfully preserves.

Figure 8: Scientific / medical reasoning. The nail finding is Beau’s lines, transverse ridges left by repeated arrest of nail-matrix growth, which point to cyclical chemotherapy. Only OpenAI o3 reaches this. Gemini identifies the pattern as Muehrcke’s lines and reasons fluently to nephrotic syndrome; Gemma-3-12B reasons to psoriasis; Qwen2.5-VL-7B concludes none of the options apply. Each wrong answer arrives with a confident, clinically phrased causal chain. This is the category with the highest rate of confidently wrong explanations, and the reason we treat it as the clearest safety concern for deployment.

Figure 10: The four-stage annotation loop. Duties are separated so that no annotator validates an item whose reasoning trace they wrote, and an item that fails Stage 4 returns to its author for revision instead of being silently accepted or discarded. Stage 2 produces the human reference length Lgt i that CORE uses and the reference content that trace alignment uses.

Table 7: Trace alignment for all 25 evaluated systems, sorted by gap. “Sim.” is the mean over gold trace steps of the maximum cosine similarity to any step of the model response. The gap is positive for every variant: responses that reach the correct answer track the human reasoning trace more closely than responses that do not.

Table 2: Accuracy (%) of all 25 evaluated systems across the five PRISM-BENCH categories, against the human baseline (5 annotators × 50 items per category). No system exceeds 66% overall, or 84% in any single category. The newest frontier systems lead on OCR yet remain near 47% on navigation, where humans reach 86%: recent gains concentrate on recognition rather than spatial grounding.
Table 1: PRISM-BENCH dataset statistics. The three answer-choice rows partition all 1,000 items; most are 4-way or wider multiple choice, and 11 items are open-ended or binary.

Table 6: Reflective-token analysis for 12 representative models. “Reflective tokens” counts hesitation and backtracking phrases (“Wait”, “Actually”, “Let me reconsider”) per response. More self-correction does not yield higher accuracy: Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking averages 17.0 reflective phrases and 1,812 tokens to reach 36.0%, while its instruct counterpart averages 2.6 phrases and 737 tokens to reach 40.0%.

papers.title: PRISM-BENCH: Diagnosing Grounded and Faithful Multimodal Reasoning Beyond Final-Answer Accuracy
papers.tldr: PRISM-BENCH shows that multimodal reasoning quality depends on grounding, faithful reasoning, and efficiency—not final-answer accuracy alone.

papers.abstract: Handwritten civil-status registers across Sub-Saharan Africa are being photographed, but rarely transcribed, which leaves their content unsearchable. Local administrations that hold these records typically lack GPUs, reliable connectivity, and the budget for external digitization services. We study whether a frugal pipeline, with consumer-grade capture and CPU-only inference, can make such registers machine-readable. We introduce a corpus of 1,568 smartphone images of handwritten birth, marriage, and death records from a municipal registry in Chad, with line-level transcriptions for 185 records. Our pipeline combines a fully classical preprocessing stage, running at about 2.6 images per second on a laptop CPU, with a Kraken recognizer fine-tuned from a pretrained model in about four hours on a free-tier GPU. On manually corrected line segmentation and a single-registry test set whose writers also appear in training, fine-tuning reduces the character error rate from 14.53% to 0.50% and the word error rate from 56.93% to 3.37%. On a six-core laptop CPU, the recognizer weighs 61 MiB, peaks below 2.6 GiB of RAM, and processes an image in under 6 s on average, excluding line segmentation. Finally, a downstream information-extraction task shows that residual recognition errors cost about 9 F1 points on role resolution, compared with a 36.7-point gap between the fine-tuned and pretrained recognizers. These results are evidence of feasibility within one registry, not of performance on unseen writers or sites; we discuss these limitations in detail.
authors: Ousmane Hamadou, Jean Louis Kedieng Ebongue Fendji
bullets: Targets digitization barriers in Sub-Saharan administrations lacking GPUs, reliable connectivity, and external-service budgets.
Introduces 1,568 smartphone images from 185 handwritten birth, marriage, and death records in a Chadian municipal registry, with line transcriptions.
Combines classical preprocessing with a Kraken recognizer fine-tuned on a pretrained model; inference runs on a laptop CPU without a GPU.
On manually corrected segmentation and a same-writer test setting, fine-tuning reduces character error rate from 14.53% to 0.50% and word error rate from 56.93% to 3.37%.
Residual recognition errors reduce downstream role-resolution F1 by about 9 points; results demonstrate feasibility only within the studied registry.
papers.selection_reason: Develops a frugal pipeline for handwritten text recognition that optimizes for CPU-only inference and memory usage, relevant to memory efficiency.
papers.title: Frugal Handwritten Text Recognition for Sub-Saharan Civil-Status Registers: A Smartphone-to-Records Pipeline with CPU-Only Inference
papers.tldr: A frugal smartphone-to-CPU pipeline can make handwritten civil-status records searchable within a single registry, but its strong accuracy has not been validated on unseen writers or sites.

papers.abstract: Humans are dexterous, but traditional data collection paradigms such as teleoperation, kinesthetic teaching, and wearable exoskeletons force humans to act through the robot embodiment, bottlenecking their dexterity. Retargeting can avoid this. However, existing methods purely translate kinematics and ignore the real-world contact dynamics essential for task success. We present CARD: Contact-Anchored Retargeting for Dexterous Manipulation, a simulator and object-free framework that retargets human demonstrations to robot actions by explicitly preserving contact force targets. CARD unifies human data sources including video, motion capture, and tactile gloves via a shared hand--contact representation and generates explicit contact force targets in addition to kinematics. To maintain these contact targets during hardware open-loop replay, CARD also introduces a tactile tracking controller. For video which does not contain an explicit tactile source, we present Vid-HACO, our video-to-contact model that sets a new state of the art. Across our video, glove, motion-capture data and the GRAB dataset, CARD maintains contact on $43$--$78\%$ of contact frames, while kinematic and object-aware retargeting methods maintain contact on $<10\%$ and $22.5\%$ of the frames respectively. Further, integrating our formulation into physics-based retargeting improves strict task success from 12\% to 32\% on GRAB dataset. Finally, we show that our tactile tracker is critical to reproduce demonstrated forces during hardware replay. These results establish that contact preservation via CARD is a scalable interface for transferring human dexterity to robots.
authors: Cunxi Dai, Botao He, Francois R Hogan, Wei Pan, Rao Fu, Wen-Han Hsieh, Ruoshi Liu, Jitendra Malik, Guanya Shi, Akash Sharma
bullets: Addresses the failure of kinematics-only retargeting to preserve the contact dynamics needed for successful manipulation.
Uses a shared hand–contact representation for video, motion capture, and tactile-glove data, generating both robot actions and contact-force targets.
Introduces Vid-HACO for inferring contacts from video and a tactile tracking controller for hardware open-loop replay.
Maintains contact on 43–78% of contact frames, compared with under 10% for kinematic and 22.5% for object-aware retargeting.
Improves strict task success on GRAB from 12% to 32% when integrated with physics-based retargeting; hardware results show tactile tracking is essential for reproducing forces.

figures.caption: Figure 2. CARD overview. Video, glove, and motion capture are converted into a unified hand–contact representation, a MANO mesh with one contact force target per semantic link (Sec. 3.1). Geometric initialization maps human joint angles to the robot skeleton, followed by contact-anchored retargeting that aligns the corresponding robot pads with the contact force targets (Sec. 3.3). Joint and contact force targets are replayed by a tactile tracking controller (Sec. 3.4) on hardware.

Figure 7. Replay on hardware. We show a series of snapshots of CARD trajectories replayed on the SHARPA Wave hand, Wuji Hand 2, and Unitree Dex3-1. The articulated Rubik’s cube and the bending deck of cards use the same pipeline as the rigid objects.

Figure 4. Contact-anchored vs. kinematic retargeting on two video clips. Per clip: the human source, CARD, DexPilot, AnyTeleopK, AnyTeleop-P, and CARD’s geometric initialization (init only), the columns of Tab. 1. The scanned object is for visualization only, and orange spheres are the contact force target. Kinematic baselines reach the object but do not track the contact.

Figure 3. Demonstration sources. We show some demonstration exmaples from monocular video (Vid-HACO contact), tactile glove (taxel pressure), and motion capture with the tactile glove (taxel pressure).

Figure 6. Tactile tracker ablation. We show the same trajectories replayed with (top) and without (bottom) tactile tracking. Tactile tracking maintains the desired contact forces, enabling stable grasps and successful task execution.

Figure 5. Tactile tracker. Each finger uses fingertip force feedback to track the desired contact force through an admittance loop whose curls form the joint offset ∆q, while feedforward torque directly applies the target force through the joint impedance controller (Appendix F).

Figure 13. Force tracking on the SHARPA Wave. (a) The index finger follows a 0–4N periodic contact force target against a fixed object: the measured force reaches the peaks within a few tenths of a newton and lags the target by about 0.2 s. The floor near 0.5N is the preload the state machine keeps while in contact. (b) A three-finger grasp with step targets during mustard bottle pick-up replay (thumb 9.7N, middle 7N, index 2.6N): the forces rise to their set-points within a second of the step, the thumb overshoots while the object settles, and release returns every finger to zero within about a second.

Figure 9. Initializer vs. solution on six video clips (hanger, can, cup, cards, marker, bowl): the geometric initializer qinit (left of each pair) seats the hand near the contact force target. The contact solve (right) closes the last millimeters. Orange spheres are the contact force target.
Figure 11. Semantic regions. The 18 regions shared by every source and robot, three per finger, the palm, the upper palm, and the pinky base, each with its region center of pressure.

Figure 12. Pseudo-object for video. Left to right: the contact force target of every frame of a video clip, mapped into the wrist frame and accumulated (registered contact cloud); their convex hull, the pseudo-object that serves as the collision field; the MANO hand at the peak-contact frame grasping the translucent hull; and the input video at the same frame. The first three panels are drawn in the camera frame of that frame, so their orientation matches the video.

Figure 8. Cross-embodiment transfer. Two GRAB demonstrations (rows) retargeted to SHARPA Wave, Wuji Hand 2, Unitree Dex3-1, and a parallel-jaw gripper (columns, after the human source). Only the semantic map changes. Orange spheres are the contact force targets.

Figure 10. Semantic maps. The human hand (left of each pair) and the robot it is mapped to, colored by semantic region: the same color marks a human region and the robot link that receives its contacts. Skin marks human regions the embodiment has no link for, and grey marks unmapped robot bodies. SHARPA Wave and Wuji Hand 2 take the 15 finger regions and the palm one-to-one, and SHARPA also the pinky base. The Unitree Dex3-1 folds middle, ring, and pinky onto its third finger, and the parallel-jaw gripper assigns the thumb to one jaw and the four fingers to the other.

Underline: best published baseline. On GRAB we additionally compare against ReGrind ported to SHARPA Wave, which takes the GRAB mesh as input. CARD uses only the contact-reconstructed pseudo-object (Fig. 12), and the GRAB mesh only to score penetration. The glove+motion capture gap combines the two beds’ medians weighted by anchor-frames.

Percent, threshold 0.52 except for the threshold-free AP. Vertex metrics are pooled over all vertices and frames. Frame F1 measures whether any vertex is in contact.

Table 4. Vid-HACO training data. Contact: what the hand touches. View: egocentric, third-person (exo, including ARCTIC’s eight allocentric cameras), or web images.

papers.selection_reason: Contact-anchored retargeting of human demonstrations to dexterous manipulation, including video-to-contact model; strongly relevant to robot manipulation and learning from human video.
papers.title: CARD: Contact-Anchored Retargeting for Dexterous Manipulation
papers.tldr: CARD retargets human dexterous manipulation to robots by preserving contact forces—not just hand kinematics—across multiple demonstration modalities.

papers.abstract: We present CPG-ENN, a trainable quadruped locomotion framework that combines explicit neural coordination with learned motion realization. A symmetry-based eight-neuron central pattern generator (CPG) supplies gait rhythms, while a pretrained, leg-shared execution neural network (ENN) maps rhythmic signals and trajectory parameters to joint-angle references without online inverse kinematics. A single feedback policy modulates six physically interpretable trajectory variables. The controller tracks planar velocity and yaw-rate commands across walk, trot, pace, bound, and pronk without gait-specific learned controllers or transitionspecific rewards. Simulation yields 99.39% transition success across all 20 directed gait pairs and all source-target speed combinations from {0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0} m/s. Ablations show high cross-gait transition feasibility without transition exposure; exposure mainly refines gait acquisition and velocity transients. Comparisons with AllGaits and Walk These Ways demonstrate accurate gait-speed regulation, and Unitree Go2 experiments validate five gaits and their transitions.
authors: Xiyan Liu, Yide Liu, Guoyong Mao, Shaoxing Qu
bullets: Targets robust velocity and yaw-rate control across walk, trot, pace, bound, and pronk.
Uses an eight-neuron CPG for gait rhythms and a pretrained leg-shared ENN to generate joint-angle references.
A feedback policy adjusts six physically interpretable trajectory variables.
Simulation achieved 99.39% transition success across 20 directed gait pairs and tested speed combinations.
Experiments on a Unitree Go2 validated all five gaits and their transitions; transition exposure mainly improved gait acquisition and velocity transients.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of the CPG–ENN framework. The CPG coordinates gait rhythms, and a single feedback policy adjusts six motion parameters. The pretrained ENN, shared across all four legs and fixed during policy training, maps rhythmic signals and motion parameters to joint-angle targets tracked by a proportional–derivative (PD) controller.

Fig. 5. Shared ENN architecture. Each leg’s 17-D input combines six global features (5-D gait encoding and body height) with eleven per-leg features. All four legs share one MLP, whose three joint-angle outputs per leg are concatenated into a 12-D reference.

Fig. 10. Gait–speed transition benchmark. (a–c) CPG–ENN; (d–f) AllGaits; (g–i) WTW. Columns show forward-speed RMSE over 0–2 s after switching, speed-pair success rate, and gait-pair success rate. Rows and columns within each matrix denote source and target conditions, respectively. Each speedpair cell summarizes supported gait transitions across switch times; each gait-pair cell summarizes speed pairs across switch times. RMSE uses only each method’s successful trials; success is defined in Sec. IV-A. Blue indicates lower RMSE or higher success; red indicates the opposite. Speed-matrix diagonals include gait changes at constant speed. Dashes mark excluded same-gait cases; hatching marks unsupported WTW transitions involving walk.
Fig. 1. Go2 gaits: walk, trot, pace, bound, and pronk. Red: flight phases and foot clearance (bound: 4.1 cm; pronk: 5 cm).

Fig. 8. Gait transitions: (a) walk→trot→pace→bound→pronk; (b) reverse sequence. Rows show forward velocity, policy height ht and measured base height, and roll/pitch. Solid curves show the mean, and shading indicates ±1 standard deviation across time-aligned rollouts with 10 randomly sampled sets of switch times. Vertical lines mark gait switches.

Fig. 9. Forward-speed tracking across five gaits: CPG–ENN (Ours), AllGaits, and WTW. (a–e) Walk, trot, pace, bound, and pronk. Dashed diagonals indicate ideal tracking. Filled/open markers denote in-distribution (ID)/out-of-distribution (OOD) commands relative to each controller’s gaitspecific training range. Crossed markers denote failed trials, displayed at zero; stars denote trials with no forward motion. WTW excludes walk (N/A).

Fig. 6. Velocity tracking under piecewise-random commands. Columns show walk, trot, pace, bound, and pronk; rows show body-frame forward velocity vbx, lateral velocity vby , and yaw rate ωbz . Dashed curves show commands; colored curves and shading indicate the temporal mean and ±1 standard deviation within centered sliding windows, without crossing command changes.

Fig. 4. Foot-trajectory parameters for offline ENN training. (a) Body height h, ground clearance gc, ground penetration gp, and step length ls in the sagittal plane. (b) Planar trajectory rotation by ψ about the +z-axis of the hip-abduction frame.

Fig. 7. Policy outputs versus target velocities (left to right): step length ls,t and height ht versus forward velocity; trajectory orientation ψt versus lateral velocity; and left–right step-length difference ∆ls,t versus yaw rate. Colors denote gaits.
Fig. 3. Phase relationships of the five gaits generated by the eight-neuron CPG. Numbers denote normalized leg-phase offsets within one gait cycle.

papers.selection_reason: Trainable CPG framework for quadruped locomotion with learned execution network; directly relevant to legged robot control.
papers.title: A Trainable CPG Framework for Quadruped Locomotion
papers.tldr: CPG-ENN combines a symmetry-based CPG, shared neural motion execution, and feedback control to produce and transition among five quadruped gaits without gait-specific transition training or online inverse kinematics.

papers.abstract: Differences in musculoskeletal morphology challenge policy reuse across individual models. Here we present MyoAcross, a framework that combines individual musculoskeletal model construction, morphology-conditioned policy learning and virtual model augmentation to enable muscle-driven reference-motion tracking without individual fine-tuning. Across 31 held-out individual models, MyoAcross achieves 99.24% completion and reduces tracking error by 22.60% relative to an unconditioned multilayer perceptron. Policy reuse extends to models of 22 held-out individuals constructed from single-image shape estimates, measured height and body mass, and, with asymmetry augmentation, to models with unilateral lower-limb shortening. Comparisons with measurements from 120 additional individuals show agreement in vertical ground reaction force waveforms and channel-dependent agreement between simulated muscle activations and electromyography. These results establish a common control framework for comparative simulations of movement across individual musculoskeletal models.
authors: Bozhao Wang, Yinglei Zhu, Zhengqing Li, Zhiyuan Zhang, Weiming Kang, Yiheng He, XinJun Liu, Senhao Hou, Huichan Zhao, Xiaoqiang Tang
bullets: Addresses policy reuse challenges caused by differences in musculoskeletal morphology.
Combines individualized model construction, morphology-conditioned policy learning, and virtual model augmentation.
Achieves 99.24% completion across 31 held-out models and reduces tracking error by 22.60% versus an unconditioned MLP.
Generalizes to single-image-based models and models with unilateral lower-limb shortening.
Simulations agree with measured ground-reaction forces and show channel-dependent agreement with electromyography.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the MyoAcross framework. a, The 64 source motions comprise 8 clips in each of 8 locomotion categories. CCW, counterclockwise; CW, clockwise. b, SKEL derives target skeletal measurements from SMPL body shape. Skeletal-guided regional scaling and mass calibration adapt the MyoFullBody template to construct 141 individual musculoskeletal models. Retargeting the source motions to each model produces 9,024 reference motions. c, Skeletal measurement fitting error across the 141 models. Template, Global fit and Regional fit denote the unchanged MyoFullBody template, fitting a single global scale factor and skeletal-guided regional scaling, respectively. Each point represents one model’s mean absolute error across 17 target skeletal measurements. Boxes span the interquartile range, central lines indicate medians, and whiskers extend to the most extreme values within 1.5 times the interquartile range. The inset enlarges the distribution for regional scaling. d, Original models of 110 training individuals and their virtual variants support policy learning in parallel simulations; 31 individuals are held out for evaluation. A morphology encoder maps model-derived morphology features to a learned morphology representation, which conditions the actor and critic through feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM). The actor generates muscle excitations, and training uses proximal policy optimization (PPO).

Figure 5: Virtual model augmentation supports policy reuse across individual and asymmetric models. a, Training schemes and evaluation protocols. V0 uses 110 original training models without virtual model augmentation. Standard augmentation (V10) and asymmetry augmentation each add 10 virtual models per training individual, yielding 1,210 training models. Asymmetry augmentation increases the asymmetry perturbation scale while retaining the other covariance settings. All schemes use the MyoAcross policy architecture and the same interaction budget, with evaluation at 15,000 training iterations on models of 31 held-out individuals and 64 reference motions per individual. b, Completion, reference coverage and tracking error on the original held-out models for V0 and V10 (standard augmentation). Faint points represent individual-model means over the 64 reference motions; squares (V0) and circles (V10) indicate means across individuals. Out-of-range points appear as left- or right-pointing triangles at the corresponding axis limits, labelled with their measured values. c, The same metrics for standard augmentation and asymmetry augmentation under unilateral lower-limb shortening. Thigh and shank regional scale factors are reduced together by 1%, 2.5%, 5% or 10% on either the left or right side, giving nine conditions including the original model at 0%. Each test model retains its corresponding original model’s reference motions. Circles and dashed lines denote standard augmentation (labelled Standard); triangles and solid lines denote asymmetry augmentation. Symbols indicate means across individuals. Error bars in b and c show 95% percentile bootstrap confidence intervals from 10,000 subject-level resamples of the 31 individuals. Tracking error includes executed frames from incomplete trials.

Figure 3: Policy reuse across held-out individual musculoskeletal models. a, Training schemes and shared evaluation protocol for the template-trained MLP (labelled Template MLP), unconditioned MLP, Concat and MyoAcross. The unconditioned MLP is trained across individual models without morphology input. The three policies trained across models share the same training model bank, reference motions and interaction budget. Each policy is evaluated at 15,000 training iterations on 31 held-out individual models, with 64 corresponding reference motions per model and no individual fine-tuning. b, Completion, reference coverage and tracking error. Faint points represent individual-model means over the 64 reference motions; diamonds indicate means across individuals. Detail views enlarge completion and reference coverage for the three policies trained across models. c, Paired comparisons of individual-model tracking error. Each point compares MyoAcross with the unconditioned MLP or Concat for the same individual. Dashed lines indicate equal error; points below these lines indicate lower error for MyoAcross. d, Tracking error across eight motion categories for the unconditioned MLP, Concat and MyoAcross. Each category contains eight motions per model; symbols indicate means across individuals. Dotted, dashed and solid lines connect category means for the unconditioned MLP, Concat and MyoAcross, respectively, as guides to the eye. Error bars in b and d show 95% percentile bootstrap confidence intervals from 10,000 subject-level resamples of the 31 individuals. Tracking error is measured in world coordinates without alignment and includes executed frames from incomplete trials.

Figure 4: Biomechanical assessment of walking across individual musculoskeletal models. a, Workflow from labelled motion-capture markers and recorded body mass to individual musculoskeletal simulation. MoSh++ estimates SMPL-H body shape from the markers. SKEL-derived skeletal measurements guide regional scaling of the MyoFullBody template, and mass calibration matches recorded body mass. Model-derived morphology features condition the pretrained policy, which generates muscle excitations to track reference motions. Eight medium-speed KIT walking motions are retargeted to each of 120 Gait120 individual models. All policies are evaluated at 15,000 training iterations, with policy parameters and normalization statistics fixed and without individual fine-tuning. b, Subject-level tracking error for MyoAcross, Concat and the unconditioned MLP (n = 120 subjects per policy). c, Simulated vertical ground reaction force (GRF) profiles for MyoAcross and measured level-walking profiles from the corresponding Gait120 subjects, shown separately for the left and right feet. Forces are normalized by body weight (BW), and complete stance phases are interpolated to a common phase grid. Lines and shaded bands show population means and standard deviations, respectively (n = 101 subjects for the left foot and 107 for the right). d, Subject-level GRF agreement, quantified by Pearson correlation (left) and BW-normalized root-mean-square error (RMSE; right). Metrics are calculated separately for each foot and averaged within subjects with valid bilateral measurements (n = 101 per policy). e, Subject-level agreement between simulated muscle activations and measured electromyography (EMG), expressed as the mean Pearson correlation across 12 EMG channels (n = 120 per policy). In b, d and e, points represent individual subjects. Boxes span the interquartile range, central lines indicate medians, and whiskers extend to the most extreme observations within 1.5 times the interquartile range. Waveform correlations are calculated within each subject before population aggregation. No correlation-maximizing temporal shifts are applied.

Figure 1: Muscle-driven control across individual musculoskeletal models. a, Four example models illustrate variation in body dimensions, body mass and bilateral symmetry: A, 1.70m and 65 kg; B, 1.86m and 73 kg; C, 1.62m and 75 kg; and D, 1.67m and 65 kg, with 10% unilateral lower-limb shortening on the right side. Colours identify the same models throughout the figure. b, Motion sequences illustrate reuse of the pretrained MyoAcross policy across the four models for slow, medium-speed and fast walking, backward walking, left and right turns, and counterclockwise and clockwise circling. Each sequence shows four frames per model. Small coloured curves indicate the corresponding movement paths. CCW, counterclockwise; CW, clockwise.

Figure 7: Single-image model construction and policy reuse. a, Human Skeleton and Mesh Recovery (HSMR) estimates SKEL shape parameters from a single photograph. The resulting skeletal measurements are calibrated to measured height and combined with recorded body mass to construct an individual musculoskeletal model. Source motions are retargeted to the constructed model, which supplies its own morphology features. Control uses the pretrained MyoAcross policy trained with standard augmentation (V10) at 15,000 training iterations, without individual fine-tuning; the snowflake denotes frozen policy weights. The individual shown in a is an author of this study and provided informed consent for publication of the image; the face is anonymized. b, Sequential medium-speed walking poses of the image-derived model of MoVi Subject 65. Red muscles and warm-coloured bones depict the policy-controlled model; translucent purple bones depict the corresponding reference motion. Each model–reference pair is translated together for horizontal presentation. c, Completion and tracking error for 88 image-derived models, each evaluated on 64 reference motions. The cohort includes 63 individuals from the original training split (blue), 22 from the held-out split (orange) and three outside the registered training and evaluation collections (grey). Each point represents one model’s completion and mean tracking error over the 64 reference motions; the inset enlarges the high-completion region. Tracking error includes executed frames from incomplete trials.

Figure 6: Policy sensitivity to morphology feature and reference-motion input errors. a, Input perturbation design for the unconditioned MLP, Concat and MyoAcross, evaluated on 31 held-out individual models with 64 reference motions per model. Physical models, policy parameters and normalization statistics remain fixed. Perturbations affect only the inputs supplied to the policy; initialization, reward computation, termination and scoring use the unperturbed reference motions. Each perturbation type includes an unperturbed baseline and three nonzero levels. b, Completion, reference coverage and tracking error under relative biases of 2%, 5% and 10% in morphology features. c, The same metrics under angular offsets of 2.5◦, 5◦ and 10◦ in lower-limb reference joint targets supplied to the policy. d, Combined morphology feature biases and reference-motion input offsets, paired as 2% with 2.5◦, 5% with 5◦, and 10% with 10◦. The unconditioned MLP receives no morphology features, so morphology feature perturbations leave its inputs unchanged in b, and only reference-motion input perturbations apply to it in d. Each nonzero level uses three perturbation-sign samples, with signs held fixed throughout each trial. Metrics are averaged over samples and motions within each individual, then equally across individuals. Symbols indicate these means; error bars show 95% percentile bootstrap confidence intervals from 10,000 subject-level resamples of the 31 individuals. Tracking error includes executed frames from incomplete trials.

papers.selection_reason: Morphology-conditioned generalist policy for muscle-driven control; transferable learning-based control across embodied models.
papers.title: A generalist policy for muscle-driven control across individual musculoskeletal models
papers.tldr: MyoAcross enables one muscle-driven control policy to track reference movements across diverse individual musculoskeletal models without per-model fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Attention Matching (AM) compacts a KV cache by keeping some keys per head, refitting their values and adding a bias to each kept key's logit. FlashAttention and vLLM's paged caches have no input for it. We fold the bias into the keys along one closed-form direction per head, fitted on context queries, giving a plain cache with AM's size and head dimension and the model's own query path; the output error is bounded by how far each query's projection on that direction is from 1. With equal per-head budgets, unmodified vLLM serves folded caches through a KV connector, matching Hugging Face's answers on all 51 Qwen3-4B questions and its greedy output on 180 of 200 Qwen3-14B LongBench samples. With equal budgets on QuALITY (Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, 8B, Llama-3.1-8B) and LongHealth (three Qwen3 models), the fold is within noise of AM's accuracy in 13 of 14 settings, with lower KL to the full cache than dropping the bias in all 12 where both ran. Under the published per-head budgets, on Qwen3-4B, its Instruct-2507 variant and Llama-3.1-8B, it is within noise of AM in 9 of 10, no longer beats dropping the bias in KL, and the two each win once in accuracy.
bullets: AM compresses KV caches by retaining selected keys, refitting values, and adding per-key logit biases—but standard kernels cannot consume those biases.
The proposed closed-form, per-head key adjustment absorbs each bias along one fitted direction, preserving the model’s normal query path and cache dimensions.
Unmodified vLLM serves the folded caches through a KV connector; outputs closely match Hugging Face and retain most greedy generations in the reported tests.
Across equal-budget evaluations, folding matches AM within noise in 13 of 14 settings and generally produces lower KL divergence than omitting the bias.
Under published per-head budgets, folding remains comparable to AM in 9 of 10 settings, though its KL advantage disappears.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The fold moves each retained key along one shared direction u by βj √ d, so a query near the hyperplane q · u = 1 (shaded) sees the logit shift βj (q · u) ≈ βj . Left: AM, a scalar bias βj per retained key kj . Right: the fold. For the orange open circle, a query far from the hyperplane, AM still adds βj while the fold scales it by q · u.

Figure 2: On the median head the default fold stays within about 5% of AM at every distance (the mean, worse far out, is in Appendix A.12). Median relative attention-output error over heads on Pride and Prejudice, on 512-query windows starting ∆ tokens after the compacted context. Thin lines: interquartile range over heads for keep (dotted) and AM (solid). Shaded: median AM error above median keep error.

Table 6: Folded caches of larger models served by unmodified vLLM 0.18.1 (default FlashAttention backend, bf16, one A100-80GB, random weights of the real architectures, 51 QuALITY questions). Capacity: concurrent requests that fit the KV pool with 256 generated tokens each. Decode: the highest rate measured, in tokens/s, at the batch in parentheses. At 5% the 14B model reaches vLLM’s limit of 256 concurrent sequences, and at 10% its pool holds 255, one short of it. The ×2 and ×4 rows repeat each article to lengthen the context. 14B peak rates are measured at batch ≤ 128 and are lower bounds. Fold columns at the native length are injected caches; at the longer lengths they are plain prompts of the fold’s length, which decode at the same rate.

Table 7: Logit terms of compaction and merging methods. Static: one scalar per cache entry, the same for every query, which the fold handles. Fold applies: structurally, since the fold has been tested only on AM, one capped log-count merge and two of KV-Surgeon’s compactors.

Table 2: On QuALITY no fold−AM accuracy difference in these settings is beyond noise. Fold−AM and drop−fold: paired differences with their 95% bootstrap intervals over the 30 articles below them, accuracy differences in points. Bold: beyond noise. KL>1: questions with KL above 1 under drop and under the fold. 534 questions. Each column’s AM fit was chosen on the test set for AM’s lower KL (Setup). Drop was not run with the AM-style fit on QuALITY, so the Qwen3-1.7B columns have none, and Table 13 gives drop under our fit.

Table 3: On LongHealth the fold keeps AM’s accuracy gain over keep on Qwen3-4B and 8B and loses it on Qwen3-1.7B at 10%. Our AM fit throughout. Layout as in Table 2, with intervals over the 20 patients (398 questions).

Table 8: The fold under each model’s published per-head budgets: level with AM in nine of the ten cells, and below it on Llama-3.1-8B LongHealth at 5%. AM-style fit with the published NNLS weighting, bf16; Qwen3-4B QuALITY on a Tesla T4, the rest on an A100. Below each paired difference, its 95% bootstrap interval over the 30 articles (534 questions) or 20 patients (398); accuracy and agreement in %, differences in points. Bold: beyond noise.

Table 13: QuALITY under our AM fit, on all four models at 20% and 2% and on Qwen3-1.7B also at 10% and 5%: the fold’s KL is below AM’s beyond noise only on Qwen3-8B at 2%, above it on Qwen31.7B at 20% and 10%, and level elsewhere. ∆: fold minus AM, with the 95% bootstrap interval over the 30 articles below it; accuracy in %, ∆acc in points. 534 questions; full-cache accuracy 55.6, 69.1, 73.0 and 71.3% (55.6 here and 55.8 in Table 2: run-to-run variation, Appendix A.10).

Table 18: With launch cost removed by CUDA graphs, AM’s bias costs little in single-sequence decode and most at batch-8 decode. Top: 512–4096 cached entries, which covers our compacted caches. Bottom: 16k–32k. CUDA-graphed per-call times, one run per model. papers.abstract: Agentic life-science benchmarks give an agent evidence about a named entity and score an answer against a recorded outcome. That score tests reasoning over evidence only if the evidence, rather than the name, determines the answer. We examine this distinction by varying identity and evidence independently on a clinical-outcome benchmark and published tasks from Biomni and LAB-Bench. Blinding identity matters little when a prompt contains a decisive sequence or passage. It matters a great deal when the prompt is mostly a name and candidate list (0.742 named versus 0.082 blinded; chance 0.093). Across 96 LAB-Bench LitQA2 questions, the gap increases under one fixed passage-redaction scheme (+0.000 to +0.135; per-instance slope +0.147, p= 0.004). On the clinical benchmark, a no-evidence recall probe matches prediction accuracy and recovers a database-specific programme count. So, we argue that benchmarks intended to measure evidence-dependent reasoning should report identity-blinded results, retrieval telemetry, and positive controls.
bullets: The study independently varies entity identity and provided evidence on a clinical-outcome benchmark and Biomni/LAB-Bench tasks.
Identity blinding has little effect when prompts contain decisive sequences or passages, but greatly reduces performance for name-and-candidate-list prompts (0.742 to 0.082; chance 0.093).
Across 96 LAB-Bench LitQA2 questions, performance gaps increased under passage redaction, with a reported per-instance slope of +0.147 (p=0.004).
A no-evidence recall probe on the clinical benchmark matched prediction accuracy and recovered a database-specific programme count.
The authors recommend identity-blinded evaluation, retrieval telemetry, and positive controls for benchmarks measuring evidence-dependent reasoning.

papers.abstract: Multimodal forgery detection is commonly studied under a static assumption: training attacks are expected to approximate those encountered after deployment. This assumption becomes increasingly fragile as generators, editing systems, and multimodal large language models continually introduce new forgery mechanisms and forensic evidence. We formulate this problem as attack-incremental continual multimodal forgery detection, where the binary real/fake interface remains fixed while emerging attacks must be learned without forgetting previous ones. We introduce Fable-Bench, which organizes attack evolution through complementary joint-modality, text-side, and image-side protocols. We further propose ARISE (Authentic Reference-Informed Stability Enhancement), motivated by the open-ended forged class and the comparatively reusable geometry of authentic content. ARISE fits a real-only Gaussian mixture model to projected authentic replay representations as a compact historical reference. Meanwhile, the proposed Gaussian-Responsibility-Aware Stability Preservation (GRASP) derives a sample-adaptive anisotropic metric that strongly constrains historically stable representation directions while retaining plasticity elsewhere. Our Vulnerability-Aware Replay (VAR) further estimates stage-wise vulnerability from authentic-density degradation, forged-to-authentic boundary confusion, and authentic-mode occupancy drift, then assigns bounded replay emphasis to fragile stages. All adaptive signals are obtained from training-time replay statistics, while inference uses only the original multimodal backbone and binary classification head. Experiments across three attack-evolution protocols and multiple detector architectures demonstrate improved historical retention and final average performance over representative continual-learning baselines.
authors: Yuchen Zhang, Yaxiong Wang, Yujiao Wu, Lianwei Wu, Qi Zhang, Li Zhu, Chaofeng Dong, Le Wu, Zhedong Zheng

Introduces Fable-Bench with joint-modality, text-side, and image-side attack-evolution protocols.

Uses VAR to prioritize replay for stages vulnerable to authentic-density degradation, boundary confusion, or mode drift.
Across three protocols and multiple detector architectures, ARISE improves historical retention and final average performance over representative continual-learning baselines.

papers.abstract: Humanoid behavior foundation models (BFMs) provide reusable whole-body motion priors: given a kinematic reference, they generate coordinated joint commands for motion replay, teleoperation, and VLA control. However, trained primarily on flat-ground motion, BFMs lack an explicit mechanism to adapt foot placement, swing clearance, and contact timing to local terrain. Many terrain-aware BFM approaches address this limitation by retraining or fine-tuning the tracker together with perception, incurring substantial data and computation costs while coupling ordinary tracking to the perception pathway. To bridge this gap, we propose GRAFT, a geometry-aware residual adaptation framework for frozen behavior trackers. GRAFT preserves the BFM parameters and motion-reference interface, while a lightweight adapter adds terrain-conditioned corrections only to lower-body execution targets. The adapter is trained with task and foot-geometry rewards, regularized to suppress unnecessary corrections on flat ground, and distilled from privileged terrain observations to onboard depth. Because the frozen BFM already provides whole-body reference tracking and nominal locomotion, GRAFT reduces terrain learning to a focused execution-adaptation problem. We instantiate the framework on four frozen trackers and evaluate stairs, gaps, and platforms in simulation. We further validate it through real-world deployment on a Unitree G1, where the adapted SONIC tracker traverses terrain with onboard depth and unmodified references.
authors: Liang Li, Guoyao Zhang, Xingyu Chen, Sikai Wu, Qianyang Wu, Yuhang Lin, Renjing Xu, Mingliang Zhou, Diyun Xiang
bullets: Targets missing terrain adaptation in flat-ground-trained behavior foundation models, especially foot placement, swing clearance, and contact timing.
Adds a terrain-conditioned residual adapter that modifies only lower-body execution targets while preserving the frozen tracker and reference interface.
Trains with task and foot-geometry rewards, suppresses unnecessary corrections on flat ground, and distills privileged terrain information to onboard depth.
Evaluated on four frozen trackers across stairs, gaps, and platforms in simulation.
Demonstrated real-world terrain traversal on a Unitree G1 using the adapted SONIC tracker, onboard depth, and unmodified references.

papers.abstract: Web fashion images support applications such as visual product search and consumer-to-shop matching, yet their visual heterogeneity makes reliable garment segmentation challenging. Despite advances in promptable segmentation, autonomously identifying and correcting garment-specific errors without human-provided spatial prompts remains difficult. We propose GarmentSegAgent, an autonomous framework that integrates semantic planning, spatial execution, and visual evaluation through iterative textual self-refinement. At its core, we introduce CAST (Constrained Attribution-guided Selective TextGrad), which connects visual error attribution with targeted textual optimization. CAST identifies instruction components responsible for segmentation errors, selectively updates them through textual gradients, and validates the resulting instructions against garment-specific constraints. This enables image-specific error correction at inference time while keeping the underlying foundation models frozen. Experiments on DeepFashion2, ModaNet, and Fashionpedia demonstrate consistent improvements in region overlap and boundary accuracy, alongside more reliable refinement than conventional TextGrad. By enabling visual feedback to guide controlled instruction updates, GarmentSegAgent offers a promising direction for autonomous garment understanding, with potential applications in scalable fashion content analysis, visual retrieval, and consumer-to-shop matching on the Web.
authors: Jia Chen, Chao Huang, Xinrong Hu, Mingdi Huang, Ruyang Zhao, Jun Bai
bullets: Addresses unreliable garment segmentation caused by heterogeneous web fashion imagery and the need for spatial prompts.
Combines semantic planning, spatial execution, and visual evaluation in an iterative self-refinement framework.
Introduces CAST, which attributes errors to instruction components, selectively optimizes them, and checks garment-specific constraints.
Evaluations on DeepFashion2, ModaNet, and Fashionpedia show consistent gains in region overlap and boundary accuracy, with more reliable refinement than conventional TextGrad.
Foundation models remain frozen; refinement occurs at inference time through image-specific instruction updates.

papers.abstract: Video models answer from sampled frames and may miss the decisive moment. A common remedy is to commit to an answer, re-examine the video, and confirm or revise it, a loop now mainly learned with reinforcement learning (RL). We find that RL erodes the initial answer, a phenomenon we term confidence erosion, where confidence means the label-verified reliability of the initial answer instead of self-reported certainty: because errors can be repaired later, a correct initial answer earns less reward, and the initial answer stalls even as the final answer's gain over it rises. We propose the principle confident first, reflective second: the initial answer must stay reliable on its own, above a floor set by a reference policy, and reflection may only add to it. Our method, CoFire, implements this principle with one mechanism for each erosion channel: reward incentives, parameter drift, and gradient interference. CoFire reaches 67.0% mean accuracy on Video-MME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench, 1.7 points above the strongest compared 7B method, and improves initial-answer and final accuracy over outcome-reward RL by 4.1 and 3.7 points on average: a stronger initial answer carries through to a stronger final one.
authors: Zihao Lin, Jingyuan Liu, Yucheng Zhang, Yuguang Yao, Lifu Huang
bullets: RL-based reflection can cause confidence erosion: correct initial answers are undervalued because later correction is rewarded.
CoFire enforces a reference-policy reliability floor for the initial answer and allows reflection to add, not replace, its value.
It addresses reward incentives, parameter drift, and gradient interference as sources of erosion.
CoFire achieves 67.0% mean accuracy across Video-MME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench, 1.7 points above the strongest compared 7B method.
Compared with outcome-reward RL, it improves initial and final accuracy by 4.1 and 3.7 points on average.

papers.abstract: We propose Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion-Uni (NLD-Uni), a unified discrete diffusion large language model (DLLM) for visual understanding and generation tasks. Compared with prior unified diffusion models, NLD-Uni introduces two major innovations. First, we propose a unified cross-paradigm on-policy distillation (OPD) framework that successfully transfers the visual understanding ability of autoregressive VLMs and visual generation ability of continuous flow models, to a unified DLLM. Second, NLD-Uni incorporates a novel progressive self-refining diffusion process that gradually corrupts each token across multiple steps during training, as opposed to adopting the conventional masked diffusion formulation that directly corrupts a clean image token to an uninformative mask token. At inference, this design allows NLD-Uni to make intermediate commit to a token, enabling progressive self-refinement for better visual quality. Through extensive experiments, we show that NLD-Uni achieves state-of-the-art performance among unified DLLMs on diverse tasks including visual question-answering, multi-modal reasoning, object grounding, text-to-image generation, and image editing.
authors: Shufan Li, Hanrong Ye, Greg Heinrich, Yonggan Fu, Haotian Zhang, Sifei Liu, Aditya Grover, Pavlo Molchanov
bullets: Transfers capabilities from autoregressive vision-language models and continuous flow models into one unified diffusion model.
Uses cross-paradigm on-policy distillation to train visual understanding and generation abilities.
Introduces progressive self-refining diffusion, gradually corrupting tokens instead of replacing them directly with masks.
Enables intermediate token commitments during inference for progressive visual refinement.
Reports state-of-the-art unified-DLLM performance across VQA, multimodal reasoning, object grounding, text-to-image generation, and image editing.

figures.caption: Figure 2 | NLD-Uni supports diverse multimodal tasks by adopting an Elastic-MoT architecture with three elastic views of a single model. The VLM view uses the 8B understanding branch; the T2I view combines 4B understanding parameters with the 8B generation branch; and the interleaved view uses both full branches (16B). Each view loads only the parameters needed for its task. Yellow and green blocks denote understanding and generation layers, gray blocks indicate omitted layers, and blue arrows denote joint attention. Representative examples demonstrate visual reasoning, object grounding, text-to-image synthesis, and image editing guided by reasoning and localization.

Figure 3 | Overall Framework of NLD-Uni. NLD-Uni is a unified diffusion model whose input and output are both multimodal. Images in the input stream are represented by both continuous embeddings of a semantic encoder and discrete tokens of a VQ encoder. Images in the output stream are represented solely using VQ codes. NLD-Uni is trained to predict the clean token distribution given partially masked inputs. For image generation, we incorporate an intermediate masking state.

Figure 6 | On-Policy Distilling from Continuous Flow Models. Given a student output, we generate a teacher-refined output by adding noise to the student sample and re-denoise it with the teacher model. For reference, we also show an independent teacher generation. We observe that the teacher’s refinements are closely aligned to the student’s output while having better visual fidelity and source image preservation.

Left: AR on-policy distillation loss aligns the student’s AR distribution with a frozen AR teacher. Right: Consistency loss aligns the student’s diffusion view to its own AR view. The diffusion prediction is obtained by evaluating the student on randomly masked AR rollouts. We apply stop-grad to the AR target.

Figure 10 | The design of SBD formulation. (Left) SBD adopts a two-stream training process that concatenates clean blocks and noisy blocks in the sequence dimension. It applies AR CE loss on the clean blocks, and diffusion CE loss on the noisy blocks. (Right) SBD models use a specialized attention mask with a causal mask in the clean blocks and block-bidirectional mask in the noisy blocks. Each noisy block can attend to all other tokens in itself and all tokens in preceding clean blocks.

papers.abstract: We study 3D visual grounding in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), where a referring expression should identify a target object as both a rendered 2D mask and a set of explicit 3D Gaussians. Prior methods typically extract 3D targets by applying heuristic thresholding or top-ratio filtering to dense primitive-level relevance scores. However, these scores often vary substantially across scenes and prompts, making such heuristics sensitive and leading to unstable targeting. ClusterSplat addresses this by reframing 3D target selection as cluster-level selection over scene-adaptive candidates. The method first learns instance-aware Gaussian features, forms feature-aware seed voxels, and merges neighboring seed voxels when a description-length criterion decreases, producing a scene-specific set of cluster candidates. Given a referring expression, a query-conditioned cluster scorer ranks the cluster candidates with a lightweight MLP, and the selected cluster directly defines the explicit 3D target while its cluster score is rendered for the 2D mask. On ScanRefer, ClusterSplat achieves the best rendered 2D segmentation and explicit 3D target metrics among the compared 3DGS baselines. It also obtains the best average Ref-LERF scores, supporting the same trend under fine-grained referring descriptions. On ScanNet v2 class name queries, ClusterSplat achieves the strongest rendered 2D results and the highest 3D matching accuracy, while maintaining competitive 3D IoU. Our project page is available at https://jaesung8.github.io/clustersplat/ .
authors: Jaesung Lee, Hyeontaek Hwang, Gabriel Manalu, Daeyoung Kim
bullets: Targets referring expressions as both rendered 2D masks and explicit sets of 3D Gaussians.
Learns instance-aware features, builds feature-aware seed voxels, and merges them using a description-length criterion.
Uses a query-conditioned lightweight MLP to rank cluster candidates and select the 3D target.
Reports the best results among compared 3DGS baselines on multiple 2D and 3D grounding metrics across ScanRefer and ScanNet v2.
Scope: performance is evaluated on referring descriptions and class-name queries in indoor 3D scenes.

figures.caption: Figure 2: ClusterSplat overview. The pipeline first performs Instance-Aware Gaussian Feature Learning and Scene-Adaptive Clustering: it learns instance-aware Gaussian features, forms featureaware seed voxels, and merges them into scene-adaptive cluster candidates. It then performs QueryConditioned Cluster Scoring: the referring expression conditions the cluster tokens, and the MLP scorer ranks the candidates to select the Top-1 cluster as the explicit 3D target. Finally, Cluster-Level Mask Rendering assigns the selected cluster scores to Gaussians and renders a 2D mask supervised by the mask loss.

Figure 3: Qualitative examples on ScanRefer. Each row shows a referring expression with rendered masks and top-down 3D selections. ClusterSplat localizes the referred object more coherently and reduces distractor support compared with score-discretized baselines.

Figure 4: Illustration of how we prompt GPT-4.1 to obtain five diverse pseudo-captions for a trainingframe instance mask. The specific view shows two tables, and the mask/bounding-box cue enables GPT-4.1 to generate captions that are descriptive and localized to the selected instance.

Figure 5: Sensitivity of primitive-level target extraction to the top-ratio hyperparameter. We evaluate the 3D targeting performance (mIoU) of OpenGaussian [6] and Dr.Splat [10] across 10 ScanNet v2 scenes by sweeping the selection ratio ρ ∈ [0.01, 0.10]. The optimal ratio is highly scenedependent, and the performance often drops sharply away from the peak, indicating that primitivelevel score discretization requires careful calibration for robust open-vocabulary 3D targeting. This motivates cluster-level Top-1 (argmax) selection, which relies on relative cluster ranking rather than absolute score thresholds.

Figure 6: Ref-LERF qualitative results. Each row shows a fine-grained referring description with attributes, surface cues, or spatial relations. ClusterSplat produces compact masks that better follow the referred object across the shown examples.

Figure 7: ScanRefer qualitative results on the first five evaluation scenes. Each row shows the groundtruth mask, rendered mask predictions, and top-down 3D target selections for a referring expression. The examples illustrate compact, object-aligned support with reduced distractor responses.

Figure 8: ScanRefer qualitative results on the remaining five evaluation scenes. The examples cover attribute-based and spatial referring expressions, showing consistent 2D mask concentration and top-down 3D target localization across the evaluation scenes.

Figure 9: Top-down ScanNet v2 19-class visualization across all 10 evaluation scenes. The first two columns compare annotated ScanNet v2 point-cloud labels with Gaussian pseudo labels, followed by class-level predictions from 3DGS baselines and ClusterSplat.

papers.abstract: Do vision-language models (VLMs) share our ability to communicate visually? We share preliminary findings, starting from a surprising observation: simple visual symbols like a red heart can strongly influence model behavior on seemingly unrelated tasks, such as steering models towards recursive solutions on simple coding problems. Notably, this steering effect is largely implicit, as models' direct interpretations and thinking traces about visual symbols diverge substantially from their observed behavior. In visual communication between models, this leads to a generation--interpretation gap: while models tend to send shape primitives that they (and humans) find intuitive, these visual cues often fail to steer other models. In further communication games involving abstract concepts and stories, models can creatively use visuals to transmit meaning to one another, although some communications remain non-intuitive to humans. These findings reveal that VLMs might be capable of rich, creative, and visually-grounded communication, but their interpretation and production of visual meaning diverges from human conventions in surprising ways. Together this work highlights both the promise and challenges of visual communication between humans and VLMs.
authors: Alexa R. Tartaglini, Zhengxuan Wu, Thadd\"aus Wiedemer, Martin Wattenberg, Been Kim, Yuxuan Li
bullets: Simple symbols, such as a red heart, can implicitly steer VLM behavior toward recursive solutions on coding tasks.
Models’ stated interpretations and reasoning about symbols may differ substantially from the behavior those symbols induce.
Visual communication between models shows a generation–interpretation gap: intuitive shape-based cues often fail to steer other models.
In communication games, VLMs can creatively convey abstract concepts and stories, though some messages are unintuitive to humans.
The work highlights both the promise and challenges of human–VLM visual communication.

figures.caption: Figure 1 | Simple visual symbols steer model behavior on a coding problem. A) Evaluation methodology. We append an image of a simple colored shape (e.g., a blue triangle) to a coding prompt (binary tree traversal) and instruct the model to look at the image while solving the problem. Across 𝑛 sampled generations, we compute the proportion of recursive solutions 𝑃(recursion) and measure the visual steering effect Δ𝑃(recursion) as the change in 𝑃(recursion) relative to the no-image baseline. B) Visual symbols steer toward recursion far more strongly than random noise or matching text descriptions. Star-patterned bars show average Δ𝑃(recursion) for Gemini 3.1 Pro and Claude Opus 4.7’s top three steering symbols (symbols shown below each bar), which nearly matches the effect of directly instructing the model to use recursion (light gray bars). By contrast, matching text descriptions (e.g., “an image of a pink heart”; hatched bars) and Gaussian noise images (dark gray bars) induce minimal to no steering. C) Models display different steering landscapes over a library of 288 visual symbols. Heatmaps show Δ𝑃(recursion) across 12 colors (𝑥-axis) for each model’s 8 highest- and 6 lowest-steering shapes (𝑦-axis; full heatmaps in Sec. B.2.1).

Figure 2 | Models generate creative visualizations to communicate concepts, but exhibit a generation–interpretation gap. A) Communication game methodology. A sender model generates a visualization to convey a target coding strategy (e.g., recursion), concept, or story to a receiver model, refining its visualization through multi-turn feedback. B) Multi-turn feedback enables models to converge on effective visualizations. Bars show the average number of turns to succeed using visual symbols (top bars) versus free-form PIL drawings (bottom bars). Symbol-based communication requires more communication turns to align sender and receiver than free-form drawing. C) Senders choose intuitive symbols to communicate recursion rather than the symbols that actually steer them. Top symbols selected by Claude Opus 4.7 as a sender (left, sized by selection frequency) compared to the symbols with the largest empirical steering effect Δ𝑃(recursion) (right). D) Models construct creative scenes using free-form code and abstract symbols. Examples show successful visualizations generated by Gemini 3.1 Pro to communicate the concept “art” (left) and a threesentence story about a knight removing a thorn from a dragon’s paw (right).

Figure 3 | Visual steering associations diverge from both human intuition and models’ own explicit interpretations. A) Optimizing symbol communication for model receivers reduces human legibility, whereas free-form drawings remain interpretable. Bars show human accuracy (%) at identifying the target coding strategy (recursion vs. iteration), concept, or story from visualizations on the first communication turn (blue; unsuccessful for the receiver) versus the final turn (red; successful), using visual symbols (top bars) or free-form PIL drawings (bottom bars). B) Models’ direct interpretations of visual symbols poorly predict their empirical steering effects. Each point represents one or more of the 288 visual symbols (sized by count), plotting the proportion of trials in which a model explicitly classifies the symbol as “recursion” (𝑥-axis) against its behavioral steering effect Δ𝑃(recursion) (𝑦-axis).

Figure 22 | Steering results for all binary choice semantic pairs. The labels along the 𝑥-axes indicate the direction of steering away from each model’s unsteered baseline preference (from 𝐴 to 𝐵), with icons below each bar showing the visual symbols that drive the shift.

Figure 4 | All shapes and colors in the visual symbol library. Each symbol shows an example of the color and shape indicated by the label; the library includes all 288 combinations of the 12 × 24 colors and shapes.

Figure 5 | Full steering heatmaps for inorder binary tree traversal, where the model is instructed to look at the image (“Explicit image instruction prompt,” Appendix B.1). Each heatmap is one model; rows are the 12 colors, and columns are the 24 shapes. Cell values are the steering effect (i.e. delta Δ𝑃(recursion) relative to that model’s text-only baseline), on a diverging scale from −1 (red, towards iteration) to +1 (blue, towards recursion).

Figure 6 | Recursion steering heatmaps aggregated across baseline-iterative coding problems: 𝑁 = 4 problems for Claude Opus 4.7, 𝑁 = 3 for Gemini 3.1 Pro, and 𝑁 = 4 for GPT-5.4. Because all problems for each model have baseline iterative solutions, the cell values show steering towards or away from recursion. Axes and color scale are as in Figure 5.

Figure 7 | Iteration steering heatmaps aggregated across baseline-recursive coding problems: 𝑁 = 2 problems for Claude Opus 4.7, 𝑁 = 3 for Gemini 3.1 Pro, and 𝑁 = 2 for GPT-5.4. Because all problems for each model have baseline recursive solutions, the cell values show steering towards or away from iteration. Axes and color scale are as in Figure 5.

Figure 15 | Placing images at the end of context rather than the beginning changes which symbols steer for recursion. A) The steering effect at the start and end of context decouple most strongly for Claude Opus 4.7 and GPT-5.4. The 𝑦-axis shows the steering effect of visual symbols when placed at the start of context, while the 𝑥-axis shows the end of context. Gemini 3.1 Pro remains somewhat correlated. B) Top steering symbols appear to shift from more geometric to more semantic. Lines show the steering effect for four individual symbols when placed at the start, middle, and end of context (symbols are visualized next to their lines). Claude Opus 4.7 and GPT-5.4 exhibit a marked shift where more intuitively “recursive” shapes like branching arrows or spirals begin to exert the strongest steering effect. Interestingly, this appears to line up with these models’ interpretations and choices in communication games. Gemini 3.1 Pro’s top steering shapes remain largely the same.
Figure 23 | Cross-model correlations (Pearson 𝑟) in visual steering on inorder binary tree traversal. Shapes are generally more correlated than colors.

Figure 31 | Example free-form vs. symbol library visualizations for short story communication. Visualizations generated by A) Claude Opus 4.7, B) Gemini 3.1 Pro, and C) GPT-5.4. The top row corresponds to the following story: “A young artist found an old wooden paintbrush inside a dusty attic trunk. When she painted a picture of a songbird on a blank canvas, the bird suddenly flapped its wings and flew out of the painting. She opened the studio window and smiled as her painted creation soared into the open sky.”; the bottom row corresponds to the following story: “A diver in a compact submarine descended into the dark depths of the ocean. Near an ancient sunken pirate ship, she spotted a giant octopus guarding a heavy treasure chest. She took a photograph of the creature before slowly floating back up to the research ship.” Interestingly, models appear to arrive at largely similar layouts for visualizing stories.

Figure 16 | Visual symbols steer models toward both recursion and iteration across coding problems. Bars show the mean shift away from each model’s unsteered baseline strategy (±1 SEM across problems and top-3 symbols, shown below each bar). A) Aggregated recursion steering across baseline-iterative problems (𝑁 = 4 for Claude Opus 4.7, 𝑁 = 3 for Gemini 3.1 Pro, and 𝑁 = 4 for GPT-5.4). B) Aggregated iteration steering across baseline-recursive problems (𝑁 = 2 for Claude Opus 4.7, 𝑁 = 3 for Gemini 3.1 Pro, and 𝑁 = 2 for GPT-5.4). On baseline-recursive problems, Claude Opus 4.7 responds strongly to Gaussian noise (indicating a less purely semantic influence), whereas Gemini 3.1 Pro and GPT-5.4 maintain the selective visual-symbol steering pattern from Sec. 3.

Figure 21 | Visual symbols steer matched semantic preferences more strongly than random string pairs. Bars show the mean shift away from each model’s unsteered baseline preference (𝑁 = 9 pairs per split). A) Steering on matched semantic pairs, like “summer” vs. “winter.” B) Steering on length-6 random strings.
Figure 24 | Recursion steering results for smaller models.

Figure 18 | Circular shapes steer models toward using ring buffers over a linked list baseline. Box plots depict the steering effect (Δ𝑃(Ring Buffer)) driven by individual shapes across doubly linked list vs. ring buffer coding problems (𝑁 = 3), computed the same way as Fig. 17. GPT-5.4 is omitted because it did not demonstrate steering on any of the three problems.

Figure 19 | Writing style steering heatmaps aggregated across 𝑁 = 5 topics for optimistic vs. melancholic (Claude Opus 4.7, top) and verbose vs. terse (Gemini 3.1 Pro, bottom). Warm colors tend to steer Claude Opus 4.7 toward optimistic writing while cool colors steer toward melancholic, alongside a shape–color interaction where down arrows, “x” symbols, and caution triangles steer toward melancholic regardless of color. Gemini 3.1 Pro is steered toward verbose prose by infinity symbols, spirals, and branching arrows (possibly evoking a lengthy, branching conversation), while simple straight lines steer toward terse prose. Axes and color scale are as in Figure 5.

Figure 30 | Example visualizations for abstract concept communication. A) Zero-shot communication. Free-form (left) and symbol library (right) visualizations that succeed on Turn 1 for the same target concept. B) Multi-turn communication. First-turn vs. final-turn free-form visualizations across refinement trajectories. Edits across turns are sometimes a bit opaque; i.e. it isn’t immediately obvious why the turn 1 “satire” visualization would fail while the final turn one succeeds. C) Unsuccessful visualizations. Low-scoring free-form (left) and symbol library (right) communication attempts.

Figure 29 | Example free-form visualizations for recursion vs. iteration steering. A) Multiturn communication. Three-turn refinement trajectories toward recursion, with receiver steering proportions (𝑛 = 10) shown below each image. B) Successful & unsuccessful visualizations. Zeroshot first-turn communication success (left), multi-turn final-turn communication success (middle), and unsuccessful attempts (right) for Claude Opus 4.7 (top), Gemini 3.1 Pro (middle row), and GPT-5.4 (bottom).

Figure 8 | The steering effect of text captions largely does not match that of images. A) Top three steering captions for each model. The colors of the text show the corresponding color. Captions are formatted as, e.g., “An image of a brown spiral.” B) The steering effect of captions decouples from the steering effect of images of visual symbols.
Figure 10 | Naturalistic animal images (𝑁 = 20) used to measure the ImageNet steering baseline.

Figure 11 | Disrupting shape structure via pixel shuffling disrupts visual steering at high enough percentages. A) Example pixel-shuffled stimuli. Progressive pixel shuffling (0% to 100%) preserves global color proportions while progressively destroying shape geometry and adding low-level noise (shown for the pink heart and blue triangle). B) Recursion proportion 𝑃(recursion) across pixel shuffle levels. Lines show 𝑃(recursion) on inorder binary tree traversal across five symbols (visualized next to their lines) for Claude Opus 4.7, Gemini 3.1 Pro, and GPT-5.4.

Figure 12 | Visual steering is highly sensitive to symbol orientation. A) Example rotated stimuli. Visual symbols rotated from 0◦ (prototypical upright orientation, outlined in bold) to 315◦ in 45◦ increments. B) Recursion proportion 𝑃(recursion) across rotation angles. Lines show 𝑃(recursion) on inorder binary tree traversal across the three orientation-dependent symbols for Claude Opus 4.7, Gemini 3.1 Pro, and GPT-5.4.
