papers.abstract: Traditional multiple sclerosis (MS) image analysis has primarily focused on retrospectively detecting and segmenting lesions. This study investigates whether baseline FLAIR MRI can identify regions at risk for future lesion formation beyond population-level spatial patterns. We introduce FORESEE-MS, an evaluation protocol that uses a fold-specific population-prior atlas as a baseline and assesses predictions using pooled voxel-level discrimination (AUROC and AUPRC) and within-patient lesion localization (Recall@Top-K%), with patient-level bootstrap confidence intervals. We evaluated five deep learning models (3D U-Net, Attn+ResBlock+VAE, ViT, and two SwinUNETR variants) using 5-fold cross-validation on 39 subjects from the MSSEG-2 dataset. The atlas achieved the highest pooled voxel-level AUROC and AUPRC, with no deep learning model reliably outperforming it on either metric. However, the 3D U-Net and Attn+ResBlock+VAE achieved higher mean voxel-level within-patient Recall@Top-K% than the atlas at all evaluated thresholds, although most paired confidence intervals for the differences included zero. These findings suggest that baseline FLAIR may contain patient-specific predictive information, but in this small cohort, it remains uncertain whether this information improves lesion forecasting beyond a population-prior atlas.
authors: Maryam Akhavan Aghdam, Sudip Mittal, Noorbakhsh Amiri Golilarz, Shahram Rahimi
bullets: Tests prospective lesion forecasting rather than retrospective lesion detection or segmentation.
Compares five deep learning models with a fold-specific population-prior atlas using voxel-level discrimination and within-patient localization metrics.
Evaluates models with 5-fold cross-validation on 39 subjects from the MSSEG-2 dataset.
The atlas performed best on pooled voxel-level AUROC and AUPRC, while 3D U-Net and Attn+ResBlock+VAE had higher mean within-patient Recall@Top-K%.
Most paired confidence intervals included zero, so improvement over the atlas remains uncertain in this small cohort.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of the FORESEE-MS workflow. (a) Training-subject follow-up new-lesion masks are used to construct the fold-specific population-prior atlas and supervise the deep learning models. (b) At inference, the models receive only baseline FLAIR and the distance-to-brain-boundary map. (c,d) The atlas and each deep learning model independently produce voxelwise risk maps for future lesion formation. (e) Risk maps are evaluated using pooled voxel-level AUROC and AUPRC and within-patient Recall@Top-K%. (f) Held-out follow-up lesion masks are used only for evaluation.

Fig. 3: Qualitative comparison of predicted risk maps for three MSSEG-2 subjects. (a) Subject 057 (hit): deep learning models assign high risk around a ring-shaped FLAIR hyperintensity adjacent to new lesions, while the atlas produces smaller periventricular hotspots. (b) Subject 021 (partial hit): most methods highlight the smaller lesion but miss the larger lesion above it. (c) Subject 094 (miss): no method places a hotspot directly on the lesion in the displayed slice, although some models assign high risk to nearby regions. In each map, blue to red indicates low to high relative risk within the brain.

Fig. 2: Recall@Top-K% across methods: (a) voxel-level recall averaged over 28 lesion-positive subjects and (b) lesionlevel recall pooled over 147 lesions. Error bars indicate 95% patient-level bootstrap CIs for each method.

Table 1: Pooled voxel-level AUROC/AUPRC from 5-fold cross-validation across 39 subjects, with 95% CIs estimated from 1,000 patient-level bootstrap resamples. Best values in each column are shown in bold.

papers.selection_reason: Predicts future 3D states (lesions) from baseline MRI using deep learning, aligning with the concept of environment dynamics forecasting in world models.
papers.title: FORESEE-MS: Toward Prospective Spatial Forecasting of Future Multiple Sclerosis Lesions from Baseline FLAIR MRI
papers.tldr: FORESEE-MS evaluates whether baseline FLAIR MRI can predict future MS lesion locations beyond a population-prior atlas, finding suggestive but inconclusive patient-specific predictive information.

papers.abstract: Low-cost arms such as the SO-101 have become the most common entry point to robot learning, yet no released policy performs spatially constrained, language-conditioned tasks on them out of the box, and existing SO-101 benchmarks run only on physical hardware with simple tasks and few held-out objects. We introduce SO-101 Bench, a simulated benchmark for language-conditioned spatial manipulation built on an Isaac Lab digital twin of a real SO-101 setup. It has four tasks scored as five families, 138 objects in seen, unseen-instance and unseen-class splits, 916 evaluation episodes with subsets for held-out appearances, rotate-to-fit planning and occlusion memory, and 3,629 simulated demonstrations on which every learned policy is fine-tuned under an equal compute budget. The twin ranks policies as the real robot does: five policies trained without real data, four VLAs and an LLM agent, keep their exact ranking when the same weights run on the physical arm in an unseen environment with unseen objects (Spearman rho = 1.00, MMRV = 0.000), although simulation overestimates success. Across nine VLAs and world-action models, the best learned policies score near 61%, with spatial placement, unseen object classes and rotate-to-fit planning remaining open. An LLM agent that writes code and hands grasping to a learned policy scores 83.2%, and an ablation shows that this lead comes from the choice of harness and the choice of language model.
bullets: Targets low-cost SO-101 arms, addressing the lack of accessible benchmarks for spatially constrained, language-conditioned tasks.
Provides four tasks across five evaluation families, 138 objects, seen/unseen splits, 916 episodes, and simulated demonstrations in an Isaac Lab digital twin.
Policy rankings in simulation exactly matched physical-robot rankings for five policies tested, though simulation overestimated success.
Best learned policies achieved about 61%, while an LLM code-writing agent paired with a learned grasping policy reached 83.2%.
Spatial placement, unseen object classes, and rotate-to-fit planning remain open challenges.

papers.selection_reason: Simulated benchmark for language-conditioned spatial manipulation on low-cost arms, evaluating VLAs and LLM agents; directly embodied manipulation and VLA.
papers.title: SO-101 Bench: Accessible Spatial Manipulation
papers.tldr: SO-101 Bench is a simulated, language-conditioned spatial manipulation benchmark whose digital twin reliably ranks policies but exposes substantial challenges in generalization, planning, and spatial placement.

papers.abstract: Compact electroencephalography (EEG) decoders enable embedded brain--computer interfaces (BCIs), but compression can alter adversarial robustness without proportional hardware savings. We present ORBITAL, a robustness-constrained framework combining hardware-realizable structured compression, recovery-aware operating-point selection, multi-attack evaluation, and native edge validation. Across nine subjects and three seeds on BCI Competition IV-2a, S25-TRADES achieves the highest observed mean true-union robustness among compressed EEGNet models (23.06% vs 21.27% for standard Full), with 26.27% fewer parameters and 25.10% fewer MACs. Matched controls identify TRADES as the main source of robustness recovery, improving S25 union accuracy by 6.74 percentage points over clean recovery (p=0.0039), while per-example analysis reveals boundary redistribution rather than uniform margin expansion. On Jetson Orin Nano, FP16 compression reduces board energy by up to 16.20% and latency by 8.00%. Despite 99.3% prediction agreement, native INT8 Q/DQ incurs about twice the FP16 latency and energy, demonstrating the need for joint robustness and hardware-aware optimization.
bullets: Structured compression can change adversarial robustness without matching hardware gains.
S25-TRADES achieved the highest observed mean true-union robustness among compressed EEGNet models, while reducing parameters and MACs versus Full.
TRADES was the main driver of robustness recovery, improving S25 union accuracy over clean recovery in matched controls.
On Jetson Orin Nano, FP16 compression reduced energy by up to 16.20% and latency by 8.00%.
Native INT8 Q/DQ showed roughly twice the FP16 latency and energy despite 99.3% prediction agreement, highlighting hardware-dependent trade-offs.

Fig. 3. TRADES union-accuracy gain over clean recovery across EEGNet compression levels. Markers denote subject means; intervals show 95% subjectbootstrap confidence intervals.
Fig. 4. Worst-case post-attack margin differences between S25-TRADES and standard Full, grouped by per-example union-robustness outcome. Intervals denote 95% confidence intervals.

Fig. 1. Motivation for robustness-constrained EEG compression. ORBITAL’s accuracy–robustness–hardware trade-off under structured EEG compression. S10 satisfies predefined screening constraints, S25 achieves the highest observed mean true-union robustness among compressed candidates, and S50 offers greater structural and measured hardware savings.

papers.selection_reason: Robustness-constrained low-precision compression for edge inference, reducing memory, energy, and latency; relevant to efficient AI via memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: ORBITAL: Optimization of Robust Brain--Computer Inference Through Architecture-Aware Low-Precision Compression
papers.tldr: ORBITAL jointly optimizes compressed EEG decoders for adversarial robustness and real edge-hardware efficiency, with FP16 compression offering the strongest practical trade-off.

papers.abstract: Self-driving laboratories couple a learned design surrogate to an instrument, and on every new target domain it must answer four questions: when it can be trusted, how many target measurements it needs, which to make first, and when to stop adapting, switch models or escalate. We state a framework making each measurable (a competence ratio, a budget $k^*(\varepsilon)$, a time-to-target and a priced decision) and instantiate it without wet experiments on six public droplet-microfluidic and liposome tables as offline laboratories: 107 leave-one-group tiers whose rows are hidden labels. A sealed, pre-registered programme (two sealed negative validations and a pre-registered test on three more tables) and seven frozen closed-loop protocols, each run twice, yield 23 findings. Shift cost is stratified by shift type; no label-free statistic certifies individual candidates; random-split model-family rankings predicted neither the sealed nor the loop rankings. Warm-start residual boosting returns a surrogate to $1.25\times$ its development reference within 20 target rows in 94% of chemistry tiers (27% under a strict noise-floor reading), 90% of laboratory and 40% of device tiers, and a budget planned from the shift type on other tables is not measurably worse on a new one. In the loop, one gain survives drift and shuffled-label controls on all tiers, carried by the sparsely sampled ones: proposing at once and warm-starting on every measurement reaches a 10% target in 2.80 measurements against 3.31 for the reference, and in 5.72 against 11.35 for random proposals on 301 hard units at a 3% tolerance. No label-free acquisition rule survives the shuffled-label control, no interval-aware proposal or other model family does better, and no threshold rule on the tested diagnostics beats always continuing once escalation is priced. No wet-lab validation is claimed.
bullets: Evaluated 107 leave-one-group tiers across six public droplet-microfluidic and liposome tables using sealed, preregistered offline protocols.
Formalized measurable trust, target-measurement budget, time-to-target, and cost-aware decisions for adapting, switching, or escalating a surrogate.
Warm-start residual boosting recovered near-reference performance within 20 target rows most often in chemistry tiers, less often in laboratory and device tiers.
Propose-then-update reached a 10% target in 2.80 versus 3.31 measurements for the reference, and 5.72 versus 11.35 for random proposals on hard units at 3% tolerance.
Shuffled-label controls invalidated label-free acquisition rules; no tested stopping threshold, interval-aware proposal, or alternative model family consistently improved decisions.

papers.selection_reason: Offline closed-loop framework for adapting learned surrogates on new target domains; relevant to test-time and continual adaptation.
papers.title: When Can a Learned Design Surrogate Be Trusted in a Self-Driving Microfluidics Laboratory? An Offline Closed-Loop Framework Built and Tested on Six Public Tables
papers.tldr: An offline study defines and tests when learned surrogates can be trusted and adapted in self-driving microfluidics, finding that warm-start closed-loop updating helps on sparse, shifted settings but no label-free stopping or acquisition rule is reliable.

papers.abstract: Modeling multi-scale dynamics in urban road networks is essential for intelligent transportation systems but is often hindered by the computational cost of long-range historical context and the challenge of fusing heterogeneous modalities. Existing spatio-temporal frameworks face a trade-off between sequence length and memory overhead, while frequently neglecting the transient effects of exogenous factors such as road incidents and weather. To address these limitations, we propose SpecLST, a frequency-enhanced long-short-term spatio-temporal multimodal framework. SpecLST leverages a fast Fourier transform-based frequency-domain representation module to efficiently encode multi-week historical dependencies, bypassing the memory bottlenecks of standard attention mechanisms over raw long sequences. Heterogeneous context is integrated through attention-based fusion, followed by a sparse Mixture-of-Experts backbone with graph augmentation for spatio-temporal representation learning. Additionally, a frequency-enhanced residual head isolates high-frequency transients, improving sensitivity to abrupt traffic anomalies. At the 60-minute horizon, SpecLST achieves mean relative error reductions of 14.10% in MAE, 10.35% in RMSE, and 15.78% in MAPE across eight neural forecasting baselines and four datasets, with the dataset- and metric-specific average reductions ranging from 5.63% to 22.21%.
authors: Kenan Kang, Matthew M. Y. Kuo, Weihua Li
bullets: Addresses the memory cost of long historical sequences and weak handling of heterogeneous, time-varying factors such as incidents and weather.
Uses FFT-based frequency representations to encode multi-week dependencies more efficiently than attention over raw long sequences.
Fuses heterogeneous context with attention, then applies a sparse Mixture-of-Experts backbone with graph augmentation.
Adds a frequency-enhanced residual head to capture high-frequency, abrupt traffic anomalies.
At a 60-minute horizon, reports average error reductions of 14.10% in MAE, 10.35% in RMSE, and 15.78% in MAPE across four datasets and eight baselines.

papers.abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has become a key mechanism for efficiently specializing foundation models into many task- and user-specific variants. Serving many LoRA adapters under a shared resource budget turns post-hoc compression into a two-level allocation problem: rank must be distributed across layers within each adapter and across adapters within the fleet. Although trained LoRAs contain substantial spectral redundancy, spectral reconstruction alone does not determine how much compression an adapter can functionally tolerate. We formulate fleet compression through a functional rank-distortion frontier for each adapter, followed by fleet-level minimax allocation under a shared rank budget. Given exact frontiers, this decomposition is equivalent to joint optimization over all layer ranks. We introduce Functional Rank Allocation (FRA), an unlabeled method for constructing practical frontiers. FRA measures isolated module truncations end to end, uses these measurements as an additive search surrogate solved by dynamic programming, remeasures every complete candidate, and takes the lower-risk envelope with a complementary spectral proposal before exact minimax allocation over the constructed frontiers. Across 78 adapters from three public fleets, FRA improves worst-case and tail utility over uniform spectral compression in constrained-budget regimes. Fixed-budget probes show that isolated costs rank candidates well, but their calibration shifts across proposal shapes; end-to-end verification and the spectral proposal therefore limit functional-search error.
bullets: LoRA fleet compression must allocate rank both across layers within adapters and across adapters under a shared budget.
The method builds per-adapter functional rank-distortion frontiers from isolated module truncation measurements and dynamic programming.
Complete candidates are re-evaluated end to end and combined with a spectral proposal before exact fleet-level minimax allocation.
Across 78 adapters from three public fleets, FRA improves worst-case and tail utility over uniform spectral compression in constrained-budget settings.
Isolated measurements rank candidates effectively, but calibration varies with proposal shape, making end-to-end verification important.

papers.abstract: Perceiving human body motion is critical for multimodal systems that understand and assist people. Yet current evaluations of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) largely focus on objects, scenes, and coarse actions, leaving their ability to reason about the body itself poorly assessed. This is especially challenging from the egocentric perspective, in which the body is only partially visible and motion must be inferred from occluded and temporally distributed cues. We introduce SOMA, a benchmark for fine-grained body-motion understanding from egocentric video, comprising 1,632 human-verified questions across three capability axes: body configuration, motion dynamics, and temporal reasoning. We evaluate 37 leading closed-source, open-source, and specialized egocentric MLLMs, complemented by an extensive human evaluation. We find that humans also find this task difficult from video alone (68.5% accuracy), yet clearly outperform the strongest MLLM (Qwen3.6-27B), which reaches 50.0% zero-shot accuracy. Our error analysis shows that MLLMs often misread the wearer's own body, misjudge events in time, and are prone to biases such as favoring the right hand or under-counting repetitions. To narrow the gap to human performance and support further progress, we introduce a training dataset of aligned video, body motion, and language supervision, and a multimodal baseline that jointly learns from these modalities. By identifying common failure modes and missing capabilities in current MLLMs, we hope SOMA will inspire future research on body-motion understanding and multimodal reasoning. Full benchmark, training data, and code will be released at: https://cnai.epfl.ch/soma
authors: Matea Tashkovska, Na\"el Ouerghemi, Haozhe Qi, Alexander Mathis
bullets: Introduces 1,632 human-verified questions spanning body configuration, motion dynamics, and temporal reasoning.
Evaluates 37 closed-source, open-source, and specialized egocentric MLLMs, alongside human evaluation.
Humans achieve 68.5% video-only accuracy, compared with 50.0% for the strongest evaluated MLLM, Qwen3.6-27B, in zero-shot evaluation.
Finds recurring errors in interpreting the wearer’s body, temporal events, repetition counts, and hand-side biases.
Provides aligned video–body-motion–language training data and a multimodal baseline to support future research.

papers.abstract: For efficiency, industrial large language model (LLM) labelers often pack many candidate labels into one prompt and generate a YES/NO answer for each, even when each decision depends only on the entity and one candidate. Generating these independent decisions as one answer list couples them, spends decoding on the list, and relies on the list being well-formed. In this paper, we present an end-to-end recipe that reformulates the labeler as semantic scoring, fine-tuning it on single-candidate prompts to return each decision as one answer-token score from a prefill-only pass. We also adapt Multiple-Item Scoring (MIS) to score hundreds of candidates in one sequence with attention masked between them. Deployed for profile qualification labeling at LinkedIn, semantic scoring changes at most 0.01% of decisions when candidates are reordered and matches the agreement with reference labels that packed generation reaches only with about 4.7x as many training pairs. The MIS-based stack raises throughput over the deployed stack by 1.24x offline and 1.9x in model serving under a one-second p99 latency target. For offline batch inference, we implement MIS-based scoring as a reusable, model-agnostic Ray Data API proposed for upstream adoption. Model serving uses MIS support contributed to SGLang.
authors: Jian Sheng, Sriram Vasudevan, Sundara Raman Ramachandran, Yang Hu, Junyu Zhou, Xiaojing Ma, Haolan Qin, Tiffany Zhou, Vedant Vipul Jhaveri, Ashwini Bhingare, Chinmay Kini, Qing Lan, Xiaoqing Wang, Suleyman Cetintas, Fedor Borisyuk
bullets: Packed generation couples independent candidate decisions, wastes decoding, and can fail when the output list is malformed.
The proposed method fine-tunes single-candidate prompts to produce one answer-token score and uses attention-masked Multiple-Item Scoring to evaluate hundreds of candidates together.
Semantic scoring changes at most 0.01% of decisions when candidate order changes and reaches reference-label agreement with roughly 4.7× fewer training pairs than packed generation.
The MIS-based system improves throughput by 1.24× offline and 1.9× in serving under a one-second p99 latency target.
The work includes a reusable Ray Data API for offline inference and MIS support contributed to SGLang.

papers.abstract: Robotic agents operating in real-world environments must adapt continuously from a stream of multimodal demonstrations, often under constraints that preclude storing or revisiting past data. In this replay-free, single-pass lifelong imitation learning setting, sequential updates can progressively distort the representation space, making expert-based approaches particularly sensitive to routing interference, causing expert selection to degrade over time. We propose HIDRA, a structured routing framework that mitigates this issue through a hierarchical dual-attention mechanism, which decouples instruction-level expert retrieval from context-dependent refinement. To further stabilize routing under representation drift, HIDRA introduces a key-level geometric regularization that enforces both alignment within tasks and separation across tasks. The resulting approach enables reliable expert selection while supporting an expandable set of experts for continual adaptation. We evaluate HIDRA on several LIBERO benchmark suites, including more challenging variants with heterogeneous task sequences and paraphrased language instructions. Our approach consistently outperforms both replay-free and replay-based baselines, improving AUC and forward transfer while maintaining low forgetting, with stronger gains under high interference and language variation. The code is available at: https://github.com/yfqi/HIDRA.
authors: Fanqi Yu, Matteo Tiezzi, Cigdem Beyan, Tommaso Apicella, Vittorio Murino
bullets: Targets sequential learning from multimodal demonstrations without storing or revisiting past data.
Uses hierarchical dual attention to separate instruction-level expert retrieval from context-dependent refinement.
Adds key-level geometric regularization to align representations within tasks and separate them across tasks.
Supports an expandable expert set for continual adaptation and reliable expert selection.
On LIBERO suites, including heterogeneous and paraphrased tasks, it improves AUC and forward transfer while maintaining low forgetting; gains are stronger under interference and language variation.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of HIDRA. A frozen pretrained multimodal policy produces an instruction query qinst and a context query qctxt . These drive a two-stage hierarchical dual-routing attention mechanism. Stage I performs instruction-level retrieval via qinst to select an anchor expert j∗ and an instruction candidate set Sj∗ over task-level keys {kinsj }. Stage II then uses qctxt to perform context-level refinement within Sj∗ using context keys {kctxj }, producing fused routing scores and selecting the active experts. Key-space regularization (Reg.) promotes intra-task compactness and inter-task separation, enabling stable and interference-resistant expert selection as new task-specific experts are introduced during replay-free lifelong adaptation.

papers.abstract: We tackle the challenge of building real-time interactive video worlds with user-defined behaviors. Such worlds must track object states, apply interaction rules, and render the resulting consequences as users act. Yet existing end-to-end video world models typically learn interaction dynamics within the generator, making it difficult to specify object-level rules and reason about their consequences. In this work, we introduce BoxWorld, which separates interaction reasoning from generative rendering. Given user-specified rules, a coding agent creates a Box World Engine that determines interaction outcomes and exposes the resulting object states through a lightweight interface of layout boxes, persistent object attributes, and dynamic status variables, leaving appearance and physical effects to generative rendering. A Box-State Generative Renderer then renders this evolving state stream into video autoregressively, enabling online control over object motion, state switches, and conditional events. Rendering this state stream is non-trivial: the renderer must respond to object-level state updates in real time while remaining coherent with the generated history. To this end, we introduce a three-stage training strategy that learns object grounding from open-domain videos and state transitions from gameplay videos, both annotated automatically, and finally performs rollout distillation on self-generated histories. We further propose PairedStateBench, a paired benchmark for fine-grained interaction control. BoxWorld substantially outperforms end-to-end world models and remains competitive across multiple public benchmarks. Project page: https://boxworld-web.github.io.
authors: Zike Wu, Ahmed Hatem, Chintan Trivedi, Wallace Michel Pinto Lira, Xuebin Qin, Lele Wang, Renjie Liao
bullets: A coding agent converts user-defined rules into a Box World Engine that tracks object states and determines interaction outcomes.
A Box-State Generative Renderer turns state updates into coherent autoregressive video while supporting online control of motion, switches, and conditional events.
The system uses a three-stage training strategy covering object grounding, state transitions, and rollout distillation.
PairedStateBench is introduced to evaluate fine-grained interaction control.
BoxWorld substantially outperforms end-to-end world models and remains competitive on multiple public benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Prefix caching enables a Large Language Model (LLM) servers to reuse the Key-Value (KV) states and accelerate prefill computation stage for requests that share a prefix with earlier prompts, thus reducing latency and serving cost. With limited memory resource, the KV cache eviction policy becomes a decisive factor in determining the overall benefits of prefix caching. Production traffic may have single-turn, multi-turn, agentic, or a mixture of any combination of these request types. Our findings indicate that agentic steps return within seconds and favor recency, while popular prompts and long conversations return after many other requests and favor frequency. Across 20 mixes, no single policy is always best: vLLM's default strategy LRU provides 12% higher cache hits as compared to the frequency-oriented S3FIFO on agentic-heavy mixes but trails it by up to 22% elsewhere, and even a single workload parameter can flip the winner even for any particular mix. We present WAKMan, a workload-aware KV cache manager that picks its eviction policy from live traffic without knowing request types or reading prompts. It improves hit rate over LRU by 5 percentage points on average, with the lowest mean and worst-case optimality gap of all policies.
authors: Suhas Kumar Morisetty, Vaibhavi Lokegaonkar, Sachin Mathew Varghese, Wesley Harris
bullets: Prefix caching benefits depend heavily on how KV-cache entries are evicted under limited memory.
Agentic requests favor recency, while popular prompts and long conversations favor frequency.
No single eviction policy is consistently best across diverse workload mixes.
WAKMan selects an eviction policy from traffic behavior without identifying request types or reading prompts.
It improves hit rate over LRU by 5 percentage points on average and has the smallest mean and worst-case optimality gaps among evaluated policies.

papers.abstract: Multi-task learning (MTL) improves model efficiency by sharing representations across related vision tasks, but it often suffers from negative transfer when task updates interfere with one another. Existing conflict-mitigation methods typically operate in gradient space, requiring explicit task-gradient manipulation and additional optimization steps. We propose Conflict-Resolution through Low-Rank Matrices for Multi-Task Learning (CRLoMTL), a parameter-efficient framework that mitigates task interference in the low-rank parameter-update space. CRLoMTL learns task-specific LoRA updates through task-specific passes, where each task updates its own low-rank matrices, and integrates these updates through global shared-subspace fusion. Specifically, we introduce a shared-subspace resolver based on singular value decomposition (SVD), referred to as the SVD resolver, which extracts a common low-dimensional orthonormal basis across task adapters and projects task updates into this shared space before merging them into a single deployment-time update. The resulting update can be folded into the backbone, preserving the inference structure of the original model without additional runtime branches. Experiments with Swin Transformer backbones on PASCAL-Context, NYUD-v2, and CelebA show that CRLoMTL achieves a favorable accuracy-parameter trade-off, improving over single-task baselines by up to 2.77% on PASCAL-Context, 5.03% on NYUD-v2, and 3.50% on CelebA, while training only a small fraction of the parameters used by single-task models.
authors: Ahmed Agiza, Tasneem Shaffee, Rahil Badkul, Sherief Reda
bullets: Addresses interference between task updates while avoiding explicit gradient manipulation and extra optimization steps.
Learns task-specific LoRA updates and merges them through a shared subspace extracted with SVD.
Fuses the resolved updates into the backbone, preserving the original model’s inference structure.
With Swin Transformer backbones, reports gains of up to 2.77% on PASCAL-Context, 5.03% on NYUD-v2, and 3.50% on CelebA over single-task baselines.
Uses only a small fraction of the parameters required by single-task models, targeting a favorable accuracy–parameter trade-off.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) perform well across many real-world tasks but remain prone to hallucination, limiting their reliability in domains such as biomedicine and healthcare, where answers must be grounded in established knowledge. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) mitigates this problem by incorporating external information, but often overlooks logical relationships and relies heavily on the LLM's own reasoning, which can compromise answer faithfulness. We propose OA-RAG, an agent that integrates formal reasoning with LLM reasoning, drawing on both the logical structure and informal annotations of domain ontologies. For each answer, OA-RAG reports the ontology observations used as evidence and a model-assessed grounding level (entailed, supported, related, or unrelated) that characterises the strength of that evidence. Across benchmarks derived from three large-scale ontologies and six real-world medical question-answering tasks, OA-RAG achieves the best overall performance among the evaluated ontology-fine-tuned and popular RAG methods, with particularly strong results on reasoning-intensive tasks. The reported grounding levels also offer a useful indication of answer reliability, with stronger grounding generally associated with higher accuracy. Finally, our results demonstrate the value of ontologies as knowledge sources: OA-RAG is competitive with, and sometimes outperforms, domain-specific RAG systems that draw on sources such as textbooks.
authors: Hui Yang, Jiaoyan Chen, Yongsheng Gao
bullets: Addresses hallucinations and weak logical grounding in conventional RAG, particularly in biomedical and healthcare applications.

Performs best overall among evaluated ontology-fine-tuned and popular RAG methods across ontology benchmarks and medical QA tasks.

papers.abstract: Video Large Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in video understanding and reasoning, but processing long visual sequences incurs substantial computational, latency, and memory overhead. This survey examines training-free inference acceleration, focusing on reducing inference costs while preserving task-relevant spatiotemporal evidence. We organize existing methods by their intervention stages in the inference pipeline, covering input, visual encoding, projector, prefill, and decoding. Post-training quantization (PTQ) is discussed separately as a cross-stage extension with varying calibration requirements. We analyze how intervention position affects evidence preservation and computational savings, and why local efficiency improvements may not translate into end-to-end acceleration. We complement this analysis with quantitative evidence from prior studies and our own experiments under a shared evaluation setting to assess accuracy-latency trade-offs.
authors: Yuqi Li, Chuanyue Yan, Neil Rodrigues, Xianglong Wang, Xiaoqin Feng, Junming Liu, Xi Xiao, Zhongwei Cheng, Wei Li, Lin Chen, Yingli Tian
bullets: Video VLMs face high computation, latency, and memory costs on long visual sequences.
Methods are categorized by intervention stage: input, visual encoding, projector, prefill, and decoding.
Post-training quantization is treated as a cross-stage approach with different calibration requirements.
The survey examines how intervention location affects preservation of task-relevant spatiotemporal evidence.
Prior results and shared-setting experiments assess accuracy–latency trade-offs and highlight that local gains may not yield end-to-end speedups.

papers.abstract: Large-scale linear programs with millions of variables and constraints strain time and memory budgets. First-order methods such as the primal-dual hybrid gradient scale to this regime because they avoid matrix factorizations, but they require many iterations. Learned accelerators can reduce these iterations, yet fewer iterations do not guarantee a shorter solve. Learning inference also takes time, and running the accelerator longer trades solver time for inference time. Existing unrolled accelerators handle this trade-off poorly: each layer processes every variable and constraint, the predicted iterates still need solver refinement, and every instance runs the same layers. We therefore ask: What neural accelerator design achieves end-to-end speedups on large-scale linear programs across sizes and target accuracies? We introduce AHEAD, an accelerator that predicts step sizes for first-order linear programming solvers while keeping their update rules. Its weight-shared predictor reads compact solver statistics and rescales the primal and dual step sizes, so each warm-start iteration stays inexpensive and a short warm-start phase hands the solver a warm start. A learned handoff policy sets the number of warm-start iterations for each instance and target accuracy, after which the solver finishes under its own termination criterion. On packing linear programs with up to $10^7$ variables, AHEAD achieves $6.5$--$11.6\times$ end-to-end speedups over Gurobi's first-order solver from a cold start, including on instances of unseen sizes and distributions. The gains extend to PageRank linear programs and hold across difficulty levels and target accuracies.
authors: Sihao Liu, Zhichao Hou, Huayue Gu, Raiyan Rahman, Liang Wu, Ruozhou Yu, Xiaorui Liu
bullets: Targets the high iteration counts and inference–solver trade-off in learned acceleration for massive linear programs.
Uses a weight-shared predictor over compact solver statistics to rescale primal and dual step sizes while preserving the solver’s update rules.
A learned handoff policy selects the warm-start duration based on each instance and target accuracy.
Evaluated on packing LPs with up to 10^7 variables, including unseen sizes and distributions, and on PageRank LPs.
Reported gains hold across difficulty levels and target accuracies.

papers.abstract: Monocular outdoor navigation requires robust camera motion estimation and a dense, navigable map, where 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM serves this task through an explicit differentiable parameterization and closed-form projection. However, typically, the geometry is recovered by associating 2D pixels with 3D points, so a modular SLAM system absorbs tracking error into the map, leading to cascading degradation. To address these gaps, we present SG^2SLAM, which couples streaming spatial geometry with a ray-conditioned 3DGS kernel. Streaming spatial geometry replaces the per- frame cross-dimensional correspondence with a chunk-level metric prior that supervises tracking and mapping from one source. A ray-conditioned kernel extends each primitive with a viewing-direction subspace that senses the monocular camera viewpoints. The joint optimization over spatial geometry and poses ensures a globally consistent map and trajectory outcome. Experiments on the KITTI and Waymo Open datasets show that our SG^2SLAM surpasses the per-frame association baselines in the monocular outdoor navigation task. Code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.
authors: Ziang Guo, Didar Seyidov, Yixiao Zhou, Xuefeng Zhang, Ali Alridha Abdulkarim, Chen Min, Zufeng Zhang, Dzmitry Tsetserukou
bullets: Addresses cascading map degradation caused by absorbing monocular tracking errors into the map.
Uses chunk-level streaming spatial geometry as a metric prior to supervise both tracking and mapping.
Introduces a ray-conditioned 3DGS kernel that models viewpoint-dependent information.
Jointly optimizes geometry and poses to produce globally consistent maps and trajectories.
Outperforms per-frame association baselines on KITTI and Waymo Open datasets.

The chunk fusion is solved over the spatial geometry and poses via a global joint graph.

papers.abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms have been observed to lose the ability to adaptively learn from new data, a phenomenon termed Loss of Plasticity (LoP). While many metrics have been shown to correlate with it, the causal mechanisms and the geometric conditions from which it can arise have not been clearly identified. We analyze LoP in Proximal Policy Optimization with isotropic Gaussian policies, the state-of-the-art formulation for many continuous action spaces in RL. We report multiple metrics which characterize the effect that the policy standard deviation $\sigma$ has on LoP, and we also suggest related explanations for the effectiveness of widely adopted LoP mitigation techniques. We observe a significant effect of $\sigma$ on the extent of LoP, and accompany this with both theoretical and experimental supporting arguments. Our experimental validation consists of LoP benchmark evaluations against standard baselines as well as real-world policy deployment on a 7-DoF robotic arm.
authors: Andrea Vasco Grieco, Evelyn D'Elia, Edoardo Caldarelli, Raffaello Camoriano
bullets: Analyzes loss of plasticity (LoP), where RL agents become less able to learn from new data.
Studies PPO with isotropic Gaussian policies and examines how policy standard deviation σ relates to LoP.
Provides theoretical and experimental evidence that σ substantially affects the extent of LoP.
Connects the findings to why commonly used LoP mitigation techniques may be effective.
Validates the analysis on LoP benchmarks and through deployment on a 7-DoF robotic arm.

papers.abstract: Memory-agent benchmarks often collapse retrieval and answer generation into one score, making it hard to tell whether a failure comes from missing an update or from not using an update that was already retrieved. We examine this distinction on the single-hop FactConsolidation task of MemoryAgentBench. With Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on 6K-history BM25 accuracy drops from 45% to 32% when the retrieved evidence budget grows from 64 to 512 tokens, even though a gold-assisted post-hoc audit finds the newest statement in every retrieved set. Most of the errors occur on questions that also contain an obsolete statement version. Under a frozen prompt and equal four-statement evidence size, replacing one unrelated statement with the obsolete competing statement reduces accuracy from 100% to 44.6% for Qwen2.5 and from 100% to 87.8% for Qwen3-14B, with all 50 harmful paired flips classified as stale. A 32K-history replication likewise favors BM25-64 over BM25-512 (69% versus 58%). These results suggest that retrieving the correct fact is not enough. An obsolete competing statement can be more harmful than an unrelated piece of evidence of the same size.

papers.abstract: Navigation vision-language-action (VLA) policies repeatedly invoke costly semantic reasoning even when the next command remains unchanged. Command reuse can reduce computation but risks missing instruction-dependent turns or stops. We introduce ASPEN, an event-triggered scheduler based on command persistence prediction: estimating whether the frozen base policy would reissue its previous command. A lightweight multimodal predictor combines temporal observations, language instructions, execution history, and cached VLA confidence. At eligible command boundaries, sufficient predicted persistence permits command reuse. Otherwise, ASPEN triggers fresh semantic reasoning from the VLA. Evaluated with frozen NaVILA on cross-dataset RxR-CE val-unseen, ASPEN reduces VLA calls by 9.5% and estimated inference time by 8.1%, including scheduling overhead. It maintains comparable navigation performance and preserves identical baseline action sequences on 92.1% of episodes.
bullets: Targets redundant semantic reasoning in navigation VLAs when the next command is likely unchanged.
Uses a lightweight multimodal predictor over observations, instructions, execution history, and cached VLA confidence.
Reuses commands when predicted persistence is sufficient; otherwise triggers fresh VLA reasoning.
With frozen NaVILA on RxR-CE val-unseen, reduces VLA calls by 9.5% and estimated inference time by 8.1%.
Maintains comparable navigation performance, with identical baseline action sequences in 92.1% of episodes.

papers.abstract: Complex whole-body loco-manipulation requires executing diverse maneuvers, such as crouching, grasping, and locomotion, within a single long-horizon task. While performing simple pick-and-place behaviors is well-established, scaling to complex, long-horizon tasks remains difficult. Currently, this challenge is addressed by relying on human motion data and correspondingly humanoid platforms, which limits platform independence and introduces substantial data processing overhead. Instead, we extend proximal policy optimization (PPO) to train a single policy for multi-phase tasks across diverse robotic hardware, leveraging prior task structure to shape behavior. Our method adapts PPO using a phase-conditioned critic, phase-gated reward functions, and a multi-phase reset curriculum to guide exploration. To support varied hardware, we employ a decoupled hierarchical control architecture that separates lower-level balancing dynamics from high-level phase execution. We demonstrate multi-stage loco-manipulation skills on hardware on both the Unitree G1 and a Boston Dynamics Spot equipped with a manipulator arm, and validate our design choices through ablations. Our approach enables the acquisition of complex loco-manipulation behaviors purely through environment interaction while directly incorporating high-level task structure into policy learning.
authors: Simone Manni, Annika Wollschl\"ager, Dario Bellicoso, Abel Gawel, Marco Hutter, Simon Le Cleac'h, Jan Br\"udigam
bullets: Targets long-horizon tasks combining maneuvers such as crouching, grasping, and locomotion.
Uses a phase-conditioned critic, phase-gated rewards, and a multi-phase reset curriculum to structure exploration.
Employs decoupled hierarchical control, separating low-level balance from high-level phase execution.
Demonstrates multi-stage skills on Unitree G1 and Boston Dynamics Spot with a manipulator arm.
Ablation studies validate the proposed design choices.

figures.caption: Fig. 3: Overview of the phase-conditioned PPO framework. An environment state machine segments the task into phases (ψk) via local success conditions (e.g., distance d and phase-specific thresholds ϵ). To tackle exploration bottlenecks, a multiphase curriculum initially resets episodes into later stages before progressively shifting back to the initial phase as training advances. The actor outputs delta actions updating command targets ct, while an auxiliary head enforces phase internalization via cross-entropy loss (LCE) against the true environment phase. The critic conditions value estimation on state st and phase one-hot encoding ek, combining a base value Vbase with phase-specific residual heads. These are constrained by Lreg to keep the main learning burden on the base head. Finally, task rewards are dynamically gated based on the active phase ψk and combined with rewards for forward phase transitions and penalties for backward regression.

Fig. 5: Algorithmic Ablation Study on Spot and G1: Task success rate across training steps on (a) spot tire rolling and (b) g1 push two boxes, comparing our method (Ours) against baseline architectures (MLP, Multihead), an unguided variant (No phase prediction), and execution without multi-phase episode initialization (Initial phase reset). Solid curves and shaded regions denote the mean and variance across 3 random seeds, respectively. (c) Spot Phase Analysis: Evaluation of phase-prediction accuracy across 1,000 successful episodes of spot tire rolling task. Because individual phase durations vary across rollouts, evaluation episodes are temporally anchored at phase transitions with intermediate timesteps linearly warped to uniform phase durations. The top plot shows that the auxiliary head’s online phase predictions tightly track the ground-truth phase steps with minimal variance, while the bottom plot highlights the object-to-goal distance as a proxy for task progression.

Fig. 2: Overview of the low-level whole-body policy. The policy commands leg and waist joints to execute stable locomotion, low crouching, and crouch-walking. Training stability is achieved via inverse kinematics (IK) keyframe initializations that spawn the robot in valid postures, coupled with a feasibility-constrained command space. For standing environments, this region is bounded by the convex hull of admissible IK keyframes, whereas for dynamic environments, the feasible command envelope dynamically contracts as target tracking velocity increases.

Fig. 4: Hardware deployment of the g1 lift box task using onboard state estimation and ArUco marker detection. The right panel shows the Unitree G1 humanoid executing the lift, while the insets display the state estimation visualization (top-left) and the onboard first-person camera view tracking the ArUco marker (bottom-left).

papers.abstract: Are concepts and mechanisms unified across modalities in current AI models, or instead implemented separately for each one? We operationalize this broad question of modality unification by studying cross-modal steering: 1) finding vectors that successfully steer generation on tokens of one modality, which then 2) transfer zero-shot to steer generation when added to tokens of another modality. Our study goes beyond simple correlational alignment (e.g. representational similarity) because steering is fundamentally causal. We study cross-modal steering in several unified multimodal models (UMMs), since they possess shared parameters for language and image generation, focusing on these two modalities. Across diverse steered concepts such as emotion and object size, we show that steering vectors transfer zero-shot in both directions (text-to-image & image-to-text). Even for concepts that are highly unique to one modality (e.g. formal vs. colloquial language), steering vectors often induce a consistent, interpretable effect in the other modality, such as formal clothing and design. This transfer has a geometric signature too: despite a clear modality gap separating text and image representations, steering vectors with strong cross-modal transferability tend to point in similar directions for the same concept. Our findings shed light on how vision and language interact inside unified multimodal models and point towards more general, modality-agnostic approaches for controlling their behavior.
authors: Donghao Zeng (Mila, McGill University), Nishant Subramani (Carnegie Mellon University), Tamar Rott Shaham (MIT CSAIL), Benno Krojer (Mila, McGill University, Northeastern University)
bullets: Tests whether concepts and mechanisms are unified across language and vision models.
Finds bidirectional transfer: text-derived vectors steer images, and image-derived vectors steer text.
Transfer works for concepts including emotion, object size, and modality-specific language style.
Cross-modal vectors often have similar geometric directions despite a pronounced modality gap.
Suggests modality-agnostic methods for controlling multimodal model behavior.

papers.abstract: The information bottleneck (IB) trades compression of an input $X$ against prediction of a target $Y$ through a multiplier $\beta=1/\lambda$, yet each operating point is usually served by training, or fully conditioning, a new encoder. For jointly Gaussian data, we show that the IB solution factorizes as $A(\beta)=D(\beta)W$: the information-bearing directions $W$ do not depend on $\beta$, and $\beta$ acts only through scalar gains. We ask whether this separation of \emph{representation} from \emph{rate control} survives beyond Gaussian models, treating the budget as a given operating parameter rather than a quantity to be optimized. For a budget-free representation \(F(X)\), the \emph{separation gap} is controlled by the \emph{sufficiency deficit} $\epsilon_F=I(X;Y\mid F(X))$: We show there is at least $\epsilon_F$ in the worst case for finite inputs, and it is bounded uniformly in $\lambda$ by a function of $\epsilon_F$ for finite label alphabets. The same certificate extends to a new target distribution and to pooled multi-domain data, where a conditional-alignment term appears. On MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR-10 and STL-10 (10 seeds, eight prespecified budgets), a frozen CNN representation with one compressor--decoder pair per budget reduces estimated training multiply--accumulate operations (MACs) by $7.7\times$ and wall-clock time by about $2\times$ relative to end-to-end VIBs, and attains higher budget-averaged accuracy ($65.6\%$ versus $57.3\%$ per domain; $67.1\%$ versus $57.1\%$ pooled), with the advantage concentrated at strong compression, where the VIBs collapse. At weak compression ($\lambda\le0.036$), VIB has higher cross-entropy and ECE; its surrogate Lagrangian is higher per domain, indistinguishable from the pooled VIB in the macro average, and lower on the pooled test set.
bullets: For Gaussian data, the IB encoder’s informative directions are independent of the compression parameter, which only changes scalar gains.
Beyond Gaussian models, the separation gap is controlled by the representation’s sufficiency deficit, with extensions to new targets and pooled multi-domain data.
Experiments on MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR-10, and STL-10 show 7.7× fewer training MACs and roughly 2× lower wall-clock time than end-to-end VIB training.
The frozen-representation approach achieves higher budget-averaged accuracy, especially under strong compression where VIBs collapse.
At weak compression, VIB has better cross-entropy and calibration, so the proposed approach does not dominate on every metric or operating regime.

papers.abstract: Dyadic relationship recognition aims to identify the latent social relationship between two individuals from their multimodal interactions. Existing methods typically project heterogeneous cues into a shared representation and optimise a flat classification objective, overlooking that relationships may rely on different interaction patterns. For instance, distant relationships can often be inferred from direct behavioural correspondence, whereas close relationships are better reflected by coordinated affective, behavioural, and multimodal responses. To address this limitation, we propose HiRe-DRR, a Hierarchical Multimodal Interaction Reasoning framework that organises relationship evidence from three complementary perspectives: feature level, interaction type, and relationship hierarchy. HiRe-DRR decomposes facial, bodily, acoustic, and textual cues into low- and high-level representations and constructs homogeneous and heterogeneous cross-participant interactions. We further introduce the Mixture-of-Interaction Transformer (MoI-Former), which treats diverse interactions as specialised experts and employs relation-aware sparse routing to identify relationship-relevant evidence while preserving contextual interaction information. The proposed Hierarchical Conditional Loss (HC-Loss) exploits the hierarchical nature of social relationships through coarse-to-fine supervision, enabling structured relationship reasoning. Extensive experiments on three dyadic relationship benchmarks demonstrate that HiRe-DRR outperforms recent representative image-, video-, and multimodal methods. Our routing analysis further reveals that distant relationships tend to rely on low-level homogeneous interactions, whereas closer relationships focus on high-level heterogeneous interactions. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/tw-repository/HiRe-DRR.
authors: Wang Tang, Fethiye Irmak Dogan, Linbo Qing, Ce Zhu, Hatice Gunes
bullets: Addresses the limitation that different social relationships depend on different interaction patterns.
Decomposes facial, bodily, acoustic, and textual cues into low- and high-level representations with homogeneous and heterogeneous cross-participant interactions.
Uses MoI-Former with relation-aware sparse routing to select relevant interaction evidence while retaining context.
Applies HC-Loss for coarse-to-fine supervision aligned with relationship hierarchies.

Experiments on three benchmarks show improvements over representative image-, video-, and multimodal methods; routing analysis links distant relationships to low-level homogeneous interactions and closer relationships to high-level heterogeneous interactions.

papers.abstract: Offline-to-online reinforcement learning uses offline pretraining to accelerate subsequent online learning. While many methods assume the offline dataset remains available throughout fine-tuning, there are many settings where this is not the case. Prior work attributes failures in this setting primarily to critic recalibration under distribution shift. We identify a complementary actor-side failure: once the offline data disappears, continued behavioral cloning (BC) no longer preserves the offline behavior distribution and instead refits the behavioral model to the agent's limited, and nonstationary, online experience. We demonstrate that stopping online behavioral fitting while preserving the pretrained expressive prior substantially improves no-retention fine-tuning across implicit flow Q-learning (IFQL), flow Q-learning (FQL), and action-chunked RL (QC) on seven OGBench domains. We trace this failure to a behavioral feedback loop: continuing online behavioral cloning rapidly erases the pretrained prior, inducing representational collapse and action diversity loss that starves the critic of useful exploration. Freezing the prior breaks this cycle, preserving offline coverage while allowing value learning to drive continuous improvement.
authors: Sami Nur Islam, Johan Obando-Ceron, Doina Precup, Aaron Courville, Pablo Samuel Castro
bullets: Identifies an actor-side failure: continued online behavioral cloning refits the policy to limited, nonstationary online data.
This creates a feedback loop that erases the offline prior, reduces action diversity, and limits useful exploration for the critic.
Stopping behavioral fitting preserves offline coverage while allowing value learning to improve the policy.
The approach improves no-retention fine-tuning across IFQL, FQL, and action-chunked RL on seven OGBench domains.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Stopping BC enables no-retention fine-tuning. Left: After offline pretraining, we freeze the behavioral prior and continue updating the critic using online data. Right: Aggregate performance across seven OGBench tasks after 1M offline gradient steps (gray) and 1M online environment steps (white). Stopping BC consistently improves methods with expressive policies.

Figure 3: Stopping BC improves no-retention fine-tuning across expressive policy classes. Performance of IFQL, FQL, and QC (Action-Chunked RL) across five OGBench domains (25 tasks). The vertical dashed line marks the transition from offline pretraining to online fine-tuning. Continuing BC without offline data (BC-ON, orange dashed) causes catastrophic performance collapse. BC-OFF (red dashed) rescues online fine-tuning and often approaches the performance of the standard retaineddata baseline (blue solid). The full plot with the seven domains can be found in the Appendix B.4.

Figure 4: When does freezing the behavioral prior enable no-retention fine-tuning? Col 1: In IFQL, fine-tuning succeeds with a standard Bellman double critic (navy) but collapses entirely when its expressive flow prior is ablated in favor of a Gaussian actor (blue). Col 2: Removing ReBRAC’s BC penalty (BC-OFF) does not prevent collapse (scaled 0.0− 0.2 to highlight the immediate drop), demonstrating that omitting BC without a decoupled prior is insufficient. Col 3: A frozen flow prior supports continued online improvement without retention even after pretraining on low-quality offline data. Cols 4 & 5: Seeding replay with 25k online transitions prevents BC-ON from flatlining across both IFQL and FQL, yet BC-OFF consistently achieves superior asymptotic success.

Figure 8: Online BC induces actor collapse and critic data starvation. (Middle) When BC remains active without offline data, the behavior prior’s internal representations degenerate (feature rank collapses), which destroys the policy’s cross-state and within-state diversity across both IFQL and FQL. (Right) Confined to narrow data collection, the critic is starved of diverse, high-value trajectories. This causes the critic’s own feature rank to collapse, destroying its ability to accurately separate high-return states from low-return states (shrinking quantile gap). BC-OFF rescues this entire chain. The details of how these metrics are computed are covered in Appendix C.

Figure 9: Spatial collapse and degraded exploration under online Behavioral Cloning. Left: PCA projections of online rollouts onto the offline manifold at 1.2M steps. Stripped of its exploratory capacity by BC, the agent is forced into repetitive failure modes, leading to severely restricted state-space coverage. Right: Short-horizon state displacement on cube-double. Continued BC restricts the agent to increasingly localized behavior, while BC-OFF preserves purposeful, wide-area navigation.

Figure 5: Online fine-tuning on Robomimic under no data retention. Removing the BC objective (BC-OFF) prevents catastrophic degradation and matches offline retention performance across human demonstrations.
Figure 6: Effect of turning BC off with diffusion priors (IDQL). Performance across Cube Double and Ant Soccer.
Figure 11: Online fine-tuning across all seven OGBench domains. Performance across 35 tasks (5 per domain) for IFQL, FQL, and QC.

Figure 7: Continued online-only BC forgets the pretrained behavior. Left and middle: Held-out offline action MSE for IFQL and FQL, respectively. Continuing BC without retaining offline data sharply increases error, whereas BC-OFF preserves the pretrained behavior. Right: BC Loss on the offline data (log scale).

Figure 10: Online BC drives progressive parameter drift and candidate collapse. Left: Per-layer relative drift (log x-axis). Under BC-ON (solid), drift penetrates chronologically, beginning with the output-adjacent layer (103–104 steps). BC-OFF (dashed) exactly freezes IFQL and anchors FQL via distillation. Middle: Macroscopic drift and downstream impact for IFQL on cube-double. Under BC-ON, unbounded parameter drift occurs from the pretrained initialization. Right: Adam’s secondmoment estimate (v̂, log scale). Under BC-ON (solid), gradient magnitude plummets immediately at the onset of online training and remains orders of magnitude below BC-OFF (dashed), indicating a weakened optimization signal.

Figure 2: Sensitivity to the BC loss weight. Online fine-tuning performance across varying BC loss weights (0.1× to 10× default) without offline data retention. Scaling the BC weight up or down (yellow to dark brown) fails to prevent collapse in both IFQL and FQL. Only removing the BC loss entirely (BC-OFF, green) avoids collapse and enables sustained online learning.

papers.abstract: Long-video question answering is challenging since the answer often hinges on a few decisive moments scattered throughout the video, while memory constraints force Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to sample frames at extremely low rates, resulting in sparsity that risks omitting key evidence. Though aggressively enlarging the context size is intuitive, we argue that performance remains fundamentally constrained by the bias, \emph{i.e.}, the misleading cues caused by spurious \textit{linguistic} correlations and salient yet irrelevant \textit{visual} observations. In this paper, we first introduce {S-MME}, a benchmark designed to systematically diagnose shortcut-biased behavior in MLLMs. To mitigate this failure, we further propose a training-free framework, Counterfactual Long-video Evidence-Aware Reasoning (CLEAR). By treating the full video-question pair as a complete view, CLEAR estimates bias effects via augmented views by only keeping the question or locally salient visual clips. Then, we intervene hidden states to mitigate the discrepancy at inference such that the correct answer can be predicted confidently. With experimental studies across five benchmarks, we show that our method is generalizable and can be integrated in different MLLMs, yielding consistent gains in prediction and robustness. We hope CLEAR can offer a complementary direction in test-time scaling for long-video understanding.
authors: Xusheng Liang, Jianqiao Sun, Hao Zhang, Yulei Niu, Hengshuang Zhao, Jiawei Ma
bullets: Long-video QA is difficult because sparse frame sampling can miss decisive evidence, while spurious cues can still mislead models.
S-MME benchmarks shortcut-biased behavior from misleading language correlations and salient but irrelevant visual content.
CLEAR estimates bias using question-only and locally salient-clip views, then intervenes on hidden states at inference.
Experiments across five benchmarks show consistent gains in prediction and robustness across different MLLMs.
CLEAR is presented as a complementary test-time scaling approach; the abstract does not specify detailed limitations.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of CLEAR. (a) The full-video path produces the final answer, while questiononly and salient-view probes reveal spurious linguistic correlations and salient-yet-misleading visual observations. The salient view is formed by selecting top-K locally relevant clips according to query-conditioned visual attention. (b) CLEAR extracts the hidden state of the shared decision token z at selected late decoder layers, and constructs residual vectors rql = hf l − hq l and rsl = hf l − hs l from the restricted-view probes to the full-video state. These residual vectors are injected into the full-video path to steer its hidden state away from shortcut anchors before final decoding.

Figure 2: Construction pipeline of S-MME. We first mine candidate questions with explicit long-video evidence requirements, then use restricted views to identify shortcut-consistent distractors, followed by human validation of answer uniqueness, evidence sufficiency, and shortcut plausibility.
Figure 4: Effect of intervention location. Latelayer intervention performs best, with the last block achieving the highest accuracy.

Figure 1: MLLMs often fail despite the presence of decisive evidence, either by following spurious linguistic correlations or by over-relying on salient but misleading visual observations. CLEAR diagnoses these shortcut-biased trajectories with controlled probes and steers the full-video representation toward evidence-consistent prediction.
Figure 5: Context scaling analysis. CLEAR consistently improves accuracy and reduces ShortErr under the same frame budget.
Figure 6: Qualitative effect of CLEAR on open-ended video QA.

papers.tldr: The paper diagnoses shortcut biases in MLLMs for long-video QA and introduces training-free CLEAR to reduce misleading linguistic and visual cues during inference.

papers.abstract: Monocular 3D human mesh recovery (HMR) remains unreliable under weak observations caused by long camera-to-person distances, occlusion, and motion blur. In challenging scenarios such as sports, these factors make the problem highly ambiguous, as different 3D poses may yield similar 2D projections. This ambiguity is especially severe for one-stage HMR, which recovers all meshes directly from the full image without person crops or external 2D cues. To handle this ambiguity, we present UT-HMR ( Uncertainty-guided Temporal HMR), to our knowledge the first one-stage HMR framework to capture correlated pose uncertainty across joints. Each person query predicts a Gaussian distribution over the full SMPL pose with a compact low-rank-plus-diagonal covariance, which is converted into joint-wise precision weights for heteroscedastic supervision while keeping inference deterministic. Temporal early fusion further injects neighboring-frame evidence before pose decoding, supplying the visual evidence needed to resolve the ambiguity that the uncertainty captures. With a lightweight ViT-B backbone, UT-HMR achieves state-of-the-art results on VIP-HockeyPose-v2 (ice hockey) and WorldPose (soccer), reducing MPJPE, PA-MPJPE, and PVE by up to 4.7%, 3.8%, and 5.6%, and remains competitive on 3DPW against methods with larger backbones and higher input resolutions.
authors: Zhibo Wang, Sirisha Rambhatla, Yuhao Chen, Maria Koshkina, David Clausi
bullets: Addresses unreliable monocular HMR under long-distance views, occlusion, motion blur, and fast sports motion.
Predicts a Gaussian distribution over the full SMPL pose using compact low-rank-plus-diagonal covariance.
Converts uncertainty into joint-wise precision weights for heteroscedastic supervision while retaining deterministic inference.
Uses temporal early fusion to provide neighboring-frame evidence before pose decoding.
Achieves state-of-the-art results on VIP-HockeyPose-v2 and WorldPose, with reported metric reductions of up to 4.7% MPJPE, 3.8% PA-MPJPE, and 5.6% PVE; remains competitive on 3DPW.

The predicted covariance is supervised by the distribution loss and converted into joint-wise precision weights for the heteroscedastic joint loss.

papers.abstract: The Persona Selection Model (PSM) posits that post-training selects a persona the model learned during pre-training. Work on subliminal learning has shown that models can impart covert signals (like "love of owls") into semantically unrelated outputs like strings of numbers, and that students trained on these outputs inherit those traits. In this work I show that by evaluating the likelihood of such outputs under the base pre-trained model with an appropriate header, a method I call persona-header likelihood evaluation (PHLE), one can decode these subliminal signals and classify between them. For example, PHLE distinguishes number sequences generated by a post-trained model prompted with "You love owls" from those prompted with "You love eagles", and distinguishes answers from a model with a secret desire to harm the user, filtered to remove any noticeable misalignment, from those of a model with no system prompt. In both cases prompted classifiers, including the generating model itself, remain near chance. The signal partially persists across model families, with the Qwen base model reading signals generated by Olmo and vice versa. This is evidence for a non-trivial prediction of the PSM, and the method may be practically useful for auditing the hidden objectives of models.
bullets: Introduces persona-header likelihood evaluation (PHLE), which scores outputs under a base model using an appropriate header.
PHLE decodes subliminal signals embedded in semantically unrelated outputs, such as number sequences.
It distinguishes hidden owl-versus-eagle preferences and filtered harmful intentions from neutral behavior, while prompted classifiers stay near chance.
Signals partially transfer across model families, with Qwen and Olmo base models decoding one another’s signals.
The findings support the Persona Selection Model and suggest PHLE could help audit hidden model objectives.

papers.abstract: Despite rapid progress in visual understanding and document transcription, modern vision-language models (VLMs) struggle with a fundamental accessibility task: reading Braille from images. We introduce BrailleBench, a manually curated benchmark of 259 real-world Grade-1 and Grade-2 Braille images. We evaluate proprietary, open-weight, OCR-specialized, and tool-assisted multimodal systems and find that standalone general-purpose models perform poorly at directly transcribing Braille images, whereas tool-assisted systems perform much better. We design a synthetic Braille generation pipeline with diverse layouts and image perturbations. A 2B VLM model trained on our synthetic data reaches 87% exact match on Grade-1 and 61% on Grade-2 BrailleBench, outperforming standalone VLMs and achieving the highest Grade-2 exact match score among the evaluated systems. We further show that high accuracy on synthetic validation data does not guarantee high accuracy on real photographs in our experiments: models trained on prior synthetic data reach up to 96% on their synthetic validation set but at most 3.26% on Grade-1 BrailleBench. Our results identify an accessibility-relevant capability gap in multimodal systems and show that targeted synthetic supervision can improve real-world Braille transcription.
authors: Kartik Jangra, Atharva Gawane, Siddharth Pulipaka, Hemachandran Karah, Raj Dabre
bullets: BrailleBench contains 259 manually curated real-world Grade-1 and Grade-2 Braille images.
Standalone general-purpose VLMs perform poorly, while tool-assisted systems perform much better.
A synthetic Braille generation pipeline uses diverse layouts and image perturbations for training.
A 2B VLM trained on the synthetic data achieves 87% Grade-1 and 61% Grade-2 exact match on BrailleBench.
Synthetic validation accuracy may not transfer to real photographs: prior models reached up to 96% synthetically but at most 3.26% on Grade-1 BrailleBench.

papers.abstract: Learning velocity fields directly in pixel space is difficult and slow. We show that coarse second-order image statistics can ease this task: frozen Wiener estimates improve velocity learning, with gains extending beyond the linear predictions they explicitly provide. Moreover, we observe similar but complementary gains from frozen bases and pixel decoding. These observations motivate Wiener-informed Decoding (WiD), which uses statistical knowledge both for direct prediction and to organize decoder computation without modifying native blocks. WiD combines a trainable Wiener prediction path with coefficient interfaces that inject features into the native decoder and return its predicted coefficient corrections, with these components initialized with data statistics. All introduced parameters, including the spectrum and coordinate transforms, are trained jointly under the original pixel-space velocity objective. Across model scales and decoder architectures, WiD accelerates training and improves generation quality with modest parameter overhead. It also yields smoother gradient trajectories and remains effective with representation alignment. WiD improves class-conditional and text-to-image generation across different resolutions. On ImageNet 256 x 256, PixelDiT-XL with WiD reaches FID 1.53 after 500 epochs, achieving comparable quality to PixelDiT with 37.5% fewer training epochs. Statistical denoisers contribute beyond the estimate: their computational structure can also ease pixel-space training.
bullets: Frozen Wiener estimates improve velocity-field learning beyond their direct predictions.
WiD combines a trainable Wiener path with coefficient interfaces that augment native decoder computation without changing its blocks.
Statistical initialization, smoother gradients, and compatibility with representation alignment support training across model scales and decoder architectures.
On ImageNet 256×256, PixelDiT-XL with WiD reaches FID 1.53 after 500 epochs, matching PixelDiT quality with 37.5% fewer epochs.
The approach improves class-conditional and text-to-image generation across resolutions, with modest parameter overhead.

papers.abstract: We measure, without sampling error, the probability a language model assigns to each integer from 1 to N when asked for a random number. For a fixed prompt the model defines one probability vector, which we compute by summing over each integer's scored spellings rather than estimate by sampling, removing the noise that limits earlier studies [1, 4]. We evaluate 18 open-weight model lines at five ranges up to N = 100, under 29 decoding configurations, on two inference stacks; 15 of them have matched base and instruction-tuned checkpoints that both give usable answers. Instruction tuning makes the distribution less uniform in all 15 pairs. It installs one heuristic, round-number avoidance, and sharpens another, endpoint avoidance. Base checkpoints do not avoid round numbers once the endpoints are removed from those sets; tuned checkpoints avoid them, multiples of 10 almost completely. Base checkpoints return the endpoints 1 and N at 0.30 to 0.60 of the interior rate; tuned checkpoints almost never return them. A preference for odd numbers is consistent across tuned checkpoints only at N = 100, where base checkpoints also show it weakly. Endpoint avoidance and the odd preference fit the account Kubovy and Psotka [6] proposed for human number choice; round-number avoidance is not part of that account, and the midpoint avoidance it predicts is essentially absent, with one slight exception at N = 100. Tuning does not install a new favourite integer shared across models: above N = 10 no modal integer is shared by more than 42 percent of tuned conditions, and P (17) rises in 10 of 15 pairs and falls in 5. The concentration is present in the model's own distribution: at temperature 1.0, nucleus truncation at top-p 0.95 adds a median of 0.035 to the total variation distance.
bullets: The study computes exact integer probabilities by summing over each number’s scored spellings, avoiding sampling noise.
Across 15 matched base/instruction-tuned model pairs, tuning reduced distributional uniformity under varied ranges and decoding settings.
Tuning installed round-number avoidance—especially for multiples of 10—and sharpened avoidance of the endpoints 1 and N.
Odd-number preference appeared consistently only at N = 100; midpoint avoidance was largely absent.
Tuning did not produce a shared favorite integer across models; the concentration was intrinsic to the model distributions rather than caused mainly by top-p sampling.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has rapidly become the preferred representation for high-fidelity novel view synthesis and 3D scene reconstruction. However, the learned representation encodes sensitive visual information including human faces, license plates, documents, and computer screens, raising significant privacy concerns when trained splats are shared or deployed. In this work, we address the underexplored problem of privacy preservation in Gaussian Splatting by proposing a representation-level anonymization framework that directly anonymizes a trained splat. Given a trained splat and a user-provided reference view identifying sensitive content, our method localizes the corresponding regions in the underlying 3D representation and directly anonymizes them, ensuring that the sensitive information is absent from all subsequently rendered novel views while preserving the overall scene geometry and visual fidelity. We achieve this post-training anonymization in less than 1 second. Furthermore, we extend our framework with a privacy-by-design training strategy that prevents sensitive content from being embedded into the representation during optimization, enabling the generation of privacy-preserving splats directly from training images. Our method achieves a remarkably low Face Similarity Measure (FSM) of 9.79% at a retained Face Detection Rate (FDR) of 39.47% and makes sensitive text completely unreadable with an OCR Character Error Rate of 1.00. Our work aims to serve as the primary stepping stone towards privacy-aware 3D representations and motivates further research along these directions.
authors: Gaurav Behera, Abhinav Raundhal, Archisha Panda, Saumya Balina, Gargi Shroff, Ponnurangam Kumaraguru
bullets: Addresses privacy risks from faces, license plates, documents, and screens encoded in trained Gaussian splats.
Localizes sensitive regions from a user-provided reference view and anonymizes them at the representation level.
Post-training anonymization takes less than 1 second and preserves overall scene geometry and visual fidelity.
Also introduces privacy-by-design training to prevent sensitive content from being embedded during optimization.
Reports 9.79% Face Similarity Measure, 39.47% retained Face Detection Rate, and 1.00 OCR Character Error Rate for sensitive text.
