papers.abstract: Geometry foundation models recover camera poses and dense geometry from a set of images with a feed-forward network, but they expect pinhole images. That assumption is inside the backbone too: the positional encoding and the training loss both bind an image position to a direction in space, and both depend on the lens. We condition both on the dense ray field, the unit direction through every pixel, which describes any central camera without a lens type, distortion coefficients or a bound on field of view. Angular coordinates give the rotary encoding the measured ray angle of each patch, evaluated per view, and solid-angle weighting scales the point loss by the area each pixel covers on the sphere, so neither the encoding nor the supervision depends on the lens. Any3R is therefore a feed-forward model that takes any central camera, and is robust to mixing many camera types per scene, with no retraining per lens. On a benchmark of thirteen central cameras across three datasets, where every method reconstructs with its own predicted camera poses, it is the most consistently accurate method. Any3R enables scalable 3D reconstruction from heterogeneous crowdsourced and archival imagery collections sourced across diverse camera types. Project page: https://jingong-chen.github.io/Any3R/
authors: Jingong Chen, Qingwen Zhang, Youming Deng, Chulwoo Pack, Olaf Wysocki, Boris Jutzi, Kwanghee Won, Kyle Gao
bullets: Addresses the limitation of geometry foundation models that assume pinhole cameras and lens-dependent image-position representations.

Evaluated across 13 central cameras and three datasets, Any3R is reported as the most consistently accurate method while predicting camera poses itself.
Supports heterogeneous imagery collections, including crowdsourced and archival images from diverse cameras.

papers.abstract: Test-time updating lets a language model change persistent state after training---such as model weights, adapter parameters, or a memory module---before or while answering queries. Existing evaluations often compare systems using update count or frequency and performance measured immediately afterward. These summaries omit what is updated, where, when, and in what order. The same total can therefore hide an important difference: one system may answer after one update while another answers after two. We introduce the Control Map, an evaluation framework that records the committed updates preceding each scored answer and separately evaluates behavioral changes, immediate learning (acquisition), later recall (retention), preservation of unrelated behavior (locality), and performance in new settings. We prove when counts alone determine final state and show, under stated assumptions, how differences between pre-answer histories limit differences in average scores. Using ControlMap, our experiments reveal three insights. First, update scheduling matters: at a 760M-parameter checkpoint, 24 schedules with the same update count yield 19.7%--34.2% accuracy. Second, learning an edit does not guarantee that it lasts or remains contained: all six selected CounterFact LoRA settings learn the new information, while ROME retains edits at all 13 operating points but fails locality at each. Third, no editor performs best consistently across models, benchmarks, and tests. Evaluations should therefore report update histories and assess acquisition, retention, and locality separately.
authors: Zehao Zhao, Shangjian Yin, Rui Liu, Chongyang Bai, Mark Ibrahim, Kavosh Asadi, Yuchen Lu, Hang Cui, Hamed Firooz
bullets: Update count alone can hide differences in what is updated, when, and in what order before an answer is scored.

The authors prove when update counts suffice to determine final state and bound score differences caused by different update histories.
Experiments show scheduling strongly affects accuracy: 24 equal-count schedules at one checkpoint range from 19.7% to 34.2%.

papers.abstract: Image and video generators can produce spatially consistent visual content, but how to use this capability to improve spatial understanding remains underexplored. We study this problem from two perspectives: geometric supervision during training and explicit geometric evidence during inference. To this end, we introduce a unified geometric understanding and generation model (GeoUG) that integrates depth and multi-view generation with spatial understanding. First, we design a multi-scale depth codec that enables metric-depth generation using a pretrained visual autoencoder, and show that joint training yields task-dependent gains in spatial understanding. Second, we introduce 3DCueBench to control geometric difficulty while balancing selected 2D cues, and find that generated depth provides larger reasoning gains on questions requiring fine-grained geometric discrimination. Building on this finding, we develop adaptive interleaved reasoning, in which GeoUG first drafts an answer and then decides whether to generate geometric evidence to confirm or revise it. We train this decision through reinforcement learning, balancing accuracy gains over retaining the draft against generation cost. GeoUG achieves circular accuracies of 97.9%, 90.8%, and 94.2% on CV-Bench-3D, 3DCueBench, and DA-2K with fewer generation calls than always generating.
authors: Rui Yang, Yanwei Li, Sili Chen, Jingjia Huang, Yi Lin, Hengshuang Zhao

Finds generated depth particularly helps fine-grained geometric reasoning.
Uses reinforcement-learned adaptive interleaved reasoning to decide when to generate evidence; reports 97.9%, 90.8%, and 94.2% circular accuracy on three benchmarks.

papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) offer a promising framework for embodied intelligence, yet mainstream approaches remain centered on video foundation models or vision-language models. Even when geometric features extracted by 3D models such as VGGT are incorporated, they are typically passed into a video model or VLM that serves as the primary backbone, leaving 3D geometry as an auxiliary input or prediction target rather than the native foundation for world modeling. We present E0.5, a geometry-native world-action model built directly on 3D foundation models. E0.5 introduces two key innovations. First, it adopts a 3D foundation model as the primary backbone, making 3D geometry the native representation for both world modeling and action prediction. Second, it explicitly predicts future 3D states together with actions, enabling the model to capture geometric world dynamics beyond action-only modeling or future video prediction. Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0 first demonstrate the effectiveness of E0.5 without embodied-data pretraining, achieving success rates of 89.90\% and 50.09\% under clean and randomized settings, respectively. Building on these results, we further pretrain E0.5 on more than 160k robot trajectories from AgiBotWorld-Beta, jointly learning robot actions and future geometry within the pretrained 3D foundation. This embodied pretraining improves mean real-world manipulation success rates by approximately 15 and 7 percentage points on AgileX Piper and Zerith H1, respectively. Together, these results demonstrate the potential of geometry-native foundations to acquire robot interaction knowledge and transfer it to physical manipulation. E0.5 embodies this geometry-native approach as a member of the VWA family of world-action models.

papers.abstract: Sparse expert execution does not remove the stored states needed to adapt a mixture-of-experts language model. We present DuplexTune, a framework for replaying coupled hidden states through pretrained attention and expert modules. Trainable width bridges connect two residual streams to the backbone. Bridge warm-up precedes backbone adaptation, with router weights kept frozen. We analyze the implicit state-recovery equation and identify the convergence and replay conditions needed for reconstruction. On Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B, the single-H800 evaluation reports 38.8 GB peak memory, versus 64.8 GB for supervised fine-tuning with checkpointing, and throughput of 25.1 versus 19.9 samples/s. DuplexTune achieves 67.2% MMLU, 75.6% GSM8K, and 7.69 MT-Bench, with a weaker multilingual score than the checkpointed baseline. The results characterize a configuration-dependent tradeoff among state storage, throughput, and adaptation quality.

Reports 67.2% MMLU, 75.6% GSM8K, and 7.69 MT-Bench, while multilingual performance is weaker than the checkpointed baseline.

papers.abstract: Variable-length training creates conflicting parallelism requirements across the layers of a hybrid-attention model. The longest samples require wide sequence-parallel (SP) groups of 16 or 32 ranks for full attention, whose cost grows quadratically with sequence length. Sparse-attention layers, dominated by near-linear MoE work, can instead balance most evaluated workloads within node-local SP8 groups. Reusing the wide groups for these layers pushes their all-to-all communication across nodes, where the observed effective rate is 7.0x lower. Yet switching to smaller groups changes which ranks own each sample; a separate redistribution at every full-sparse boundary would introduce another data transfer. Layerwise Repacking keeps each SP16/32 parent for full attention and repacks its samples into node-local sparse children at SP{1, 2, 4, 8}, where hidden states persist between full layers. The layout change rides on the two existing full-layer Ulysses sites: at each, one variable-size all-to-all performs both the head exchange and the sample repacking, so no redistribution pass is added. Because the balance the children can reach depends on which samples share a parent, an auxiliary parent solver rebalances parent membership before the children are formed. On all 22 steps with SP16/32 parents among the first 200 training steps of a 1F3S hybrid-attention model (one full-attention layer per three sparse-attention layers), repacking alone reduces the mean end-to-end time by 5.95% and raises model FLOPs utilization (MFU) by 3.75 percentage points over the baseline with repacking disabled; with the improved solver, end-to-end time falls by 7.61% and MFU rises by 4.83 percentage points.
authors: Jiahao Zhang, Junwei Feng, Dongliang Huang, Xiaoling Zhou, Yiqiao Liao, Chengru Song

The method repacks samples from each wide parent group into smaller sparse-attention child groups at existing Ulysses all-to-all sites.
An auxiliary solver rebalances parent membership to improve the load balance achievable by the sparse children.

papers.abstract: Conditional memory layers, such as DeepSeek's Engram, attach large hashed n-gram tables to a language model, and removing them from DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash costs 36.8 PopQA points. Low-bit quantization loses long-tail facts first, and the standard remedy, giving more bits to frequently accessed rows, backfires: refining lookups by access frequency is worse than refining them at random. We trace this to the gate that scales each retrieved row. A lookup's quantization error is weighted by its gate, which is small for frequent n-grams, large for the rare n-grams of long-tail entities, and computable from a 1-bit code. GateRQ therefore stores each row as a ladder of 1-bit residual codes, keeps level 1 in GPU memory to compute the gate, and reads deeper levels only for the lookups the gate ranks highest. Without retraining, GateRQ cuts GPU table memory by 7.8x on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, which raises vLLM throughput by 11%-31% over FP8 tables, while losing about 1 PopQA point at 1.50 bits read per lookup and 0.2 points at 2.10 bits across two models.
authors: Tianqi Chen, Xunchao Li, Linchuan Xie, Guanghua Yu, Jianchen Zhu, Peisong Wang, Jian Cheng
bullets: Frequency-based precision allocation can hurt because frequent lookups often have small gates, while rare long-tail entity lookups have larger gates and greater quantization impact.
GateRQ stores each row as progressively refined 1-bit residual codes and uses an always-resident first level to estimate gates.
Deeper residual levels are fetched only for lookups ranked as most important by their gate values.
Without retraining, it reduces GPU table memory by 7.8× and improves vLLM throughput by 11%–31% over FP8 tables.
It loses about 1 PopQA point at 1.50 bits per lookup and 0.2 points at 2.10 bits across two models.

papers.selection_reason: Gate-aware quantization of conditional LLM memory drastically cuts table memory and improves throughput while preserving long-tail fact recall.
papers.title: Let the Gate Decide: Per-Lookup Precision for Quantized Conditional Memory in LLMs
papers.tldr: GateRQ improves quantized conditional memory by allocating extra precision per lookup based on the row’s gate value, preserving long-tail facts while reducing memory and improving throughput.

papers.abstract: Deploying LLM agents in specialized domains often require fine-grained task-specific procedures and knowledge a general model lacks, yet parameter training is costly and non-interpretable, and hand-engineered agent systems shift the cost to expert labor. Episodic memory updates at context level, but single agent adaptation struggles to alleviate cross-task interference, especially with complex tasks such as multi-application navigation or data pool analysis. Although multi-agent evolution alleviates this problem, existing methods lack clear definitions on update rules and rely on the backbone model to decide where and how much the system changes. This ill-scoped evolution makes learning follow the backbone's structural preferences rather than the observed failures: one backbone accumulates skills while another spawns agents. We present EMMA (structured Episodic Memory for Multi-Agent workflow synthesis), which treats the configuration of a multi-agent system (controller routing memory, specialists inheriting a generalist prompt, and per-step procedural skills) as episodic memory. EMMA makes the ownership and admissibility of updates explicit: a reflector assigns each diagnosed failure to the scope owning its correction and proposes one edit within it, and backbone-independent guards keep every accepted edit scoped, incremental and bounded. Across KramaBench, AppWorld and BBEH with five backbones and four baselines (ACE, GEPA, EvoMAS and ADAS), EMMA attains the best overall performance on every benchmark, up to 32.5% over the strongest baseline, maintains consistent improvements across backbones, and uses 17-38% fewer training executions than the most efficient baseline.
authors: Ruijia Niu, Kaiwen Liu, Rose Yu, Kristina Klinkner
bullets: Addresses cross-task interference and costly, opaque adaptation in specialized multi-agent systems.
Represents controller routing, specialist prompts, and procedural skills as distinct episodic-memory scopes.
Uses a reflector to assign failures to the responsible scope and propose one bounded edit.
Backbone-independent guards enforce scoped, incremental, and admissible updates.
Outperforms four baselines across KramaBench, AppWorld, and BBEH, with up to 32.5% higher performance and 17–38% fewer training executions.

figures.caption: Figure 2: EMMA architecture. The controller selects controller-memory entries, plans, and dispatches one step at a time to a sub-agent with its assigned skills; step outputs drive replanning, and a step that overflows its sub-agent is re-split. The three memory levels persist across tasks and are written only during training; the execution environment is created per attempt and discarded.

Figure 3: EMMA training procedure. (1) Rollout in a fresh environment; (2) a binary gate from the task’s own signal; (3) structured reflection over the whole trajectory (localize, classify, generalize, minimize); (4) one guarded edit within the designated scope; (5) re-run until success or the revision budget is spent, then an end-of-task controller update; the memory is frozen after one pass.

Figure 1: Ill-scoped versus scoped updates. (a) Without scope constraints, the update is a backbone habit: Opus 5 accumulates skills, DeepSeek v3.2 repeatedly creates agents (one mark per created artifact). (b) EMMA assigns the diagnosed failure to a scope and makes one bounded edit within it.
Figure 4: Cross-family consistency. Held-out performance per backbone (from Tables 2 and 3); shaded columns are open-weight backbones.
Table 6: Configuration of EMMA.

Table 3: AppWorld, TGC / SGC (%) on test_normal (168 tasks) and test_challenge (417 tasks). Best in bold, second underlined, ranked per metric. For ADAS on DeepSeek v3.2 and Kimi-K2.5, no discovered program beat the hand-written seed, which is reported.
Table 5: Ablations on KramaBench with Opus 4.5. Top: learned memory levels. Bottom: training-split episodic learning vs. testsplit adaptation.
Table 4: Training task executions, mean over five backbones (lower is better). Best in bold, second underlined.
Table 2: KramaBench (macro accuracy over 76 held-out tasks) and BBEH-mini (accuracy, 368 held-out examples). Best per column in bold, second underlined; Mean averages over backbones.
Table 1: Ownership rules: failure scopes z and available actions Act(z). A lesson at the wrong level never fires again or contaminates unrelated tasks; the scope–action guard enforces this table.

papers.tldr: EMMA structures episodic updates across multi-agent workflows, improving performance consistently while reducing training executions.

papers.abstract: While progress in informal mathematics has come largely from scaling the chain-of-thought and agentic reasoning of frontier language models, formal theorem proving has increasingly relied on human-designed workflows around these models, such as planning, decomposition, and orchestrating specialized provers. This raises a bitter-lesson question: can a simple agentic loop that scales test-time compute match these workflows? The answer matters as formal verification must scale to keep up with frontier models producing research mathematics, yet new workflows rarely settle it, as their gains are often confounded with stronger models or more compute. We study this question with h1, a simple harness that gives a model an efficient interface to Lean 4 and keeps it working through verifier feedback and self-reflection, without imposing a decomposition or search structure. h1 reaches state-of-the-art results on PutnamBench, FATE-X, and FormalConjectures100-Solved, settles eight open problems in FormalConjectures, and, at matched models, matches or outperforms specialized workflows such as Goedel-Architect and AlphaProof Nexus, surprisingly showing that a single attempt (pass@1) can often scale to solve open problems. Through ablations and matched-model comparisons with Claude Code and AxProverBase, we find that simplicity alone is not enough: an efficient Lean interface largely determines cost and solve rate. We thus recommend that future work evaluate frontier models with efficient execution feedback before prescribing workflows, at the risk of bitter lessons.
authors: Skander Moalla, Ahmad Rammal, Niket Patel, Remi Munos, Julia Kempe
bullets: Motivation: formal theorem proving needs to scale with frontier models, but workflow gains are often confounded by stronger models or more compute.
Method: h1 provides an efficient Lean 4 interface with verifier feedback and self-reflection, without predefined decomposition or search structures.
Results: h1 achieves state-of-the-art performance on PutnamBench, FATE-X, and FormalConjectures100-Solved, and settles eight FormalConjectures open problems.
Matched comparisons show h1 can match or outperform workflows such as Goedel-Architect and AlphaProof Nexus, with pass@1 often solving open problems.
Ablations indicate that simplicity alone is insufficient; the efficiency of the Lean interface strongly affects cost and solve rate.

figures.caption: Figure 1 (Left) Simple scaling Pareto-dominates specialized systems. On PutnamBench (672 competition problems), h1 with DeepSeek V4 Flash Pareto-dominates Goedel-Architect’s best of four runs (pass@4) seeded with natural-language proofs. With GPT-5.5, it solves every solvable problem, as Humanfia and Aleph Prover do, at lower cost. (Middle) Longer attempts can outperform repetition. On five open Erdős problems, a single h1 attempt (pass@1) beats three attempts of AlphaProof Nexus’s basic agent (APN basic, pass@3) at lower mean cost per success, can be cheaper than repeating h1 itself, and Pareto-dominates the full APN system. (Right) Simple harness design is important for scaling efficiency and effectiveness. On a 100-problem PutnamBench subset, Gemini 3 Flash trails Opus 4.5 in the AxProverBase loop but overtakes it in h1 at matched budget through more efficient tool use and caching.

Figure 3 Generalist models reach frontier results through simple scaling. On FC100-solved (left) and FATE-X (right), increasing h1’s inference budget takes generalist models beyond published benchmark scores. On FC100-solved, h1 with Gemini 3.1 Pro matches the DeepMind (DM) prover agent’s score at a quarter of its budget cap; with GPT-5.6 Sol, it solves 78, and 90 on FATE-X. With DeepSeek V4 Flash, h1 surpasses AlphaProof on FC100-solved and Leanstral 1.5 on FATE-X. Baseline markers show the best published results as of August 27, 2026.

Figure 5 (Left) h1Pareto-dominates AxProverBase on Putnam100. For each of six model settings, the arrow goes from AxProverBase to h1, labelled with the gain in solves at a comparable or lower budget cap. (Right) Claude Code improves with our Lean tools but still falls short of h1 on FATE-X. With Opus 4.8, replacing Claude Code’s built-in shell and file tools with our prompt and Lean tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) raises its solves from 63 to 73, while h1, which also enforces validation, repair, and reflection, reaches 83 (Putnam100: Figure 6).

Figure 2 h1: a simple harness that scales. An LLM agent edits a Lean file through reasoning and tool calls (ReAct; Yao et al., 2023) until it submits or reaches the T -turn limit, forcing submission. An external validator then checks the proof. On failure, a reflection LLM compacts the transcript and feedback for the next iteration. The loop provides Lean tools without prescribing a proof search structure. Search uses LeanExplore (Asher, 2025), Loogle (Breitner, 2023), and grep; proof fragments run in the Lean read–eval–print loop (REPL) (leanprover-community, 2023); the language server (LSP) reports goals and definitions; SafeVerify (GasStationManager, 2024) performs validation.

Figure 4 (Left) Detailed prompts sustain progress on open problems. With Gemini 3.1 Pro on six open Erdős problems and a $150 cap per attempt, a single attempt with detailed prover and reflection prompts, which among other things deflect giving up and cheating, outperforms six attempts with brief ones. (Right) Moderate numbers of turns between reflections outperform both extremes. Solves with Gemini 3 Flash on Putnam100 ($20 cap) and Gemini 3.1 Pro on FATE-X ($50 cap) as the number of turns between reflections varies.

papers.selection_reason: Scaling test-time compute with a simple LLM agentic loop and verifier feedback is directly relevant to large language model reasoning and evaluation.
papers.title: h1: A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving
papers.tldr: h1 shows that a simple Lean-feedback agent loop, scaled with test-time compute, can match or outperform specialized formal-proving workflows and solve new open problems.

papers.abstract: Solving long-horizon agentic tasks requires language agents to interact with their environments over multiple steps, and reliable performance often comes from the expensive capable models available through cloud providers. Meanwhile, alternative efficient models with inferior performance but a much lower cost are emerging, including lower-tier cloud models and smaller open-weights models deployable on local hardware. This raises a natural question that remains less explored than traditional query-level routing: can capable and efficient models collaborate within a single long-horizon agentic task to substantially reduce cost while preserving task accuracy? In this paper, we systematically investigate key design choices for such collaboration through model handoffs, where one model takes over from another, focusing on handoff direction and context transfer. We find that efficient-to-capable handoffs generally underperform capable-only execution with limited or even no cost reduction, whereas capable-to-efficient handoffs at suitable stages of task progress largely preserve or even improve accuracy while substantially reducing cost. These findings suggest that a one-time, simple, well-timed handoff strategy is good enough for cost-effective agent collaboration, motivating AgentBaton, a lightweight detector that learns when to hand off from recurring patterns in task progress. Across 11 model pairs and two representative benchmarks, AgentBaton reduces API costs by 65.9% on average while largely preserving task accuracy, with accuracy gains of up to 8.8 percentage points over capable-only execution. Experiments across various reasoning-effort settings further show that AgentBaton extends the empirical accuracy-cost Pareto frontier.

papers.abstract: Distributed speculative decoding has emerged as a promising approach for device--server collaborative large language model (LLM) inference, but its decoding speedup is often limited by the vocabulary-scale communication overhead. In existing distributed speculative decoding methods, exact rejection sampling requires transmitting full token distributions over the LLM vocabulary between the device and the server, which becomes costly in bandwidth-constrained environments. To address this issue, we propose DISCO, a communication-efficient framework for distributed speculative decoding, that eliminates vocabulary-scale distribution transfer while preserving the exact target distribution. DISCO achieves this by introducing a server-side replica of the draft small language model (SLM), which enables the server to locally obtain the draft-side distribution required for rejection sampling. As a result, DISCO exchanges only drafted token indices and scalar probability values between the device and the server. Experimental results on multiple datasets show that DISCO consistently achieves higher decoding speedup than existing distributed speculative decoding methods, particularly under stringent bandwidth constraints.

papers.abstract: Low-bit weight--activation quantization reduces the memory and computation needed to deploy large language models, but activation rounding can still degrade accuracy after calibration. Reconstruction from rounded inputs cannot distinguish activations within the same quantization bin. We propose ResCom, a low-rank correction that uses the activation rounding residual to compensate for the resulting layer-output error. An output-aware calibration procedure selects residual directions by their contribution to output reconstruction and computes the correction in closed form, without gradient training or updates to the calibrated weights. On Llama-3-8B with 4-bit weights and activations, rank-32 attention corrections reduce WikiText-2 perplexity from 7.708 to 7.147, improve MMLU by 2.89 percentage points, and raise five-shot GSM8K accuracy from 23.96 to 36.16 percent. Evaluations on models from 1B to 70B parameters and on held-out C4 test the method beyond this setting. The evaluated FP32 implementation adds 2.25 percent to 4K prefill time; a separate compact-storage implementation retains a 27.7 percent peak-memory reduction relative to FP16.
authors: Ning Yang, Bohan Cui, Zhuowen Liu, Yuting Wang
bullets: Targets accuracy loss caused by activation rounding in weight–activation quantization.
Selects output-relevant residual directions during calibration and computes corrections in closed form without gradient training or changing calibrated weights.

Evaluations span 1B–70B models and include held-out C4 testing.
The evaluated FP32 version adds 2.25% to 4K prefill time; compact storage preserves a 27.7% peak-memory reduction versus FP16.

papers.abstract: Autonomous vertical landing of reusable launch vehicles is a critical yet formidable challenge in aerospace engineering, primarily due to highly nonlinear dynamics, stringent precision require- ments, and inherent environmental uncertainties. While reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a promising alternative to traditional model-based control, existing approaches frequently rely on flat training paradigms and highly simplified initial conditions, drastically limiting their real-world applicability. This paper proposes a comprehensive curriculum-driven deep reinforcement learning framework designed to master both far-range navigation and precision landing. By employing a three-stage curriculum augmented with a critic warm-up procedure and a rehearsal mechanism to prevent catastrophic forgetting, alongside a high-dimensional observation vector utilizing a full 3 X 3 rotation-matrix, the agent is trained to navigate from an initial horizontal distance of 1,000 to 1,500 units vastly farther than prior benchmarks before executing a soft touchdown. Crucially, we intro- duce a redesigned reward function that reduces unnecessary computational overhead and addresses limitations of earlier formulations, including poorly calibrated reward components and potentially conflicting optimization objectives. The redesigned function bounds the per-step reward magnitude by (O(1)), while its progress term accumulates the total distance closed over the trajectory. The available 100,000-episode results report a 99.98% success rate for the proposed policy and 68.31% for the baseline under the evaluation conditions. In the evaluation, the proposed policy retained 69.1% of its initial fuel capacity and achieved a mean final distance from the pad centre of 7.07 units, compared with 13.10 units for the baseline. Landing visualizations are available in Video 1 and Video 2.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of combining long-range navigation with precision vertical landing under nonlinear dynamics and uncertainty.
Uses a three-stage curriculum, critic warm-up, rehearsal to limit catastrophic forgetting, and observations containing a full 3×3 rotation matrix.
Introduces a bounded, computationally simpler reward function whose progress term tracks cumulative distance closed.
Under the reported evaluation, the policy achieved 99.98% success versus 68.31% for the baseline.
The proposed policy retained 69.1% initial fuel and had 7.07 units mean final pad-distance, compared with 13.10 units for the baseline.

papers.abstract: Emergent generative AI technologies, while remarkably beneficial across several tasks and domains, can suffer from unforeseen vulnerabilities and difficult-to-anticipate failure modes. Such failure modes can disparately affect vulnerable communities. This paper investigates two well-known vision language models (VLMs) and inspects how these models encode protected identities while generating images. We show that when VLMs are requested to transform human face images to reflect race identities (e.g., Hispanic, Black, White, or Asian) and sexual orientation (e.g., gay or straight), VLMs often comply with such requests. We demonstrate that compliance (and refusal) is non-deterministic, group-sensitive, and generated images are statistically distinguishable, often accentuating deep-seated stereotypes. We further show that representation biases introduced during image generation can re-emerge in textual reasoning and characterization tasks. Finally, we show that this worrisome finding is not limited to racial identity or sexual orientation, image generation can perpetuate bias around criminality, raising concerning possibilities of AI-assisted profiling.

papers.abstract: Image quality assessment (IQA) underpins embodied imaging pipelines by judging whether visual quality satisfies downstream tasks, yet most existing methods learn task-agnostic scores aligned with generic human ratings on static benchmarks. This objective mismatches embodied and interactive settings, where image adequacy depends on task goals, context, and action requirements that shape an agent's decisions. We argue that IQA should shift from score regression to goal-conditioned judgment defined by embodied task utility. To this end, we propose an MLLM-based embodied IQA agent framework that reasons about task requirements, grounds quality evidence, and produces decision-facing assessments. A compact VisDrone evidence study shows that conventional perceptual metrics and generic MLLM-based IQA scores are weak proxies for downstream VLM task success, while a task-conditioned utility score better predicts whether visual input supports the target task. These findings support a task-utility-oriented reframing of IQA for embodied, explainable, and decision-aware visual perception.
authors: Jirong Zha, Yanwei Liao, Yemin Wang, Xiangmin Yi, Siqi Peng, Yingfeng Chen, Chen Gao, Xinlei Chen

The paper proposes an MLLM-based embodied IQA agent that reasons over task requirements, grounds quality evidence, and produces decision-facing judgments.

Task-conditioned utility scores better predict whether visual inputs support the target task.
The proposed reframing targets embodied, explainable, and decision-aware visual perception.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a task-utility oriented Image Quality Assessment framework for embodied agents, connecting visual understanding to task requirements and actions.

papers.abstract: Object-wise reconstruction increasingly inserts generated meshes into captured scenes as editable proxies for observed objects. This use creates a requirement absent from isolated-asset scores and pose estimates: at the captured metric state, the proxy should reproduce calibrated observations of the same instance. We present ObjectTwin, a scan-grounded measurement protocol that freezes the instance, cameras, scan-projected support and recorded depth, metric anchor, and evaluation denominator, then replaces only the object representation. The resulting asset correspondence gap measures lost observation agreement relative to scan-derived visible geometry without treating the scan as complete physical ground truth. Across two indoor RGB-D capture domains and two generation backends, visible, anchored generated assets lose 0.302-0.497 MaskIoU under this replacement. Every tested scene-level estimate is positive, while same-input generator preference reverses across capture domains. Coverage and overlap-depth analyses locate disagreement in both visible support and surface placement; the evaluated conservative pose refinement does not systematically recover it. These results establish capture correspondence as a separately measurable interface between generated-asset quality and stronger physical or task-level evaluation.
bullets: Addresses a gap in isolated-asset and pose metrics: editable proxies must match the same object instance in its captured metric state.
Freezes the instance, cameras, scan-derived support, recorded depth, metric anchor, and evaluation denominator while replacing only the object representation.
Defines the asset correspondence gap as lost observation agreement relative to scan-derived visible geometry, without assuming the scan is complete ground truth.
Across two indoor RGB-D domains and two generation backends, generated assets lose 0.302–0.497 MaskIoU; disagreement involves both visible support and surface placement.
The evaluated conservative pose refinement does not systematically recover the mismatch, and generator preferences reverse across capture domains.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses the asset correspondence gap in digital twins, providing a metric for evaluating generated assets against captured observations, relevant to 3D reconstruction and foundation models.
papers.title: ObjectTwin: Measuring the Asset Correspondence Gap for Capture-Anchored Digital Twins

papers.abstract: Changing a deployment policy can invalidate a world model's uncertainty while leaving the physical transition mechanism and predictor unchanged. For one-step prediction, if source and target laws share the conditional mechanism $P(Y|X)=Q(Y|X)$, then the intervention is identified by the pre-outcome change of measure $w(X)=dQ_X/dP_X$. For policy-controlled dynamics this ratio factors into state-occupancy and action-propensity terms. Weighted conformal calibration transports marginal coverage to the target law; with an estimated ratio $\hat w$, $P_Q\{Y \in C_{\hat w}(X)\} \ge 1-\alpha-TV(Q,\hat Q) \ge 1-\alpha-E_P|w-\hat w|$. Population log-loss regret for a source-versus-target domain classifier bounds the same ratio error. If $h$ is its clipped target posterior, $\rho$ is the target-domain prior, and $\Delta(h)$ is population log-loss regret, then $E_P|w-\hat w_h| \le (1/(\rho\gamma))\sqrt{\Delta(h)/2}$. An exact cancellation improves the dependence from a generic odds-map bound of order $\gamma^{-2}$ to $(\rho\gamma)^{-1}$. Our experiments use a released DINO-feature world model and physical Franka trajectories. Under the strongest controlled state-action shift, ordinary 90% conformal sets cover 55.0%, whereas oracle and learned-ratio calibration cover 91.0% and 90.9%. The learned surrogate remains within 0.9% total variation of the target law. Calibration is relative to the deployment law: the model can remain fixed while calibration follows the intervention. We machine-check in Lean 4 the finite-support algebraic and causal identities used in the classifier-regret argument, including its coverage-composition step.
bullets: Under shared transition mechanisms, policy changes affect calibration through a pre-outcome density ratio over states and actions.
Theoretical bounds relate target coverage loss to ratio-estimation error, which can be controlled using domain-classifier log-loss regret.
An exact cancellation improves the classifier-based error dependence from order γ⁻² to (ργ)⁻¹.
In experiments, ordinary 90% sets covered 55.0%, versus 91.0% with oracle and 90.9% with learned-ratio calibration under strong shift.
The approach is validated on DINO-feature world-model predictions and physical Franka trajectories; key finite-support identities are machine-checked in Lean 4.

papers.tldr: Weighted conformal calibration can preserve uncertainty coverage after policy interventions by reweighting fixed world-model predictions toward the deployment distribution.

papers.abstract: AI applications often invoke a model before they determine whether inference is necessary. That default is useful for ambiguous generative tasks, but it is poorly matched to work that is structured, deterministic, policy-bound, lookup-oriented, or directly verifiable. KORA introduces deterministic-first execution control: a pre-inference control layer that represents requests as task paths, attempts deterministic or structured routes first, validates route outcomes, records telemetry, and escalates to a model-candidate path only when deterministic handling is insufficient. This paper presents KORA as a deterministic-first execution-control architecture and reports bounded evidence from reproducible benchmark and validation workloads. In a reproducible 100-task deterministic-heavy benchmark, KORA-controlled execution avoided 80 of 100 simulated model invocations versus a naive direct baseline, with zero mismatches in the deterministic subset. The workload is intentionally deterministic-heavy: it includes categories such as FAQ lookup, policy/rule checking, schema or format validation, deterministic transformation, and a smaller set of model-needed ambiguous or generative tasks. A separate synthetic customer-support local/no-network validation workload demonstrates route measurement and avoided model-call accounting in an application-shaped setting. These results support bounded model-invocation reduction and validation visibility in documented workloads. They do not establish production behavior, real-provider outcomes, energy outcomes, API-cost reduction, or broad superiority.
bullets: Targets structured, policy-bound, lookup-oriented, and verifiable workloads that do not always need inference.
Uses a pre-inference control layer with task paths, deterministic/structured routing, validation, telemetry, and model escalation.
Avoided 80 of 100 simulated model invocations with zero deterministic-subset mismatches in a deterministic-heavy benchmark.
A synthetic local customer-support workload demonstrated route measurement and avoided-call accounting.
Evidence is bounded to documented workloads; production, cost, energy, and broad-superiority claims remain unestablished.

figures.caption: Figure 1: KORA request-routing overview. Incoming requests are mapped to task paths and routed through deterministic, lookup, or policy handlers before model invocation. Validated deterministic outputs return without a model call, while failed, unmapped, or model-required routes conservatively escalate to model fallback. Telemetry records routing, validation, escalation, and avoided-call events.

Figure 3: KORA-controlled request path. KORA routes requests through deterministic or structured handling before model invocation, returning validated deterministic outputs when possible and conservatively escalating invalid, unmapped, or model-required routes to model fallback.

Figure 2: KORA benchmark evidence workflow. The 100-task deterministic-heavy benchmark compares a naive direct baseline with KORA-controlled execution. KORA avoids 80 of 100 simulated model invocations while checking 80 deterministic outputs with zero mismatches; this result is bounded to the documented reproducible workload and is not production, cost, energy, or broad-superiority evidence.
Table 2. Customer-support triage local/no-network validation scope and boundary.

papers.selection_reason: Pre-inference deterministic-first execution control reduces unnecessary model invocations, directly supporting efficient AI goals of reducing compute and latency.
papers.title: KORA: Deterministic-First Execution Control for AI Workloads
papers.tldr: KORA reduces unnecessary AI model calls by trying validated deterministic routes before escalating ambiguous tasks to a model.

papers.abstract: Direct-policy World Action Models (WAM) have demonstrated the benefits of decoupling action generation from explicit future visual prediction for efficient inference in autonomous driving and embodied control. However, they still require tens of denoising steps to achieve competitive action quality, incurring substantial latency and hindering real-time deployment. Simply reducing the number of denoising steps will collapse the nonlinear multi-step denoising trajectory into coarse updates, substantially degrading action quality. To reduce the denoising steps while enabling real-time action generation, we present an effective world action model with one-step action generation, namely OSWAM, for autonomous driving and embodied control. We argue that it is the absence of structured action priors in random noise initialization that forces direct-policy WAMs to recover coherent action sequences through iterative denoising. Hence, we construct imagination tokens to initialize the diffusion process, providing physical priors and action-conditioned representations. We further introduce privileged information distillation with future conditioning to enhance future-aware action generation. As a result, OSWAM can efficiently and effectively generate high quality actions in just one diffusion step. Our experiments demonstrate that OSWAM achieves comparable or even better results in both autonomous driving and embodied control than direct-policy WAM and Joint-WAM that require tens of steps. It obtains approximately $3\times$ speedup over direct-policy WAM baselines and supports real-time compiled inference with latency as low as 40ms on an NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPU. The project page is available at https://gwenzhang.github.io/OSWAM/
bullets: Direct-policy world action models typically need tens of denoising steps, limiting real-time deployment.
OSWAM uses imagination tokens to provide physical priors and action-conditioned representations at diffusion initialization.
Privileged information distillation with future conditioning improves future-aware action generation.
Experiments report comparable or better performance than multi-step direct-policy and Joint-WAM baselines, with about 3× speedup and latency as low as 40 ms on an NVIDIA RTX 5090.
The abstract evaluates autonomous driving and embodied control, without specifying broader domains or limitations.

papers.abstract: Multimodal medical AI requires a common visual interface for encoding heterogeneous imaging evidence for patient condition modeling. However, existing medical visual tokenizers are often tied to a specific dimension and imaging modality, forcing multimodal systems to rely on fragmented and poorly reusable representations. We introduce MedVTok, a general-purpose visual tokenizer that maps 2D images and 3D volumes from diverse imaging modalities into a unified token space. Building such a tokenizer poses two key challenges: preserving anatomical structure across dimensions and capturing clinical semantics across modalities. To this end, MedVTok introduces (i) slice differential regularization, which explicitly models inter-slice anatomical coherence missing in previous per-pixel/per-voxel supervision, and (ii) multi-expert representation alignment, which integrates knowledge from multiple medical expert encoders while retaining modality-specific complementary knowledge. Trained on 28M images and 70K volumes across 9 imaging modalities, MedVTok supports classification, retrieval, segmentation, synthesis, visual question answering, and medical report generation through a single tokenizer. Across 24 benchmarks, MedVTok achieves state-of-the-art performance, demonstrating a scalable token interface that unifies medical image dimension, modality, and task usage.
bullets: Addresses fragmented tokenizers that are limited to specific image dimensions or modalities.
Uses slice differential regularization to preserve anatomical coherence across 3D slices.
Applies multi-expert representation alignment to combine clinical knowledge while retaining modality-specific information.
Trained on 28M images and 70K volumes spanning 9 imaging modalities.
Supports classification, retrieval, segmentation, synthesis, visual question answering, and report generation, with state-of-the-art results across 24 benchmarks.

papers.abstract: A robot policy needs to understand what a task is asking for in a scene, and how to move the robot to accomplish that task. To achieve these two skills, we introduce Zero-real Agent Policy (ZAP), a recipe that teaches a small off-the-shelf vision-language model to control a robot via a simple tool harness. We use a pretrained 27B parameter model to bootstrap world understanding and reasoning, followed by supervised fine-tuning and GRPO on simple simulated tasks to teach it how to move the robot. Without observing real-world robot data during training, ZAP reaches 96.7% success on real-world tasks, matching GPT-6 Astra in our harness and outperforming the MolmoAct2 VLA (33.3%), while running 3x faster and 17x cheaper than GPT-6 Astra. Furthermore, ZAP also generalizes to an unseen embodiment as well as new objects, goals and strategies never seen during training. On a single-arm Franka, ZAP reaches 55.9% on RoboLab-120, 4.9 percentage points ahead of the leading VLA/WAM baseline.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of combining task understanding with robot motion control without real-world robot training data.
Uses a pretrained 27B vision-language model, then supervised fine-tuning and GRPO on simple simulated tasks via a tool harness.
Achieves 96.7% success on real-world tasks, matching GPT-6 Astra while running 3× faster and costing 17× less.
Generalizes to unseen embodiments, objects, goals, and strategies; reaches 55.9% on RoboLab-120, 4.9 points above the cited VLA/WAM baseline.

papers.tldr: ZAP combines pretrained world understanding with simulation-based control training to achieve strong zero-real robot manipulation and compositional generalization.

papers.abstract: Latent world models are typically pre-trained offline and kept frozen at test time, so planning with them can degrade under distribution shift. Test-time adaptation (TTA) can mitigate this degradation by updating the model during deployment. Unlike pre-training on fixed data, TTA for planning is closed-loop: the planner uses model rollouts to select actions, and the resulting transitions drive the next update. This raises the question: which objective should guide TTA for planning? Under a prediction-only objective, the model is fit only to the outcomes of its own actions, so it can remain wrong about the actions that would reach the goal, and low prediction error need not translate into better planning. Inspired by reward-biased maximum likelihood from adaptive control, we introduce Optimistic Test-Time Adaptation (OpTTA). Its objective has two terms, the prediction loss on observed transitions and the planner's goal-reaching cost on its candidate rollouts, both minimized over the model parameters. The planning term biases adaptation toward models that are optimistic about reaching the goal, without any additional environment interaction. Across visual and environment shifts on manipulation, reaching and navigation tasks, OpTTA raises final planning success over the frozen model by 13.5 percentage points on average, compared with 6.9 for the prediction-only objective (AdaJEPA), when only the predictor is adapted. When the encoder is adapted as well, the gains are 13.5 and 7.5 points. These experiments span three JEPA world models with different encoders and training objectives and, for temporal straightening, both CEM and gradient-based planners. Our results suggest that test-time adaptation of world models for planning benefits from an optimistic, task-aware term in addition to the prediction loss.
bullets: Frozen latent world models can plan poorly when deployment conditions differ from training.
Prediction-only adaptation fits observed transitions but may remain inaccurate about goal-reaching actions.
OpTTA jointly minimizes observed-transition prediction loss and the planner’s goal-reaching cost on candidate rollouts.
Across manipulation, reaching, and navigation shifts, OpTTA improved final planning success by 13.5 percentage points on average, versus 6.9–7.5 for prediction-only adaptation.
The approach was evaluated with three JEPA world models and both CEM and gradient-based planners, without additional environment interaction.

papers.abstract: Robotic missions involving spatially distributed tasks often require jointly selecting rewarding locations and planning feasible motions under limited travel budgets. This paper proposes Reward-Guided RRT*, a new sampling-based framework that constructs a budget-feasible mission through a sequence of locally joint task-selection-and-motion-planning stages, evaluated directly in the continuous state space, without requiring a precomputed task-transition graph. The method incrementally builds a mission using reward-guided RRT* searches, while a return-feasibility procedure ensures that each selected task can be visited without violating the mission budget. Experiments with increasing obstacle complexity and number of tasks show solutions comparable to VNS-PRM* while requiring substantially fewer sampled states. We also extend the framework to Dubins steering and evaluate it in CoppeliaSim with a scaled car-like robotic platform, demonstrating its ability to incorporate vehicle kinematic constraints.
bullets: Builds missions incrementally through locally joint task-selection and motion-planning stages.
Uses reward-guided RRT* without requiring a precomputed task-transition graph.
Applies return-feasibility checks to ensure selected tasks remain within the mission budget.
Achieves solutions comparable to VNS-PRM* with substantially fewer sampled states in experiments.
Extends to Dubins steering and demonstrates operation with a car-like robot in CoppeliaSim.

papers.abstract: Quadrotor controller comparisons commonly report a single tracking error, although the resulting ranking also depends on tuning effort, reference information, actuator prediction, optimizer fallback, and command timing. We quantify these effects for cascade PID, hover LQR, boundary-layer sliding-mode control (BL-SMC), linear MPC with LQR fallback (LMPC-F), a preview-enabled LMPC-F, and a geometric $SO(3)$ controller on a common nonlinear plant with rotor gyroscopic coupling, motor lag, and saturation. A primary study (556 episodes at 50~Hz) combines matched twelve-candidate tuning, 400 paired evaluation episodes, and a 48-cell MPC factorial; a confirmation study (1462 episodes) repeats the evaluation on 50 fresh realizations with tuning budgets of 12, 24, and 48 candidates. A matched twelve-candidate tuning protocol changed the mean-RMSE ordering obtained with the fixed baseline settings, moving BL-SMC from last to first; the new ordering recurred on the fresh realizations, and a 48-candidate budget left it unchanged. Reference preview substantially reduced MPC tracking error and, on the figure-eight task, removed fallback activity. On an abrupt step, the outcome depended on the interplay between fallback policy, predictor, and actuator authority. Command timing also changed the outcome: replaying measured command-call delays terminated three of four nominal MPC configurations on a desktop computer and all four on a Raspberry Pi~5, whereas capping the solver at 100 iterations removed every deadline miss in the tested nominal timing profiles. Controller rankings therefore depend not only on tracking accuracy but also on the tuning protocol, reference information, fallback behavior, and implementation timing. We propose a reporting checklist covering tracking accuracy, tuning effort, completion and failure rates, fallback activity, applied-input variation, and command timing.
bullets: A matched 12-candidate tuning protocol changed the baseline RMSE ranking, moving BL-SMC from last to first; this ordering persisted on fresh realizations and with 48 candidates.
Reference preview substantially improved MPC tracking and eliminated fallback activity on the figure-eight task.
On abrupt steps, performance depended on the interaction among fallback policy, actuator prediction, and actuator authority.
Measured command delays caused most or all tested nominal MPC configurations to miss deadlines, while a 100-iteration solver cap removed deadline misses in tested profiles.
The study recommends reporting tracking accuracy alongside tuning effort, completion/failure rates, fallback activity, input variation, and timing.

papers.title: How Tuning, Reference Preview, Actuator Modeling, and Fallback Policies Change Quadrotor Controller Comparisons: A Reproducible Simulation Study

papers.abstract: Learning generalizable humanoid loco-manipulation remains bottlenecked by costly real-world demonstrations. Simulation provides a scalable alternative, but requires visually faithful, physics-ready scenes and executable whole-body motions. We present Zero-HLM, a real-to-sim-to-real framework that transforms smartphone captures and simulated source demonstrations into scalable training data for humanoid loco-manipulation. Gaussian-guided agentic real-to-sim reconstruction aligns visual and physical scenes; motion-environment co-adaptation uses rollout feedback to correct whole-body references and interaction geometry. We generate 4,800 physically validated demonstrations for zero-shot transfer across three Unitree G1 tasks. Simulation-trained GR00T N1.7 achieves 66.7% mean full-task success, versus 46.7% with real-data training. On generalized configurations, expanded simulation training raises pooled success from 23% for base-trained real-data policies to 69%, without additional real demonstrations. Project page: https://young-bit.github.io/zero-hlm/
bullets: Addresses the cost and limited scalability of collecting real-world humanoid demonstrations.

Generates 4,800 physically validated demonstrations for three Unitree G1 tasks.
Simulation-trained GR00T N1.7 reaches 66.7% mean full-task success and 69% pooled success on generalized configurations.

papers.title: Zero-HLM: Generalizable Humanoid Loco-Manipulation without Real Robot Data
papers.tldr: Zero-HLM enables zero-shot humanoid loco-manipulation transfer by generating physically validated training data from smartphone captures and simulation, without real-robot demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Animals have a remarkable capacity for autonomy---driven by intrinsic motivation---without external sensory cues or extrinsic objectives, yet the computational mechanisms behind this ability largely remain a mystery. We combine whole-brain recordings in the fruit fly (Drosophila melanogaster), which reveal neural representations of spontaneous exploratory decisions more than 10 seconds in advance, with a neuromechanical digital twin to test whether optimizing intrinsic goals yields realistically embodied artificial agents that quantitatively match fly behavior and internal representations of future volitional action during exploration. Our hierarchical policy selects from a discrete library of low-level motor primitives, consistent with ethological theories of behavioral syllables. We train agents without external reward using 20 intrinsic motivation algorithms spanning curiosity, entropy, and competency methods. The agents are evaluated in a virtual tethered-ball assay modeled on the fly experiment, comparing spontaneous locomotor statistics and internal representations and decoding future turn direction from kinematics and neural activity on the same timescales observed in flies. DIAYN, a hierarchical competency algorithm learning discrete policies that maximize behavioral entropy and the separability of induced sensory observations, achieves the strongest joint behavioral and neural prospective coding performance relative to flies. Its learned policies closely capture individual variability in fly exploration strategies, suggesting that this diversity serves to maximize state-space coverage at the population level. DIAYN's latent activity also closely captures the sum-difference rule for interhemispheric encoding of kinematics in biological flies. These results establish hierarchical, intrinsically motivated agents as a powerful framework for reverse-engineering animal autonomy.
bullets: The study investigates how animals generate autonomous exploratory actions without external rewards or sensory cues.
Whole-brain recordings show that future spontaneous decisions are represented more than 10 seconds before action.
A neuromechanical Drosophila digital twin uses hierarchical policies that select discrete low-level motor primitives.
Among 20 curiosity-, entropy-, and competency-based methods, DIAYN best jointly matched fly behavior and prospective neural coding.
The model also reproduced individual exploration variability and a biological interhemispheric kinematic encoding rule.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Agent Architecture Overview. (a) The FlyGym simulator provides visual, proprioceptive, and olfactory observations from a biomechanically realistic fly body. Modality-specific CNN and MLP encoders embed these observations into a shared representation ϕt, which is provided to the actor–critic and intrinsic drive module. When applicable, the policy is additionally conditioned on a sampled skill z. The intrinsic drive module computes an intrinsic reward from the encoded state transition and selected action. The actor outputs a categorical distribution over discrete motor primitives, while the critic estimates the state value. The policy selects a new motor primitive every 100 ms. (b) Locomotor primitives are translated into joint-level commands by a low-level central pattern generator (CPG) controller, while grooming is executed using a kinematic replay. These motor commands are applied within the FlyGym physics simulation, which is integrated with a timestep of 100µs. Thus, each policy action is executed for 1,000 physics steps before the next action is selected.

Figure 1: Environment Overview. (a) The fly policy is trained in an environment with obstacles and multiple odor sources. (b) The policy is then evaluated in a tethered-ball environment where the fly is head-fixed. The angular and forward velocities are read from the ball, analogous to the biological experiment of Brezovec et al. (2023). (c) The policy receives olfaction as a weighted sum of intensities sampled at the antennae and maxillary palps. (d) The policy’s proprioceptive input comes directly from NeuroMechFly and includes joint angles, joint velocities, and body-frame gravity, height, and linear and angular velocities. (e) Vision is also provided to the policy by simulating the ommatidia mapping of pale and yellow type cells to pixels.

Figure 4: Turning Bias. (a) Distribution of turning bias across evaluation rollouts for each method. Points indicate individual rollouts, with the mean and range shown for each method. DIAYN produces a broad distribution of turning biases spanning more of the fly-to-fly variability than the other evaluated methods. Methods with a rollout containing no turns or turns in only one direction are excluded because log(NR/NL) is undefined for those rollouts. (b) Virtual x-y trajectories integrated from the ball state of the nine flies and the nine DIAYN evaluation skills drawn from a common origin.

Figure 3: Turn-direction decoding from neural and behavioral data. Prospective coding is quantified as balanced accuracy in predicting future left/right turns. (a,c) Neural (a) and behavioral (c) prospective coding in the fly and models using elastic-net logistic regression in the −15 to −8 s window. (b) Neural and behavioral decoding before (−15 to −8 s) and during (−0.4 to +0.4 s) turns. (d) Behavioral versus neural prospective coding. The dashed line defines the fly’s behavioralto-neural accuracy ratio, which DIAYN closely matches. (e) Models with no turns or only one turn direction, precluding stratified cross-validation.

Figure 5: Low-dimensional internal structures relate to ω and v. (a) Reconstructed from Brezovec et al. (2023), the IPS of the fly brain has an interhemispheric relationship of z-scored activity that is correlated with angular (interhemispheric difference) and forward velocity (interhemispheric sum). (b) As a functional analogue of the bilateral supercluster pairs in Brezovec et al. (2023), we use PCA to find principal components in the network activation of the LSTM layer of the Actor in the policy whose difference correlates with angular velocity and whose sum correlates with forward velocity. papers.abstract: Large-scale vision, language, and video pretraining has substantially improved the perception and generalization capabilities of robotic manipulation models, but action generation for complex dexterous manipulation remains constrained by the scarcity of robot demonstrations. Limited robot demonstrations must be used to learn both action representations and task-conditioned action distributions, making it difficult to adequately learn action representations and, in turn, limiting the ability of downstream generative models to generate complex dexterous actions. To address this limitation, we propose ARPG (Action Representation Pretraining and Generation), which explicitly separates action representation learning from action generation: we first pretrain an action representation encoder on large-scale human manipulation data. We then freeze the encoder and train a compact generative backbone (130M parameters) to learn task-conditioned action distributions in the encoder's representation space. Experimental results show that ARPG achieves state-of-the-art performance on the DexJoCo benchmark and improves the average success rate on bimanual dexterous manipulation from 10.1% for $π_{0.5}$ to 44.7%. Scaling experiments further show that broader coverage of human manipulation behaviors effectively improves downstream performance. These results indicate that action representation pretraining provides an independent scaling dimension for improving complex dexterous manipulation capabilities.
bullets: Problem: Scarce robot demonstrations must support both action-representation learning and task-conditioned action generation.
Method: Pretrain an action encoder on human manipulation data, freeze it, and train a compact generative backbone in the learned representation space.
Result: ARPG achieves state-of-the-art performance on DexJoCo and raises average bimanual dexterous-manipulation success from 10.1% to 44.7% versus π₀.₅.
Scaling human behavior coverage further improves downstream manipulation performance.
Scope: The approach targets complex dexterous and bimanual manipulation, with results indicating action pretraining as an independent scaling dimension.

papers.abstract: Scaling vision-language-action (VLA) models is constrained by scarce action-labeled demonstrations and incompatible control spaces across robot embodiments. We present RynnVLA-Latent, a framework that turns heterogeneous interaction videos into scalable supervision for robot policy pretraining. At its core, RynnLAM learns continuous, 3D-grounded latent actions from visual transitions without requiring native robot controls. By combining residual future-feature prediction, camera-compensated 3D-flow supervision, and camera-motion decoupling, RynnLAM encourages representations that capture control-relevant motion rather than appearance changes alone. We apply RynnLAM to 30.1K hours of human, robot, and simulation videos, producing 745.52M latent-action descriptors. RynnVLA-Latent then learns to predict latent-action chunks from visual observations and language through flow matching, before adapting its pretrained backbone and action expert to embodiment-specific robot actions. The resulting 4B policy achieves 98.8% success on LIBERO, 84.7% on LIBERO-Plus without benchmark-specific adaptation, 51.9% average success across five VLABench tracks, and 88.6% average success on the RoboTwin 2.0 bimanual benchmark. It also achieves the highest observed success rates among the compared methods on six real-world manipulation tasks across dexterous-hand and mobile-gripper platforms. Together with representation ablations and data-scaling results, these findings demonstrate the potential of latent-action supervision for scaling robot policy learning beyond native action-labeled data.
bullets: Addresses scarce action-labeled demonstrations and incompatible control spaces across robot embodiments.
RynnLAM learns continuous latent actions from visual transitions using future-feature prediction, 3D-flow supervision, and camera-motion decoupling.
Pretrains on 30.1K hours of human, robot, and simulation videos, generating 745.52M latent-action descriptors.
A 4B policy predicts latent-action chunks from vision and language before adapting to robot-specific actions.
Reports strong results across LIBERO, VLABench, RoboTwin 2.0, and six real-world manipulation tasks, with scaling and ablation evidence supporting latent-action supervision.

figures.caption: Figure 3 Architecture of RynnLAM and comparison with existingmethods. (a) Conventional latent action models compress a frame transition into a single latent representation and reconstruct the future observation conditioned on the source frame. (b) RynnLAM factorizes transition information into motion tokens zmt , an action latent zat , and a camera latent zct . The three components are trained through complementary objectives: feature-space reconstruction, 3D dynamic-flow prediction, and relative camera-pose estimation, respectively. This factorization encourages the action representation to capture physical scene dynamics while encouraging camera ego-motion to be represented separately.

Figure 1 Overview of the RynnVLA-Latent pretraining corpus. We aggregate approximately 30.1K hours from 25 datasets, comprising 16.63M episodes and 3.057B frames. Human video and real-robot video each contribute approximately 40% of the duration, with simulation accounting for the remaining 20%. The figure summarizes source composition, dataset contributions by duration, and object and action vocabulary from public tasks.

Figure 4 Two-stage training pipeline ofRynnVLA-Latent. (a) Latent-action pretraining. RynnLAM provides shared transition descriptors for human and heterogeneous robot videos. The policy predicts these descriptors from observations and language. (b) Robot post-training. Both the pretrained RynnBrain backbone and action-expert trunk are reused. The output projection is retargeted to native robot actions, and proprioceptive state is introduced. Post-training adapts the pretrained policy to the target control space without adding a separate latent-to-action decoder.

Figure 2 Data curation pipeline. The video data is collected from diverse sources and partitioned into short clips during data preprocessing. Each clip undergoes a multi-modal annotation process: (1) Video Captioning: Qwen3-VL (Bai et al., 2025) generates detailed natural language descriptions of the video content; (2) Optical Flow Estimation: DPFlow (Morimitsu et al., 2025) computes dense per-frame motion fields; (3) Depth Estimation: Depth Anything 3 (Lin et al., 2025) produces monocular depth predictions.

Figure 6 Latent-action similarity visualization. We retrieve the nearest neighbors of several query latent actions across the multi-embodiment corpus and display the corresponding video frames. The displayed high-similarity neighbors exhibit related motion patterns across different embodiments and visual domains, providing a qualitative illustration of cross-domain transition similarity.

papers.abstract: Humanoid robots have recently achieved remarkable success in motion tracking. However, during real-world deployment, robots inevitably encounter dynamics gaps arising from either extra physical disturbances or inaccurate simulation modeling, resulting in a significant training-deployment gap. Therefore, effectively leveraging real-world data to fine-tune policies represents the crucial last mile for robust deployment. To bridge this gap, we propose HumanoidNDM, an online fine-tuning framework for humanoid motion tracking driven by a real-world-trained neural dynamics model. First, in the data collection stage, we introduce a low-frequency reference perturbation method with an adaptive intensity mechanism, balancing deployment feasibility and exploration efficiency. Second, for the model training stage, we train a robust history-based, proprioceptive neural dynamics model in Euclidean space by incorporating differentiable forward kinematics, eliminating the reliance on costly motion capture systems. Finally, in the policy fine-tuning stage, we directly fine-tune the policy via backpropagated model gradients, achieving high data efficiency. Through physical validation on the Unitree G1 robot, we demonstrate that HumanoidNDM enables rapid real-world adaptation to various perturbations, representing the first online, MoCap-free fine-tuning framework for humanoid tracking policies.
bullets: Addresses the training–deployment gap caused by unmodeled disturbances and inaccurate simulation dynamics.
Collects feasible exploration data using low-frequency reference perturbations with adaptive intensity.
Learns a robust history-based proprioceptive neural dynamics model with differentiable forward kinematics, avoiding motion capture.
Fine-tunes the tracking policy directly through backpropagated model gradients for high data efficiency.
Physical validation on a Unitree G1 shows rapid adaptation to various real-world perturbations.

papers.abstract: This paper proposes a command-aligned sampling distribution that incorporates navigation commands directly into the exploration process to improve the efficiency of sampling-based motion planning for quadcopters in three-dimensional environments. Inspired by the Language-Aided Subset Sampling Motion Planner, this paper extends command-aware subset sampling to aerial systems. Subset sampling is generalized to command-aligned regions, enabling structured 3D exploration while preserving probabilistic completeness. Natural language instructions are grounded into yaw-conditioned and altitude-aware geometric constraints using a prompt-based large language model for entity extraction and instruction validation. Extensive simulations in complex environments demonstrate that the proposed method generates collision-free, consistent trajectories while significantly reducing sampling effort compared to uniform RRT-based planners.
bullets: Targets inefficient exploration in sampling-based drone planning for complex 3D environments.
Converts natural-language instructions into yaw-conditioned and altitude-aware geometric constraints.
Uses command-aligned subset sampling to structure exploration while preserving probabilistic completeness.
Simulations produce collision-free, consistent trajectories with reduced sampling effort versus uniform RRT-based planners.
