papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D foundation models have recently reshaped multi-view reconstruction, yet dynamic 4D understanding still often relies on large-scale motion supervision or hand-crafted, architecture-specific heuristics. We ask whether frozen 3D foundation model tokens already encode motion-relevant information that can be exposed by lightweight readout functions, rather than re-learning motion-specific features with high-capacity decoders. Through probing on three representative backbones, we find that static--dynamic separation is decodable from frozen token representations. Our rank-restricted and spectral analyses on $π^3$X reveal that the recovered motion cues are concentrated in a low-dimensional subspace. Building on this, we propose Probing-based Motion Distillation (PMD), which converts pairwise motion-state compatibility scores against a fixed anchor token into dense motion masks. Trained on only 160 YouTube-VOS videos using a single 16 GB GPU, PMD transfers zero-shot to DAVIS, SegTrackv2, and FBMS-59 without target-benchmark fine-tuning. With multi-view pretrained geometric backbones, PMD outperforms training-free heuristics and approaches substantially heavier supervised and self-supervised methods, suggesting that motion decoding from frozen 3D foundation models can be lightweight and data-efficient.
bullets: Motion information can be separated from static content using simple readouts over frozen tokens.
Rank-restricted and spectral analyses on π³X indicate that motion cues lie in a low-dimensional subspace.
ProMo3D introduces Probing-based Motion Distillation, using anchor-token compatibility scores to produce dense motion masks.
Trained on 160 YouTube-VOS videos, PMD transfers zero-shot to DAVIS, SegTrackv2, and FBMS-59.
With multi-view pretrained geometric backbones, PMD outperforms training-free heuristics and approaches heavier supervised and self-supervised methods.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of Probing-based Motion Distillation (PMD). Given an input frame group, a frozen feed-forward 3D foundation model such as π3X [36], VGGT [34], or Depth Anything 3 (DA3) [21] produces token representations. A lightweight probe trained on only 160 videos maps these features into a probe-induced static–dynamic discriminative representation. PMD then converts anchor-based pairwise probe scores into dense dynamic score maps, which are thresholded into coarse masks and optionally refined with SAM2 [29]. It transfers zero-shot to DAVIS [26, 27], SegTrackv2 [17], and FBMS-59 [14], while requiring substantially less training data and trainable capacity than high-capacity motion decoders such as GeoMotion [8].

Figure 3: Qualitative comparison on DAVIS [26] and SegTrackv2 [17] against training-free methods based on feed-forward 3D foundation models. The semantic classes shown here are absent from the 160-video training subset of π3X-PMD. All binary masks shown here are generated without SAM2 [29] refinement. PMD produces cleaner dynamic score maps and more coherent coarse masks.

Figure 5: Scene-diversity starvation analysis. (a) Low-rank probing (k = 8) matches or exceeds full-rank probing under reduced training data, indicating a compact static–dynamic discriminative structure. (b) Downstream mask quality degrades gradually rather than collapsing.

Figure 2: Layer-wise motion decodability on DAVIS-all [27]. Low-rank quadratic probes expose static–dynamic discriminative cues across the multi-view geometric modules of all three backbones, outperforming linear and diagonal probes.

Figure 6: Semantic leakage in π3X-PMD. The two static background flamingos receive elevated dynamic scores alongside the moving foreground instance, illustrating imperfect separation of motion and semantic cues.

Figure 7: Stress test of the fixed anchor token a = 0 convention on a DAVIS-all [27] evaluation example for the two non-padded backbones in the main analysis. The upper-left reference patch is marked in green in the input frame. For each backbone, we compare a standard case where the fixed a = 0 patch is static with a rare violation where the same patch is fully dynamic according to the ground-truth mask. For both DA3-PMD and DUSt3R-PMD, the violation moderately increases the background response, but it does not invert the prediction: the moving foreground remains separable and is recovered by both the coarse and refined masks.

Figure 4: Low-rank structure of the probe-induced static–dynamic discriminative representation on π3X-PMD, illustrated for DAVIS-all [27]. (a) Principal Component Analysis (PCA) illustrates clear separation between static and dynamic tokens. (b) The singular spectrum decays steeply in the leading components, especially in earlier layers, revealing strong rank concentration. (c) Performance saturates at a very low effective rank, indicating that the probe-induced motion cues are compact.
Figure 8: Additional layer-wise motion decodability on DAVIS-all [27]: VGGT [34], π3 [36], and MapAnything [13].

Figure 11: Limitation: Fine-grained Motion vs. Binary Detection. PMD highlights the breakdancer with the most prominent motion and assigns moderately elevated scores to nearby people with subtler in-place motion relative to the static background. However, the pipeline ultimately produces a binary static–dynamic mask rather than distinguishing different motion types or motion magnitudes.

Figure 10: Scene-diversity starvation and layer-wise semantic leakage on π3X [36]. Visualization of PMD dynamic score maps across network depth under varying amounts of training data. While deeper representations entangle motion with semantics, reducing the training subset to only 10 videos exacerbates this leakage across all layers. The starved probe incorrectly highlights static foreground objects, whereas the 160-video model maintains a focus on actual motion, particularly in its shallow and intermediate layers.

Figure 9: Additional scene-diversity starvation analysis on DAVIS-all [27]. We report token-level Normalized Gain for the default low-rank quadratic probe (k = 8) across π3X [36], DA3 [21], and DUSt3R [35] while reducing the number of YouTube-VOS training videos. Solid lines denote the mean over available random subset seeds, and shaded bands denote one standard deviation when multiple seeds are available. Performance degrades gradually as training diversity is reduced, while the uncertainty bands remain moderate overall and widen mainly in the most data-starved regimes.

papers.abstract: Successful tool-use trajectories are not necessarily useful supervision. Even successful interactions may underrepresent multi-step dependencies or contain actions that are unjustified by the information visible to the agent at decision time. We identify two coupled requirements for effective trajectory supervision: compositional coverage, so that important observation-action dependencies are represented, and decision grounding, so that each supervised action is supported by the learner-visible interaction history. We introduce Trajectory2Gym, which constructs executable interactions around under-supported compositional structures and derives supervision only from grounded decisions in their realized executions. Structural-support selection allocates the resulting experience, while parent-normalized supervised fine-tuning preserves the semantic interaction as the unit of training weight. This reframes trajectory generation as the deliberate construction of learnable interaction experience, rather than the collection of successful trajectories. Across five Qwen3 scales, Trajectory2Gym improves Tau1, Tau2, and BFCL at every tested scale, increasing the equal-weight three-benchmark mean by 16.9-29.8 percentage points. The gains are strongest in stateful and multi-turn interaction, where later decisions depend on earlier observations and feedback. Our results suggest that scaling tool-use agents depends not only on collecting more successful trajectories, but on constructing interactions whose dependencies are represented and whose decisions are learnable from the agent's visible history.
bullets: Successful trajectories can still provide weak supervision when multi-step dependencies are missing or actions are unsupported by visible information.
The method builds executable interactions around under-supported observation–action structures and supervises only decisions grounded in their realized histories.
Structural-support selection allocates experience, while parent-normalized fine-tuning keeps each semantic interaction as the training unit.
Across five Qwen3 scales, it improves Tau1, Tau2, and BFCL, with the largest gains in stateful and multi-turn tasks.
The study argues that learnable interaction construction matters more than simply collecting additional successful trajectories.

papers.abstract: As the applications of AI continue to expand across various multimodal and multilingual domains, ensuring safe and responsible deployment of these systems has become an important concern. A wide-range of interventions have been proposed to make AI responses safer and more reliable. They often incur substantial computational or annotation costs, or cannot be extended to multilingual settings. In this work, we propose Selective Detection And Targeted Editing (SEDATE), a training-free approach based on detect-edit-verify strategy. SEDATE first detects the responsible neurons, edits them as and when necessary and finally verifies the model responses; all without any additional model training. We evaluate SEDATE across 7 languages and 4 model families. We further evaluate its effectiveness across 4 out-of-distribution languages and 4 additional datasets. We show that SEDATE achieves substantially superior safety scores across all languages and models over the best-performing baseline while retaining the general capabilities and incurring negligible overhead. Our results are robust, with the trends remaining similar for out-of-distribution languages and datasets.
bullets: Addresses the cost and limited multilingual applicability of existing safety interventions.
Detects responsible neurons, selectively edits them when needed, and verifies the resulting responses without additional training.
Evaluated across 7 languages, 4 model families, 4 out-of-distribution languages, and 4 additional datasets.
Reports substantially higher safety scores than the strongest baseline across languages and models, with negligible overhead and retained general capabilities.
The abstract does not specify the exact aggression circuit structure or provide numeric results.

papers.abstract: Rubric-based rewards enable effective reinforcement learning on non-verifiable tasks. However, because these rewards are typically defined as a weighted measure of rubric coverage, models are trained primarily to maximize a recall objective. As a result, RL-trained models produce responses that are more complete but also more verbose and contain more unnecessary or factually incorrect content, leading them to be less preferred than responses from the base model. To address this issue, we present the FORK reward, which jointly optimizes recall and a novel precision objective, which requires each unit of a model response to be both necessary and factually correct, as measured by rubric-driven necessity credits and a factual-correctness grader, respectively. Our experimental results show that FORK outperforms existing rubric-based RL methods and achieves Pareto-optimal performance that balances rubric coverage and overall response quality. Compared to the original recall-based reward, FORK substantially improves precision and reduces response length while achieving similar rubric coverage, which leads to significantly higher win rate compared to the base policy (e.g., from 10.6% to 68.0% on RubricHub-Medical and from 22.1% to 74.1% on HealthBench).
bullets: Recall-focused rubric rewards can produce overly verbose responses with unnecessary or incorrect content.
FORK adds a precision objective based on rubric-driven necessity credits and factual-correctness grading.
The method improves precision and shortens responses while maintaining similar rubric coverage.
It achieves Pareto-optimal coverage–quality tradeoffs and higher win rates against the base policy on medical evaluation benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Reward hacking in rubric-based RL and our mitigation method. With the standard coverage reward, recall (i.e., weighted coverage of rubrics) quickly saturates, while precision and win rate against a base model continually decreases and responses become more verbose. With a precision objective included in the reward (FORK), the model reaches similar recall while gradually increasing precision and win rate and generating less verbose responses. Here, we train Qwen2.57B-Instruct on RubricHub-Medical and evaluate it on an in-domain test set.

Figure 2: Training with FORK. Given a prompt, a policy model samples a response, which is then divided into units. An LLM grader matches rubrics to units to assign each unit a necessity credit and determines a credit threshold for unit necessity. In parallel, the grader assesses the factual correctness of all units. Precision is defined as the fraction of necessary and factually correct units, and recall follows the standard definition of weighted rubric coverage. We update the policy model using their weighted harmonic mean as a reward.
Figure 3: Recall vs. Win Rate using a training grader. We report recall against win rate for rubric-based RL methods evaluated with the training grader on RubricHub-Medical.

papers.abstract: We present MOTIO, an agentic skill-engineering system that turns ordinary human-action videos, reality-grounded 3D assets, motion references, and reusable robot skills into executable humanoid loco-manipulation programs. Through in-context task and contact reasoning, an agent constructs staged robot-native interactions and improves them using physics execution, multi-frame feedback, and human validation---without task-specific teleoperation or robot demonstration collection. Agentic 3D supplies metric product and environment assets, while existing whole-body, inverse-kinematics, and dexterous-hand interfaces realize the programs. Across 33 timestamped first approvals, the median recorded agent-turn time is 97.0 minutes and request-to-approval duration is 2.80 hours. Simulation-side layout and object variation prepare a long-horizon bottle-disposal skill for a continuous 101.75-second physical G1 execution in a scanned office; physical refinement reduces screw-tightening thread residual by 76.0%. Agent-generated skills additionally supervise BC/DAgger distillation into one shared reference policy, completing 18 simulated tasks under the same checkpoint without inference-time expert intervention. Project page: https://iiiiqiiii.github.io/motio/
bullets: Uses in-context task and contact reasoning to build staged, robot-native interactions.
Improves programs through physics execution, multi-frame feedback, and human validation.
Combines metric 3D assets with whole-body, inverse-kinematics, and dexterous-hand interfaces.
Demonstrates a 101.75-second physical bottle-disposal task and reduces screw-tightening thread residual by 76.0%.
Generated skills can supervise BC/DAgger distillation into one policy that completes 18 simulated tasks without inference-time expert intervention.

papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents with tool use exhibit inconsistent behavior across independent runs from identical states, calling different tools, producing contradictory outputs, or pursuing divergent strategies. This variability compounds over time and undermines deployment reliability. Existing evaluation metrics primarily measure task correctness via completion-based scores and do not capture consistency in agent behavior across executions. Separately, agent behavior is analyzed either at the token level using probability distributions or at the single-response level using semantic clustering, but neither captures how inconsistency propagates across future turns of a trajectory. We introduce Recursive Semantic Divergence (RSD), an unsupervised trajectory-level consistency metric adapted from bisimulation metrics in reinforcement learning. RSD measures the expected cumulative semantic disagreement between two independent rollouts of the same agent from the same state, using natural language inference to detect logical inconsistency. It is defined recursively over future states and approximated by a neural network trained on independent rollouts. The learned metric estimates future divergence from the current state, providing a consistency score at each turn without requiring the full trajectory to complete. When used as a reward signal for fine-tuning, RSD reduces the variation in task progress from 132% to 91% on tau2-bench and from 90% to 44% on toolsandbox, while improving performance across benchmarks and model scales. Training with RSD as an additional reward signal matches supervised fine-tuning performance with substantially lower variance, without requiring ground-truth labels.
bullets: Addresses the inability of task-completion metrics to capture trajectory-level consistency and inconsistency propagation across future turns.
Defines RSD as expected cumulative semantic disagreement between independent rollouts, using natural language inference and a recursive formulation inspired by bisimulation metrics.
Trains a neural network on independent rollouts to estimate future divergence at each turn without waiting for the full trajectory to finish.
Using RSD as a fine-tuning reward reduces task-progress variation on tau2-bench and toolsandbox while improving benchmark performance across model scales.
Matches supervised fine-tuning performance with substantially lower variance and requires no ground-truth labels.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Diagram illustrating Recursive Semantic Divergence (RSD) in LLM agents. The first three panels display trajectory spreads for perfectly consistent, mostly consistent, and highly inconsistent agents over time. The final panel maps an agent’s expanding and converging semantic action space alongside its corresponding RSD score, demonstrating how the metric tracks the variance of semantic divergence at each turn.

papers.title: Recursive Semantic Divergence for LLM Agent Consistency
papers.tldr: Recursive Semantic Divergence (RSD) measures and reduces how much LLM agent behavior diverges across repeated tool-using runs from the same state.

papers.abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) enable flexible generation through iterative masked denoising, but incur substantial inference cost because token representations are repeatedly recomputed across denoising steps. Existing cache-based methods reduce this cost by reusing intermediate results across denoising steps and recomputing only a subset of positions at each step, chosen either on a fixed schedule or by heuristic signals of change. Our trajectory experiments instead point to decoding trajectory as the more relevant quantity. Cached generation remains accurate when it stays close to the full-denoising trajectory, with errors concentrated around unmask-order deviations and reduced as longer reference prefixes are recovered. This suggests a more direct principle: limiting representation error helps, but keeping generation on the full-denoising trajectory is a more direct route to accurate decoding. We therefore formulate efficient dLLM inference as trajectory-guided querying. Rather than broadly repairing representation error, we use full-denoising trajectories to supervise which unresolved positions should receive limited fresh computation. Based on this formulation, we introduce TRACEQUERY, a lightweight sparse decoding framework that predicts a small set of near-future trajectory-relevant positions, queries only those candidates, and lets the backbone select which one to commit from their fresh predictions. TRACEQUERY delivers the strongest quality-computation trade-off among cache-based approaches, sustaining high accuracy with substantially fewer fresh token computations, and generalizes across tasks, model variants, and families. Code: https://github.com/fish1928/tracequery.git
bullets: dLLMs are expensive because token representations are repeatedly recomputed during iterative denoising.
The authors find that decoding accuracy depends more directly on staying close to the full-denoising trajectory than merely limiting representation error.
TRACEQUERY predicts a small set of future trajectory-relevant positions, computes fresh predictions only for them, and lets the backbone choose which position to commit.
It achieves the strongest quality–computation trade-off among cache-based methods and generalizes across tasks, model variants, and model families.
The approach relies on full-denoising trajectories as supervision for efficient sparse querying.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Two-stage ablation of TRACEQUERY. (a) Stage I selects the router configuration by varying the feature combination, router architecture, ranking loss, normalization, and query horizon during router training. (b) Stage II fixes the selected configuration and evaluates alternative feature groups under closed-loop cached decoding. Results are averaged across four models and reported as accuracy change relative to the adopted configuration. Bars show paired 95% bootstrap confidence intervals; filled markers indicate intervals excluding zero, and gray dots denote per-benchmark changes.

Figure 2: Overview of TRACEQUERY. Full denoising first provides an offline reference trajectory describing the future order of decoding decisions. The router is trained to recover the near-future portion of this trajectory from inexpensive signals available during decoding. At inference time, after step t commits At, the router ranks the remaining unresolved positions and selects a small query set Qt+1. Only these positions receive fresh computation, while other positions reuse cached representations. The backbone dLLM then makes the final commitment from the freshly queried candidates. Periodic broad recomputation is retained to control accumulated approximation error.

Figure 1: Trajectory agreement and dependence on trajectory guidance. (a) We compare decoding progress under full denoising and cached decoding. Each underlying observation corresponds to a token position, paired by the step at which it is unmasked under full denoising and its corresponding step under cached decoding. Rather than plotting individual observations, we show the 80% density contours. Concentration along the diagonal indicates agreement with the fulldenoising unmask order, while broader deviations reflect trajectory divergence. (b) Accuracy on examples solved by full denoising as the injected full-denoising prefix is progressively removed.

Figure 3: Quality–compute and batch-scaling comparison. (a) Average score across benchmarks as a function of total computation, measured in TFLOPs. The red dashed line marks the score of full denoising without caching. TRACEQUERY reaches higher scores under comparable compute budgets. (b) Supported batch size as a function of wall-clock time per document. TRACEQUERY supports larger batches at comparable latency, demonstrating improved batch-scaling efficiency.

Table 2: Persistent KV-cache memory for the illustrative BF16 LLaDA-8B configuration under batch size 1. Relative memory denotes model weights plus KV cache divided by model-weight memory alone.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces TraceQuery, a trajectory-guided sparse decoding framework for diffusion LLMs to reduce recomputation costs during inference.
papers.title: TraceQuery: learning what to recompute from full-denoising trajectory in diffusion language models
papers.tldr: TRACEQUERY accelerates diffusion language model decoding by using full-denoising trajectories to predict which masked positions need fresh computation, preserving accuracy with fewer token updates.

papers.abstract: Transformer-based large language models (LLMs) impose substantial computation and memory costs as context sizes increase, motivating methods that compress a context into a shorter representation before inference. Existing soft-prompt compression methods typically use the same Transformer backbone as used in the target model, where producing the compressed representation leads to significant latency overheads. This restricts them to the offline setting where context is compressed once and then reused across many queries. We propose the Boa Compressor, a plug-and-play online context compressor built on a Mamba state-space model (SSM) that encodes arbitrary-length context in a single linear-time pass, producing a representation on which we condition a frozen target LLM. The SSM is trained by distillation, matching the next-token logit distribution from the LLM ingesting the full context (as teacher) to the same LLM ingesting the compressed representation (as the student). At equal compression ratios, Boa matches or surpasses the performance of existing state-of-the-art offline compression baselines, while being an order of magnitude faster than Transformer-based implementations, thereby reducing end-to-end latency rather than adding compression time overhead. We demonstrate that Boa also scales well to longer contexts and to compression ratios as aggressive as 16x. By enabling effective compression that is cheap enough to run on every query at inference time, Boa becomes a practical and general tool for efficient long-context inference.
bullets: Addresses the latency and memory costs of long contexts and the overhead of Transformer-based compression.
Distills a state-space encoder to match the target LLM’s next-token distributions from full versus compressed context.
Matches or surpasses state-of-the-art offline compression at equal compression ratios.
Runs an order of magnitude faster than Transformer-based compressors, reducing end-to-end latency.
Scales to longer contexts and compression ratios up to 16×, supporting per-query compression.

papers.abstract: Energy-based models have shown promising properties for domain-specific tasks but remain challenging in modeling general-purpose scenarios. To bridge this gap, we design energy-steered models (ESMs) for foundational language modeling. ESMs integrate energy steering and token generation within a single architecture to leverage the energy-guided search to refine token generation. Specifically, ESMs first optimize a latent state over the energy landscape, then leverages the refined latent state for token generation. By performing such energy-guided pre-training on large-scale corpora, ESMs learn generally effective energy landscape where favorable tokens correspond to lower energy values. To explore the scaling behavior of ESMs, we pre-train ESMs on three large-scale corpora, then evaluate across 26 downstream tasks spanning a broad range of domains. Our results demonstrate that ESMs have promising scaling behaviors with increasing model size and training data, and outperform GPTs on most downstream tasks. These findings highlight ESMs as a promising architecture for large-scale pre-training and general purpose problem solving. We fully release the model weights and training infrastructure to enable the community to completely reproduce and extend our results. GitHub: https://github.com/datamllab/openesm HuggingFace: https://huggingface.co/collections/guan-wang/openesm
bullets: Targets the challenge of extending energy-based models from domain-specific tasks to general-purpose language modeling.
Combines energy steering and token generation in one architecture by optimizing a latent state over an energy landscape before decoding.
Pre-trains models on three large-scale corpora and evaluates them across 26 diverse downstream tasks.
Reports favorable scaling with model size and training data, outperforming GPTs on most evaluated tasks.
Releases model weights and training infrastructure for reproduction and extension.

papers.abstract: KV caching reduces the serving cost of large language models (LLMs), but the growing KV cache footprint is increasingly exceeds GPU and host-memory capacity. Therefore, people use SSD to expand the KV cache storage capacity with high I/O bandwidth. However, in production LLM workload, such as multi-round conversation and LLM agents, the total amount of KV cache writes significantly exceeds SSD capacity, shortening SSD lifetime from years to months. To improve SSD lifetime, a natural solution is to reduce the KV cache writes by gating the KV cache writes via historical access patterns. However, that significantly lowers the KV cache hit rate (and increase the LLM serving cost) since KV caches from different attention types might have identical historical access pattern but different future access patterns. Our insight is that, to reduce KV cache writes without hurting KV cache hit rate, one need to not only consider the access pattern, but also application-level information such as the attention type of KV cache. Leveraging this observation, we propose Gandalf , the first SSD KV cache offloading system with SSD life time awareness. Gandalf prioritize the admission of full-attention KV cache into SSD over the cache generated by other types of attention, which significantly increases SSD lifetime without sacrificing cache hit rate. Our evaluation shows that Gandalf extends the SSD lifetime by 7.3X on average, while having negligible impact on cache hit rate across multiple workload traces and wide range of hardware capacity. Gandalf design can be extended to other flash-based storage, such as High Bandwidth Flash (HBF).
bullets: LLM KV-cache writes can overwhelm SSD capacity in workloads such as multi-round conversations and LLM agents, reducing device lifetime from years to months.
Write gating based only on historical access patterns can lower cache hit rates because different attention types may share similar histories but have different future reuse.
Gandalf combines access patterns with application-level attention-type information to guide SSD cache admission.
It prioritizes full-attention KV caches over caches from other attention types, reducing writes while preserving cache effectiveness.
Across multiple workload traces and hardware capacities, Gandalf extends SSD lifetime by 7.3× on average with negligible cache-hit-rate impact; the design may also apply to high-bandwidth flash.

papers.abstract: Force-sensitive manipulation requires contact and load information that is not provided explicitly by visual observations. We present CW-WAM, a world action model that jointly predicts video, motion, and contact wrench. Inspired by hybrid motion-force control, it contains a unified interaction module that treats both motion and contact wrench as modeling targets and predicts time-aligned motion-wrench chunks as control references. A pair-causal attention mechanism structures the motion-wrench dependencies, while a long fixed-length wrench memory retains past interaction information. The predicted wrench chunk acts as a force reference for a 20-Hz outer-loop admittance controller within a slow-fast control system that maintains force feedback and smooth motion between model queries. CW-WAM improves contact prediction and increases the insertion success rate from 25% to 70% for square pegs with 1-mm clearance per side and from 40% to 95% for power adapters, compared with WAM without wrench input. It also improves lifting-height accuracy across different loads. Our framework with an admittance controller reduces force-reference RMSE from 4.8 to 2.7 N for peg insertion and from 2.0 to 1.3 N for wiping, respectively, with smaller force fluctuations during successful execution. Project website: https://cw-wam-project.github.io/
bullets: Addresses the lack of explicit contact and load information in visual observations.
Jointly predicts video, motion, and time-aligned contact-wrench chunks using pair-causal attention and long wrench memory.
Uses predicted wrench as a force reference for a 20-Hz outer-loop admittance controller in a slow-fast control system.
Compared with WAM without wrench input, insertion success rises from 25% to 70% for square pegs and from 40% to 95% for power adapters.
Reduces force-reference RMSE from 4.8 to 2.7 N for peg insertion and from 2.0 to 1.3 N for wiping, while improving lifting-height accuracy across loads.

papers.abstract: The microphysics of dark matter (DM) is imprinted on cosmological structure across an enormous dynamic range. Nonlinear cosmological observables are most reliably modeled with N-body and hydrodynamic simulations. However, systematic N-body scans over DM theory space are prohibitively expensive. Machine learning emulators provide a possible solution, but are currently limited by either low resolution or only the ability to emulate specific observables. We introduce Astrolabe, a flow-matching-based generative emulator designed to be free of both constraints. Astrolabe acts directly on the 6N phase-space coordinates of N individual particles. With no voxel grid in the output, there is no voxel-resolution ceiling, and in principle any observable can be measured from inference. Astrolabe is computationally tractable via a field-particle hybrid transformer in which every particle cross-attends to multiscale field tokens, so compute and memory are linear in N. Astrolabe incorporates physical flow matching by taking the prior distribution for the flow to be approximate COmoving Lagrangian Acceleration (COLA)-based coordinates rather than unphysical noise, with momentum and mass conservation enforced at all points along flow time. In the Lambda-CDM cases we test, Astrolabe produces realistic fields with accurate power spectra, halo mass functions, velocity profiles, and halo density profiles. We also observe out-of-distribution generalization, with accurate emulation of dark-acoustic oscillation initial conditions. Astrolabe is also capable of being fine-tuned to simulate very large N and we demonstrate this by emulating a TNG50-3-dark simulation at a fraction of the cost. This method represents a first step toward a general and powerful cosmology simulation surrogate, which may eventually permit the inclusion of baryonic physics and a systematic exploration of richer dark sector interactions.
authors: Ibrahim Elsharkawy, David Curtin, Yonatan Kahn, Neal Weiner
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost of scanning dark-matter theory space with N-body and hydrodynamic simulations.
Generates all 6N particle phase-space coordinates directly, avoiding voxel-resolution limits and restricting inference to predefined observables.
Uses a field-particle hybrid transformer with linear-in-particle compute and memory, plus COLA-based priors and enforced momentum and mass conservation.
Produces realistic power spectra, halo mass functions, velocity profiles, and density profiles in tested ΛCDM cases, and generalizes to dark-acoustic oscillation initial conditions.
Can be fine-tuned for very large particle counts, demonstrated on a TNG50-3-dark simulation at lower cost; broader baryonic and dark-sector applications remain future scope.

papers.selection_reason: A generative emulator for cosmology simulations using flow matching, which predicts future environments and acts as a world model for physical dynamics.
papers.title: ASTROLABE: A 3D Particle-Level Surrogate for Cosmology Simulation with Physical Flow Matching
papers.tldr: Astrolabe is a particle-level flow-matching emulator that efficiently generates cosmological simulations while preserving physical constraints and supporting flexible observable measurements.

papers.abstract: Stochastic order-independent transparency enables efficient and elegant rendering of primitive-based radiance fields like 3D Gaussian Splatting models, but remains impractical due to the inherent visible noise in the output. We propose a principled approach to minimize high-frequency noise, addressing its sources at the representation and image synthesis level. During stochastic rendering, our history-based spatial resampling scheme drastically accelerates image convergence, while temporal importance resampling ensures coherence under camera movement. During training, a color regularizer implicitly reduces the variance along view rays in the 3DGS models. With these properties, our optimized, Vulkan-based renderer effectively mitigates output noise at low and high sample counts, achieving a substantial 13~dB PSNR increase in quality over previous stochastic methods at 1 sample per pixel and quickly converging to sorted 3DGS with an average L1 error of less than $10^{-4}$.
bullets: Targets visible high-frequency noise that limits stochastic order-independent transparency for primitive-based radiance fields.
Uses history-based spatial resampling to accelerate convergence and temporal importance resampling to maintain coherence during camera movement.
Applies a color regularizer during training to reduce variance along view rays in 3DGS models.
An optimized Vulkan renderer improves quality by 13 dB PSNR over prior stochastic methods at 1 sample per pixel.
Converges quickly toward sorted 3DGS, reaching an average L1 error below 10⁻⁴.

papers.abstract: The Muon optimizer applies spectral orthogonalization to matrix-valued updates and has shown strong performance in large-scale neural network training, yet the mechanisms of this transformation in feature learning remain poorly understood. In this work, we investigate this question through a tractable factual-recall model, where a fact maps each subject-relation pair to an answer, and a linear transformer learns the subject- and relation-dependent information required to recover this mapping. The transformer is optimized with gradient flow (GF), spectral GF, or Sign GF, which are continuous-time limits of gradient descent, Muon, and Adam, respectively. Prior studies (Nichani et al., 2025) have shown that when the number of subjects exceeds the number of relations, GF learns relation-dependent information before subject-dependent information, producing a feature-separation phase during training. We characterize this separation with the learning times when the subject- and relation-dependent components of the prediction reach a target accuracy. With $S$ subjects and $R$ relations, GF has a learning-time ratio of $\widetildeΘ(\sqrt{S/R})$, whereas Spectral GF reduces this ratio to $\widetildeΘ(1)$. In addition, for fixed $S$ and $R$, the subject- and relation-dependent errors decay as $1/(T\log T)$ in training time $T$ under GF, but as $\exp(-\mathrm{poly}(T))$ under spectral GF. Finally, we show that GF and spectral GF are equivariant under orthogonal transformations of the token embeddings, whereas Sign GF is not: Different orthonormal embeddings can potentially produce no feature separation, a large feature-separation phase, or even a reversed learning order. These results provide a mechanistic view of how spectral orthogonalization can fundamentally reshape feature-learning dynamics.
bullets: A tractable linear-transformer factual-recall model separates subject-dependent and relation-dependent learning.
Standard gradient flow learns relation information first, with a learning-time ratio of approximately √(S/R) when subjects outnumber relations.
Spectral gradient flow reduces this ratio to approximately constant order and changes error decay from 1/(T log T) to exp(−poly(T)).
Gradient flow and spectral gradient flow are invariant to orthogonal token-embedding transformations, while Sign GF is not.
The analysis offers a mechanistic explanation for how spectral orthogonalization reshapes feature-learning dynamics.

papers.abstract: Among on-policy deep reinforcement learning methods, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) has become the de facto standard, due to its consistently strong empirical performance across diverse application domains. However, on-policy methods are inherently sample inefficient: fresh data collected under the current policy is used for just a few updates before being discarded. Off-policy methods avoid this inefficiency via experience replay, achieving notable sample efficiency gains, but at the cost of training instabilities or extensive tuning. This motivated the rise of hybrid strategies that augment PPO with off-policy data reuse. Existing sample-reuse variants of PPO demonstrated improved sample efficiency over vanilla PPO, yet a systematic study of when reuse helps, in which scenarios, and to what extent remains missing. In this work, we study the effectiveness of sample reuse in PPO by instantiating two variants within a multiple importance weighting framework. Both retain the core PPO mechanics, reusing only samples from a window of recent iterations, thereby isolating the effect of data reuse from other factors. The variants, termed wPPO-U and wPPO-BH, employ vanilla importance weights or balance-heuristic-corrected ones, respectively. For both, we derive policy improvement lower bounds providing theoretical grounding for their respective losses. We use them to empirically study when and how data reuse improves sample efficiency or final performance of PPO across continuous control tasks.
bullets: Introduces two PPO reuse variants within a multiple-importance-weighting framework: wPPO-U and wPPO-BH.
Reuses samples only from a window of recent policy iterations to isolate the effect of data reuse.
Uses vanilla importance weights in wPPO-U and balance-heuristic-corrected weights in wPPO-BH.
Derives policy-improvement lower bounds to theoretically support both objectives.
Evaluates when and how reuse affects sample efficiency and final performance across continuous-control tasks.

papers.abstract: Recent Recommendation Agents (RecAgents) offer a promising alternative by shifting recommendation to an active, user-side paradigm, where generative agents autonomously perceive external platforms, reason over user preferences, and execute decisions. However, existing RecAgents still suffer from two critical limitations: brittle item perception based on noisy and heterogeneous item pages, and inefficient long-context reasoning over extended user histories and multi-step interaction traces. To address these challenges, we propose a novel recommendation agent framework, termed as ReMem, that combines OCR-based multimodal perception with time-evolving dynamic memory. Instead of parsing raw HTML, ReMem observes item pages through screenshots and extracts structured multimodal information via an OCR tool, enabling a more humanoid and platform-agnostic perception mechanism. To support long-horizon preference modeling, ReMem further introduces a chunk-wise sequential memory update strategy, where the agent selectively maintains a fixed-size memory of informative historical interactions while processing arbitrarily long contexts with linear inference complexity and bounded context length. This design allows the agent to preserve evolving user preferences without relying on external memory modules or disrupting the standard autoregressive generation process. To enhance the dynamic memory instruction, we further develop a multi-memory GRPO variant, which propagates the final-answer advantage to all intermediate conversations that contribute to the final response. Extensive experiments on three datasets demonstrate that ReMem consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving an average improvement of 5.16\% across three recommendation agent tasks, namely searching, ranking, and judging.
bullets: Addresses brittle item understanding from noisy, heterogeneous webpages and inefficient reasoning over long interaction histories.
Uses screenshots and OCR to extract structured multimodal item information without relying on raw HTML.
Maintains evolving preferences through chunk-wise sequential updates to a fixed-size memory, enabling arbitrarily long contexts with linear inference complexity.
Introduces multi-memory GRPO to propagate final-answer advantages to intermediate conversations involved in generating the response.
Across three datasets and searching, ranking, and judging tasks, ReMem reports an average 5.16% improvement over state-of-the-art baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of the proposed ReMem framework. Inspired by how humans browse item pages while maintaining time-evolving memory, ReMem consists of three key components. a) Instead of relying on raw HTML, ReMem adopts an OCR-based perception module that represents item pages through a unified multimodal view of natural text, images, and interactive elements, better matching users’ browsing behavior. b) User interaction history is processed as a sequential stream of chunks, from which the model maintains a compact, fixed-length memory that is continuously updated to capture evolving user preferences. c) To teach the model what to remember and how to update memory in multi-turn interactions, ReMem employs Multi-Mem GRPO, which propagates the final-answer advantage to all intermediate memories that contribute to the final response.

(b) The proposed ReMem follows a more human-like principle: see item pages through OCR-based multimodal perception and memorize only evolving preference abstractions through dynamic memory, enabling robust modeling of time-evolving user preferences.

papers.abstract: Deterministic dynamics modeling of tendon-driven continuum robots remains challenging owing to uncertainties in material behavior, tendon transmission, friction, and contact. Measured joint configurations and nominal tendon commands do not fully characterize these internal mechanical factors, leaving uncertainty in the subsequent motion. We therefore develop a history-conditioned, physics-informed flow-matching framework for probabilistic dynamics prediction, using motion and actuation histories to predict the distribution of the next complete joint configuration. By recursively sampling next-step configurations under prescribed commands, the model predicts distributions of future whole-body motions. In simulation, scenario-specific models achieve five-second trajectory Energy Scores (lower is better) of 12.05 mm under internal friction variation and 9.29 mm under unobserved actuation disturbances. Relative to the conditional variational autoencoder and diffusion baselines, Flow attains lower Energy Scores and coverage closer to the nominal level in both scenarios. Ablations support history and structural conditioning in both scenarios. On the physical robot, predictions under two tendon-command profiles excluded from training capture the principal motion sequences, with five-second Energy Scores of 11.91 and 11.42 mm, lower than the compared baselines. The predicted-to-measured spread ratios are 1.65 and 1.22 (closer to 1 is better). These results support history-conditioned probabilistic dynamics prediction under incomplete mechanical observations.
bullets: Addresses uncertainty from material behavior, tendon transmission, friction, and contact that is not captured by current configurations and nominal commands.
Uses motion and actuation histories with structural conditioning to predict distributions of the next complete joint configuration.
Recursive sampling produces distributions of future trajectories under prescribed tendon commands.
In simulation and physical-robot tests, the method achieved lower Energy Scores than variational and diffusion baselines, while capturing principal motion sequences.
Results support probabilistic dynamics prediction under incomplete mechanical observations, with evaluation focused on tested friction, actuation-disturbance, and command-profile scenarios.

papers.abstract: Large-scale manipulation demonstrations are essential for learning robust visuomotor policies, yet real-world data collection is expensive and difficult to scale. Simulation offers a promising alternative, but physical and visual discrepancies can limit the transferability of synthetic data, particularly for manipulation with soft grippers. We present PhyVisGen, a physically and visually high-fidelity framework for scalable robotic manipulation data generation. On the physical side, PhyVisGen introduces an arm-gripper coupling method based on the Incremental Potential Contact (IPC), enabling high-fidelity soft contact throughout complete manipulation trajectories. On the visual side, it combines real-scene reconstruction with real-time path tracing to generate visually realistic observations while preserving captured scene appearance. Quantitative evaluations demonstrate the physical and visual fidelity of PhyVisGen. Policies trained exclusively on synthetic manipulation demonstrations achieve 65-95% success across five real-robot tasks, without real-robot demonstration data or policy fine-tuning.
bullets: Addresses the cost and scalability challenges of collecting real-world robotic manipulation data, especially with soft grippers.
Uses Incremental Potential Contact (IPC) for high-fidelity arm–gripper coupling and soft-contact simulation across complete trajectories.
Combines real-scene reconstruction with real-time path tracing to produce realistic observations while preserving scene appearance.
Quantitative evaluations show high physical and visual fidelity.
Policies trained only on synthetic data achieve 65–95% success across five real-robot tasks without policy fine-tuning.

The demonstrations are used for imitation learning. The learned policies are zero-shot deployed in the real world.

papers.abstract: Closed-loop evaluation of surgical robots requires tissue that deforms, can be grasped and lifted, and reproduces the anatomy in which the robot will operate. We present a simulator in which this tissue is reconstructed from a fixed-view RGB-D recording of the surgical field, composited to remove the instruments, closed into watertight volumes and tetrahedralised; the pipeline was applied unchanged to three specimens of two species (thirteen organs, 146,061 tetrahedra, no inverted elements). For one specimen, the organs are placed in a bimanual cell in which two Franka FR3 arms operate motorised instruments through 6 mm trocars. The core contribution is the numerical and contact design that keeps this cell stable: implicit integration, simulation meshes separate from collision meshes, numerical guards, and a grasp constraint captured at the live tissue pose. In 45 repeated grasp-lifts, a friction grasp held the tissue in 0 of 15 trials and each constraint grasp in 13 of 15; on displaced tissue, a rest-pose constraint produced one-step snaps of up to 17.8 mm, which live-pose capture eliminates. Against the recording, front-surface depth error is 1.33 to 1.41 mm, organ silhouette IoU is 0.80, and in five grasp-lifts reproduced from video the landmark displacement RMSE is 11.8 mm against 14.2 mm for a static prediction. Biofidelity is not claimed; the environment is intended for closed-loop feasibility, safety, contact and policy screening.
bullets: Reconstructs watertight, tetrahedralised organs from fixed-view RGB-D recordings with instruments removed, applied to 13 organs across three specimens and two species.
Uses implicit integration, separate simulation and collision meshes, numerical safeguards, and grasp constraints captured at the live tissue pose for contact stability.
Constraint grasps succeeded in 13/15 trials, while friction grasps succeeded in 0/15; live-pose capture removes displacement-induced snaps up to 17.8 mm.
Simulation matched recordings with 1.33–1.41 mm front-surface depth error and improved landmark displacement RMSE from 14.2 mm to 11.8 mm versus a static prediction.
Designed for feasibility, safety, contact, and policy screening; the authors do not claim full biofidelity.

papers.abstract: Prioritized experience replay (PER) improves sample efficiency by replaying high-priority transitions, usually according to absolute temporal-difference error. In stochastic environments, PER can distort the distribution of realized outcomes replayed from transitions with the same state-action pair. We call this within-group self-selection. We quantify the resulting changes in within-group outcome frequencies and mean Bellman targets. We decompose PER into between-group allocation and conditional sibling selection, and derive fixed-buffer corrections that preserve current group-level priority mass: SAMPLE selects a group through PER and trains on a uniformly sampled sibling; AVG averages sibling Bellman targets; and MODEL samples from an empirical full-outcome model. In exact state-action environments with rare high-magnitude outcomes, sibling-aware replay improves learning efficiency over PER, although matched parameter sweeps show that tuning can narrow some gaps. In MinAtar, approximate VQ-VAE groups with SAMPLE mitigate degradation under mean-preserving reward tails in four of five games. Sibling-aware replay thus retains the focus on high-priority state-action regions while recovering their empirical outcome frequencies.
bullets: PER can overselect particular stochastic outcomes among transitions sharing a state-action pair, distorting outcome frequencies and Bellman targets.
The paper separates PER into group-level allocation and conditional sibling selection.
It proposes SAMPLE, AVG, and MODEL corrections that preserve group-level priority mass while restoring or modeling sibling outcomes.
In exact state-action settings, sibling-aware replay improves efficiency for rare high-magnitude outcomes; in MinAtar, approximate SAMPLE mitigates degradation in four of five games.
Benefits depend on tuning and the quality of approximate state-action grouping.

papers.abstract: The paper proposes a novel data-driven framework for designing and training a feedback linearizing controller by explicitly incorporating relative degree based conditions into the learning process. This enables the conventional feedback controller components to be replaced by neural Lie derivatives, thereby facilitating a fully data-driven feedback linearization framework. Furthermore, practical closed-loop stability is established by deriving sufficient conditions under which bounded identification errors lead to bounded tracking errors. The derived theoretical results are validated through their application to an armature controlled DC motor.
bullets: Targets fully data-driven feedback linearization without requiring conventional analytical controller components.
Incorporates relative-degree conditions directly into neural controller training.
Uses neural Lie derivatives to construct the feedback-linearizing controller.
Derives conditions showing bounded identification errors yield bounded tracking errors, supporting practical closed-loop stability.
Validates the theoretical results on an armature-controlled DC motor.

Fig. 7. Closed-loop reference tracking performance under noisy operating conditions. The system output follows the reference trajectory with bounded tracking error while maintaining a bounded control input.

Fig. 3. Validation simulation evaluating true continuous state trajectories against the trained model predictions across four distinct initial state configurations. papers.abstract: Global vision--language similarities compress an image and a caption into one vector, preserving semantics but not which word corresponds to which region or how those regions are arranged; a model can recognize every word and object yet prefer a compositionally incorrect caption. We argue that a frozen encoder retains this association structure, so the problem is to read it rather than to rebuild it beside the pretrained similarity. We introduce BindCLIP, a pairwise scorer built on one latent object: a balanced token--patch--depth optimal-transport coupling that places both candidate captions and several visual depths in a single plan. Semantic, entity, order, and spatial evidence are read as energies of this state, and exchanging the candidates permutes the plan, making the score exactly antisymmetric. A geometric refinement inside the coupling contracts moves that the candidates and the visual depths do not support. No task label, parser, relation inventory, or detector is used. One checkpoint and one inference path improve the official What'sUp, ARO, and SugarCrepe benchmarks over frozen global CLIP, with the strongest transfer on the relation splits. Controls rule out patch access and caption-length shortcuts, and an inference-time lesion localizes spatial arrangement to the coupling.
bullets: Addresses the failure of global image–caption similarity to capture word–region correspondences and spatial composition.
Builds one balanced token–patch–depth optimal-transport plan jointly over candidate captions and multiple visual depths.
Derives semantic, entity, ordering, and spatial evidence from coupling energies; candidate exchange yields an exactly antisymmetric score.
Uses no task labels, parsers, relation inventories, or detectors, and follows one checkpoint and inference path.
Improves frozen CLIP on What'sUp, ARO, and SugarCrepe, with strongest transfer on relation splits; controls identify spatial arrangement in the coupling.

papers.title: BindCLIP: One Balanced Coupling For Compositional Vision Language Scoring
papers.tldr: BindCLIP reads compositional token–region structure from frozen vision–language encoders via a balanced optimal-transport coupling, improving relation-sensitive caption scoring without extra supervision.

papers.abstract: Simulation-trained humanoid proprioceptive odometry faces two transfer challenges: training trajectories generated by specific robot control policies intended for deployment cover only a limited range of motions, while sim-to-real mismatch can make unconstrained predictions unreliable. We address both with Prior-Informed Odometry from Human-Motion Tracking (PRIMO). On the data side, we generate odometry supervision by having the humanoid track diverse retargeted human motions in simulation, decoupling supervision from the deployment policies and broadening the training motion distribution. On the model side, a Prior-Informed estimator uses physics- and symmetry-informed priors to structure velocity and rotation prediction and a coarse raw-context pathway to preserve sensor context alongside encoded features, thereby strengthening sim-to-real generalization. Under a unified real-robot protocol, PRIMO reduces mean error by 31.6%-61.7% relative to the strongest evaluated external baseline in each domain-metric comparison. Across two locomotion-policy revisions, policy specialists exhibit symmetric crossover, whereas Tracking-Locomotion training reduces mean opposite-policy simulation error by 86.8%-94.6%. On real dynamic motion, Tracking-Locomotion training reduces mean error by 69.2%-81.7% relative to training on the union of both deployment policies. Across the tested motion compositions, the Prior-Informed estimator consistently lowers mean trajectory errors relative to its Unconstrained counterpart in both simulation and real-robot evaluation. Code is available at https://github.com/Agibot-Spatial-Intelligence/PRIMO.
bullets: Addresses limited training-motion coverage and sim-to-real mismatch in simulation-trained humanoid odometry.
Generates supervision from diverse retargeted human motions, decoupling training from deployment-policy trajectories.
Uses a Prior-Informed estimator with structured velocity/rotation prediction and a raw-context pathway.
Reduces mean error by 31.6%–61.7% versus the strongest evaluated external baselines under a unified real-robot protocol.
Tracking-Locomotion training and the Prior-Informed estimator consistently improve simulation and real-robot performance across tested motions.

papers.abstract: Low-cost planar air-bearing testbeds have matured into a standard proxy for free-flying spacecraft GNC, but they remain largely thruster-only and are rarely equipped for contact-rich, inertia-coupled manipulation. Building on the open-source ATMOS testbed, we contribute a reaction wheel and two force/torque-sensed robotic arms (LEVION) with interchangeable end-effectors, integrated as first-class control actuators through a unified ROS 2 abstraction layer. On top of the software stack we build a reinforcement-learning training environment and digital twin, and a controller that exploits these added degrees of freedom, letting classical optimal controllers and learned policies be swapped on the same hardware without modification. We validate the integrated system, PINGU, across four benchmark tasks: point-to-pose navigation (classical LQR vs. sim-to-real PPO), dynamic disturbance rejection under arm-induced center-of-mass shifts, reaction-wheel momentum stabilization, and force-controlled docking. The results show that these additions extend an ATMOS-class emulator into the contact-rich regime and bridge classical optimal control and reinforcement learning on one reproducible platform.
bullets: Addresses the limitation of thruster-only planar spacecraft testbeds for inertia-coupled manipulation and contact-rich operations.
Integrates a reaction wheel and two force/torque-sensed robotic arms with interchangeable end-effectors through a unified ROS 2 interface.
Provides a reinforcement-learning environment and digital twin supporting interchangeable classical optimal controllers and learned policies.
Validates the system on navigation, disturbance rejection, momentum stabilization, and force-controlled docking tasks.
Demonstrates an ATMOS-class emulator extended into the contact-rich regime on a single reproducible platform.

papers.abstract: We present Elevator-VIGS, a visual-inertial 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM system that keeps tracking and mapping through elevator rides. Inside a moving elevator, the two sensors are in conflict. The camera sees only the robot's motion relative to the elevator, while the IMU senses that motion plus the elevator's motion relative to the world. This conflict is challenging for existing visual-inertial estimators. If vision dominates, the estimator tracks only the robot's motion within the elevator and misses the elevator's rise, and if the conflict remains, the estimator diverges. We observe that the conflict comes from forcing both observations into a single coordinate frame. We instead estimate the robot's pose in the elevator's coordinate frame, and the elevator's motion relative to the world as a per-keyframe transport state, the elevator's rise and vertical velocity, within dense visual-inertial bundle adjustment. Elevator-VIGS detects rides zero-shot with a vision-language model and a depth network, and constrains the transport state at the departure and the arrival. We record real-world and simulated elevator sequences. On these sequences, Elevator-VIGS achieves state-of-the-art tracking and rendering performance. On four elevator-free public benchmarks it keeps the state-of-the-art performance of VIGS-SLAM. Project page: https://ruizhou-cn.github.io/elevator-vigs/.
bullets: Addresses the conflict between camera observations of robot-relative motion and IMU measurements that also include elevator motion.
Estimates robot pose in the elevator frame while modeling elevator transport—rise and vertical velocity—per keyframe.
Detects elevator rides zero-shot using a vision-language model and a depth network.
Constrains transport at elevator departure and arrival within dense visual-inertial bundle adjustment.
Reports state-of-the-art tracking and rendering on elevator sequences while retaining VIGS-SLAM performance on elevator-free benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: System overview. Elevator-VIGS takes RGB frames and IMU readings as input, tracks the camera online and trains a Gaussian map in parallel, extending VIGS-SLAM with the components outlined in red. Each keyframe, selected by optical flow and initialized through IMU preintegration, holds VIGS-SLAM’s 15-dimensional state of pose, velocity and bias together with its disparities. In the frontend, a ConvGRU refines the dense visual correspondences iteratively, and visual-inertial bundle adjustment optimizes the sliding window at every new keyframe. The ride detector ❺ arms on a semantic and a geometric cue from the RGB frames, and the IMU detects the departure and the arrival within the armed window. From the departure until the fold, each keyframe’s position and velocity decompose into an elevator-frame part and the transport state ❶, the elevator’s rise and vertical velocity. The solve then widens to 17 dimensions, the departure and arrival constraints ❷ constrain the transport state, and the update projection ❸ preserves the transport state through every optimization. Once the keyframes from the elevator leave the sliding window, the deferred fold ❹ writes the rise into the poses and returns them to the world frame. The mapper initializes Gaussians from each new keyframe’s depth and refines the map with color and depth rendering losses. Loop closure proposes keyframe pairs from optical flow, a same-floor gate ❻ rejects pairs on different floors, and each detected loop triggers pose-graph bundle adjustment and a Gaussian update.

papers.abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving maps current observations directly to future trajectories, yet those trajectories must remain valid as the scene evolves. Future state modeling aims to address this temporal mismatch, but general representations often contain information unrelated to ego planning and affect trajectory generation only through auxiliary supervision, static conditioning, or proposal evaluation. We propose FeasibleFlow, a one-step end-to-end generative framework that jointly transports a configuration-space feasibility field and multimodal ego trajectories. Our Asymmetric Joint MeanFlow uses the pathwise Jacobian-vector product in the MeanFlow identity to incorporate field evolution into trajectory transport. Because safety feedback is sparser than progress feedback, we further introduce the Anchor-relative ranker (ARR) and Pareto-ReinFlow to balance safety and progress in candidate selection and generation, respectively. Experiments on the NAVSIM benchmark demonstrate the strong performance of FeasibleFlow and validate both the joint transport of feasibility and trajectories and the proposed safety-first mechanisms.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between static observations and trajectories that must remain valid as scenes evolve.
Introduces Asymmetric Joint MeanFlow to couple feasibility-field evolution with trajectory transport via a pathwise Jacobian-vector product.
Uses Anchor-relative ranker and Pareto-ReinFlow to prioritize sparse safety feedback while balancing safety and progress.
NAVSIM experiments demonstrate strong performance and support the value of joint feasibility–trajectory transport and safety-first mechanisms.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overall architecture and training pipeline of FeasibleFlow. (a) During supervised training, a DeepSets encoder and implicit decoder learn the feasibility field from logged configuration labels. Field and action states are transported by the Asymmetric Joint MeanFlow, and the Anchor-relative ranker (ARR) selects the final candidate through its Imitation ranker and Outcome ranker. (b) Pareto-ReinFlow uses the frozen ranker to select a reference trajectory, evaluates exploratory trajectories by their relative safety and progress, and updates only the online action MeanFlow.

Fig. 1. Motivation and key mechanism of FeasibleFlow. A trajectoryonly generator leaves future feasibility implicit. FeasibleFlow instead jointly transports a graded configuration-space feasibility field and multimodal ego actions. The evolving field enters action transport through the cross-JVP term of the Asymmetric Joint MeanFlow, while inference remains a single transport step.

Fig. 4. Qualitative comparison with MeanFuser [14]. The top and bottom rows show off-road and collision cases, respectively. From left to right, each row presents the front-camera image, the MeanFuser result, and the FeasibleFlow result. Red circles mark the critical regions.

Fig. 3. Visualization of configuration-space feasibility. From left to right: the front-camera image, multimodal trajectory candidates with the selected plan, and the predicted feasibility field. Brighter regions in the heatmap indicate higher predicted feasibility. The field view overlays the exact configuration-space boundary, selected and ground-truth trajectories.

papers.abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has become a key technology for serving large-scale personalized large language models and diffusion models in the cloud. However, the co-occurrence patterns, resource contention relationships, and evolutionary regularities of adapters under production inference workloads have not been systematically or quantitatively studied. Based on GenTD26, Alibaba's production diffusion model inference dataset, this paper adopts a graph-theoretic framework to construct an adapter co-occurrence network and conducts a characterization from both static structure and dynamic evolution. Our main findings are as follows. (1) The co-occurrence network is extremely sparse, and adapter usage frequency follows a significant heavy-tailed distribution. (2) Introducing the first adapter incurs a 66.1% execution-latency overhead, with diminishing marginal costs afterwards. (3) Co-occurrence relationships are driven by base models: in 90.6% of multi-adapter requests, all adapters share the same dominant base model; 66.2% of significant co-occurrence edges connect same-model adapter pairs; and in 85.8% of multi-adapter requests, all adapter pairs form significant co-occurrence edges. (4) The adapter ecosystem exhibits a core-periphery bipolar structure, with a weekly Jaccard similarity of 0.696 at the model level and a churn rate of 54.5% for the top-10 hottest models within a 12-hour window. Based on these findings, we propose a preloading strategy built on top-k co-occurrence statistics; offline experiments show that it covers 81.0% of test-set co-occurrence pairs at k=3, and sensitivity analyses across frequency thresholds and time windows verify the robustness of the conclusions. These results provide a data-driven basis for cache preloading, adaptive scheduling, and GPU memory management in LoRA inference services.
bullets: Adapter usage is highly heavy-tailed, while the co-occurrence network is extremely sparse.
Adding the first adapter causes substantial latency overhead, with diminishing marginal costs for additional adapters.
Co-occurrence is strongly organized by base models: most multi-adapter requests use adapters from the same dominant model.
The adapter ecosystem has a core-periphery structure with both persistent model-level patterns and rapid turnover among the hottest models.
A top-k co-occurrence preloading strategy covers 81.0% of test co-occurrence pairs at k=3 in offline evaluation.

papers.title: Co-occurrence Patterns of LoRA Adapters in Production Diffusion Model Inference Services
papers.tldr: A graph-based analysis of production LoRA usage reveals sparse, base-model-driven co-occurrence patterns and supports top-k preloading for more efficient diffusion inference services.
